News.title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
News.content:
The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.

Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.

These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.

The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.

Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.

He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."

Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.

"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."

News.title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
News.content:
People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.

Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by Â£1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.

Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.

The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.

In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a Â£100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.

But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.

"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.

"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.

However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.

News.title: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
News.content:
Laura Brand said she knew before they met that "he liked women", and found out that while they were dating that he had been having sex with others.

"I wasn't interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people", she said.

"I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."

She said she remained friends with Brand while he was married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012, and got back together with him in 2015.

Asked if she was "aware of his promiscuity" during their time apart, she said: "I was very aware of it. I could read about it regularly in the papers, so I was aware of it and he also told me."

Turning to their relationship now, she said: "We have a very honest, frank, and clear relationship and marriage.

"It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest."

The charges against Brand relate to allegations made by six female complainants spanning a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The entertainer has displayed little emotion during the course of his trial, but was seen smiling broadly during parts of his wife's evidence.

He let out a laugh when she told the court: "We do have many friends and there are colleagues, and we are grateful for those people."

Her evidence came a day after the star appeared in the witness box himself.

He told the jury the allegations had a "devastating" impact on his relationships with friends and colleagues, meaning they would not touch him "with a bargepole".

He also said on Wednesday he had been promiscuous but believes sexual consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".

On Thursday, the court also heard statements from two of Russell Brand's ex-girlfriends

Elia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, and described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".

She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with".

"When I said no, however, he accepted it," she said in a statement.

Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.

Amanda Alguero Alejos told the court in a statement that Brand had also repeatedly cheated on her.

"He was undoubtedly promiscuous, never in front of me and never when I was around. That was not what mattered to me at the time," she said.

She recalled women "circling" around Brand "like birds", even when they were out as a couple.

The trial continues, with the jury likely to retire to consider the verdicts on Tuesday.

News.title: Met refers itself to police watchdog over letter about Meghan's father
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police complaints watchdog over its handling of a letter with allegations against Thomas Markle, which was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.

The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.

Markle has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".

The force said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) "in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex."

The Met added it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".

The letter that will be considered by the IOPC was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Roslyn Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.

The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".

Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason for not visiting Thomas Markle and not allowing him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".

Confirming that it had referred itself to the IPOC, the Metropolitan Police said it was aware of media reports that it had try to obtain a copy of the letter.

"While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," it said.

It added that the Met has carried out an initial review in recent days which has led to the voluntary referral to IOPC.

The watchdog will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas, it contained claims of alleged offences.

There are also reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to get a copy from the Sussexes.

Meghan, in a statement last week, said she believed the allegations in the letter "were being investigated".

But the watchdog will have to consider what happened to the warnings.

There are also likely to be questions about what royal officials knew about the letter, which was sent when Meghan was still a working royal, and which was forwarded to the Sussexes' office rather than to her personally.

Jim Gamble, former head of the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre, previously told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he would have expected the police to have shared any warnings.

"If you get information that comes to you about someone from a foreign jurisdiction who represents a threat to children, there's a well-worn path and generally you'd expect a UK police force to share that information," said Gamble.

"I would have expected the Metropolitan Police to have gone to the FBI to say, 'Look, this isn't proven, it's an allegation, you might want to look at it'.

The letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.

Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims.

Philippine Police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.

However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

News.title: Jury shown CCTV of Huntingdon train staff using frying pan in defence
News.content:
CCTV footage of a crew member using a frying pan to fend off a knifeman aboard a train has been shown in court.

Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said Samir Zitouni showed "sheer courage and bravery in seeking to save lives and defend others", during the mass stabbing on the Doncaster to London King's Cross train.

Jurors at Cambridge Crown Court saw footage of Zitouni using the pan against Anthony Williams, before the train made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies attempting to murder 10 people aboard the train, three people in Peterborough the day before and a boy at a London railway station.

The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks was not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals.

News.title: George Michael's Faith guitar sells for £180k after auction row
News.content:
The guitar George Michael performed with in his 1987 Faith music video has sold for Â£180,000 at auction, after a row over the sale of memorabilia related to the singer.

The guitar was one of more than 30 items auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant. The sale fetched a total of Â£238,000 excluding buyers' premium.

Bailey died in 2014 and the items were sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.

Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Sworders and Belcher declined to comment.

Sworders described the 32 lots, including signed photographs, invitations to events and presentation CDs and discs, as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".

Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Andrew Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.

News.title: Hundreds of GP practices lose online services after collapse of tech firm Silicon Practice
News.content:
Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.

Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England â just under 10% of the total.

Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk, have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.

GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.

Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.

Since last year, all practices in England have had to offer online appointment booking. Currently, more than 40% of appointments are made that way.

An NHS England spokesperson said while "the majority" of GP practice websites were running as normal, some using Silicon Practice will be affected.

"If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."

News.title: Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
News.content:
A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.

The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.

Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.

The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".

The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."

Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.

However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph, external.

The alleged incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.

Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.

In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.

"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.

"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."

Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there â but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."

Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."

News.title: Poundland's future hangs in the balance as chain edges towards collapse
News.content:
Poundland's future is hanging in the balance as the discount chain edges towards collapse.

The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators which will give the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.

The move comes after managing director Barry Williams told its 12,000 staff the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales.

It is understood the firm's owner, Gordon Brothers, wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future.

"This is a business that has been turned around, it employs thousands of people," he told the BBC.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal Â£1. A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale.

Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer, which has left it on the brink of collapse.

"If there is a potential owner that can continue that progress, obviously that naturally sounds like the best way forward, so if that hasn't been accepted, I want to know why that is the case," Reynolds added.

It could still be purchased out of administration in a so-called pre-pack deal, but the most likely option is for it to be broken up and for Poundland's stores to be sold off.

Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.

It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz.

It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.

News.title: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment
News.content:
The environmental performance of water companies worsened again last year despite industry investment, according to the first joint report by the regulators.

Eight of the nine companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", with only Severn Trent receiving the highest rating.

Companies were praised for reducing service disruptions but serious pollution into the environment remained a "major concern".

The chair of the environmental regulator, Alan Lovell, said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".

"I'm very angry," he told BBC News. "I think it's extremely disappointing to see the level of pollution incidents... and I completely sympathise with the public."

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said she was "demanding answers from the companies that are failing" and would be "shining a spotlight on the worst offences around the country".

Four different regulators currently oversee water companies in England and Wales - the Environment Agency (EA), Natural Resources Wales (NRW), Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate - and this marks the first time they have come together to assess the industry.

It is a nod to the commitment made by Sir Keir Starmer's government to merge the organisations covering England into a single body as part of efforts to streamline regulation.

But it is on environmental performance that the report is most critical.

Serious pollution incidents in 2025 were a "major concern", the Environment Agency said, and remained at similarly high levels to those seen in previous years.

Overall, England's water companies were awarded 16 out of a possible 36 stars for environmental performance - the worst total on record.

The EA said this was due to "declining performance in some areas but also due to our tighter performance standards".

And in Wales, DÅµr Cymru Welsh Water was given a two-star rating, out of four, by NRW.

Industry body Water UK acknowledged that "the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough".

But it also pointed out that more than half of all pollution incidents were as a result of "blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies".

"It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth, and end sewage entering rivers and seas," a spokesperson said.

Today's report did highlight some "strengths to build on", with UK drinking water quality remaining "among the best in the world".

And the regulators also noted that "leakage has reduced over the long term" but said improvement was still needed.

News.title: Chancellor's £30m pledge for train station is insult to the people of Wales, minister says
News.content:
A Â£30m rail funding pledge announced by Chancellor John Healey in the Budget is "an insult to the people of Wales", a Welsh government minister says.

Wales' Transport Minister Mark Hooper said the investment in the proposed Cardiff Parkway station was "a tiny fraction" of the cash needed to improve Welsh rail.

The Plaid Cymru-led Welsh government had called on Healey to bring forward Â£1bn of the Â£14bn the UK Labour government had promised for long-term rail funding in Wales.

UK government finance minister Emma Reynolds said the cash was part of a Â£445m package aimed at tackling years of "chronic under-investment" in rail.

Hooper made the comments after a meeting with the UK government in Whitehall on Thursday.

The proposed Cardiff Parkway in the city's eastern St Mellons area would link passengers on the South Wales Metro network to north Wales, Bristol, Manchester and London.

News.title: 'I died twice', says man saved by off-duty police sergeant
News.content:
A dad who suffered a cardiac arrest and collapsed in a shop said his 12-year-old son could have lost his dad if a "hero" off-duty police officer had not saved him.

James Ashley, 52, from Merthyr Tydfil, had just finished parkrun and was shopping in Cwmbran when he was hit by a "wave of dizziness" and fell to the floor on 4 April.

Sgt Adam Hollings from Gwent Police was nearby and immediately started CPR.

"I clinically died twice but by the time the paramedics got there, I was sitting up talking... the difference with Adam knowing what he was doing is that my son didn't lose his dad as a 12-year-old," he said, and called him an "absolute hero".

Hollings, who has spent 21 years on the force, was awarded a Royal Humane Society Resuscitation Certificate for his role in saving Ashley's life.

"We're very lucky to have the first aid training that we do, and if we can occasionally be in the right place at the right time to help people out, then fantastic," he said.

The 40-year-old from Abergavenny said that even though he was off-duty his training and life-saving skills kicked in and he acted on "autopilot".

He told someone in the shop to call an ambulance, and then used a defibrillator.

A defibrillator is a device that gives a jolt of energy to the heart. It helps get the heart beating again when someone is in cardiac arrest and their heart has stopped.

News.title: Watch the moment bridge hit at least 45 times is driven into again
News.content:
Video footage from Victoria Road resident Mark Needs shows a number of lorries and other vehicles getting into difficulty over the years, despite warning signs alerting drivers to its presence.

"The worst one was when a van with a cherry picker got stuck under it, it took four to five hours to get it out," he said.

"Another time a lorry coming down the hill hit the bridge, then a car and a telegraph pole."

Needs said there were sensors on poles set some way back on either side of the bridge. He said they activated flashing signs close by the bridge when vehicles of a certain height drove past.

The flashing sign on the Fairwood Terrace side of the bridge did not appear to flash when the lorry approached on 25 October, but Swansea council said the sensor system was functioning correctly.

Needs said there had been some interesting collisions, including a lorry transporting potatoes that got stuck.

"Everybody had free potatoes that day," he said.

Network Rail said staff carried out precautionary safety inspections following the latest incident but identified no damage.

Network Rail said: "Alongside collision protection beams, which have been in place since 2014 to protect the main railway structure from vehicle impacts and reduce the risk of damage, the bridge is also clearly marked with low-headroom warning signs, with additional advance and illuminated LED signage on the approaches to alert drivers before they reach the structure.

"We continue to work closely with Swansea Council to improve highway signage, and make sure these warning systems remain operational and effective."

Gowerton councillor Susan Jones said: "Obviously that bridge is a problem. When they extended the railway station it was strengthened - if they hadn't, I dread to think."

News.title: DUP blocks Michelle O'Neill's engagements over Drumcree
News.content:
O'Neill and other senior Sinn FÃ©in figures have been interviewed by police investigating last month's unnotified demonstrations in Portadown, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

The Sinn FÃ©in deputy leader has defended her involvement, saying it was the "right thing to do".

The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said "the DUP's sham response today was beyond pathetic" adding "the DUP is interested only in clinging to office, not principle".

Alliance leader Naomi Long said refusing to attend or preventing others from attending the meeting with the prime minister was reckless and put party interests ahead of Northern Ireland's economic future and the needs of the public.

The Ulster Unionist Party leader Jon Burrows told BBC's Evening Extra programme the situation was a "political fudge" that was "all choreography and no consequences," adding that the move would "probably galvanise Sinn FÃ©in further at the ballot box."

The Social Democratic and Labour Party's (SDLP) Matthew O'Toole said "plunging this place into more political chaos is not a sensible strategic move for unionism".

"Ultimately it's only going to make reasonable people here conclude that the largest unionist party simply doesn't want to make the status quo work," he added.

The DUP has been under pressure from unionist rivals and some within its own ranks over how to respond to the row over Drumcree.

Last week, DUP MP Carla Lockhart stepped down from the party's officer board over their leader Gavin Robinson not withdrawing Little-Pengelly to force O'Neill from their joint Stormont office.

On Thursday Lockhart said she will follow her "own course" if the party does not seek to remove Sinn FÃ©in's Michelle O'Neill as Stormont's first minister.

Robinson said that while O'Neill and her party colleagues "should be punished, that does not include punishing the rest of Northern Ireland".

The Upper Bann MP, who last week quit the DUP's ruling officer board in opposition to party leader Gavin Robinson's approach, outlined her position in a letter to colleagues which she later posted on Facebook.

Other DUP representatives including assembly member Diane Forsythe have since backed Lockhart's calls for O'Neill to be "removed from office".

On Tuesday, Forsythe said that in the absence of such "meaningful action", official engagements through the joint Executive Office should be stopped immediately as a "bare minimum".

On Wednesday, a second DUP assembly member called for O'Neill to go.

Maurice Bradley said removing O'Neill "would not, in itself, require the Assembly to collapse".

News.title: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
News.content:
Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site was once a rubbish dump but has been redeveloped and now protects 1,235 acres of mangroves.

The King walked along a new boardwalk through the wetlands to see the conservation work being done to protect this vulnerable, low lying island from climate change.

He met students carrying out field work in the wetland waters asking them about their exams and ambitions to be marine biologists.

"We've so been looking forward to this," said Joanne Smith, president of the Bahamas National Trust Council.

"We want more Bahamians to get involved in our national parks so they can use it to better themselvesâ¦ we are so pleased to have the King here, this is really significant for us."

Then it was on to the Junkanoo, where the King could be seen dancing alongside attendees dressed in feathered headdresses and bright costumes.

The history of the Junkanoo is not clear but it's believed it emerged out of the slave trade when enslaved men and women were given time off to mark Christmas.

A small protest near the parade, which had activists holding placards with the words "Pay us what you owe us", was moved on by the police.

The small group of protesters were from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.

The King acknowledged the "great suffering of the past" when he first arrived in the Bahamas, as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

Noelle Nicholls, chair of the reparations committee, said :"We are demanding an apology for those crimes, and reparations for the harm that was done."

Nicholls said the protesters' presence "amidst the pomp and pageantry of the celebrations... are for us also a sombre occasion, because this is the King returning in a way that has still not atoned for the sins of the past."

The King has confirmed that Commonwealth leaders will discuss the legacy of slavery at a major summit in Antigua next week.

News.title: Weight-loss jabs boom putting recycling centre workers at risk
News.content:
The boom in injectable weight-loss drugs, such as Mounjaro and Wegovy, is leading to more used needles turning up at recycling centres, putting workers at risk of serious injury and infection, bosses say.

At a recycling plant in Coventry, I watched staff sorting rubbish on a fast-moving conveyor belt when a crushed yellow sharps container suddenly appeared among the waste.

"A resident has put this in a wheelie bin," explained supervisor Paul Pagett.

"It then gets crushed by the recycling vehicle and then it comes to us open and obviously we've got needles then falling out on to the line putting my guys at risk."

The sharps box should never have been there.

Used needles should be disposed of separately through dedicated clinical waste services. Instead, recycling bosses say they are increasingly finding them mixed in with household waste.

"There are safe disposal routes for needles but the worst place to put them is in your recycling," said Richard Dobbs, managing director of Sherborne Recycling.

"It ends up in facilities like ours where it will be touched by people and that's inherently unsafe."

News.title: Where is Celebrity Traitors filmed and can you stay in the castle?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

AsThe Traitors' second celebrity season finale approaches, fans might be wondering where the breakfast banquets, muddy missions and turret executions actually take place.

We’ve rounded up everything you need to know about the Scottish castle hosting celebrity royalty on this series of The Traitors.



Where is The Traitors filmed?

Ardross Castle is used in both the UK version of the show and the US adaptation hosted by Scottish actor Alan Cumming.

The 19th-century castle, complete with more than 100 acres of parkland, sits on the banks of the River Alness, just north of Inverness in the Scottish Highlands.

Ardross Castle estate was purchased by the 1st Duke of Sutherland in the late 1700s, where he built a hunting lodge.

The castle as we recognise it now began to take shape once the estate was sold to Sir Alexander Matheson, an MP and opium trader, in 1845 for £90,000.

Aiming to attract tenants to agricultural tenancies, he began developing the land and enlisted the architect Alexander Ross to design the castle building in the Gothic Scottish Baronial style.

Ross added around 30 rooms to the original mansion for £7,000, along with the lawns, pond and fountain.

Ardross Castle passed between owners in the 19th and 20th centuries, and was broken up and sold in 1937. It was purchased by the current owners, the McTaggart family, in 1983, when they began renovating the property, and added new trees.

Generally, the day’s missions take place on site, while the discussions, action and banishments are filmed among the castle’s lavish interiors.

Can you stay at The Traitors castle?

Unfortunately for budding Faithfuls, the rooms of Ardross Castle are not available for individual stays.

While the action on The Traitors takes place overnight at the castle, stars of the show actually tuck into the Courtyard by Marriott hotel near Inverness’s airport during filming.

The Ardross stronghold is used as a wedding and conference venue for corporate and private events when it is not the set of bewilderment and backstabbing. The Times reports that prices to hire the castle for a wedding for up to 130 people over two nights begin at £45,000.

News.title: Dolly Parton ‘surprised’ Bono while collaborating on her final recording
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Bono has opened up about collaborating with the late Dolly Parton on U2’s new song, “Torn.”

The song, which closes the band’s forthcoming album Carnaval de Luz, is reportedly the final vocal that the Queen of Country recorded before her death in August at the age of 80.

In a new interview with Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, 66-year-old frontman Bono explained that the band had originally approached Parton about working together on a different song, that he described as being for a “Celtic Irish folk project.”

Bono continued: “I got in touch with her and we were discussing some of the songs, just her and I, across the phone line. One of the songs was called ‘Lifelong.’ I think it was kind of like a marrying song, like a wedding song. And she said, ‘That's a little too Irish for me, if you don't mind.’ And I said, ‘You're from the Appalachians, aren't you all Scots Irish?’ She said, ‘Yeah, but I'm talking about my voice.’”

He went on to explain that Parton came back with the suggestion for “Torn,” saying: “And she said, I got a song started called ‘Torn.’ Now you can take it somewhere else and I'd like to see where you could take it or something like that.”

Bono and Dolly Parton sing together on U2’s ‘Torn’, which features the late Queen of Country’s final recorded vocal ( Getty )

Bono said that when the band received the song from Parton, it was “quite traditional and we really took it somewhere else. I was really surprised that she ran with it. That's because not only was it sort of, not just American families, but arguing at the kitchen table and two brothers not speaking. You know, had some real friction of the times in it.”

He added that the group did not know how sick Parton was, explaining: “I was surprised that she ran with it and she sang it like she just took flight. Amazing vocal. And she was ill at the time. We didn't know how ill, of course. And she got out of bed to sing this song. And it meant a lot to us at the time, just knowing she was ill, that she would even consider doing something with us.”

Parton was hospitalized at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville in with “kidney and autoimmune issues” five days before she died. It was later revealed she had died after “a brief battle with cancer.” The type of cancer has not been disclosed.

Aside from the U2 collaboration, Parton recorded another song before her death, which has been sealed inside a time capsule that won’t be opened until the year 2046. The track, titled “My Place in History,” was deposited by the late queen of country in a wooden box at Dollywood’s DreamMore resort, which opened back in 2015.

In her book Songteller: My Life in Lyrics, Parton reveals that the resort’s staff have been specifically instructed to leave the box unopened until the date she specified: what would have been her 100th birthday on January 19, 2046.

U2’s Carnaval De Luz is set to be released November 13.

News.title: Some California airports could flood this holiday season thanks to El Nino, scientists warn
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Busy California airports used by millions of travelers could face flooding risks during the upcoming holiday season thanks to sea level rise and a record-breaking El Niño climate pattern, a new report warns.

While recent levee improvements have reduced the risk at Oakland International Airport, San Francisco International Airport - built on marshland - is vulnerable to flooding of 3 feet or more. That could ground flights, with takeoffs not recommended when standing water on the runway exceeds 0.5 inches.

"It doesn't mean it's certainly going to happen because it's all about timing," Fraser Shilling, director of the University of California-Davis Road Ecology Center, told KGO on Wednesday.

But with this week’s record tides seen up and down the California coast, experts fear much worse flooding is on the way.

"This was just like a preview. This is a trailer," Shilling said.

open image in gallery The holiday travel season could see flooding at California airports, a new report warns. The past week has already seen coastal records broken in the Bay Area ( Getty Images )

There are flood protection measures in place at San Francisco’s airport, which had more than 1.8 million travelers just last Thanksgiving. Those measures include vinyl sheet pile walls, concrete seawalls and concrete-capped earthen berms, Doug Yakel, a public information officer at the airport, told The Independent.

“SFO facilities staff are also making preparations to reduce flooding risk which includes clearing drainage areas, ensuring pump stations are in top condition, clearing trees that could cause power outages, and preparing sand bags,” he said.

But Shilling told KGO that it was “clear from their description that none of those things are long-term protection.” Yakel did not address that comment.

The big picture

Climate change threats to infrastructure are accelerating, especially along U.S. coasts. This past week has been a prime example, with high tides breaking records in the Bay Area and in Southern California.

San Francisco blew past its previous October high tide records at 2.01 feet on Wednesday, according to Anthony Edwards, a meteorologist at the San Francisco Chronicle. Both San Diego and Los Angeles recorded their highest coastal water levels in over a century earlier this week.

The water has stranded drivers, submerged backyards and forced residents to travel by kayak and paddleboard.

open image in gallery December tides could be 1 to 2 feet higher than this week, with peak El Niño bringing expanding seawater ( Getty )

The swelling tides - not yet king tides, per the state’s government - are fueled by near record high ocean temperatures offshore, El Niño-spurred pulses of energy known as Kelvin waves and the position of the moon.

Combining the effects of sea level rise, high tides, climate-related marine heat and the El Niño-driven Kelvin waves - which push water toward the coast - leads to a tidal height that’s at least 34 feet above normal, climate scientist Marc Alessi wrote this week in The Equation.

Recent models suggest that between 24 to 75 percent of California beaches could disappear seasonally or permanently by 2100 without taking action to make areas resilient to these effects.

With an upcoming peak in tides during the holiday travel season, December tides could be 1 to 2 feet higher than this week, according to Dr. Jeff Masters, an extreme weather and climate change expert.

Peak El Niño intensity is expected around November and December, climate scientist Daniel Swain noted in a post on his site Weather West. That means already hot, expanding seawater could continue to encroach farther on coastlines.

“Between November 2026 and January 2027, I would anticipate multiple significant coastal flood events that are worse in severity and also much more widespread than what we are currently seeing,” he wrote.

News.title: Trump cancels his appearance at weekend rally in Kansas days before midterm vote
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump has canceled an appearance at a Kansas rally on Saturday, his only scheduled campaign-trail appearance the weekend before Election Day.

The president will instead participate in a series of virtual rallies. It’s unclear whether he will reschedule the Kansas event.

Trump was scheduled to appear at Salina Regional Airport to support embattled Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, who is polling closely in a race for re-election against Democratic candidate and pastor Adam Hamilton. The last time voters in the state elected a Democratic U.S. senator was in 1939.

Pieter Miller, executive director of the Salina Airport Authority, said “all Salina events are cancelled” due to the president’s schedule.

Protesters repeatedly interrupted the president’s last appearance in the state, which Trump falsely claimed were “paid” to be there. At least 11 people were escorted from the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City that night.

open image in gallery Donald Trump has canceled a rally in Kansas scheduled for October 31, his only planned weekend rally before Election Day ( Reuters )

It was at that event where the president invoked the antisemetic slur “shylock” while defending Marshall’s history of suing former patients for failing to pay medical debt when he worked as an OB-GYN.

“And they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a shylock-type guy. And if he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law,” Trump said at the Kansas rally earlier this month. “He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability. And he didn’t do it. He has a law firm that did it.”

Kansas GOP Chair Danedri Herbert told The Kansas City Star that she heard about the president’s plans to scrap the event through the Republican National Committee.

“That’s all they told me that it was canceled and we’d get more information,” she said. “They are going to do a series of telerallies but I don’t have any information about those.”

Rob Fillion, executive director for the Kansas Republican Party, told Wichita’s CBS affiliate KWCH that “Salina and Kansas are very important to our nation, but there are a lot of other races that are in play.”

Trump being able to speak at “multiple locations at the same time is probably more valuable for his time,” Fillion said.

open image in gallery Recent polling from CNN/SSRS show Hamilton, left, leading among likely voters at 49 percent to Marshall’s 45 percent ( AP )

The White House said the president will “continue connecting directly with Americans nationwide through more than 20 telerallies before election day.”

“Telerallies give him the opportunity to highlight his accomplishments and expand his reach across the country,” the White House added.

Kansas is among several states where Democrats appear to be in striking distance to reclaim a Senate majority and tip the balance of power in Congress, according to polling data.

The results of a recent CNN/SSRS poll published Thursday show Hamilton leading among likely voters at 49 percent to Marshall’s 45 percent.

Marshall’s favorability rating among likely voters is only 36 percent to Hamilton’s 41 percent.

News.title: Man pleads guilty to 'heinous' murder of woman in Henley-on-Thames drowning case
News.content:

A 45-year-old man has pleaded guilty to the murder of a woman in south Oxfordshire earlier this year, police have confirmed.

Nelio Gouveia admitted to a single count of murder during an appearance at Oxford Crown Court on Thursday, according to Thames Valley Police.

His guilty plea follows the death of 44-year-old Jennifer Symonds in Henley-on-Thames back in March.

Thames Valley Police launched a murder probe after being called to Phyllis Court Drive at around 7.50am on 6 March, when they found Ms Symonds’ body. The force said Gouveia and Ms Symonds were known to each other.

open image in gallery Nelio Gouveia pleaded guilty during an appearance at Oxford Crown Court ( AFP/Getty )

The defendant previously lived in Phyllis Court Drive, which is also home to the Phyllis Court private members’ club on the banks of the River Thames.

Gouveia was arrested on the same day Ms Symonds’ body was found, and was charged with her murder on 8 March. A court hearing earlier this year heard that a post-mortem examination showed Ms Symonds died from drowning.

According to her LinkedIn profile, Ms Symonds previously worked for Microsoft as a senior success account manager in Reading.

Following his conviction on Thursday, Gouveia has been remanded in custody, and he is due to be sentenced at Oxford Crown Court on 20 November.

“My thoughts remain firmly with Jennifer’s family, who have lost someone who was dear to them,” senior investigating officer Detective Inspector Rob Underhill, of the Thames Valley Police Major Crime Unit, said on Thursday.

“Nelio’s actions on 6 March were heinous, and I am pleased that he has pleaded guilty. This case demonstrates Thames Valley Police’s commitment to investigating violence against women and girls.

“If you are a victim of violence, then please be reassured that we have specially trained officers who will listen and support you.”

News.title: Harry Brook hopeful for the future as England end forgettable series with a win
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Harry Brook was in upbeat mood despite England’s forgettable tri-series in Pakistan after his side broke their duck in a dead rubber against Sri Lanka in Lahore.

England failed to defend 429 for four against Sri Lanka last Thursday, while Pakistan recovered from being 154 for nine to overhaul a 242-run target and a claim a famous win over Brook’s side on Sunday.

Attention has fallen squarely on the bowlers following three successive defeats but while Pakistan and Sri Lanka will contest Saturday’s final, Brook took heart that lessons had been learned on the trip ahead of next month’s white-ball tour of Australia.

Brook said at the presentation ceremony: “The lads have learned a hell of a lot from a couple of days ago, so it was an exceptional effort.

“We haven’t had the series that we’d have wanted, we obviously would like to be in the final.

“But the lads have taken a lot of confidence from it, despite being on the wrong side. We’re scoring runs and taking wickets, and we’ve got a lot of clarity in our roles despite the losses.”

Ben Duckett continued his love affair in Lahore, making it back-to-back centuries and three in four innings at the Gaddafi Stadium with a majestic 167 off 132 balls – his best one-day international score.

open image in gallery Ben Duckett was in good form against Sri Lanka on Thursday (KM Chaudary/AP) ( AP )

Duckett made century stands with Tom Banton and Brook after England’s white-ball captain elevated himself to number three, with Will Jacks, Jordan Cox and Sam Curran relegating Joe Root further.

Root did not bat in England’s imposing 386 for five but took the crucial wicket of Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis, who thumped his bat in frustration when he gloved down the leg-side for 89 off 71 balls.

Sri Lanka kept up with the scoring rate with Pavan Rathnayake registering his second century in eight days against England, following up his 130 in Rawalpindi with a fine 118 off 77 balls in Lahore.

However, wickets tumbled more frequently despite the evening dew and once Rathnayake perished to Liam Dawson – who impressed with four for 49 – Sri Lanka were soon all out for 331 to lose by 55 runs.

open image in gallery England’s Liam Dawson celebrates claiming the wicket of Sri Lanka’s Avishka Fernando (K.M. Chaudary/AP) ( AP )

“There’s never a dead rubber playing for England,” Duckett said. “We go to Australia and that win will give us confidence because so many different people have put their hand up on this trip.

“We just haven’t got over the line in previous games but the guys have played some really good cricket.

“Tonight, the ball was skidding on and it was really tricky for the bowlers. For the guys to experience that and experience winning and getting over the line, we’ll definitely take that forward.”

As for his record at the Gaddafi Stadium, Duckett replied: “I love coming here. It’s just a good place to bat.

“I think the pitches suit me, they don’t bounce loads and they’re maybe a fraction slower but I imagine a lot of batters enjoy batting here.”

News.title: Michael Jackson estate battle: Paris asks courts to cut executor payments
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Michael Jackson’s daughter Paris is asking courts to step in to cut the payments she claims John Branca, the executor of her father’s estate, is awarding to himself.

Her court filing is the latest in a long-running legal battle over Jackson’s estate. The estate was overseen by Branca and former record company executive John McClain prior to the latter’s death in May at the age of 71.

Paris, 28, claims that Branca has paid himself over $100 million in compensation in just two years' worth of accountings. Paris says that is more than any member of the Jackson family has ever received from the Estate since her father’s death 17 years ago.

After Branca, 75, responded to call the accusations against him “nonsensical,” a representative for Paris Jackson told The Independent: “Enough of the smoke and mirrors — Paris is asking to reduce the management fee. Executor Branca has repeatedly failed to meet deadlines ordered by the judge that are in place to provide Paris and her siblings visibility about how the Estate is being run.”

The statement continued: “Since money is what motivates Executor Branca, this is the only way to enforce the timeline he agreed to.”

Michael Jackson and his daughter Paris, who is involved in a long-running legal dispute over his estate ( Getty )

Paris is asking the court to incrementally reduce the executor’s compensation for 2023 and 2024 from 15% to 10% of the gross entertainment-related income.

Back in April, Paris accused the executors of her father’s estate of using his money to publicly insult her.

She has been alleging since last July that executors Branca and McClain were mishandling Jackson’s money, ever since she reportedly noticed irregular payments. She went on to accuse the attorneys of “skimming money” from her father’s estate.

Branca and McClain denied all allegations against them. After months of court hearings and filings going back and forth between the two parties, the co-executors submitted an 83-page status report dismissing Paris’s claims once again, which prompted an April 6 filing where she accused them of trying to make her look bad in the public eye.

“This overlitigation is waste,” Paris’s filing said, according to court documents reviewed by The Independent. “At nearly every hearing… Executors try to avoid the merits by characterizing Paris’s concerns as lawyer-driven or in service of some purported desire for media attention. Neither is true.”

“This litigation is painful for Paris. It is a distraction from her own life and her own career. She would rather there be no press coverage of it whatsoever,” the filing said.

Paris’s attorneys claimed that “from the first day Paris dared to raise an objection,” Branca and McClain “have used her father’s money to attack her in the media.”

News.title: Attacker who firebombed a Jewish gathering in Colorado pleads guilty to federal charges
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An Egyptian man who firebombed a Jewish group at a demonstration in Boulder last year has pleaded guilty to federal hate crimes and other charges.

Mohamed Soliman is already serving life in prison after pleading guilty to state charges last spring in connection with the deadly June 2025 attack on elderly activists. He yelled “Free Palestine!” and threw two Molotov cocktails at a group demonstrating in support of hostages taken in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.

Soliman used a “makeshift flamethrower and threw an incendiary device” into the crowd, the FBI said.

Federal prosecutors accused Soliman of attacking the group because they were Jewish. The flames badly burned Karen Diamond, 82, and injured a dozen others. Diamond died three weeks later and her family said she suffered “indescribable pain.”

open image in gallery Mohamed Sabry Soliman is seen launching a fiery attack on demonstrators at an outdoor mall, Sunday, June 1, 2025, in Boulder, Colo. ( Lisa Turnquist )

The charges Soliman pleaded guilty to in federal court in Denver included nine counts of hate crimes, two of using fire or an explosive to commit a felony and one of carrying an explosive while committing a felony. They are punishable by life in prison after federal prosecutors declined to seek the death penalty.

Plea hearing

Soliman spoke through an interpreter at his plea hearing Thursday and said little besides “yes” and “no” to the judge’s questions. He was led out of court in handcuffs and shackles without looking at the victims in the courtroom.

“The defendant violently used the explosives to cause permanent and life-threatening injuries to several of these victims and cause the death of Karen Diamond,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Melissa Hindman said in court shortly before Soliman pleaded guilty.

A group of victims sat stoically in the courtroom and some took notes as the judge asked Soliman if he understood the proceedings. Several victims intend to make statements at Soliman’s sentencing but declined to do so in court Thursday, the judge said.

open image in gallery Rachel Amaru, an organizer for Run for Their Lives, embraces Rachel Cohen after the June 1 attack in Boulder ( Getty )

“I have not made up my mind about the sentence,” Colorado U.S. District Judge John Kane said. Soliman's federal sentencing was set for Jan. 7.

Boulder shaken by the attack

Boulder residents, particularly the Jewish community, were unnerved by the attack in the city northwest of Denver that’s home to the University of Colorado. The group “Run for Their Lives” had been demonstrating weekly downtown.

Soliman was able to get near the demonstration on Pearl Street, a pedestrian mall lined with shops and restaurants, by posing as a gardener.

He planned the attack for a year and after his arrest, he told police he wanted “to kill all Zionist people,” a reference to the movement to establish and protect a Jewish state in Israel.

Federal officials said he was in the U.S. illegally. He entered in 2022 on a tourist visa that expired the following year, then filed for asylum. He was granted work authorization, but it too expired.

Soliman was living with his wife and their five children in an apartment in Colorado Springs at the time of the attack and worked a series of low-paying jobs. The couple divorced in April and Soliman recently dropped his opposition to removing his family from the U.S.

Prosecutors in Soliman’s state case argued he planned to inflict more harm than he carried out and tried twice to buy a gun but was denied. He brought 18 Molotov cocktails — bottles filled with flammable liquid that are lit, thrown and burst into flames when they shatter — to the demonstration in a box, but only two were thrown.

Of the 29 attack victims identified by state prosecutors, 13 were physically injured. Prosecutors considered the rest victims because they could have been hurt and an injured dog led to a state animal cruelty charge.

While in court to plead guilty to the state charges in May, Soliman said he has known and respected Jewish people but questioned the deaths of innocent people in Israeli attacks on Gaza.

“Yes, I am against Israel and I can’t deny that. And that is my right,” Soliman said.

News.title: Trump administration loses grip on bird flu, experts warn
News.content:
The Trump administration has been criticised for losing control of a bird flu outbreak that has spread among mink and cattle farms across the United States.

The H5N1 virus has infected around 1,000 people since it was first detected in the late 1990s, killing roughly half of them. While it currently does not spread among humans, scientists have long worried that it could trigger a pandemic, and that each human infection raises the risk of the virus mutating.

A new variant emerged in 2020 and has since spread to millions of birds and hundreds of animal species across the globe, leading to devastating losses in both wildlife and farmed livestock and poultry.

While some countries have introduced tough measures to curb its spread, including mandatory culls of infected animals, “flockdowns” (where birds are kept indoors) and vaccination of farm workers who handle at-risk livestock, experts say the US is allowing the virus to run rampant.

For more than two months, an outbreak has raged unchecked on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur, news outlet ProPublica reported last week.

Mink in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of the farms give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate.

Mink have very similar respiratory systems to humans, increasing the risk that a virus can spread between the animals and people, and undergo a process known as “reassortment”, when two or more viruses mix together to make a new, more dangerous strain.

News.title: Britain faces unprecedented squeeze on incomes, IFS says
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. John Healey has ruled out making “crude cuts” to welfare after he failed to tackle the rising benefits bill in Wednesday’s Budget.

The Chancellor acknowledged last night that the current benefits system is “unsustainable” but said he will only look to make cuts “in a Labour way”.

Speaking to the BBC in the wake of Wednesday’s Budget, Mr Healey promised that “there will be a reduction in the benefits bill” before the next election.

However, he said this will not include “crude cuts” to payments.

He said: “We will do that in a Labour way, and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain, or progressive, to have a bigger and bigger benefits bills.

“This system is unsustainable. I’ve been clear about that. The Prime Minister’s been clear about that. It’s what you do about it.”

He added: “We have to bring the benefits bill down. You don’t do that by crude cuts, especially when people are feeling the cost of living pressures.”

His comments on welfare come after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch accused Labour of presiding over a Government that had left Britain “overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system”.

She said: “Next year, under Labour, the tax burden will be the highest in our country’s history and our benefits bill is going up by tens of billions of pounds because this Government has put welfare first.”

The latest figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility released on Wednesday revealed that benefits spending is expected to jump by almost 30pc to £431bn by 2032.

Almost half the total is pensions and disability benefits for pensioners, despite the planned abolition of the triple lock. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Healey launches tax raid on savers as welfare bill spirals | Chancellor to pull in £4.3bn from landlords and savers as Badenoch calls for ‘tough love’ on benefits

2) Gulf states face tax raid on UK property investments | John Healey’s changes risk driving investment away from Britain, industry experts warn

3) UK hands Rolls-Royce £1.25bn to fund new jet engines | British engineering giant confirms plans for £2.5bn to be invested during next decade

4) Petrol drivers face threat of stealth tax raid to boost EVs | Official review recommends forcing fuel suppliers to fund new renewable energy subsidies

5) JP Morgan lashes out at ‘unprincipled’ bank tax | Wall Street giant criticises John Healey’s Budget announcement on surcharge increase

What happened overnight

The Chancellor will have woken up to jittery markets after Google-owner Alphabet revealed higher spending on AI.

Alphabet dropped 10pc in after-hours trading, wiping nearly $400 billion off its market value. Microsoft, by contrast, beat forecasts with better-than-expected cash flows that lifted its shares by 3pc.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dropped 0.7pc, while Japan’s Nikkei fluctuated between gains and losses and was last ⁠up 1pc.

Oil prices retreated as investors latched onto hopes that peace talks to resolve the Middle East conflict could be back on the table.

European stocks were on track to edge higher at the open after the US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady as widely expected on Wednesday. The European Central Bank announces its next interest rate decision on Thursday.

News.title: Risk of Ebola spread in UK is low, experts stress
News.content:
Infectious disease experts have stressed the likelihood of Ebola spreading to the UK is low after the head of Africa’s health agency warned that the haemorrhagic fever could reach Britain.

The Democratic Republic of Congo is struggling to contain an outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the deadly virus that began in the volatile eastern region of the country. There have been 10,000 cases, including nearly 5,000 deaths, since the outbreak was first reported in May and it has now become the second largest Ebola epidemic in history.

In recent weeks the virus has spread to Kenya, where there have been nine cases including two deaths, and Nigeria. The case in Nigeria is concerning because the patient, the wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, the country’s capital, had no history of travel to the affected region of DRC. She has now been evacuated to Switzerland.

In comments reported by the Guardian Jean Kaseya, head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, described the outbreak as “unprecedented” as it was the first time that the disease had spread to three geographic regions of the continent. He warned that there was scope for further spread.

“We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

On Wednesday the United States announced that travellers arriving by air would have to sign a statement affirming that they had not been in the DRC within the previous 21 days. Anyone found to provide false or misleading information would face imprisonment or a fine.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) stressed that the risk to the UK is low. Dr Sam Collins, head of guidance, clinical and public health response at the agency, said the Ebola outbreak in DRC is serious but “the UK is well prepared to respond safely and effectively to the risk of imported cases arising here”.

UKHSA is monitoring travel routes from the affected countries and is providing information on symptoms.

The UKHSA said it is rare for Ebola to occur in returning travellers and the NHS has “well established procedures in place” for such a situation.

News.title: Wesley Fofana’s Chelsea nightmare continues as Liverpool win shoot-out
News.content:
It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

News.title: Burnham rules out calling early election
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. John Healey has promised to offer households “breathing space” in his maiden Budget today.

The Chancellor insisted the economy has shown “resilience” in the face of the energy shock from the Iran war.

However, he admitted the conflict has pushed up the cost of living, “piling pressure on the families, on businesses, and on our public finances”.

Among the measures the Chancellor is expected to announce are plans to scrap standing charges on household gas bills – saving families up to £50 a year.

Mr Healey said: “We can’t stop these shocks that hit Britain, but we can make Britain more resilient when they do.

“So, this Budget is designed to give households breathing space from some of the everyday costs, provide targeted support for businesses and self-employed people, and to start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Healey prepares to slash household gas bills by £50 | Chancellor to scrap standing charges on gas bills and curb Energy Secretary’s power

2) Minimum wage rise will drive up food prices, Healey warned | Manufacturers say they are already struggling to cover soaring production costs

3) Poundland directors quit in stand-off over administration | Board members fear owner wants to steer retailer into insolvency

4) Google attacks UK over ‘unlawful’ AI plans | Search giant fights plans by competition regulator to force it to promote rivals

5) Netherlands to cut 25,000 civil service jobs in AI push | Police and defence will be exempt from plans to trim 15pc of government workforce in next decade

What happened overnight

Ahead of the Budget, oil prices rose after an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest crude exporter, which has renewed concerns around the risks to supply in the Middle East.

Brent crude was up 1.7pc to nearly $116 a barrel, maintaining inflationary pressure on the global economy. It traded around $70 before the start of the Iran war.

Meanwhile, Asia stocks rallied amid fresh enthusiasm about AI.

South Korea’s Kospi surged more than 6pc and was on track for its largest one-day gain since July, after chipmaker SK Hynix reported a more than seven-fold jump in quarterly profit and said it would return about $75 billion to shareholders this year.

The AI rally faces its next test when technology giants Alphabet and Microsoft report earnings after market close later today, with investors looking for evidence of returns that would justify the hefty cost of the AI build-out.

In Asia, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 1.7pc, with Japan’s Nikkei adding 1.1pc and ⁠China’s CSI300 blue-chip index climbing 0.7pc.

News.title: Government remains tight-lipped on aid spending in Autumn budget
News.content:
The government made no mention of plans to restore aid spending in the Autumn budget and is on track to miss its current aid commitment.

It had been rumoured that a Burnham government planned to reverse the overseas aid cuts made by Sir Keir Starmer, who reduced an already shrunken aid budget from 0.5 to 0.3 per cent of gross national income (GNI) in February 2025.

The current 0.3 per cent allocation is the lowest proportion of national income spent on aid since 1999.

It was expected the reversal would be drawn up as part of a wider shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) under Ed Miliband as foreign secretary, The Telegraph reported in September.

But there was no mention of any timeline for restoring Britain’s overseas development assistance to the legally enshrined 0.7 per cent of gross national income GNI target on Wednesday.

The UK is now also on track to miss its 0.3 per cent aid spending commitment, equivalent to £9.2 billion per year, following a failure to confirm any upwards adjustment to the UK aid budget to account for inflation.

The shortfall is estimated to fall at £410 million this year, an analysis from the Centre for Global Development (CGD) found.

Britain’s aid money is spent across the world in sectors like health, education, disaster relief, and helping to promote democracy.

News.title: Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history
News.content:
An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

The League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

Max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

“We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta said: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.



“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”



Full team news on the way shortly.

Sports.title: Max Dowman to serve THREE-game ban as Arsenal star, 16, has red card appeal rejected by FA
Sports.content:
Next

MAX DOWMAN’s bid to overturn his first professional red card has been rejected.

The 16-year-old was given his marching orders in the 85th minute of Arsenal’s stunning Carabao Cup fourth-round exit at the hands of Fleetwood Town on Tuesday.



The winger reacted angrily to a firm challenge from Harrison Neal on the touchline, KICKING OUT at the Fleetwood star.

Referee Michael Salisbury didn’t hesitate to send the winger for an early shower after the ensuing fracas died down.



Arsenal immediately appealed Salisbury’s decision to dismiss the England Under-19 international.

But the FA have REJECTED the appeal, meaning the teenager will serve a three-match ban.

“An independent Regulatory Commission has dismissed claims of both wrongful dismissal and excessive punishment for Max Dowman.

“The Arsenal player was sent off during their EFL Cup game against Fleetwood Town on Tuesday 27 October and will be suspended for three matches.

“The Regulatory Commission’s written reasons for its decisions will be published in due course.”
