Sports.title: England’s Ivan Toney to stand trial during Euro 2028 after denying assault charge
Sports.content:
Ivan Toney has in effect been ruled out of Euro 2028 after his trial for assault occasioning actual bodily harm was scheduled for 12 June 2028.

Toney appeared at Southwark crown court and stood in the dock to confirm a not guilty plea. The striker is accused of head-butting and punching Saber Da Silva at a Soho nightclub on 6 December last year.

Setting the trial date for 20 months’ time, Judge Hehir apologised to Toney for the delay. “That’s a long way, I’m sorry about that,” he said. “As you may know, the crown courts are operating under a great deal of pressure.” Toney – wearing a black button-up cardigan, white shirt and tie – was told he was in a queue of defendants awaiting crown court trials.

Quick Guide How do I 

Toney was part of Thomas Tuchel’s England squad for the 2026 World Cup, coming on against Argentina in the semi-final and starting the third-place playoff victory against France. Toney, who plays for the Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged by the Metropolitan police three weeks after the tournament. He was not part of Tuchel’s next squad for the Nations League fixtures at the end of September and early October.

It appears inconceivable the England manager would select a player for Euro 2028, which is due to be held in the UK and Ireland, while the player faces a criminal trial during the group stage.

Toney was released on unconditional bail and told it was “very important” and “a matter of common sense” that he stayed in regular contact with his solicitors while awaiting trial.

Judge Hehir told Toney that the law obliged him to give the footballer a formal warning, as with any defendant on bail awaiting trial, about the consequences of failing to attend court. “It’s a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment,” he said. The case would likely be tried in his absence if he did not appear, the judge added.

View image in fullscreen Ivan Toney (right) in action for England against France at the World Cup. Photograph: Marco Bello/Reuters

When Toney appeared at Westminster magistrates court to enter his plea at the start of October, the court was told by the prosecutor, Tom Heslop, that Toney and Da Silva exchanged words that resulted in them “squaring up” to one another before Toney “lunged forward and head-butted the complainant, followed by a few punches”. Da Silva sustained injuries to his nose and fingers, it was alleged. After pleading not guilty, Toney requested that his trial be heard at a crown court.

After the Metropolitan police announced Toney had been charged, a spokesperson for the player said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”

Toney, who has 10 England caps, started his career at Northampton before moving to Newcastle and Peterborough. His career took off at Brentford, where his goals helped them win promotion to the Premier League in 2021 before he established himself as one of the leading top-flight strikers. He moved to Al-Ahli for £40m in 2024.

Sports.title: Mussolini’s first Serie A goal marks high-flying Lazio’s thrashing of Sassuolo | Nicky Bandini
Sports.content:
Serie A had its second scoreless draw of the season on Wednesday evening. Parma and Udinese were the culprits, though perhaps they can be allowed some grace. The game was not short on incident, Maduka Okoye saving a penalty for the Friulians, who had been on a six-game losing streak, midway through the second half. Mariano Troilo made a goalline clearance for Parma soon after.

An open, end-to-end game was made to look drab in the context of this bonkers campaign. While Parma and Udinese stymied one another at the Tardini, Milan came from behind to lead Bologna at San Siro. And then collapsing to a 4-2 defeat.

The previous evening saw three matches played and 18 goals scored. Como recovered from 1-0 down after 80 minutes to beat Torino 3-1, with another star turn from Nico Paz. Roma fell behind at home to Cagliari, turned things around before half-time, conceded a late equaliser to Daniel Maldini, then won 4-2 anyway.

Breathless spectacle everywhere though most compelling of all were scenes at the Mapei Stadium, where Lazio smashed Sassuolo 6-2. Lazio were the away team. That much was told in the stands, where 10,000 of their fans had shown up with banners, flags and flares. More than the total attendance for their last home game against Parma, and a great deal louder. Despite the game taking place on a weeknight, almost five hours’ drive from Rome.

The mass boycott of Lazio’s home games, and the reasons for it, was covered by this column in September. It is the culmination of a years-long feud between organised supporters groups and the club’s owner Claudio Lotito. He stands accused of neglecting his football team and disrespecting fans in ways both broad and highly specific.

An unexpectedly brilliant set of results has done nothing to heal this rift. Lazio’s win over Sassuolo was their eighth in nine games, the only misstep coming in a 2-2 draw at home to Milan. They briefly sat atop Serie A on Tuesday night, before Inter pulled back level with an underwhelming win away to Venezia on Wednesday.

This has been Lazio’s best ever start to a season, and the joint-second best of any club in the Italian top-flight, surpassed only by their city rivals Roma in 2013-14 (Roma won 10 out of 10, and still finished behind Antonio Conte’s Juventus). Yet average attendances for their games at the Stadio Olimpico have collapsed, from the mid-40,000s earlier this decade to less than 30,000 last season and barely over 10,000 so far in this one.

View image in fullscreen Kenneth Taylor has made his peace with Gattuso and has hit form. Photograph: Emanuele Pennacchio/SOPA Images/Shutterstock

To demonstrate the grievance is only with Lotito, and not the team itself, Lazio’s supporters have travelled in vast numbers to away games. They were doing it already in preseason, when thousands attended friendlies in Ascoli and Frosinone. A sense of gathering momentum reached new heights on Tuesday, when they outnumbered and outvoiced the home support.

An easier thing to do at the Mapei Stadium than elsewhere. Sassuolo are a modestly-supported club, representing a town of 40,000 people, whose home ground is not even in that town but 20 miles up the road in Reggio Emilia. Still, the noise and choreography of Lazio’s support was spectacular. At kick-off, the stadium roiled like a turbulent blue sea. A pair of banners stretched out across the full width of the away end with the message: “You are our glory, you are my victory, my flag in the wind.”

Then the chaos really took over. Kenneth Taylor gave Lazio the lead in just the second minute, punishing a half-clearance with a side-footed finish. After a video assistant referee check confirmed the goal, Sassuolo equalised almost immediately, an off-target shot by Kristian Thorstvedt deflected in via the shoulder of the defender Josip Sutalo.

Lazio were back in front by the 13th minute, Mattia Zaccagni cutting in from the left and squaring for Gustav Isaksen to finish. Moments later it was 3-1. Another story within the story, as Romano Floriani Mussolini – great-grandson of the former Italian dictator Benito Mussolini – scored his first Serie A goal.

The player, who wears the name “Romano” on his shirt, has said politics does not interest him, though his family’s history makes it hard to avoid. His mother, Alessandra, is a right-wing politician who has defended her grandfather’s legacy. At the time of Romano’s only previous professional goal, on loan for Juve Stabia in 2024, he was wearing “F. Mussolini” on his shirt, and some fans appeared to celebrate with fascist salutes.

Sassuolo were reduced to 10 men in the 31st minute, when Thorstvedt planted his studs into Zaccagni’s ankle. Despite this, they reduced the deficit before half-time through Sebastiano Esposito. Then Zaccagni extended it again, heading in a cross from Isaksen.

The second half was more one-sided. Tijjani Noslin smashed in a pair of goals from outside the box to complete Lazio’s win. The margin of victory could have been bigger. Stefano Turati saved a pair of penalties for Sassuolo, first from Zaccagni and then Davide Frattesi. A fun detail: in La Gazzetta dello Sport’s fantasy football system, this meant that, despite conceding six times, the keeper avoided a negative score.

As the final minutes ticked away, Lazio’s head coach Gennaro Gattuso allowed himself a moment. “I closed my eyes and imagined we were in a full Stadio Olimpico,” he said. “Ten thousand people travelling 300km on a Tuesday makes me happy.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Of all the unlikely comebacks we have seen in Serie A lately, none could compare to that of a man whose last management position ended with a tearful apology to the nation after failing to qualify Italy for the World Cup in April. To say expectations were low for him at Lazio would be an understatement. His contract has a clause written into it guaranteeing an extension if the team finish as high as 12th.

View image in fullscreen Romano Floriani Mussolini has a famous great-grandfather but says he has no interest in politics. Photograph: Emmanuele Ciancaglini/Getty Images

Perhaps Lazio will not be able to sustain their momentum for a full campaign. Though Gattuso’s insistence they are still working toward top-flight safety is starting to ring hollow. Fans were – jokingly – in uproar after Frattesi broke a tradition of posting how many more points they needed to reach 40 on his Instagram stories after each win.

The simple truth is that Gattuso has got under the skin of his players and is getting more from this squad than anyone thought possible. Taylor, who also scored the opener in the win over Parma at the weekend, is emblematic. Gattuso chased him out of training one day in the summer, ordering him to the changing room for speaking out of turn. Last week, before these two goals, the manager singled the player out for praise, noting that he is pressing more consistently than he used to.

Similar stories of personal connection could be told for so many others. A phone call from Gattuso was said to have persuaded Zaccagni – perhaps the standout talent of Lazio’s last few years – to stay in the summer. Noslin appears to be blossoming in his new role as a centre-forward.

Quick Guide Serie A results Show Sassuolo 2-6 Lazio, Roma 4-2 Cagliari, Torino 1-3 Como, Parma 0-0 Udinese Venezia 0-2 Inter, Milan 2-4 Bologna, Genoa 2-0 Juventus, Monza 1-4 Napoli Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

It has added up to a run of results that nobody inside or outside the club could have imagined back when Lazio were losing their first competitive game of this season, 2-0 to the Serie B side Mantova in the Coppa Italia.

The only question hanging over this extraordinary story is whether Gattuso can do the truly unthinkable, and bridge the gap between the supporters at Lotito. “Of course I’ll talk to him,” said Gattuso on Tuesday. “He’s a very intelligent person, but the choices are his. I would love to see lots of fans at the stadium, but I can’t change their minds or the president’s. That’s a question for them.”

Sports.title: A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?
Sports.content:
By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them.

And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings.

Yet, apparently, a crisis of a sort has been churning just below the surface of what is, by broad consensus, Europe’s best home support.

On Friday, Dortmund had announced a kind of bribery scheme. A rewards program is probably a kinder way of putting it. Fans who stayed off their phones during the bout with Eintracht had the chance to win signed jerseys and earn gift cards to the club’s merchandise store. If they activated a so-called “fan mode” on the club’s app – a name so phenomenally passive-aggressive you can only applaud whoever came up with it – the club could count who unlocked their phones the fewest times during the game. For every minute the fans left their phones alone, they got points.

Dortmund are not the only German team to pick a fight with phones.

Second-division clubs Hertha Berlin and Dynamo Dresden have banned commercial influencer-style videos in their stadiums altogether, fearing for both the integrity of the TV rights they sell and the experience of their fans. Dortmund, likewise, appear motivated by the incursion of influencers, who are siphoning off and monetizing footage of the famous match-day experience and growing into a nuisance for regulars.

This problem has also afflicted the tennis majors. The US Open now resembles an influencer convention more than it does a tennis tournament. When the US Tennis Association credentialed more than 100 content creators this year, the influencers grew so disruptive that a match was stopped when a chair umpire had to ask them to turn off a ring light. Wimbledon has refused to credential influencers for just this reason, which doesn’t stop them from getting in with regular tickets or through sponsors.

Dortmund’s attempt at shaping fan behavior, however, goes further than warding off the cultural content parasites. This please-stop-holding-up-your-phones-and-just-live-in-the-present plea raises quasi-existential questions about sport and its consumption.

“Over 81,000 people in the stadium, singing, cheering, and holding their breath together: this here and now is irreplaceable,” Dortmund chief executive Carsten Cramer said. “And that’s exactly what we’re putting front and center together.”

“Anyone at a soccer game should experience the moment and the emotions – not just a cell phone screen,” added Marcel de Groot, the chief executive of Vodafone Germany, both a cellphone service provider and a Dortmund sponsor. “Let’s leave our smartphones in our pockets more often at the stadium and instead focus on what’s happening on the field and in the stands.”

These were statements delivered with unshakeable confidence in their righteousness, yet there is evidence to suggest this simply isn’t how some fans want to behave at stadiums.

Which begs the question: can, and should, professional sports teams get to dictate how their ticket-buying fans experience their games? It’s surely a question that’s crossed the mind of all the musicians who now perform to a sea of cell phones, their flashlights on, obscuring the faces in the crowd. Did their fans buy the right to experience the concert as they please? Or does this objectify the musicians and diminish the performance, somehow?

View image in fullscreen The incentives didn’t keep all Dortmund fans from using their phones at the match. Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPA

It goes back to the question of whether sport is entertainment, and whether its consumers get to sit back and let the proceedings and the attendant stimuli wash over them. Or whether they are something else entirely: active participants in the games they attend. If that is so, then fandom amounts to a parasocial relationship conferring membership to a community with attendant behavioral expectations.

What are the responsibilities of the ticketholder? Do teams get to purity-test their supporters? What do fans owe their teams? Is live soccer just content? A day out, not unlike going to the movies or a museum, where nobody expects total focus and for you to cheer on the thing you’re looking at? Is it heresy to even suggest this?

The latter tends to be the view, or at least the vibe, in most American sports leagues where fans are often less engaged, told by an announcer and a jumbo screen when and what to clap or stomp or chant. This has always contrasted with the feel of global football, where the folklore is usually organic, sparked and dictated by the fans themselves. It’s why all of those pre-game and half-time concerts at the World Cup final rankled, drowning out the thrum of the throaty Argentina fans.

It feels both instructive and fitting that this debate broke out at Dortmund. The Bundesliga’s rules on safeguarding fan majority ownership of very nearly every club have preserved the league as a kind of supporters’ paradise, with relatively cheap tickets and policies that put fans first. Dortmund, for their part, have been held up for years as a paradigm for their following – thus attracting the influencers, of course.

The latter will be dealt with, it seems. In an age when soccer clubs are essentially production houses who also field company teams, it always seemed inevitable that these interlopers would be expelled from the premises. The fans, however, are not so easily corrected on behavior their teams have deemed undesirable. And they will vote with their credit cards.

Sports.title: Arsenal’s Slegers hails ‘role model’ Russo after historic hat-trick sinks Benfica
Sports.content:
Alessia Russo wrote herself into the history books once more as she became the highest English goalscorer in the Women’s Champions League. Her hat-trick gave Arsenal a vital 3-0 win against Benfica to send the Gunners up to second in the league phase table.

“I’m so happy. I think we’ve found a nice dynamic as well with the last two games,” Russo’s manager, Renée Slegers, said. “She’s one of the leaders and she does it her way. She cares for everyone around her and connects well with her teammates. She leads the way as a role model, doing the right things consistently.”

It was a statement performance from the 27-year-old who has shaken off the early-season cobwebs. Her three goals at Meadow Park on Wednesday took her tally up to 10 in her past seven appearances for club and country, hitting a rich vein of form just when Arsenal have needed her most.

It is safe to say Arsenal’s season has yet to fully burst into life. Struggles in front of goal and unforced errors have defined the opening two months but the gritty north London derby win on Saturday did feel like it could be a springboard for momentum.

There was no less pressure coming into this Champions League match against Benfica, another must-win game with Arsenal’s European form mirroring their domestic struggles. A last-ditch win against HB Køge and a heartbreaking draw against Paris FC (in which they surrendered a two‑goal lead) left them fifth in the league phase table before kick-off, with Barcelona and OL Lyonnes looming.

Slegers made three changes to freshen things up. Ona Batlle returned to her more natural right‑back role while the summer signings Élisa De Almeida and Géraldine Reuteler made their full debuts.

Ivan Baptista’s Benfica arrived in confident form on the back of consecutive wins domestically. Slegers was keen to highlight their strong identity pre-match, having had first‑hand experience of their resilience in last year’s league phase. So it proved once more in a first half in which Arsenal dominated, but struggled to break through against a well-structured opposition.

View image in fullscreen The Arsenal head coach, Renée Slegers, has eased pressure on herself with back-to-back wins over Spurs and Benfica. Photograph: David Cliff/EPA

It was the visitors, in fact, who had the best opportunity of the first half hour. Frøya Dorsin was left beating the turf in frustration after spurning a glorious opportunity to catch out a stranded Misa Rodríguez with a lob. It was a moment that jolted Arsenal into life as they upped the tempo and began to rain pressure on Benfica’s goal. First Olivia Smith set up Russo for a low shot that went narrowly wide before Smith herself forced Lena Pauels into a fine save.

Arsenal found their breakthrough just before half-time when Russo produced a sublime finish after a well‑worked move down the left.

It was like a switch had flipped for Arsenal after the break as they exuded confidence, zipping the ball around the turf with increasing ease. Smith looked more and more comfortable in her central role while Caitlin Foord came alive down the left, the latter denied a clear shot by a superb last-ditch challenge.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The conductor behind them all was Russo as she pressed and stretched the play to her tune. The captain on the night was at the heart of things once more as the hosts doubled their lead, rising high to glance home a corner. She completed her hat-trick shortly afterwards, converting from the spot after Foord was brought down by Catarina Amado.

Quick Guide Roundup: Chelsea roll past Roma, Bayern and Real draw Show Chelsea maintained their strong start to this year’s Women’s Champions League campaign as second-half goals from Ellie Carpenter [pictured, centre] and Kadeisha Buchanan secured a 2-0 win over Roma at Plough Lane. After a goalless first half, substitute Carpenter combined with Wieke Kaptein to open the scoring in the 51st minute. The Australian made a powerful run, found Kaptein and then met her cross from the right with a low shot which took a deflection off Roma defender Winonah Heatley before going in. Central defender Buchanan wrapped up the win in the 89th minute, heading home to ensure a second win in three European matches for Sonia Bompastor’s unbeaten team. Roma were left to rue chances missed by Maya Doms and Alayah Pilgrim as they extended their scoreless Champions League start to three games. 'I’m pleased with the fact we scored really early in the second half. We could probably have killed the game a little bit earlier,' said the Chelsea head coach, Sonia Bompastor. 'It’s important for us in these games to be able to be clinical and ruthless as early as possible. But we find different ways to impose ourselves in the game and to score goals. So it’s good.' Bayern Munich fought back from two goals down to draw 2-2 against Real Madrid and preserve their unbeaten home record in the pre-knockout phase. Last season’s semi-finalists have now not lost any of their 17 home games in the group stage or league phase thanks to Momoko Tanikawa's second-half equaliser. Athenea del Castillo pounced from Linda Caicedo’s cross in the seventh minute, before Lineth Beerensteyn headed in from close range to double Madrid’s lead midway through the first half. Edna Imade nodded in to reduce the deficit on the half-hour and Tanikawa levelled soon after the restart, before Sophie Proost hit the post for Bayern in stoppage time. Eight-time champions Lyonnes cruised to an emphatic 6-0 home victory over Internazionale, with Marie-Antoinette Katoto scoring twice before Lily Yohannes made it three on the hour mark. Vicki Bècho came off the bench shortly after and hit a hat-trick as the French giants went top of the table on goal difference. Swiss side Servette claimed a historic maiden Champions League win at the ninth attempt as they brushed aside OH Leuven 5-1 in Geneva. Paola Hernández and Gloria Marinelli both struck twice to leave the Belgian champions winless so far in this season’s league phase. Press Association Photograph: Andrew Redington/Getty Images Europe Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

It was a finish that marked the 200th goal of Slegers’s tenure and one that further eases the pressure on the head coach. With every minute that passed the hosts looked increasingly like themselves and could have added more to their tally.

“It looks like there is something off our shoulders,” Slegers said. “We were playing like us tonight and I am so happy. The players enjoyed themselves – they connected, they expressed themselves and they played with intensity. We backed the last performance up. We need to do it again at the weekend.”

There will no doubt be sterner tests to come in Europe, more immediately away to Barcelona in a fortnight’s time, but this was a victory that signified something more important than just climbing up the Champions League table.

Sports.title: Time and owners not on Moyes’ side as he tries to end Everton trophy drought
Sports.content:
A European challenge plus a concerted effort to end a trophy drought that will soon stretch into a 32nd year were Everton’s stated aims for this season, although that was before the club’s owners turned the taps off in the transfer market and announced they were looking to sell up. An abrupt change of direction and ambition from The Friedkin Group (TFG) has not altered the demands on David Moyes, however. It is as you were for the Everton manager, regardless of the tools at his disposal.

Newcastle’s visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium in the Carabao Cup fourth round on Thursday – when they will be backed by 7,732 fans after Everton allocated their opponents 15% of the ground – is timely on several counts. It is, first and foremost, an opportunity for Moyes’s team to advance in a competition that Everton have never won and edge closer to realising one stated aim for the campaign. It is also a chance to restore positivity after consecutive defeats against Chelsea and Arsenal, Everton’s only losses of the season.

This will be the first of two games in a row between the sides, with Everton going to St James’ Park in the league on Monday. Newcastle serve as a potent reminder of the League Cup’s power to lift a club out of trophy torment, in their case 56 years, with victory in the 2025 final.

Newcastle, though, had Alexander Isak leading the line at Wembley in 2025. Everton have Thierno Barry and no alternative striker as a result of the calamitous end to the summer transfer window when TFG first signalled the change in the club’s financial landscape by accepting a £35m bid from Nottingham Forest for Harrison Armstrong. The young midfielder’s form and value have continued to improve in the following weeks, just as the Evertonians who protested against his sale during the draw at Bournemouth knew they would.

Barry started his second season in English football encouragingly, with four goals in the first two games. But as the misses have racked up from the 24-year-old French forward – he leads the way in the Premier League this season with 12 big chances missed – so Everton have looked disheartened at times and their performances have dipped.

It is not all on Barry, of course. Brennan Johnson and Jack Grealish need to contribute much more from out wide than they have this season. Moyes’s sparing use of Hayden Hackney, Tyrique George and Tyler Dibling has also invited criticism that his resources, while extremely limited, are not being maximised. Jordan Pickford’s recent form has been an added, uncharacteristic cause for concern.

“We need to start picking up results,” James Tarkowski, the club captain, said. “Even though we won against Ipswich, it feels, not like a slump, but it feels like we need to work our way out of this. It’s a big game on Thursday in the cup.”

Moyes gave a fine speech when receiving a tribute award from the Football Writers’ Association North in Manchester on Sunday night. In a wide-ranging analysis of a managerial career spanning more than 1,200 games, he spoke of the importance of working for owners with resolve and foresight, his desire for more British coaches to work abroad and his envy at the trophy collections of other long-serving peers such as Sir Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger and José Mourinho.

The unadulterated joy that he and West Ham got from winning the Europa Conference League in 2023 – ending that club’s 43-year wait for a major trophy – is a feeling that Moyes longs to experience again with Everton. But time and TFG are not on his side.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The 63‑year‑old Scot’s contract expires at the end of this season and talks over an extension have been kicked repeatedly down the road. Moyes has restored stability on the pitch while TFG has stabilised Everton’s finances off it, but is a manager’s contract and long-term planning on the owner’s agenda now it is trying to sell the club in a difficult market?

View image in fullscreen David Moyes’ contract expires at the end of this season. Photograph: Silvina Brodersohn/CameraSport/Getty Images

Moyes has quickly – though not as quickly as fans would like – constructed a team that could challenge for Europe with quality additions in attack, at right-back, and with a lot of luck with injuries. Everton made a £25m profit in the last transfer window and are the lowest net spenders in the Premier League over the past five years. Yet it seems highly unlikely that a wantaway owner would invest in the squad as required in January.

“Look, it’s never going to be easy,” Moyes said last month when dissecting Everton’s damaging end to the transfer window. “You know what happens in these situations, there’s only one person who tends to get called out at the end of it. You know what I mean?” That may be true but there is realism regarding Everton’s latest predicament, along with a recognition of how important a win over Newcastle could be.

Sports.title: Chelsea star linked with Man City transfer accused of ‘going soft’
Sports.content:
Major concerns have been raised about Malo Gusto following Chelsea’s Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool.

Xabi Alonso’s side were beaten on penalties at Anfield in another blow for the Blues in the space of a few days.

4 Gusto played as a right-back for Chelsea on Wednesday night Credit: Getty

This followed a disappointing 2-0 defeat to Tottenham at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

Gusto was the target of plenty of Chelsea fan ire as he was booed off when he was replaced in the 67th minute.

Chelsea and their performance were the subject of debate on talkSPORT’s Daily Football Podcast, hosted by Adrian Durham and former Republic of Ireland striker Andy Townsend.

Malo Gusto ‘gone soft’

The 23-year-old joined Chelsea in 2023 from Lyon for around £26m.

He has been a regular fixture in the team and has even been linked with a move to Man City in recent windows.

However, Durham and Townsend raised concerns about his performance.

Durham said: “There were cheers from the Chelsea fans at Anfield when he was taken off. He was awful.

“One Chelsea fan messaged me saying I don't want to see him in a Chelsea shirt again.

“Players go through this, but it feels like it could be the end of the road. He was actually linked with Man City in the summer, and they're talking about him going Man City in January.

“I don't really understand what City see, but I'm being a very harsh critic of a footballer here.”

4 Gusto's theatrics did himself no favours, according to Townsend Credit: Getty

When asked if he can see why Chelsea fans are so upset with him, Townsend said: “Do you know what I'm seeing? He's gone a little soft to me. He's taken the easy options now.

“What I liked about him previously in a Chelsea shirt was that he busts the gut to get from halfway line to get to the dead ball line at the other end of the field to maybe swing across him.

“He's better suited on the right. Tonight he played on the left. That's not him, really. He's better suited as a right full-back or a right wing-back.

“But I've always admired his willingness to run flat out at pace as often as he can. Now I'm seeing a player, whether his confidence has taken a knock, whether others have got in and he thinks he's perhaps not going to be a regular, but he's now hitting the floor under no pressure. He's looking for free-kicks.

“We know that referees are reluctant to give those soft ones, which is great, because soft free-kicks have been the scourge of Premier League football in recent years.

“A couple of times tonight, Malo Gusto dropped onto the floor as if he's been hit by a steamroller and there's been no contact whatsoever.

“Get up, get back into your defensive position and do your job. When he does that, I think he can be a very useful player.

“At the moment he's looking a bit fragile and a bit brittle, and he's taken the easy option. He's going down when he needs to man up a little bit more to me.”

Fofana’s mistakes

Wesley Fofana was another man in for criticism following their Carabao Cup exit.

He gave away a penalty in the first half, before missing a spot-kick in the shootout.

4 Fofana has played just 78 times since his big money move from Leicester Credit: Getty

Fofana cost Chelsea £70m from Leicester, but has played just 78 times in more than four years due to persistent injury problems.

Townsend said: “It was quite a lot of money that they paid for Wes Fofana. He has his assets, he's athletic, he's quick, and he's a willing boy.

“He wants to do well, but he's never got rid of that mistake that he's kind of lurking at some point at any moment in the 90 minutes.

“It can be a lack of concentration as it was when he conceded the penalty this evening. It was unnecessary to do that. Or it can be he dives in, or it can be he makes a bad decision in the box.

“Unfortunately, he's one of those players that when he makes a mistake, it often gets punished.

“Some people get away with it, make a mistake, and nothing happens because of it.

“Wesley Fofana's one of those players that every time he makes a bad decision, it gets punished. Every time he does something that we can't quite explain, it ends up in the back of the net, or he concedes a penalty.

“He's just one of those guys, I'm afraid. It might well be the case for all of his career.

“There have been defenders like it before, and there'll be defenders like it again.”

Chelsea’s front three

Chelsea’s team have been electric in attack, but shaky in defence this season.

They have scored 17 goals in the Premier League, but conceded 15 in just eight games. Only Ipswich and Crystal Palace have let in more.

The usual front three of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers has been disrupted in recent games because of injury and suspension.

4 Rogers cost Chelsea £117m from Aston Villa in the summer Credit: Getty

Pedro is out for a few weeks with a thigh injury, meanwhile Palmer’s red card against Spurs saw him miss the Liverpool match.

This left a makeshift front three that failed to deliver the knockout blow against Liverpool.

Palmer will be back to face Man United on Saturday, with the 12:30pm kick-off live on talkSPORT.

Durham said: “All the talk has been about how exciting and full of goals this Chelsea front three is going to be this season or has been so far this season.

“But Joao Pedro out injured and Cole Palmer out suspended, Morgan Rodgers maybe felt, I know that Welbeck is more experienced than this, the pressure is on me and possibly couldn't handle it maybe?”

Sports.title: ‘Doomsday’ – Jamie O’Hara stunned as Chelsea fan makes Xabi Alonso sack ultimatum
Sports.content:
Jamie O'Hara was left stunned by one Chelsea fan who claimed that should they lose to Manchester United at the weekend, he wants Xabi Alonso sacked.

The Blues have had a bad week with just a second ever Premier League defeat to Tottenham Hotspur at Stamford Bridge came before crashing out the Carabao Cup.

4 Alonso's start to life at Chelsea has been mixed Credit: AFP

Despite that, Chelsea are still fifth in the league and have won four of their first eight.

They are the third top goalscorers in the division but have conceded as many as Coventry, meaning they only have a goal difference of +2.

Chelsea have no European football and will not have a cup fixture until the FA Cup third round in January.

Rob the Blues fan lost it on The Sports Bar, and O'Hara couldn't believe what he was hearing.

Alonso given sack ultimatum

Rob told O'Hara and Jermaine Pennant: "Saturday is doomsday. If we lose to Manchester United - Alonso out.

"Alonso out. I know a few Sunday League managers and [Malo] Gusto and [Valentin] Barco are Sunday League players at best."

Pennant then suggested that the reason Chelsea fans don't like the Spaniard is because he played for Liverpool and thus contributed to dumping them out of the Champions League.

Rob responded: "I get what you mean because that was the problem we had with Rafa [Benitez].

"Alonso was a fantastic player. But against Tottenham on Saturday, the outlet was Danny Welbeck up top because the ball just kept coming back at us - it was obvious.

"We didn't really look like we were going to win that game [against Liverpool]. But every time Liverpool attacked, they looked like they were going to score."

4 Alonso is already facing a battle to get some Chelsea fans back onside Credit: Getty

4 O'Hara was totally baffled by what the fan had to say

O'Hara suggested that the defeat to Tottenham Hotspur at Stamford Bridge has changed the feeling.

Rob agreed, saying: "It has affected us massively. Spurs played well against Man United and then played really well against us.

"But we made you look like you were going to win the league."

Huge contest

talkSPORT has live and exclusive coverage of Chelsea's next Premier League game against Manchester United on Saturday, kick-off 12:30pm.

Michael Carrick will be in charge for the match despite it initially looking as if he would be sacked.

But despite just one win in the top-flight this season, the Red Devils are keeping the Englishman around.

4 Alonso's opposite number on Saturday is on the brink in his job Credit: Getty

Man United start the day in 16th place as they head to Stamford Bridge with a lot of pressure Carrick and the team.

The main one being the fact Spurs and the Blues are such big rivals, with their inner-city foes basically unable to win against Chelsea.

But that all changed on Saturday, and though there are absolutely no suggestions that Alonso is in trouble, Rob isn't the only fan who will be starting to have concerns over the former Real Madrid boss.

Sports.title: Ex-Chelsea player calls out Xabi Alonso over controversial post-match comment
Sports.content:
Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has done himself no favours with his comments after the club's Carabao Cup exit.

The Blues were beaten on penalties by Liverpool in the fourth round on Wednesday night.

3 Alonso has put 'more pressure' on Chelsea's next match, says a former Blues hero Credit: Getty

Wesley Fofana missed the crucial spot-kick as Alonso's side were dumped out at Anfield.

The match had finished level at 1-1 after 90 minutes after goals from Morgan Rogers and Cody Gakpo.

Following the final whistle, Alonso claimed the Carabao Cup was the least important competition for his club this season, even with the complete absence of European football.

Former Chelsea goalkeeper Asmir Begovic believes the Spaniard was wrong to disregard the tournament in such a way.

Begovic reacts to Alonso comments

Speaking to Paul Hawksbee and Laura Kirk-Francis on talkSPORT, he was asked if he agreed with Alonso's post-match comments.

Begovic replied: "No, I wouldn’t have said that. I think especially as in his pre-match comments he was trying to take everything very seriously.

"To say that post-match won’t sit well with the Chelsea fans, knowing them the way I do. I think he’s got to be a little bit careful with that.

"I think that puts a little bit more pressure as well on the game on the weekend against Manchester United.

"If he gets a result there, things will get a little bit rosier. Definitely not the best thing to do to downplay any competition."

Begovic, who won a Premier League title during two years with Chelsea, made five League Cup appearances for the club.

3 Fofana's penalty miss consigned Chelsea to a fourth round Carabao Cup exit Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

What did Alonso say?

The former Bosnia & Herzegovina international had been reacting to remarks made by Alonso immediately after the defeat to Liverpool.

Speaking at the final whistle, the Chelsea boss admitted: "It’s a small setback in this competition.

"It’s probably the least important competition for us in the year, so we need to move on.

"As soon as we leave Anfield, our focus is Saturday’s Premier League [game]. This is the main and the most important thing."

Chelsea host Manchester United at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, with kick-off at 12.30pm, live on talkSPORT.

Their Carabao Cup exit leaves the Blues with only two trophies left to play for this season, the Premier League and the FA Cup.

3 Chelsea have just two trophies left to play for after their defeat to Liverpool Credit: Getty

It follows their failure to qualify for any European competitions last season.

Chelsea ended the previous campaign in 10th, missing out on a Conference League berth by a single point.

Whilst they do not enter the FA Cup until January, their league campaign is firmly underway.

The Blues currently sit fifth in the table after eight matches following a 2-0 defeat at home to Tottenham Hotspur last weekend.

Sports.title: Marcus Rashford actively considered for Premier League transfer according to club insider

Marcus Rashford actively considered for Premier League transfer according to club insider

Everton are discussing a January move for Manchester United forward Marcus Rashford, according to the club's former chief executive.

Rashford returned to Old Trafford in the summer following loan spells with Aston Villa and Barcelona.



2 Everton are weighing up a January move for Rashford, says their ex-CEO Credit: Getty

Despite scoring 14 goals, adding 15 assists and winning LaLiga last term, though, Barca decided against making his move permanent.

The 28-year-old has since featured eight times for United without providing a goal contribution so far this term.

Everton eye Rashford?

Former Everton CEO Keith Wyness has now suggested Rashford could be heading to the Hill Dickinson Stadium.



Speaking to Football Insider, he explained: "This is definitely being talked about and quite strongly, and I think that could be an interesting solution.

"Rashford did well when he was on loan at Villa and at Barcelona as well.



"I think it could work, and I think being close to where he is in Manchester, just along the M63, could also benefit him greatly as well.

"We've seen Jack (Grealish) moving across that way as well, and when he's fit, Jack is certainly a big asset for Everton.



"So I think Rashford would be a very interesting signing, and I'm hearing there's a lot of smoke here; it's definitely being discussed.

"I wouldn't be surprised to see something happening in January."

Jack Grealish is into his second season-long loan spell with the Toffees from Manchester City.

2 Rashford has been backed to follow in Jack Grealish's footsteps by joining Everton Credit: Getty

The 31-year-old was on the cusp of an England re-call last term before suffering a season-ending injury in January.



As for Rashford, he was part of the Three Lions squad which finished third at the World Cup in North America.

His form from last season's loan spell has yet to re-emerge during the current campaign, though.

A recent injury has also seen Rashford miss out on United's last two fixtures against Como and Bournemouth.

The forward is currently being assessed ahead of Saturday's trip to Chelsea, live on talkSPORT.



Meanwhile, Everton currently sit 11th in the Premier League following back-to-back defeats to Chelsea and Arsenal.

David Moyes' side were unbeaten through their first six matches, including a 2-2 draw at home to United in September.

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp facing major blow as best player to fix 12-year problem could switch allegiance
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp facing major blow as best player to fix 12-year problem could switch allegiance

German football is celebrating Harry Kane winning the Ballon d'Or but their national team are struggling with the same problem as England.

That is the verdict of Raphael Honigstein, who admitted Die Mannschaft may also miss out on the next Miroslav Klose.



4 Kane won the Ballon d'Or for his incredible campaign for Bayern and England Credit: Getty

The German football expert joined talkSPORT on Wednesday to react to England captain Kane scooping the game's top individual honour.

The Bayern Munich striker beat out Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal to become the first Englishman to win the Ballon d'Or in 25 years.

Honigstein told Breakfast duo Alan Brazil and Dean Saunders: "German football on a whole in a celebratory mood because we haven't had too many things to celebrate in recent years.



"You have to go back to 2020 when Bayern won the Champions League, but there was COVID, and he made sure that people are talking about Bayern, people are talking about the Bundesliga.

"The reaction in Germany is more one of this reflects on Bayern rather than the league because Bayern are in a league of their own.



"But it still brings attention, it still brings eyeballs, and these days it's not just about what happens on the pitch; what happens beyond that.

"The Ballon d'Or, all the showbiz is an extension of that, and it's become very important to be seen and to be a player on that level as well, and Harry's done that for Germany."



Kane will be 36 years old at the time of the 2030 World Cup, but his ex-Tottenham teammate Toby Alderweireld backs him to still play.

His immediate successor for England remains unclear, with Liam Delap and Will Lankshear both touted as future Three Lions stars.

Honigstein admitted Germany are in a similar issue with their No.9 position, having never found the heir to Miroslav Klose's throne.

4 Klose, Lahm and Schweinsteiger all lifted the World Cup in their final match at the finals Credit: Getty



Germany's all-time leading goalscorer retired from football after helping his country win the World Cup in 2014.

12 years later, new boss Jurgen Klopp is still trying to find the answer, with Kai Havertz and Nick Woltemade among the options.

Nicolò Tresoldi might opt for Italy

Honigstein named the Club Brugge striker as the best potential option for Germany - if they can keep him out of their rivals' clutches.

Tresoldi, who has seven goals in nine Belgian Pro League games this season, was born in Italy but is a Germany Under-21 international.



On Germany's striker issues, Honigstein added: "We've had the problem for many years; it's nothing new.

4 Tresoldi was born in Cagliari to an Italian father and an Argentinian mother but moved to Germany as a teenager Credit: Getty

"Ever since Miroslav Klose retired, there's been a bit of a vacancy up front," Honigstein continued.

"Various players have tried to fill it; we are yet to find somebody who can play consistently and score goals consistently at that level.



"The best player, Nicolo Tresoldi, might opt for Italy because he's Italian-born, so not an ideal position.

"But I think you have to go through all of Europe and, with the exception of maybe France, there's a problem all around because it is a position that's only one player on the pitch and most teams don't play with two centre forwards, so unless you happen to be the best guy at your club, you're not going to play.

"So the overall number of strikers have just gone down over the last year."

4 His hat-trick against St Truiden on Sunday was his third treble in the space of just 26 days for club and country Credit: Getty



Tresoldi, who scored 19 goals in his debut Belgian Jupiler Pro League campaign, bagged a hat-trick in a 4-3 win over Inter Milan this month.

He narrowly missed out on a place in Germany's World Cup squad, with then-boss Julian Nagelsmann suggesting 'his time will come'.

Yet the 22-year-old has since been holding talks with Roberto Mancini and Italy technical director Claudio Ranieri at the FIGC over a switch.

Sports.title: Liverpool Confidential: Inside Harvey Elliott's difficult start to life in Valencia, why experts think move is doomed despite efforts off the pitch, the loanee who IS thriving in Spain and club's stance on making Ronald Araujo deal permanent
Sports.content:
Liverpool Confidential: Inside Harvey Elliott's difficult start to life in Valencia, why experts think move is doomed despite efforts off the pitch, the loanee who IS thriving in Spain and club's stance on making Ronald Araujo deal permanent

Harvey Elliott is working hard to right the wrongs of his first few months at Valencia as another loan away from Liverpool threatens to become a 'significant disappointment' due to concerns over his form, fitness and discipline.

The English midfielder is on loan at the Estadio Mestalla after a rotten year at Aston Villa but he has struggled for game time under two different managers, making just six substitute appearances so far.

And last weekend he suffered the ignominy of being sent off just 19 minutes after coming off the bench at home to Villarreal, who then scored a 90th-minute winner seconds later to leave Valencia second-bottom after 10 games.

Liverpool staff are in constant contact with all their loanees and their clubs to check on players' progress and the last word back from Valencia was that Elliott, 23, is putting in quality work off the pitch to improve physically.

But as Julian Burgos, a Valencia expert, tells Liverpool Confidential: ‘At the moment, I don’t think he has adapted… he has been a significant disappointment, especially considering he arrived with the pedigree of coming from Liverpool.

‘It is true that he has been putting in the work over the last few weeks, and he appears to be in better physical shape.

Harvey Elliott is on loan at Valencia but 'has been a significant disappointment' says Julian Burgos, a Valencia expert

Elliott was sent off against Villarreal at the weekend despite coming on as a substitute

‘Honestly, if the option to terminate the loan arises, Valencia will likely pursue it. With a new sporting director and manager – compounded by the team’s poor form – it seems they will look to undo many of the moves made by the previous sporting director, the Scotsman Ron Gourlay.'

Valencia sacked their previous coach, Carlos Corberan, in mid-September after they picked up just one point in their opening five matches of the season.

‘They need to free up space within the salary cap to make changes to the squad,' Burgos adds, 'so they will likely take any opportunity to cut ties with players brought in under the previous regime.’

Last year, the midfielder was stuck at Aston Villa. Clearly not fancied by their manager Unai Emery, the club prevented him from playing the 10 games that would have meant the deal becoming permanent for £35million, which seemed a foregone conclusion when he joined.

As Elliott featured for Liverpool at the start of last season – a five-minute cameo off the bench in their second game of the campaign – he could not head out on another loan because of a FIFA ruling that states players can only represent two clubs on the pitch in one season.

There is no option or obligation to make his deal permanent at Valencia, whose new manager is Javier Aguirre, whom England fans may remember for his touchline antics with Mexico at the World Cup. Aguirre will give Elliott time to turn his fortunes around. There is an understanding he needed to build fitness after barely playing last year.

The club have appealed last week's red card – for two yellows – and Elliott is said to have apologised to team-mates.

Elliott had a miserable time at Aston Villa last season when he hardly featured for the club

…but it’s not all worrying news in Valencia!

Now let’s head across the city to fellow La Liga club Levante, where one Liverpool loanee is thriving.

Centre back Ifeanyi Ndukwe has been touted as having the potential to be ‘one of the best in the world in his position’.

Burgos adds: ‘Since his debut against Sevilla four matches ago, he has established himself as a starter for the manager Luis Castro, who asserted that he possesses the qualities to become one of the best players in the world in his position.

‘Against Sevilla, he recovered from an early mistake to score the equalising goal in stoppage time, and he has been a fixture in the side ever since. At 18, he has an impressive physique, remarkable coordination for his height, and the makings of a great footballer – both for the present and, even more so, for the future.’

Ndukwe could not stay at Liverpool this season due to a work permit issue. Apparently he now has the required points to return to Anfield and a recall clause is included in the deal.

But it might be better to keep Ndukwe there, where he is playing every week, and bleed him into the first-team squad next year.

Liverpool centre back Ifeanyi Ndukwe has shone at Levante this season and is now a regular starter for his manager Luis Castro

Ndukwe could not stay at Liverpool this season due to a work permit issue. He now has the required points to return to Anfield

Is it £47m or bust for ‘Big Ron’?

The story of the week at Liverpool has been Ronald Araujo after his man-of-the-match performance against Brighton. The Uruguayan’s status as a cult hero continues to grow and grow.

But are fans naive to fall in love with a loan player? Will Liverpool make the temporary move permanent? And can they do it for less than the clause of £47m?

Last week, I said I’d answer fans’ questions every week in this column and the answers to the Araujo inquiries are…

Absolutely, fans are right to fall in love with him! Liverpool are open to making the move permanent if this form continues, for sure – otherwise why would they insert the option to do so in the deal? People may point to the fact Liverpool would not usually sign a 28-year-old (Araujo turns 28 in March) but look at Virgil van Dijk, still going strong at 35.

And yes, they will be able to negotiate the fee down from the pre-agreed figure with Barcelona.

Ronald Araujo has been sensational for his manager Andoni Iraola this season

Debate about Trent rockets

Lots of talk about Trent Alexander-Arnold this week given he has fallen out of favour with new Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho. It has led many to debate whether Liverpool should re-sign him but Confidential is told Alexander-Arnold remains happy in the Spanish capital.

Regardless, would it be a wise move? Financially, no. Does the team lack his creativity from right back? Yes. Would the fans welcome him back with open arms? No… but stranger things have happened.

Nothing in it right now though!

Trent Alexander-Arnold has fallen out of favour at Real - but a return to Anfield looks unlikely

Quiet away end

Fans of French club Lens have been banned from buying tickets for their team’s Champions League trip to Anfield.

Lens, who finished second in Ligue 1 last year under now Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage, come to Liverpool in the new year. But they will do so – as it stands – without supporters after UEFA banned them from selling away tickets following events in Belgium last week.

In Lens' loss at Bruges, fans were punished for lighting and throwing pyrotechnics – which injured disabled supporters.

The club banned its own fans from buying tickets for this week’s trip to rivals Lille and said in a statement: ‘This situation goes far beyond the realm of the displays that sometimes accompany popular expression in the stands. A red line has been crossed. This line was not implicit.’

Anfield also had an empty away end last year when Galatasaray came to town in the last 16, a match which the Reds won 4-0.

Big Mama’s best night… no thanks to dud water bottle

An important night for Giorgi Mamardashvili against Chelsea on Wednesday.

The big Georgian has had mixed reviews since his arrival from Valencia, with some indifferent performances.

But this was perhaps his best performance yet – not just for his fine penalty save, but some other notable stops as both he and Mike Penders kept the scores level.

Liverpool’s No 2 can poke fun, though, at whoever provided the notes for his water bottle ahead of the shootout. None of the instructions were correct and Mamardashvili was left diving the wrong way several times.

Giorgi Mamardashvili celebrates his side's victory over Chelsea with his team-mate Kostas Tsimikas. It was the goalkeeper's finest performance in a Liverpool shirt

The week ahead… will Szoboszlai be fit?

Sunday’s clash with Arsenal is the biggest game so far in the Andoni Iraola era for one reason: it sets the tone for the rest of the season. Lose and Liverpool are nine points behind the champions. Win, though, and it’s only three – with confidence they can beat anyone.

Will Liverpool get some players back?

Dominik Szoboszlai is pushing to return but here is a question for you to ponder to finish this week’s column: does last year’s player of the year get back in Iraola’s best XI?
