Sports.content:
'It's a travesty and not what they were promised': Glazers' anger at Sir Jim Ratcliffe's reign revealed - and why Man United have become debt-loaded inconvenience for absentee landlords as they splash cash on true loves

Ian Herbert Deputy Chief Sports Writer

From a safe distance in Florida, out of the line of fire, the Glazer family are happy for others to let it be known they are disenchanted with how they believe the British businessman who paid them £1.5billion for a minority share in Manchester United has mismanaged the club.

‘It’s a travesty and not what they expected or were promised,’ a source with a social connection to the family tells Daily Mail Sport of Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s disastrous custodianship. ‘They have never run the club this way.’

Another source told the US broadcaster ESPN this week that the Glazers believe Ratcliffe ‘couldn't have masterminded a worse situation’. His ‘downgrading in all departments’ at Old Trafford was ‘the opposite of what he said his strategy is’.

It would be unwise to characterise this Glazer concern as sentiment. Cash is the motivating factor, just as always. United are two points off the bottom of the Premier League ahead of Saturday’s trip to Chelsea and the $6bn (£4.5bn) valuation which the Glazers put on the club when seeking a buyer, four years ago, is looking more unrealistic than ever.

The Glazers control any sale. A clause in their deal with Ratcliffe, completed in 2024, lets them force him out of his 28 per cent stake – and out of the entire landscape – if they sell the club to a third party, without him having any say, unless he can match that offer and buy the entire club himself. Which is highly improbable.

Whatever displeasure they might feel, they can’t buy back Ratcliffe’s piece of the United pie. But from next February, Ratcliffe will be powerless to stop them selling the entire club for a price lower than the $33 (£25) a share he paid for his chunk. As of Thursday, the United share price was just $20.77 (£15.60).

Sir Jim Ratcliffe (right) with Man United co-chairman Avram Glazer, who is rarely seen at Old Trafford and has never given a meaningful interview about the club he owns

United fans make clear their disgust at the way the club is being run by the Glazers and Ineos

Ratcliffe’s Ineos are cutting their losses in football. They put their Swiss club FC Lausanne-Sport up for sale this week and have slashed the asking price for their French club Nice.

They could sell their chunk of United to someone else if at least two of Ineos’ three shareholders – Ratcliffe and company co-founders Andrew Currie and John Reece – agree to it. The Glazers, for their part, may want to see United’s new stadium built, hiking up the value, before selling. That might not be completed until 2035.

More than ever, the Glazers are absentee landlords. A family with far bigger fish to fry than their struggling Premier League asset where fans sing against them. A family who have been extremely active elsewhere while Old Trafford burns.

In February, Avram Glazer, one of the six siblings, bid $1.32bn (£1bn) for the Royal Challengers Bengaluru franchise in cricket's Indian Premier League, where the enormous market and broadcasting rights deals have seen stratospheric returns on investment. Only as the franchise’s valuation approached a prohibitive $2bn (£1.5bn) did Glazer withdraw. His bid for the Rajasthan Royals was also retracted.

And then there is the love of the Glazers’ lives – their Tampa Bay Buccaneers NFL franchise – where their active involvement provides a striking contrast to their loveless 21-year ownership of United.

While the family have managed to go all these years without a single meaningful UK media interview about United – Avram Glazer hastily climbed into his Aston Martin and drove off when doorstepped by a Sky TV reporter in Florida, five years ago – a recent Amazon series about the Buccaneers provided a rare glimpse into the world of these billionaires.

Like so many such series, Raise the Flags is sanitised and glossy, with Ed Glazer, another of the siblings, one of its executive producers. But it paints a revealing picture of how the NFL-mad Glazers tried and failed for years to buy into the sport, which was intrinsic to the siblings’ childhoods, until the death of Bucs owner Hugh Culverhouse finally gave Malcolm Glazer, their father, his chance in 1995.

They were seen as saviours at a franchise which was ridiculed for always losing and at risk of relocation to Baltimore, Maryland, 1,000 miles away. They transformed it, appointing rookie coach Tony Dungy and even changing the colours from garish neon orange to red and pewter grey.

Joel Glazer, who last visited Old Trafford in 2019, becomes emotional as he tells filmmakers about the team’s legendary win under Dungy, against the San Francisco 49ers in 1997, which set them on the way from hapless also-rans to two-time Super Bowl winners.

Manchester United co-owner Joel Glazer celebrates Super Bowl glory in 2021 when his beloved Tampa Bay Buccaneers beat the Kansas City Chiefs

The Bucs, not United, is what gets the Glazers out of bed. It’s what they spend their own money on – and that will include a $1bn (£750m) rebuild of the team’s Raymond James stadium

‘You know, you felt we’d turned the corner,’ he says, his voice breaking. There is an authenticity about this.

The Bucs, not Manchester United, is what gets these brothers out of bed in the morning. It’s what they spend their own money on – and that will include a $1bn (£750m) rebuild of the team’s Raymond James stadium – the ‘RayJay’ – which is old, dated and lacks the roof required for Tampa to host a lucrative Super Bowl. Within two months, the Glazers and the Bucs will outline plans for the overhaul, to conform with a deadline for a lease extension on the ground.

United have their own stadium plans, of course. But the Glazers didn’t even attend the event at Old Trafford in March 2025, at which architect Sir Norman Foster’s proposals, with their distinctive, canopy-like roof, were presented.

While United are a globally recognised brand and the Bucs are a franchise little known beyond the US, there is no doubt which of these two Glazer sports businesses holds most financial value.

The wild expectation that United would fetch $6bn was born of the values of NFL franchises such as Washington Commanders, on the market for $8bn (£6bn) at the time they put United up for sale. The Commanders were eventually sold for $6.05bn (£4.45bn) to a consortium led by Josh Harris, who also has a big chunk of Crystal Palace. There was no offer anywhere in that vicinity for United.

In part, NFL teams have become so valuable because of a US tax break which allows owners to claim tax deductions on things their teams own or pay for and shrink the amount of profit they pay tax on. It means billionaire owners like the Glazers can end up paying a lower percentage of their income in tax than the workers who keep the stadium running.

In the NFL, the Seattle Seahawks were sold in early September for $9.6bn (£7.2bn), a world record for a sports franchise that lasted just a few days until basketball’s LA Lakers changed hands for $12.5bn (£9.3bn) – more than double United’s industry valuation.

With a precious NFL asset to protect and build, United, whose football operations have been ceded to Ratcliffe, are a minor consideration.

Joel and Avram Glazer are often seen in and around the Bucs - but are rarely spotted at Old Trafford

Former Bucs head coach Tony Dungy was once under pressure like Michael Carrick is now but the Glazers stood by their man - and felt the benefits

Though the Amazon series is PR-friendly and soft focus, it offers an intriguing insight into what active Glazer involvement can look like. When the first draft under their ownership takes place, some of the brothers are in the Buccaneers ‘War Room’ witnessing the squad being built.

When Coach Dungy struggles with no wins in five in his second season and faces a critique like the one Michael Carrick is now encountering, the Glazers call him in for lunch. Rather than tell him he is fired – as he expects – they talk things over for four hours and put him at ease. Dungy’s testimony corroborates the notion that they helped him.

Joel Glazer was often seen as a meddling man of interference at United, prior to Ratcliffe moving in. He would ask for higher fees and drive harder deals when executive chairman Ed Woodward or others were trying to negotiate.

The family never wanted an Amazon documentary about United and only now, under Ratcliffe, has the streaming business got into the corridors of the club. The Glazers’ key United manoeuvres, still very much going on, take place behind closed doors.

The evidence of the past year points to them continuing to use the club as collateral to secure huge loans which helps them invest in other parts of their business empire, according to a study by the respected football finance expert Paul Quinn, popularly known as ‘The Esk’.

Quinn highlights a UK Companies House filing from February, ‘Charge 0018’, through which United took out a Bank of America mortgage against land near Old Trafford, and other club assets, to potentially generate cash for the Glazers. The loan arrangement, taking United’s maximum credit facility up to £400m, came a few weeks before Avram Glazer submitted his huge bids for an IPL franchise.

There is no evidence that the new borrowing secured by Charge 0018 funded an IPL bid, or that Manchester United’s money was used to finance one.

More than ever, it is the Glazers’ own elusive cash that the club need. That new £2billion stadium won’t build itself and though there are plenty of ways of finding the money, the Financial Times has pointed out while listing them that they will ‘not come cheap’.

More than ever, it is the Glazers’ own elusive cash that Manchester United need. That new £2billion stadium won’t build itself

Carrick will be fighting for his future when his United team take on Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday

Tapping into the bond market as Barcelona did to finance their $1.5bn upgrade of Camp Nou would leave the club more exposed to global interest rates. Private equity funds would want a major pay-back when the stadium is built, limiting United’s capacity to earn from the new structure.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers play Atlanta Falcons at the RayJay on Sunday and there can be no doubt that some of the Glazer brothers will be there. Bryan, Joel and Avram were in the team locker room after last weekend’s win at the Carolina Panthers, by all accounts smiling and clapping as coach Todd Bowles spoke.

They hardly ever watch United these days and will certainly not be at Stamford Bridge to see Carrick fighting for his future. Their Premier League asset is an inconvenience, loaded down with debt payments, running up losses for the past seven years and, on Ratcliffe’s watch, reduced to selling clumps of Old Trafford turf for £125.

Where are the Glazers? More than 4,000 miles away from all that.

Sports.title: Bruno back in from the cold - after clear-the-air talks: Fernandes KEEPS Man United captaincy, Michael Carrick confirms, and will go back into the team after being axed over interview
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick insists that he isn’t surprised to still be Manchester United’s head coach despite intense speculation over his future at Old Trafford – and confirmed that 'fully committed' Bruno Fernandes will remain as club captain. United this week decided to give Carrick more time to turn the club’s wretched season around despite overseeing their worst start in 40 years. The 45-year-old reiterated that he didn’t know what to expect after Sunday’s 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth at Old Trafford left United one place above the relegation zone, but insists he doesn’t need reassurances over his position from club bosses. Asked if he is surprised to still be in charge, Carrick said: ‘No, I'm here to do my job. I'm here to do the best for the team and I'm desperate to make us better and improve things. So I'm not surprised no. ‘I don't need any assurances from anyone. I totally get the position, I understand the job, I understand the responsibilities, I understand what comes with that. So I really don't need any assurances from anyone in that regard. ‘I care about what the supporters think, I care about what it feels like in the stadium. They're travelling to games to come and see us and support us. I care about what we give them and what we offer them and what they see. 'I genuinely don't take any notice of anything else. I know this job, I know what it brings, I know what we need to do to be better. I don't need anyone else to tell me anything else. Michael Carrick confirmed Bruno Fernandes will be back in the fold for the clash with Chelsea ‘The outside is not anything for me to focus on. I know what we can affect, I know what we need to improve. So that's part of my direct role, is the players who I care about and can affect the most directly. ‘Of course, we spoke. we have meetings as we do every single week, but some of the meetings go in different ways depending on results and the situation and the feeling. I have to say the boys are hungry. We're hurting because we haven't won enough football games. But there's an intensity, there's a bit of an edge, there's a disappointment, there's a hunger to do better for sure.’ Carrick nodded when asked if Fernandes will stay as captain after being dropped against Bournemouth following his criticism of United’s tactics in the Champions League defeat to Como. Harry Maguire wore the armband against Bournemouth, but Fernandes held clear-the-air talks with Carrick this week and is expected to lead the team at Chelsea on Saturday. ‘There's no decision to be made on that,’ said the United boss. ‘It was a decision (based on) what we felt for the game. That's it. Bruno's fully committed to this football club and there are absolutely no issues with that. We move forward, we make decisions as we go and we're looking forward to the game on Saturday now.

Your browser does not support iframes.

‘Listen, we're clear with the situation of the team, and as a football club at the moment. As I've just said, he's an important player for this group. He has been and he will be. ‘Between us, we've got to make a difference and we've got to push things in a good direction. 'He's fully committed to this football club, and he's fully committed to making things better. It doesn't change for me. He's the one that's kind of led the team so well for many a game and many a year, and he'll continue to do that.’ Carrick confirmed that Benjamin Sesko faces a long lay-off which could last until the New Year as he recovers from a troublesome shin injury. It leaves United without a recognised striker having decided not to sign one in the summer. ‘Unfortunately Ben looks like he's going to be out for a period of time,’ said Carrick, who also confirmed that Kobbie Mainoo has returned to training. ‘We're still not clear of exactly how long, but it's going to be for a longer period of time. ‘It was the process and we had to go through the process. It was a bit of a healing process for the injury to see how it would react and what direction to go with that. So even now we're still working through it. 'Not having him available is obviously a blow, but we’ll try and get him back as quickly as we can.’

Sports.title: Man United are the worst transfer operators in EUROPE as new study reveals Red Devils have made a £334MILLION loss on signings - with fellow Premier League club joining them in bottom three
Sports.content:
When it rains it pours at Old Trafford, and not just through the leaky roof. The beleaguered club, facing a managerial nightmare, dressing room unrest and unprecedented fan fury at the board and owners - have now been named the worst transfer operators in Europe. Stats boffins at CIES Football Observatory have put the business of hundreds of clubs around the world under the microscope. And the findings make for grim reading for United, who are the lowest ranked European team having lost £334m over the last five years. It is another black mark against Ineos, who have run the football operation for a chunk of that time frame having taken over football operations in 2024. Only big-spending Saudi side Al-Hilal are below the Red Devils in the overall standings. Antony (left) and Rasmus Hojlund (right) were both sold for a massive loss by Man United - who rank as the worst transfer operators in Europe

Your browser does not support iframes.

The data compiled by CIES ranks every team in world football who have spent more than £42m on transfer fees since 2021, including add-ons. They then calculated the balance between fees paid to sign players and money received for selling (loans do not count). And the value of players still owned by the club is also taken into account. A high ranking in the list points to a shrewd, well-run transfer strategy and teams lower down have conducted poor business. In Man United's case, they have lost approximately £156m from player sales and the value of players in under-fire Michael Carrick's squad decreased by a further £184m. It doesn't take long to understand how these gruesome numbers came to be. United splashed out £85m on Antony from Ajax in 2022 and he left for only £21.7m to Real Betis. Jadon Sancho arrived to much fanfare from Borussia Dortmund, costing the club £73m. They did not recoup any fee and he remains a free agent. Rasmus Hojlund came for £72m in 2023 and later signed for Napoli for a £34m loss. Andre Onana (£47m), Mason Mount (£60m) and Joshua Zirkzee (£36m) remain on the books but have struggled to make an impact. The CIES study is a damning indictment of Sir Jim Ratcliffe's INEOS, who have run football operations since buying a stake in the club

Your browser does not support iframes.

The failure is therefore not simply an inability to recoup transfer fees but also demonstrates the club's struggle to correctly identify the right players at the right prices in recruitment. At the very top of the list, Bundesliga outfit Eintracht Frankfurt boast an increase in value of approximately £441m. Real Madrid are behind them with £440m, while Champions League holders PSG sit in third on £394m. Manchester City are among the top performers - in fifth just behind Benfica - with an increase in value of around £374m, although there is clearly the enormous caveat that they have been found guilty of breaking financial rules between 2009 and 2018, a period that provided the foundation for the five years studied by CIES. Man United are not the only Premier League side with a dreadful recent record in the market. Tottenham's total value went down by £157m and the value of their players has dropped by £195m. Richarlison signing from Everton in 2022 for £60m and Dominic Solanke's £65m addition are two significant outlays that have failed to deliver. It remains to be seen how Spurs' massive summer outlay on Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Co will age but Spurs are ranked fourth last on the entire CIES list. Brighton are among the best performing club in terms of transfer strategy Leicester City, now languishing in League One, have seen a decrease of £73m, while relegated West Ham depreciated by £63m. Unsurprisingly, Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford, often heralded for being among the best-run clubs, ranked highly with gains of £292m, £271m and £253m respectively. Liverpool, who lost Trent Alexander-Arnold and Ibrahima Konate at the end of their contracts and have broken the £100m barrier on three players in two years, barely broke even with a value change of £13m. Chelsea, despite spending approaching £2bn, have sold well and are up £179m in value change over the time frame. Nottingham Forest are another side who have been extremely busy in the market and have a rise of the same amount as the Blues. Of the Premier League sides on the list, Man United a the worst performing by CIES metrics by a significant margin. The crisis club have chosen to give Carrick a stay of execution and fans' lack of faith in the running of the club will only be strengthened by the brutal transfer failings of half a decade laid out in black and white.

Sports.title: Derry City TEAR UP James McClean's contract: Poppy protest footballer's nightmare return to childhood club comes to an end amid claims he was 'permanently incapacitated'
Sports.content:
The ugly dispute between James McClean and Derry City is finally over after his contract was torn up.

Earlier this month, McClean, 37, branded it 'incomprehensible' and a 'dangerous precedent' for the club to try and terminate his deal due to his physical issues when they claimed he was 'permanently incapacitated'.

But the Republic of Ireland international, who refused to wear a poppy on Remembrance weekend while representing English and Welsh clubs at the height of his career, has now come to an agreement with his boyhood side. He had two years left on the deal.

It is a nightmare end to what was supposed to be a fairytale homecoming having signed in January and McClean had not been included in a matchday squad since July as the relationship soured.

'I am pleased that we have reached a resolution to settle these matters, his statement read. 'While my return to the Club did not work out as I had hoped, Derry City FC will always hold a special place in my heart.

'I want to thank the fans for their support, and I wish the squad, the management, staff, and the supporters the very best for the future. In particular, I want to wish the team the best of luck in the FAI Cup Final against Waterford FC.'

James McClean's return to Derry City is over after his contract was torn up

Derry City chairman Philip O’Doherty thanked McClean for his 'dedication'.

'His achievements extend far beyond the Brandywell; amassing 103 senior caps for the Republic of Ireland is a remarkable milestone, and we want to formally acknowledge his immense contribution to Irish football as a whole,' he said.

'We wish him the very best for the future. Neither the club nor James McClean will be making any further comment on this matter.'

Derry attempted to axe McClean in August – despite signing him in January on a multi-year deal – reportedly claiming he is unable to fulfil his contract's terms because he is not fit enough to play or train.

The former Wrexham man insisted he was ready to feature when called upon in a defiant statement.

'This has been one of the most difficult periods of my life, both personally and professionally,' McClean said in a statement on the PFA Ireland website on October 6.

'When I agreed to come home from Wrexham, I did so in good faith, based on commitments made to me both playing wise and regarding my future after football. I uprooted my family midway through the school year because I believed in the vision presented to me, both for the short term and the long term.

'I accept that some of my actions over the past few months were misjudged, and my frustrations should have remained in-house. I take responsibility for that - and I apologise. Derry City is my club, and I respect everyone who cares about it as much as I do.

'I was asked to help drive standards, to speak up, and to use my experience to further professionalise my hometown club. From the start of the season, I tried to do this to the best of my ability, but I felt when I did my opinions were not well received.

McLean is pictured alongside Adam O'Reilly before Derry City's UEFA Conference League game against HNK Rijeka back in July

McClean has regularly made headlines throughout his career for his refusal to take part in Remembrance Day commemorations

'While I'm happy to hold myself accountable when I am wrong and when my performances have not been to the levels I expect of myself, I cannot understand or accept that I have been treated this way over the past few months.

'For any club to feel it is OK to attempt to terminate a player's contract without any due process or just cause is incomprehensible, and it sets a dangerous precedent for every player in this league.'

But now that fractious relationship is over, with a mutual agreement over the contract termination reached.

McClean is most famous on these shores for his refusal to take part in wearing a poppy and has previously spoken out about his reasons for not doing so, a decision he first made while playing for Sunderland in 2012.

He maintained that stance throughout his career in England, despite being regularly targeted with abuse.

The winger grew up on the Creggan estate in Londonderry, an area that was directly affected by the Bloody Sunday massacre in 1972 when British soldiers shot 26 unarmed civilians during a protest march, with 14 killed.

A quote in the 37-year-old's biography The Walls sheds light on his thinking, speaking about the IRA.

It reads: 'I’m not claiming that every action was justified. Obviously, I don’t support anyone innocent being killed. But I am saying that I supported the original end goal, even if that involved bloodshed '

After being asked about those comments in this interview, McClean added: 'When you grow up listening to the stories there’s a part of you thinking: "These are heroes. I wish I was part of that or born a decade earlier". I’d be a hypocrite if I sat here and said I didn’t support their cause.

'Don’t get me wrong; I don’t believe that anybody innocent deserved to be killed, right? Unfortunately, it was a dirty war, and there were a lot of casualties on both sides.'

McClean pictured in action for West Brom against Huddersfield in 2017 not wearing the poppy

He also spoke at length about his decision not to wear the poppy two years ago: 'The poppy which originally stood for World War 1 and 2 has now been adopted into honouring and remembering British soldiers that have served in all conflicts throughout the world including those who opened fire and murdered 14 innocent civilians on Bloody Sunday Jan 1972, in my home city, as well as many other brutal crimes throughout Ireland,' McClean explained in 2024.

'That is why I never have and never will wear a poppy. If the poppy’s sole purpose was to honour World War 1 and 2 then I would have no issue wearing it, but that’s not the case.

'I respect those who do as I am fully aware we have different beliefs and upbringings, I would never force my beliefs on others, I’m not naive or stupid enough to expect the matter to be reciprocated, especially as the poppy is forced now on everyone in the UK and god forbid someone doesn’t wear it, the abuse they have to endure. The irony of all of this is that the poppy originally stood to honour those who fought for the right of freedom in both World Wars.

'Some people, no matter what, will not educate themselves or want to educate themselves, so to those who throw abuse about (matters they know nothing about), with insults like ‘hates our country’ – well I don’t. Some of my best relationships I’ve made through the years are with people born and raised in England and have completely different beliefs to me ... One thing I never have and never will do, is bend the knee to compromise my convictions.'

McClean, who has won 103 caps for the Republic of Ireland since choosing to play for them rather than Northern Ireland whom he represented in the Under 21s, said he had received 'death threats' for his stance over the poppy.

Last October, speaking during an episode of Virgin Media's Living with Lucy, he told presenter Lucy Kennedy how his family feared he would be shot while away on international duty after he first refused to wear a poppy on his shirt in 2012.

'I was getting death threats, people were saying I should be shot,' he said. 'I was getting bullets in the post, bullets sent to the club.

'That night, I met up with Ireland. The club had received threats that basically I was going to be shot. The game was on TV. I was going to be shot, this and that. (My wife, Erin) is back up in Newcastle, she’s panicking, she’s s*****g herself. They had to put security outside my hotel room door the whole night.

'Then, obviously, we’re playing the game, Erin’s watching the game, she’s panicking, she’s thinking, "He’s going to be shot on TV". Thankfully, nothing happened or nothing ever has happened.'

McClean, who has won 103 caps for the Republic of Ireland since choosing to play for them rather than Northern Ireland, said he has received 'death threats' for his poppy stance

He added: 'I was getting death threats, people were saying he should be shot and dragged across the Cenotaph.

'I could have easily just said, "I'll wear a poppy", and sold myself out and be known for my football or "I'll not wear a poppy" and be known as that but I've stayed true to myself.

'Six or seven people from the Creggan estate (where he grew up) died on Bloody Sunday that day so for me to wear a poppy in support of the people who carried out those atrocities...

'It frustrates me how people can’t see that. How is it even a debate of why I should wear the poppy?'

Sports.title: Former Chelsea star Marc Cucurella's WAG narrowly avoids being caught in Spain's deadly train crash which has killed at least 68
Sports.content:
Marc Cucurella's partner Claudia Rodriguez admitted that she was in 'shock' after revealing that she was on the train that followed Spain's deadly crash which has already claimed 68 lives. The horrifying high-speed rail accident saw one train strike another, stationary, train on the outskirts of Toledo amid a failure to communicate about the obstruction from central command. The country has been plunged into mourning as the death toll rises, with at least a further 100 people suffering injuries in the wake of the crash. Many high-profile footballers in Spain and abroad have shared their sympathies in the aftermath, but Claudia Rodriguez shared hers as she revealed how close she came to travelling on the line that day. In a story posted on Instagram, the long-time girlfriend of the Real Madrid star claimed that she had been 'on the way to Malaga on the train behind', offering all of her 'support to the victims' families and friends'. 'Guys I'm fine, my train hasn't been affected at all because there was a lot of distance from the train that has suffered the accident,' she explained in a longer post. 'We just had to turn around and go back to Madrid since it was the same route. Marc Cucurella's partner Claudia Rodriguez revealed that she had been on the train behind the one involved in Spain's fatal crash Their family moved to Madrid following the defender's summer transfer from Chelsea (Source: Instagram/Claudia Rodriguez) Spain has been plunged into three days of official warning after the horrifying crash which saw a high-speed train collide with a stationary one 'I was removed from everything. To think that if it happened later it would have happened to my train but please, nothing compared to what the people who did go on that train would have happened (heart emoji) All my strength again for those families (prayer hands emoji).' Rodriguez went on to share her support for a call to give blood in Madrid, where her family is now based following their move from Chelsea over the summer. The Spanish Football Federation confirmed that 24 Copa del Rey matches would be postponed this week as a 'mark of respect' after the crash. A number of LaLiga sides had been due to play on Wednesday evening, with revised dates and times for the fixtures planned by the RFEF. 'The entire Spanish football community stands united in grief over this tragedy and has made itself available to the authorities to assist the victims of this devastating accident,' a statement from the federation added. Three days of official mourning have begun in the country just months after the year's first fatal train crash which, like the most recent, involved a collision between one high-speed Renfe train and another from rival rail operator Iryo. More than 540 people were travelling on the two trains when the force of the crash sent two carriages skidding down a nearby slope, amplifying the damage. The crash is believed to rank as one of the most fatal in the country's history of railways. Among the footballers to share thoughtful messages of support in a challenging time was Ballon d'Or candidate Lamine Yamal. 'My solidarity and support to all the families of the victims and those affected by the Urda disaster,' he shared. 'All support and strength to everyone.'

Sports.title: 'Absolute gent' Jack Grealish lauded by Everton fans after donating £10,000 to father-of-three, 35, amid cancer battle
Sports.content:
'Absolute gent' Jack Grealish lauded by Everton fans after donating £10,000 to father-of-three, 35, amid cancer battle

Jack Grealish has been praised by fans after donating £10,000 to the fundraising campaign of an Everton supporter suffering aggressive kidney cancer.

DJ Anton Powers – an Evertonian – is believed to have shared the efforts launched by the family of Leon, 35, on Wednesday night, with Grealish quickly responding to the call-out with a generous donation.

'What an absolute gent Jack Grealish is,' Powers wrote. 'I put up an Insta story up late last night about a heartbreaking situation for a big Everton fan.

'And Jack goes on to donate to his fund. What a top guy (blue heart, hands raised emojis).'

Fans flooded the comments of Powers' missive with their own praise for the former England star, with many recalling that he has made similar impressive gestures in the past.

'Believe he makes a lot of charity donations like this, gent of the game,' one user commented. 'More players should follow (hands raised emoji).'

Jack Grealish (pictured with partner Sasha Atwood) has made another thoughtful charitable donation to a fundraising campaign

The Everton star donated to the campaign of a father-of-three who is suffering aggressive kidney cancer (Source: GoFundMe/Crystal Duffey)

'In fairness Grealish has shown over the years that he's class,' another wrote. 'Fair play (applause emoji).'

A third wrote: 'Absolute top lad is Jack. You can tell he comes from good parents and wants to help where he can.

'Never advertises what he does either it's always others that tell his story of just what a good lad he is'.

Leon's campaign details how the father of three boys aged two, three and 10 is battling 'one of the most aggressive forms of kidney cancer', having been given just one to three years to live.

The campaign has been launched by his partner Crystal Duffey, whose statement for the page stresses that the funds will be used to provide 'access to the best possible care'.

Grealish has a long history of supporting fundraising campaigns, previously donating £5,000 to the family of a woman killed in a car accident in 2021, and another £5,000 to cover funeral costs for an Aston Villa fan in 2023.

Also that year, the winger contributed £5,000 to a Birmingham City-supporting family's appeal for money to support their son Dylan Lamb's trip to America for treatment via a clinical trial to battle his blood cell cancer.

In 2025, Grealish contributed £1,000 to cover funeral fees in a different fundraising campaign, and gifted £1,400 to a man requiring specialist cancer treatment.

Grealish returned to Everton for a second loan season at the start of this term, after his first run-out was hampered by significant injury.

Sports.title: Hero driver who bravely dragged British rival from horror fireball crash opens up on their unique friendship... and reveals he was gifted a Rolex as a thank you for 'giving me more time'
Sports.content:
Hero driver who bravely dragged British rival from horror fireball crash opens up on their unique friendship... and reveals he was gifted a Rolex as a thank you for 'giving me more time'

Almost two months on from British driver Ollie Millroy's miraculous rescue from a fireball crash, he's opened up on the horrific incident with the hero who saved him.

Millroy, 36, had been racing in a China GT event at Shanghai International Circuit in September when two cars smashed into his Ferrari while navigating a bend.

In video footage of the incident, Millroy's vehicle was seen spiralling off the track while aggressive flames and huge plumes of smoke billowed above it.

Rival Dutch driver Loek Hartog, 23, pulled up beside the wreckage, jumped out and tried to free the stricken driver before scrambling to find a fire extinguisher to put out the blaze. Hartog and track staff pulled Millroy away from the fireball, saving his life.

Millroy, who is married to wife Fern with three children, broke his hand, five ribs and severely damaged his lungs but Hartog's quick thinking and bravery prevented the horrific accident from being fatal.

Millroy and Hartog have met three times since the incident and the Brit even surprised his rescuer at his birthday party, giving him a special Rolex watch engraved with the words: 'Thank you Loek.'

Ollie Millroy (left) gave his rescuer, Loek Hartog (right) an engraved Rolex watch

A British driver almost lost his life after a horrific crash China GT event sent his vehicle up in flames but Hartog saved him

Hartog told The Guardian: 'It was really special and they gave me a very special gift, because I gave them more time.'

He explained how he felt in the hours after hauling Millroy from the wreckage, adding: 'That was really emotional for me. I couldn’t sleep because I was overloaded and then Wiep, my partner, sent me a picture of Fern, the kids and Ollie at Disneyland. She was like: "You did it for them". That really struck me.

'Lots of people told me the marshals are not allowed to cross the guardrails on their own, which makes total sense on paper. But once something like this happens in front of you, I cannot believe you’re telling people to go against their feeling.

'If your gut tells you to do something, it should be your cue to act. We should mandate rules that are more human.'

Understandably, the gratitude felt by Millroy and his family is boundless, with the Brit adding: 'Thank you again Loek and don’t change. I know you won’t. This is in your nature and you’re an inspiration to all of us in sport and life in general. Fern and I now think about life differently because you really put everything into perspective.'

Millroy and Hartog shared the pictures of the Rolex watch gift on Instagram, with Hartog writing: 'Ollie and I met in circumstances neither of us could ever have imagined. One day after my birthday, he and Fern secretly flew from Dubai to Amsterdam, completely surprised me with lunch, and we spent the afternoon catching up on everything that has happened since and, more importantly, talking about what we can actually do with it all going forward.

'Somewhere along the way, Ollie, Fern, Wiep and I also just became friends. And then, as if them being there wasn’t enough, they gave me this.

'I still don’t really have the right reaction for someone handing me a Rolex across a table. I hope the first photo says enough. It is an incredibly special gift that I’ll keep and cherish forever.

The watch was given to the Dutch driver by Millroy after he flew out to surprise him

Millroy, pictured with his wife Fern, has three children and came so close to losing his life

'But the thing I’m probably most grateful for is something you can’t really photograph. On 5 September, Ollie was somebody I barely knew. Then we were sitting together in Amsterdam talking like we know each other for years. Life is weird. In this case, in a pretty beautiful way.'

Millroy is still recovering and in significant discomfort, so much so that he can't sleep, having tried to wean himself off heavier pain killers.

But the crash has not deterred the Brit from wanting to race again or encouraging his son Mylo to pursue his passion, having already started competing in karting.

In the aftermath of the crash, Millroy emotionally reflected on Hartog's heroism from his hospital bed, writing: 'I am still alive entirely thanks to one man. Loek Hartog stopped instantly with no flag marshals or fire crews in sight, and risked his own life to get me out of the car.

'I don't remember anything between 30 seconds before the crash and 1 hour after it, but I will remember his incredible act of bravery for the rest of my life.

'One day I will tell our three kids this story and Loek will be the biggest superhero in history in their eyes too.

'I'm laying here tonight with 5 broken ribs, broken collar bone, broken hand and finger and a bruised lung, but it could have been much worse.

Millroy's wife was amazed to see him alive after his fireball crash in Shanghai

'Thank you Loek. I owe you my life for your selfless act today.'

Hartog, meanwhile, posted on his own social media: 'When I saw a car turning into a huge fireball far ahead, there wasn't really a decision to make.

'From what I had seen, I genuinely believed the driver might not be able to get out by himself. I stopped, got out and went towards the car. There was never a moment of doubt.

'It was scary. There were moments where I didn't know I would actually be able to get Ollie out. But this isn't about what I did, and I'm sure many people in the same position would have reacted exactly the same way.'

Millroy's wife Fern added: 'I still can't believe he's alive, purely down to our real life superhero Loek Hartog.'

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
