World.title: Hong Kong leader apologizes for deadly fire that tested Beijing’s grip on city
World.content:
HONG KONG — Hong Kong’s leader made a rare apology Thursday for a residential fire that killed 168 people last year, announcing that a top housing official would resign after an investigation blamed corruption and regulatory failures for the Chinese territory’s worst human-caused disaster in decades.

The Nov. 26, 2025, fire at Wang Fuk Court, a high-rise housing estate in the suburban district of Tai Po, swiftly engulfed seven of its eight towers, killing 110 women and 58 men ranging in age from 6 months to 98 years old. Thousands of others were displaced from their homes at the complex, which was undergoing major renovations at the time of the blaze.

The tragedy provoked widespread public grief and anger and was widely seen as the first major test for the Hong Kong government since Beijing imposed a sweeping national security law in 2020 in response to pro-democracy protests. Critics say the law, which Hong Kong and Chinese officials say was necessary to restore stability, has been used to stifle dissent in the former British colony.

John Lee, Hong Kong’s top leader, and other officials bowed in apology during a news conference on Thursday. Zulu Lo / Sipa USA via AP

Calls for accountability and transparency after the fire were quickly met with warnings from Hong Kong and Chinese officials, who said that “external hostile forces” were trying to re-create the chaos of the 2019 protests, which sometimes turned violent.

John Lee, Hong Kong’s top leader, said he was “deeply saddened” by the fire’s impact on the community.

“After self-reflection, I have considered that the government should roll out a large number of measures for reform, and a lot of work has to be carried out,” he said at a news conference.

“In my capacity as chief executive, I apologize to all the victims and members of the public,” said Lee, who bowed in apology with seven other senior Hong Kong officials.

Lee said Housing Secretary Winnie Ho had resigned on Wednesday, making her the first official to lose her job over the fire. Ho “should bear political responsibility” for the disaster, he said, despite no evidence of personal wrongdoing.

World.title: The former youth pastor leading one of the NFL’s best offenses
World.content:
When Nate Scheelhaase was promoted to offensive coordinator of the Los Angeles Rams last winter, he stepped into one of the NFL’s most auspicious jobs, and for a Super Bowl contender, no less.

Not bad for a former youth pastor.

Fresh out of college, Scheelhaase moved to Louisville, Kentucky, in 2014 to work with teenagers at Southeast Christian Church, one of the largest megachurches in the U.S. During that time, he regularly stopped by a few dozen high schools to visit with students. For two high schools’ football teams, he volunteered as a chaplain. The role entailed building trust, finding common ground and helping those he spoke with work for something bigger than themselves.

“An impactful year,” said Scheelhaase, 35.

It wasn’t the typical starting point for a career in coaching — because even though Scheelhaase had been a four-year starting quarterback at Illinois, he wasn’t initially interested in that career path at all.

Without intending to, though, Scheelhaase honed skills while he was a youth pastor that he says helped him rise quickly within the coaching industry.

“I would say that there’s a lot of carryover,” Scheelhaase said in an interview. “From a ministry standpoint, just being around people from all different walks of life, different journeys, being able to meet them where they’re at — that’s also a football locker room. That’s a staff locker room.”

Los Angeles Rams offensive coordinator Nate Scheelhaase during training camp at Loyola Marymount University this summer. Ric Tapia / Getty

The growth of sports in the U.S. is often a story of their crossover with faith. James Naismith, basketball’s inventor, is said to have believed he could better embody what it meant to be a Christian using sports than the pulpit. Many of football’s conventions, including the huddle, numbered jerseys and padded goalposts, came from Amos Alonzo Stagg, who had gone to Yale to study divinity and began coaching to fulfill a vision of “muscular Christianity.”

Careers in sports have often led to careers in religious roles. Rocky Seto won national championships at the University of Southern California and a Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks during 16 years on Pete Carroll’s coaching staffs. In Seattle, Seto’s role eventually evolved to include a weekly address delivered in front of the entire roster and staff. He obsessively prepared his material.

“How am I going to capture the whole room?” Seto said. “It’s basically convincing them that if you learn this, this is going to help us win, help us be better.”

That experience made him feel prepared to give his first sermon. It was 2017, and Seto had just left the Seahawks to become the pastor-in-waiting at Evergreen Baptist Church, in suburban Los Angeles. Standing in front of another packed room of congregants, Seto felt his new job’s mission mirrored that of his last one — to deliver hope.

“You come to church in some ways to take a peek into heaven for a moment, and then we break. It’s like a huddle, and then we break out to basically fulfill the Great Commission outside this building, right?” he said. “And so coaching is no different. The information has to be almost like, ‘This is the greatest thing you need to know.’”

As Scheelhaase’s career was ending in late 2013, all he knew was that he didn’t envision a future in coaching.

He had gotten married a few months earlier, and he had seen enough coaches get fired and hired to question raising a family in an industry with fleeting job security and a nomadic career path. Meetings with Illini alumni in corporate jobs in Chicago also failed to inspire him. Unsure what to do, Scheelhaase called Jason Epperson, a local pastor who served as Illinois football’s team chaplain.

Scheelhaase was a four-year starting quarterback at the University of Illinois. Michael Hickey / Getty

Epperson had just taken a job at Southeast in Louisville, where there was a youth pastor role open. The idea intrigued Scheelhaase, who had grown up outside Kansas City, Missouri, as a devout Christian. When he arrived at Southeast in early 2014, he was trying “to figure out different ways to just connect with people in the area and show them that I was interested in just who they were more than just what they were doing,” Scheelhaase said. “Which I think is always a good spot to start.”

Chris Burke, an ESPN baseball analyst who lived in the area, first noticed Scheelhaase because of his athleticism during pickup games inside Southeast’s gym. Other things about Scheelhaase soon stood out, too.

“He looked perfectly suited for that job,” Burke said. “You can tell he got a kick out of being around young people. He communicated well with them. He had the patience.”

When a local mother told Scheelhaase that her eighth grade son’s father had recently died and that she needed others to be there for her son, Scheelhaase gave him rides and went to practices. The son was Nate Hobbs, the future San Francisco 49ers defensive back whom Scheelhaase still describes as one of his closest friends.

Scheelhaase stopped by Trinity High School, a local powerhouse, with a “confident humility,” said Andrew Coverdale, Trinity’s offensive coordinator at the time, who is now the passing game coordinator at Kentucky. Scheelhaase didn’t expect students to listen to him just because he had been a college quarterback.

“As somebody who taught in high school for a long, long time, I can’t really emphasize enough that kids need every form of mentorship and positive adult presence they can have, because it is brutal to be a teenage kid right now,” Coverdale said. High schoolers are “just dealing with so much and carrying so much. And so I just think having a guy like that around that you can talk to, who has life experience that he’s willing to share in a really winsome way, it was just great.”

Scheelhaase spent a relatively brief year and a half in Louisville, but he said that time shaped him immeasurably. Scheelhaase, who now has three children, said spending time around church leaders and attendees gave him role models for how he wanted to act as a husband and a father. It also changed his career path.

While he was leading a chapel service for football players at Eastern High School in 2014, he gave what he thought was a compelling, relatable speech that pulled in his athletic background and life story. It was received, he said with a smile, by proverbial crickets.

Taking a seat, he was stunned to see the reaction when the school’s head coach stood up to deliver his own pregame speech.

“Everybody was on the edge of their seat,” Scheelhaase said. “And in that moment, I thought, man, there is a cool ability to impact as a coach. And it was probably the thing that triggered the thought of, man, what would it look like to be able to impact in that way and influence in that way.”

Scheelhaase celebrates against the Buffalo Bills at SoFi Stadium near Los Angeles on Oct. 12. Katelyn Mulcahy / Getty

By the start of the 2015 football season, Scheelhaase was at Illinois coaching running backs. Technically, he was new to the profession. Yet recruiting players to campus and developing them once they were on the roster didn’t feel any different, at its core, from how he’d worked to build trust in Louisville.

“You are going to ask people to do really hard things as a coach, things that are counterintuitive to what you want to do,” he said. “Stand in a pocket where you know somebody’s going to hit you in the side of your helmet. To be somebody who loves to catch the football, but you got to go and block. To be somebody that’s willing to do the dirty work, and you’re going to ask them to do it, and the only way I know how to do that is to connect with them on a deep level. They know I not only understand what we’re asking them to do, but I care and I see them in that. And so connection, fortunately for me, it’s how I’m wired. That’s the part I enjoy the most about my job. ...

“And there probably is an element of that’s what I enjoyed even about the job as a high school pastor in Louisville, too, is just connecting with people and seeing there’s oftentimes more common ground than you think.”

In 2023, he became a coordinator at Iowa State. A year later, he left to become an offensive assistant for Sean McVay and the Rams, which to some may have seemed like a backward step; his job revolved around using software to manually draw the plays McVay wanted called each week. In the NFL, however, just being around McVay is a career springboard: The last four Rams offensive coordinators are now head coaches, and Zac Taylor was drawing McVay’s plays before Cincinnati hired him as its head coach. In 2025, a full year before Scheelhaase’s promotion to Rams offensive coordinator, McVay had called him “a special coach” and “a rising star, without a doubt.”

Last winter, as Scheelhaase was interviewing for NFL head coaching jobs, he called interim Stanford coach Frank Reich to ask about the school’s opening. The two had more in common than football. After he retired from a long career as a backup NFL quarterback, Reich attended seminary and worked as a pastor before he became an NFL head coach.

He saw carryover between the two industries, too.

“In coaching or seminary or pastoring, there are a lot of hours,” Reich said in 2019.

The hours Scheelhaase put in in Louisville have paid off in ways he didn’t expect, he said. There, his life revolved around Sundays. In ways he could never have predicted, it still does.

World.title: Russian strikes kill 14 in Ukraine but local truce brings some hope
World.content:
Kherson, Ukraine — A jet-powered Russian drone hit two passenger trains stopped at a station in Dnipro in central Ukraine Thursday, killing at least 14 people and injuring 14 more, including a 40-year-old man whose legs were amputated, officials said.

A Russian cruise missile killed two 15-year-old girls in the northern city of Chernihiv, meanwhile, and three more civilians died when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in the central city of Kremenchuk, Ukrainian authorities said.

In all, 56 people were injured in the strikes, including 10 children, as Russia continued its deadly attacks on civilians even as a localized ceasefire credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump held in the stricken city of Oleshky.

Police officers carry the body of a killed person at a railway station hit by a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Dnipro, Ukraine, Oct. 29, 2026. Stringer/REUTERS

Humanitarian aid was poised to roll into Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said Thursday, as the limited ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared away landmines.

Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, but the neighboring nations remain otherwise locked in the war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion more than 4 ½ years ago. Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.

Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv. Around half of the drones were heading to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.

The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.

Both sides thanked Melania Trump for what the White House said was her role in helping broker the temporary ceasefire so food and medical supplies can be delivered to some 2,000 desperate people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.

"The parties are fully adhering to the agreements, and no violations of the ceasefire have been reported," Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday, adding that aid deliveries were due to begin the following day.

His Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the truce was holding and that Russian engineers are working on demining Oleshky's roads.

"Both sides are fully honoring their commitments, and no violations have been recorded," she said. "This allows military personnel to continue clearing roads of mines and to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy."

Local people will also be able to evacuate, either into Russia or Ukraine, per their wishes, officials say. The mechanics of how that might work remained unclear.

Lantratova said she and her team were on their way to Oleshky for the aid delivery, adding that the operation was five months in the making.

Russian and Ukrainian representatives met in the Belarus city of Homel on Thursday to fly together to the Kherson region, Belarus state media reported.

A volunteer from Oleshky, Ksenia Arkhipova, told The Associated Press roughly 1,000 residents had told her they want to leave the city.

She said it was important that the Ukrainian delegation was present in Oleshky because many residents fear Russian authorities would identify individuals with pro-Ukrainian views or ties to Ukraine's military.

In the nearby city of Kherson, growing numbers of people were out on the streets as the truce held.

A municipal worker walks along a street over which an anti-drone net is stretched, during a ceasefire on Oct. 28, 2026, in Kherson, Ukraine. Ivan Antypenko/Suspilne Ukraine/JSC "UA:PBC"/Global Images Ukraine/Getty

Nataliia Myronenko, 42, had a steady stream of customers at her coffee kiosk since early Thursday.

"Now, during the quiet, we have people at lunchtime and in the evening, which we didn't have under the attacks," she said. "For a while, people would race down this street because they were afraid to stop."

The pause has brought a sense of relief, she said. "It's a breath of freedom, when you don't look at the sky. You keep looking at your feet because of the mines, but you're not afraid of dying. It's so great," she said, adding: "It's such a privilege and a joy, but we understand it will end soon."

Moscow and Kyiv are keen to curry favor with Washington ahead of possible three-way talks next month.

American military support is vital for Ukraine, but President Trump has waived sanctions on Russia and publicly chided Zelenskyy, indicating he is disengaging with Kyiv.

Tankers carrying Russian diesel are sailing to the United States, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is expected to attend a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, starting Friday, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.

European leaders, on the other hand, have been trying to diplomatically isolate Russian President Vladimir Putin over Moscow's invasion and what they call a campaign of sabotage across the continent.

Ukraine earlier this month reported sudden and unexpected limits on Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communications.

Putin said Russia has been in contact with the American tech titan to coordinate their orbiting activities because it is building its own equivalent of Starlink.

"Elon Musk is a genius. Truly, a real genius," Putin said late Wednesday. "We and our American partners value this relationship, and despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely together."

World.title: Items found in Pompeii home hint at life before volcanic explosion
World.content:
Ancient items found in a sealed closet in Pompeii hint at what life was like in the historic Roman city before it was destroyed in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in A.D. 79.

The closet was located in a home in the central area of the city, the Pompeii Archaeological Park said in a news release. The house had previously been excavated in 1912, but an investigation of the surrounding areas is just now underway.

Inside, archaeologists found cosmetics, an incense burner, a bronze lantern and a balsam jar. Weights, likely used for commercial activity, were also found inside a wooden chest of drawers. The researchers also found vases and pots made of materials such as bronze, glass and ceramic, and a "refined snuff bottle" decorated with pine.

Pots and vases discovered in Pompeii. Pompeii Archaeological Park

A necklace representing multiple deities and made of several materials was also found. The piece of jewelry might have been considered "magical" during the Roman era, the park said. Now these pieces are known as "crepundia," or rattles. The necklaces have amulets, meant to protect the wearer as a child. Many carried them into adulthood as mementos of childhood, the park said.

There were high levels of "geographical mobility" in the Roman world, the archaeological park said, explaining that many people, from slaves to wealthy merchants, lived far from relatives and the places they were raised.

The necklace found in the closet contains at least 20 miniature objects and materials including bone and crystal.

The wardrobe also held 38 bronze coins, preserved in a container made of plant material. The presence of the coins has led researchers to believe that the owner or owners didn't have time to recover valuable items.

It's impossible to know what happened to the people who owned these items, the archaeological park said. They may have escaped the eruption of Vesuvius and been unable to return to the site and dig for their belongings. They may have died in the disaster, along with about 15% to 20% of Pompeii's population, or afterward, without heirs who could reclaim the objects.

Little is known about the residents of the house. The items in the closet, including the paintings, and the location of the home on one of Pompeii's main streets suggest "a certain standard of living." But mouse skeletons found inside the home cast some doubt on this belief. However, such skeletons have been found in other spots of Pompeii, showing the city contended with "unwelcome guests," the park said.

A painting found in a home in Pompeii. Pompeii Archaeological Park

The home has previously been attributed to a person named Cornelius Maximus, the archaeological park said. That identification was based on the discovery of inscriptions that are no longer visible. The newly found items likely won't bring researchers closer to identifying the home's owner, but they allow archaeologists to study "the various traces of a life," said archaeological park director Gabriel Zuchtriegel in the Facebook post.

"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of those who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their daily lives," said Zuchtriegel.

Pompeii is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and popular tourist attraction. Archaeologists are also constantly exploring the ruined city, searching under heaps of volcanic ash and pumice to peer into its preserved remains.

In January, the archaeological park announced that researchers had found a 2,000-year-old love note and illustrated gladiator fight scene inscribed on a city wall. In December 2025, archaeologists found evidence suggesting that some Pompeii residents returned to live in the city after the eruption.

World.title: King faces calls for apology, slavery reparations in Caribbean
World.content:
Britain's King Charles III continued his nine-day tour of the Caribbean Thursday under mounting pressure to issue a formal apology for the U.K. royal family's historic role in the transatlantic slave trade and to support calls for reparations.

Charles was to visit Guyana on Thursday before traveling to Antigua and Barbuda for a meeting of heads of state of British Commonwealth nations, where leaders are expected to discuss the legacy of slavery.

His tour began Tuesday in the Bahamas, where the king addressed hundreds of young Bahamians and acknowledged Britain's colonial past.

"Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness," he said. "It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future."

On Wednesday, the king embraced the country's vibrant culture, joining a colorful Junkanoo street parade in Nassau surrounded by performers in elaborate costumes and feathered headdresses.

King Charles III is seen with a performer during the celebratory Junkanoo street parade in Parliament Square, Nassau, during his royal visit to the Bahamas, Oct. 28, 2026. Aaron Chown/PA Images/Getty

But around the celebrations, protesters held placards declaring: "Pay us what you owe us," demanding compensation for Britain's involvement in centuries of transatlantic slave trade.

Charles' remarks appeared to do little to satisfy campaigners who have long called for a formal apology and reparations.

Speaking to The Guardian newspaper on Wednesday, Dr. Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee, dismissed the monarch's remarks as "hollow platitudes" and said, "we deserve so much more than what was offered."

Buckingham Palace has said Charles will not offer a formal apology for slavery, saying such decisions are for the British government, not the royal family, but that he will not shy away from broader discussions about the U.K.'s involvement.

Experts say the royals are concerned that issuing a formal apology could open the door to legal claims for reparations, potentially exposing the family, and/or the British government, to substantial financial demands.

"The reason why he doesn't go further is that he's aware [of] what it will mean to actually apologize, in terms of the legal obligation to make reparation," Esther Stanford-Xosei, a lawyer and reparations expert, told CBS News in 2023, as Charles' second son Prince Harry's book "Spare" acknowledged the family had profited from the slave trade.

Stanford-Xosei said the family feared a formal apology could end up costing the monarchy, "not only money, but status … He will be exposing the criminality of this institution."

Calls for reparations

Between the 15th and 19th centuries, approximately 5 million enslaved Africans were transported to the Caribbean, including more than 2 million to British colonies, where they endured brutal conditions working in sugar, coffee and cotton plantations.

Historians have documented the monarchy's direct involvement in the trade, including investments by King Charles II and his brother James in the Royal African Company, which trafficked enslaved Africans across the Atlantic.

When slavery was abolished across most of the British Empire in 1834, the government allocated £20 million ($23 billion in today's money according to one estimate) to compensate slave owners, but not the enslaved. The compensation was part of a political compromise that helped secure abolition's passage by British lawmakers.

Britain subsequently played a significant role in suppressing the international slave trade during the 19th century, deploying the Royal Navy and investing substantial resources in abolition efforts. Its West Africa Squadron seized more than 1,600 slave ships and freed approximately 150,000 Africans between 1808 and 1869. One study estimated that Britain's wider anti-slavery efforts cost the equivalent of 1.8% of its national income annually over that period.

The debate over reparations has intensified in recent years, particularly following the global Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, which prompted renewed scrutiny of Britain's colonial past and the royal family's historical connections to slavery.

Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley has been among the leading voices calling for reparations, including investment in education, healthcare and economic development.

Speaking to The Guardian, the head of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Hilary Beckles, said people in the Caribbean wanted "proprietary justice, beginning with remorse" from British leaders.

She urged Charles to "dig deep within his consciousness" and to offer young people he meets on his visit "the empowerment that he would give to his own children."

Britain's King Charles III walks before boarding a plane to Georgetown, Guyana, at Lynden Pindling International Airport, as part of a week-long autumn tour of Caribbean nations on Oct. 29, 2026, in Nassau, Bahamas. Isabel Infantes-Pool/Getty

Not everyone in the Caribbean supports the idea of direct reparations, however.

Rasheed Griffiths, a Barbadian economist, told CBS News that "Caribbean leaders have consistently refused to implement prudent fiscal policies over the last few decades, which has led to the decay of Caribbean economies. But instead of realizing they have all the power to turn these countries around they prefer to seek scapegoats."

"The calls for reparations from the U.K. are nothing more than Caribbean leaders attempting to externalize their own failures," Griffiths said. "It should not be taken seriously by anyone, least of all the U.K. public."

Charles previously described slavery as an "appalling atrocity" that "forever stains our history" during Barbados' transition to a republic in 2021.

During a Caribbean tour in 2022, heir to the British throne Prince William and his wife Kate also faced protests over slavery and demands for reparations. William expressed his "profound sorrow" and described slavery as "abhorrent," but stopped short of a formal apology.

Many of the Caribbean nations Charles is visiting are former British colonies and several, including the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, remain constitutional monarchies, which, despite them having gained independence decades ago, makes Charles their official head of state.

World.title: These Americans remain imprisoned in Russia. Here are their cases.
World.content:
Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American retired English teacher, is finally free after spending more than four years in a Russian prison on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. For his family, the long wait is over.

But for as many as 10 other Americans, including some with dual Russian nationality, the wait continues as they remain in Russian custody.

Russian authorities tightly control all information that comes out of the country, so the detainees' circumstances can be hard to verify, but here's what we know about some of the Americans still locked up in Russian prisons and labor colonies.

Travis Michael Leake

Russian citizen Veronika Grabanchuk and U.S. citizen Michael Travis Leake attend a court hearing in Moscow, Russia on July 18, 2024. Moscow City Court Press Service/Handout via REUTERS

Travis Michael Leake, an American rock musician who fronted the Moscow-based band Lovi Noch, was arrested in 2023 on charges of organizing the sale of drugs. He was convicted of drug-related offenses and sentenced in 2024 to 13 years in prison.

In a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Leake's family said he was "left behind" when he was excluded from the August 2024 Ankara prisoner exchange that brought home three other U.S. nationals. A representative for Leake, who had lived in Moscow since 2010, maintains the American is innocent, telling CBS News: "Travis is no drug dealer."

"I'm sorry I'm not a journalist. I'm sorry I'm not a basketball player. I'm sorry I'm not somebody that's important," Leake said in a message recorded in prison advocating for his release.

Robert Woodland

Robert Woodland, who was interviewed by Russian media in 2020, is seen in a Facebook profile photo. Facebook

Robert Woodland returned to Russia after living with a U.S. foster family for most of his life, hoping to track down his birth mother. He told a Russian newspaper in 2020 that he decided to move there after connecting with her through a Russian TV show.

In 2024, Woodland pleaded partially guilty to Russian drug trafficking charges and was sentenced to 12½ years in prison. His sentence was reduced to 9½ years in 2025. Stanislav Kshevitskii, an attorney for Woodland, told CBS News in October 2026 there have been no updates to his case.

David Barnes

David Barnes was sentenced to 21 years in a high security Russian penal colony by a Moscow court. GiveSendGo

David Barnes and his Russian ex-wife were embroiled in a bitter custody battle over their two sons in Texas. During the dispute, Boricovna accused Barnes of sexually abusing the two boys, but law enforcement found insufficient evidence to file charges. Texas judges ruled repeatedly between 2014 and 2018 that Barnes should remain a joint custody guardian. After losing her bid for sole custody, his ex-wife took the boys to Russia in 2019.

When Barnes went to Russia to pursue visitation rights, his ex-wife again accused him of sexual abuse. He was convicted in a Russian court and sentenced in February 2024 to 21 years in a penal colony.

In a letter from prison to his sons, Barnes maintained his innocence, writing: "Thousands of people in America and Russia know I am innocent … You know I am innocent as well. Don't worry, we will be together again … I love you so much. I was devastated when your Mom took you from me."

Daniel Schneider

Daniel Schneider is being detained in Russia amid what a website advocating for his release describes as a "complex international child custody dispute."

Schneider traveled to Russia to reunite with his 4-year-old son, a Russian citizen. In July 2023, he was arrested while attempting to cross into Poland with the boy and was later sentenced to six years in prison for kidnapping after prosecutors said the child's mother did not consent to him leaving the country.

Gordon Black

U.S. Army Staff Sgt. Gordon Black appears in court in the far eastern city of Vladivostok on June 6, 2024. PAVEL KOROLYOV/AFP/Getty

U.S. Army Staff Sergeant Gordon Black was stationed in South Korea in May 2024 when he traveled to Russia to visit his girlfriend. U.S. officials and Russian authorities say he was arrested after she accused him of stealing money from her and was eventually sentenced to 3 years and 9 months in prison.

Last year that sentence was reduced by a Russian court to 3 years and 2 months.

Charles Zimmerman

In June 2025, retired U.S. Navy veteran and electrician Charles Wayne "Chuck" Zimmerman was pursuing his lifelong dream of sailing the world aboard his private sailboat. When he reached the Black Sea, his family says he was ordered to follow a Russian Navy vessel under threat of military action.

Zimmerman followed the vessel to Sochi, where he voluntarily declared a firearm on board. He was arrested, and later convicted of arms smuggling and given a five-year prison sentence in January 2026.

Zimmerman's sister, Robin Stultz, alleges that Russian authorities have denied her brother access to U.S. diplomatic representatives since his arrest and says she would not trust any confession they claim he made.

Andre Khachatoorian

Andre Khachatoorian was traveling from California to Armenia to visit his wife's family for the holidays in December 2021 when he was detained during a layover in Moscow. According to a website advocating for his release, he asked to access his checked bag to retrieve medication, and police noticed a locked firearm case inside.

Supporters argue that he had proper paperwork for the weapon and allege that a Russian police officer tricked him into applying for a Russian visa before removing him from the airport.

Khachatoorian was charged with arms trafficking in Russia and sentenced to eight and a half years in prison in 2023, Reuters reported.

Eugene Spector

In December 2024, a Russian court sentenced Eugene Spector to a total of 15 years in prison in an espionage case. The claims against him have not been made public by state media, and his trial took place behind closed doors.

Spector, who was born in Russia, had previously pleaded guilty to facilitating bribes to an aide to a former Russian deputy prime minister and was sentenced to three and a half years in prison in 2022.

A year later, Spector was charged with new espionage offenses, and in 2024 he was handed an additional 15-year prison sentence.

Aleksandr Antonov

Aleksandr Antonov, 66, is a naturalized U.S. citizen who immigrated from the Soviet Union in the 1990s but returned to Ukraine and Russia on business trips. Family photo

Aleksandr Antonov is a naturalized U.S. citizen who traveled to Ukraine and Russia on business trips. At a passport check in Russia in March 2025, Russian border officers noticed his U.S. passport and claimed he had Telegram messages on his phone containing anti-Russian sentiment. Antonov was detained and eventually sentenced to 6 years for inciting terrorism and extremism.

CBS News has learned from current and former U.S. officials that the State Department is debating whether to designate Antonov as wrongfully detained.

World.title: DoorDash gobbles up Instacart in $17 billion deal
World.content:
DoorDash said Thursday that it will buy Instacart for $17 billion, uniting one of the nation's top grocery delivery services with a major food delivery company.

DoorDash, which will pay $65 per share for Instacart, said the acquisition will benefit communities by enabling more supermarkets to use Instacart's platform to run their websites.

"Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day," Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said in a statement. "Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."

Consumers will benefit by having more stores to choose from, speedier delivery options and access to savings when they shop locally, DoorDash also said in announcing the acquisition.

"Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today," DoorDash said.

Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada.

DoorDash was founded a year later in San Francisco as a restaurant-delivery business and expanded into grocery delivery in 2020 amid a pandemic-induced surge in demand. The San Francisco-based company later teamed with the supermarket chain Kroger in 2022 and with Costco last month.

The deal will beef up DoorDash's grocery delivery services, making it a more potent competitor to Amazon and Walmart.

DoorDash's most recent earnings report, released on Wednesday, shows its revenue grew 34% from a year ago. Its total number of orders rose 28%, a sign the company is continuing to grow in the highly competitive delivery business. By the end of 2024, DoorDash held nearly 61% of the food delivery market share, topping Uber Eats and Grubhub, which held around 26% and 6%, respectively, according to Consumer Edge.

Survival of the biggest

The acquisition is the latest sign of consolidation in the delivery services industry, which is increasingly dominated by larger players. As competition intensifies, companies like Instacart have struggled to maintain their market share. Instacart now commands 18% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms, down from 26% five years ago, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company.

DoorDash's acquisition of Instacart also comes as more people migrate from in-person stores toward apps to order their weekly groceries. Nearly 150 million Americans grocery shopped online as of 2025, according to Capital One.

As online shopping becomes more prevalent, some companies are experimenting with personalized pricing, which involves using AI and consumer data to charge shoppers different prices for the same item.

The advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative has slammed the practice as unfair and predatory. In a months-long investigation last year, the group found that identical grocery items on Instacart could differ in price by as much as 23% from one customer to the next.

Federal regulators are now scrutinizing such practices. The Federal Trade Commission on Thursday said it has opened a probe into DoorDash and Instacart, along with seven other companies across retail and transportation, to examine how they set prices.

DoorDash, which has a market value of $73 billion, said the companies will operate as separate entities until the merger is finalized, which is expected in late 2027 or early 2028. After the deal closes, DoorDash said it plans to maintain Instacart's brand, technology and app.

World.title: Hegseth fires Pentagon's top military planner over alleged leaks
World.content:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, several sources confirmed to CBS News late Wednesday.

A Pentagon official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was accused of misconduct for allegedly leaking classified information related to the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war.

Sylvia failed three polygraph tests about sharing classified information with the press, the official said, adding that the case has been referred to the Department of Justice.

Two other Pentagon sources confirmed to CBS News that the firing was related to the polygraph tests, but said those accusations are not true.

Hegseth has made rooting out leakers at the Pentagon a priority, with sources telling CBS News last month that high-ranking military officials were subject to polygraph tests. Three staffers from his office were escorted out last year amid a leak investigation, but the Pentagon never released the results of any investigation.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell did not name Sylvia by name in a statement on social media, but said that "following an extensive Air Force OSI investigation, the Department took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information."

Maj. Gen. Brett Sylvia at Fort Campbell on May 30, 2025. Sgt. Timothy Jackson/U.S Army via AP

"To protect the integrity of the investigation, no further comment will be made regarding the individual or the circumstances of this action," Parnell continued. "This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action. Classified information is not personal property. Leaking it for personal, political or professional gain is a betrayal of the trust placed in those responsible for keeping it. Our commitment was not an empty promise. We vowed to find you, and we meant it."

Sylvia's firing comes as President Trump weighs resuming strikes against Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff, and was coordinating the Iran battle plan. Sylvia is the second general during Hegseth's tenure to be removed from what is known as a "J5" post, which is the lead on how the Iran war affects long-term planning. Sylvia's predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced to retire in October 2025.

No replacement for Sylvia has been named.

The firing was reported earlier by The Atlantic.

After initially issuing a statement extending "the deepest gratitude" for Slyvia's 32 years of service, a spokesperson for the Joint Staff retracted the statement and issued a new one.

"Upon further review, we determined that the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances," the spokesperson said. "Out of respect for the servicemember and the ongoing personnel process we will not comment further."

Sylvia is a former commander of the 101st Airborne Division with multiple deployments to Afghanistan and Iraq, earned a Bronze Star for Valor. He was a Purple Heart recipient after being wounded in battle in that gunfight with the Taliban, and he had a storied combat career that spanned 32 years.

World.title: El-Sayed's faith, family under scrutiny in campaign. Here's what we know.
World.content:
Few U.S. Senate races have captured the public's attention like the battle in Michigan between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. It pits a 63-year-old former FBI agent and former congressman who has strong backing from President Trump against a charismatic doctor and political newcomer who, if elected, would become the first Muslim U.S. senator in American history.

Trump and Rogers have made El-Sayed's identity the focus of their stump speeches. The president has called him "a jihadist" and suggested El-Sayed would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate" — derisive rhetoric denounced by critics as Islamophobic. At a recent rally in Grand Rapids, El-Sayed shot back at the president: "I don't even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November."

Recent polls show El-Sayed with a slight edge on Rogers; a new poll out Wednesday from CBS Detroit and other Michigan TV stations shows him ahead by 7 percentage points.

As Election Day nears, reports about El-Sayed's faith and background have ricocheted around the internet. Several outlets, including the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times, have discussed questions surrounding El-Sayed and his family's possible "ties" to the Muslim Brotherhood. The Democratic candidate emphatically told Fox News: "I have never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, I never will be a member of the Muslim Brotherhood."

His campaign told CBS News they consider the topic a "bad faith attack" on his religion and family, meant to distract voters. He is "a dad and a doctor. He has spent his entire career working to keep Michiganders healthy and safe," a spokeswoman said. The campaign did not respond to detailed questions.

"I'm Abdul El-Sayed, man of faith," he said in one campaign ad. "That's a good thing."

An examination of El-Sayed's past writings and new documents obtained by CBS News provides a window into his pre-campaign worldview, and sheds light on the controversy. Here's what we know:

The candidate's mother

El-Sayed was born and raised in southeast Michigan. His Egyptian immigrant parents separated when he was a toddler. Following the divorce, El-Sayed's mother, Fatten Elkomy, moved away to Missouri and worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA) as a nurse. The FBI raided her offices in Columbia, Missouri, on Oct. 13, 2004, searching for documents and financial records linking the group to overseas terrorist organizations. She described being interviewed by the FBI to her local newspaper.

The IARA, which raised $20 million and did humanitarian work with children in Africa and Asia, was shut down by the Treasury Department and Justice Department that same year, for violating sanctions and providing aid to al Qaeda and other terrorist groups. An expert witness in the case told The New York Times last week that the nonprofit was so small, with only 14 employees, that workers likely knew what was going on at the charity. Among the nearly 1,000 exhibits produced at the trial, 13 were letters Elkomy sent, documenting financial transactions between 1999 and 2001, the newspaper reported.

Elkomy was not accused of any wrongdoing.

El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, is a University of Chicago professor who posted on social media years ago that their mother had been involved with the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt. The social media posts were first reported by the Washington Free Beacon. In the 14-year-old posts, she wrote in part: "Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early '70s when she was in college."

"My family has long been MB [Muslim Brotherhood], but I have always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively," she posted on June 24, 2012.

El-Sayed told NBC News that he wasn't raised by his mother and that her ties to the Muslim Brotherhood were hearsay. "Are you serious?" El-Sayed said when pressed. "I have no ties. We have no ties."

El-Sayed described his mother as "smart, warm and charismatic" in his 2020 book "Healing Politics: A Doctor's Journey into the Heart of our Political Epidemic." His campaign said he is estranged from his mother. But there appears to have been some contact between them. The New York Post reported that his mother attended El-Sayed's medical school graduation in 2014. And in a 2021 column for his Substack, obtained by CBS News, he wrote he was "off to Columbia, MO to visit my mother for the [Thanksgiving] holiday."

The candidate's father

Mohamed El-Sayed, 74, an automotive engineer and former professor at Alexandria University, left Alexandria, Egypt, in his 20s when the government of Anwar Sadat was cracking down on militant students and professors who rebelled after the Egyptian leader made peace with Israel in the late 1970s. Abdul El-Sayed's book says his father's "political agitation against Egypt's increasingly brutal military dictatorship coupled with his proximity to young minds, made him a threat to the regime. He had to leave. There were few options."

El-Sayed's father fled to America where he pursued a PhD in mechanical engineering at Wayne State University in Detroit. The politician's book said his father was drawn to Detroit because "his name, the color of his skin and how he prayed shouldn't matter. … America was also the home of democracy, that thing he had so wanted for Egypt."

The candidate's father-in-law

Abdul El-Sayed met his wife at the University of Michigan, where both were prominent members of the Muslim Students' Association. Her father, Tayeb Jukaku, has held leading positions with Muslim community groups. Jukaku is a kidney doctor and a past president and current board member of CAIR Michigan, according to federal tax filings of the group. Jukaku also served on the founders' committee of the Islamic Society of North America (ISNA), according to their website.

Both organizations have been the subject of controversy. Supporters of CAIR, the Council on American-Islamic Relations, say it is a well-established civil rights organization focused on empowering American Muslims through legal advocacy, education and civic engagement. "Our consistent moral stance is the reason that extremist voices on all sides target our civil rights group with conspiracy theories, bigotry and even threats of violence," a CAIR spokesman said in a statement to CBS News.

Both groups were named as unindicted coconspirators in the 2007 Holy Land Foundation federal terrorism trial which found that U.S. nonprofits had funneled more than $12 million to Hamas. Neither ISNA nor CAIR was charged with any crime. Lara Burns, a retired FBI agent and the lead investigator in the Holy Land Foundation case, told CBS News that "the Muslim Brotherhood operated covertly through nonprofits" that it set up in the U.S. in the 1960s.

"The funding that flowed through the Holy Land Foundation was designed to support Hamas, primarily its social infrastructure that it used to radicalize the population to believe violence was the only solution," she told CBS News. "They claimed to provide all sorts of aid to the needy and they did, but as with all things Hamas, nothing is provided without a price."

The Trump administration designated several overseas chapters of the Muslim Brotherhood as foreign terrorist organizations in January of this year, including those in Egypt, Jordan and Lebanon.

Jukaku has donated more than $300,000 in support of his son-in-law's Senate bid, according to public records.

Muslim Students' Association

While a student at University of Michigan between 2003 and 2007, El-Sayed served as a board member and later "Brothers' Outreach Chair" for the Muslim Students' Association. The group was originally founded by Muslim students at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1963. The group spread to campuses across the country, and by the early 2000s, the largest chapter was at the University of Michigan.

The student association defined its mission around student support, religious accommodation, interfaith dialogue, and leadership development. Lorenzo Vidino, the director of George Washington University's Program on Extremism, said the group encompasses activists from various backgrounds. He says members and sympathizers of the Muslim Brotherhood played a crucial role in its founding in the 1960s. "While MSA was not a 'pure' Brotherhood organization, links to it were strong," he said.

MSA did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday.

The petition

After the Arab Spring, El-Sayed was one of 46 Egyptian-Americans who signed on to a petition to Egypt's new democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, who was a senior leader of the Muslim Brotherhood. The letter called on Morsi to crack down on allies of the country's prior authoritarian leader.

It read in part: "We, the leaders of the Egyptian community, support the revolutionary decisions taken by the president, and call on him to purge the media and the police as soon as possible…"

Some signatories have been contributors to El-Sayed's campaigns, including Amr Abbas, a cardiologist and member of Michigan's Egyptian-American community, who donated $5,000 to El-Sayed's gubernatorial primary bid in 2018.

Rogers voted in the Senate to maintain $250 million in annual aid to Egypt after Morsi came to power in June 2012.

The Substack

El-Sayed maintained a Substack column from February 2021 to at least December 2022, shared in emails with 55,000 subscribers. The columns range widely in topic and tone. CBS News viewed 233 posts. Regarding the Middle East, he wrote: "When President Biden claims 'unwavering' support for Israel, he is indeed, offering unwavering support to this status quo, which rests on the dehumanization of the Palestinian people who get neither rights or land."

"Claiming to support a two-state solution while supporting a regime that is actively destroying it isn't supporting a two-state solution," El-Sayed wrote in a column following the outbreak of violence in Israel and Gaza in 2021. "It's perpetuating a two-tiered society — freedom and democracy for Israelis, occupation and apartheid for Palestinians."

In an earlier column, El-Sayed criticized the "unquestioning support for Israel" in the U.S.

"We're told that it's because Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East," he wrote. "Yet, like Saudi Arabia, Israel's government is under the control of a small cadre of extremists — and the country has perpetrated shocking violations of human rights and international law against the Palestinians, whose land it has occupied for the better part of a century."

He added: "Perhaps there are so few democracies in the region because our country has so consistently backed dictators in the region."

In a column titled "Gaza," posted on May 20, 2021, El-Sayed was also critical of Hamas, writing: "Hamas is wrong. And its violent co-option of non-violent protest is part of the problem."

The endorsements

El-Sayed's Senate candidacy has drawn a wide range of endorsements, including from unions and grassroots groups, among them the United Auto Workers, the Teamsters and the Sierra Club.

The Democratic candidate also has received the endorsement of CAIR Action. Its super PAC, the Unity & Justice Fund, donated $115,000 to a committee supporting El-Sayed's campaign. And El-Sayed has public backing from Americans for Justice in Palestine, the political giving apparatus of American Muslims for Palestine (AMP).

Joyce and Stanley Boim, whose 17-year-old son was killed in a 1996 Hamas terrorist attack, sued AMP in Chicago federal court alleging that the organization helped fund the terror that led to their son's death. The Boims had earlier won a jury verdict against the Islamic Association for Palestine (IAP), an advocacy group started by Muslim students in 1981. They were awarded $156 million, but IAP shut down before those damages could be paid. The Boims allege AMP is the "alter-ego" of IAP. AMP calls the claim "guilt by association" and is fighting the suit.

El-Sayed's campaign didn't respond to questions about the groups' support.

World.title: US and Japan agree to establish a Japanese facility for joint missile production
World.content:
US and Japan agree to establish a Japanese facility for joint missile production

toggle caption i Rolex Dela Pena/Pool EPA via AP

CEBU, Philippines — The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said.

It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.

Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central Philippine province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.

Sponsor Message

Koizumi renews concern over China's naval activity

Koizumi raised concern Thursday about China's increasing naval activity in southwestern Japan. He said that three Chinese destroyers and a coast guard ship together crossed the Osumi Strait south of the southern main island of Kyushu and headed east to the Pacific Ocean this week. It was the first such fleet configuration his ministry has spotted, he said.

Koizumi said he cited the incident as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region" in his remark at a session Thursday. His ministry will keep watching the Chinese activity with high level of interest, he said. Japan has been accelerating military buildup in southwestern Japan to deter China.

The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.

Japan, US to bolster joint missile production capacity

The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called "Operation Supercharge" are essential for the F-35 fighter jets, Koizumi said. The two sides agreed to build a final assembly and inspection plant for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, in Japan, he said. The U.S.-made F-35s are one of the world's most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.

Sponsor Message

During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."

"We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means," Koizumi said.

Hegseth reassures US engagement in the region

Hegseth renewed the Trump administration's repeated assurances of commitment to help deter aggression in the region in a separate meeting on Wednesday with ASEAN defense ministers, who were led by the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. Like Koizumi, Hegseth did not mention China by name in expressing his security concerns in the region.

"The approach we're taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."

His message is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners," Hegseth said.

Hegseth has assured the Philippines, the oldest treaty ally of Washington in Asia, that the Trump administration will build a robust deterrence against China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. Beijing claims the busy waterway, a key global trade route, virtually in its entirety.

Australia shows commitment to defend the rule of law in the Pacific

Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said his country's forces, along with allies like the U.S., will press on with efforts to defend the rule of law despite China's increasing assertiveness, including in the South China Sea. Australia protested last year after a Chinese J-16 fighter aircraft released flares and passed within 30 meters (100 feet) of an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance jet over the disputed waters.

Sponsor Message

"That doesn't deter us from doing what we need to do and that's essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific," Marles told The Associated Press in Cebu on Wednesday. "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."

The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, all ASEAN member states, along with Taiwan, also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Confrontations have particularly escalated between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and navy vessels in disputed shoals and outlying waters.

Washington has warned that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships and aircraft come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea.

Beijing and Tokyo have a separate dispute over tiny Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea, with both sides often accusing the other of infringing on their maritime territory.

World.title: China elevates a military general to the Politburo and seeks to strengthen party discipline
World.content:
China elevates a military general to the Politburo and seeks to strengthen party discipline

toggle caption i Ng Han Guan/AP

BANGKOK — China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.

The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.

During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader.

Sponsor Message

The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China's top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission's only member besides Xi himself. It also left the Politburo without any representatives from the People's Liberation Army.

Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.

The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were "increasingly arduous," such as "uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."

It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.

The party should, "with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people," according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency.

Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.

Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.

Sponsor Message

The plenum meeting revealed wider-than-expected purges, according to analysis by Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at Asia Policy who studies Chinese politics. He calculated an attendance rate of 74 percent, the lowest since the times of former leader Mao Zedong, who ran political purges regularly.

World.title: Greetings from Baghdad, where Agatha Christie's old home presents its own mystery
World.content:
Greetings from Baghdad, where Agatha Christie's old home presents its own mystery

Jane Arraf/NPR

This, according to Iraq's culture ministry, is the one-time home of English mystery novelist Agatha Christie, on the banks of the Tigris River in Baghdad.

Fittingly, the abandoned house has its own mystery: why it's been left to decay over the last century.

Christie made dozens of trips to Iraq, including the one where she met her archaeologist husband, Max Mallowan, in 1930. They Came to Baghdad and Murder in Mesopotamia were two of her novels set in Iraq.

As for the house, it's a heritage property controlled by Iraq's culture ministry. The Iraqi government says it's willing to make the house available to anyone who will restore it. It is padlocked and literally falling down.

Sponsor Message

When we visited this month, there was a $200 electricity bill stuffed into a hole in the door — apparently reflecting years of unpaid bills in its more recent history.

World.title: A stress-free guide to organizing important paperwork and documents
World.content:
A stress-free guide to organizing important paperwork and documents

Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. 

Got piles of mail by the kitchen island? A closet full of tax documents, product manuals and old love letters? Not sure where your Social Security card is? It's probably time to organize your paperwork and documents.

Life Kit A stress-free guide to organizing important paperwork A stress-free guide to organizing important paperwork Listen · 21:30 21:30

If that fills you with dread, don't worry — Kacy Paide has advice. She's been working as a professional organizer for over two decades, and specializes in helping clients deal with paper clutter.

The key to making the process less overwhelming? Don't feel like you have to rush or organize in a certain way. "You're in control of your paper, and it's up to you how fast you want to get through it," she says.

Start with the nearest pile of paperwork

When getting started on paper clutter, don't worry just yet about what's stashed away in the garage or your office closet. Focus on sorting what's piled up around your desk or dining table. "The documents and action items that are on fire tend to be closest to us," Paide says.

Separate all those documents into two piles: active and inactive. Active requires follow up, like making a call or paying a bill. Inactive does not. That includes receipts, birth certificates and sentimental stuff, like a Valentine's Day card from your mom. Go ahead and file your inactive documents away or put them to the side for when you have a little more time to give them a deeper look.

Sponsor Message

Make the due date clear on your active paperwork. Paide likes to write it boldly with a permanent marker on a sticky note, then attach it to the document. This tactic can quickly help you identify what needs to be done and when. Be as specific with the deadline as possible — as in, "due by Nov. 15" or "start no later than 12/1" — otherwise "urgent" or "due now" will start to lose its meaning, Paide suggests.

Create a filing system that makes sense for you

There are many kinds of documents that require saving. Birth certificates and passports; product manuals for the oven and fridge; tax documents; medical records.

Storing these items away can be as simple or as complex as you want it to be. Alphabetize, color-code, label-make — or don't. The best filing system is the one you'll actually use. That said, Paide has some preferences.

Put your most important documents, like your passports and marriage certificate, in a brightly colored folder. That way they're easy to spot. As for where to put it, Paide prefers them to be a "bookend to your filing system." Put the folder at the front or the back of a file box, for instance, so you don't have to rifle through piles of paper to get to it.

Sponsor Message

You don't need fancy materials to get organized. Paide prefers to use simple file folders to organize her papers, and likes labeling those folders with sticky notes written with permanent markers. That way, she can reuse the file folders again in case she changes her mind about how she wants to sort things. She also likes buying cool file boxes for her paperwork and storing them in bookshelves. "Then you have this visual filing system that's also beautiful and approachable," Paide says.

Destroy or let go of what you don't need

Not all paperwork needs space in your desk drawers. If you're not sure whether or not to hold onto something, ask yourself: Under what circumstances would I need to produce this document? Paide shares more advice on how to let go.

You don't need to shred everything. Some people feel "like they have to shred everything with their name and address on it in order to sleep well at night," Paide says. But you really don't have to. According to the Federal Trade Commission, destroy anything containing sensitive information to protect yourself from identity theft. That includes account numbers, birth dates, passwords and pins, signatures or Social Security numbers. But of course, shred to your comfort.

Have a family member or friend help you sort sentimental or tough paperwork. That includes old letters, divorce papers or greeting cards. As you go through those documents, "voice those thoughts" about them, Paide says. In her experience, people come to conclusions about whether to keep or toss that paper "shockingly fast."

You don't have to declutter or get rid of your paper all at once. Start small if you have to, dedicate 25 minutes at a time, Paide says. And remember, organizing is an ongoing process that will require maintenance and change.

More Life Kit on home organization

5 clever design tricks to make a small home look bigger. Just because you live in a small place doesn't mean it has to look or feel cramped. Interior designers share creative strategies to create the illusion of space that work for renters and small budgets.

Sponsor Message

World.title: With days to go before the midterms, data shows the U.S. economy is doing well
World.content:
With days to go before the midterms, data shows the U.S. economy is doing well

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images North America

The U.S. economy grew faster in the summer compared to the spring, driven by consumer spending as well as investments in AI.

Gross domestic product, which broadly measures economic activity, grew at an annual rate of 3.4% July through September, according to a report from the Commerce Department released Thursday. The previous quarter GDP grew at a 2.2% annual pace.

A big driver for GDP growth in the third quarter was the strong investments from AI companies, which continue to build out data centers and spend big money in developing the technology.

Meanwhile, consumer spending was another of the big drivers of GDP growth, led in part by higher-income Americans who are better able to withstand stubbornly high inflation.

Sponsor Message

The sturdy GDP data comes just days before the midterm elections, with many Americans saying they feel gloomy about the economy as inflation jacks up the costs of many day-to-day necessities, while the ongoing conflict with Iran drives up energy costs like gasoline.

Loading...

Although consumer spending has been growing steadily, it has not spread out evenly across households, with lower-income Americans struggling more than high-earners. Wage growth has also fallen behind inflation, further squeezing many Americans.

Siri Steven, a manager at a resale store in Decorah, Iowa, says she and her husband are putting off fixing up their more than 130-year-old house.

"We barely go out to eat now," Steven said. "I really have to be mindful of our budget and make sure that we can pay all our bills and not overdraft."

She also says her family hasn't been able to save, going paycheck to paycheck. The personal saving rate for the U.S. in September is 3.8%, according to a separate report from the Commerce Department, down from 4.1% in August.

Prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, according to the same report, faster than the Federal Reserve's 2% target. The Fed watches the Commerce Department's inflation measure closely, particularly when deciding what to do with its benchmark interest rates.

Sponsor Message

Fed holds rates

Still, the central bank decided against raising rates Wednesday, with added pressure to raise rates during the next meeting in December after Thursday's reading on prices.

Economists also are concerned about the country's long term fiscal health. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, warns that despite solid GDP figures, economic growth feels delicate. That's due to business and consumers having to navigate around Trump Administration policies, such as tariffs and the U.S. war against Iran.

"We're growing," Zandi said. "The economy is moving forward but it's a very, very fragile growth. It doesn't feel like we're kicking it in on all cylinders."

World.content:
GDP report to give insight before Election Day. And, Israel's election is deadlocked

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

As Election Day approaches, data suggest that the focus is now less on whether a Democratic wave will happen and more on its potential magnitude. Democrats continue to invest in competitive Republican-dominated races, and Republicans are matching those efforts. The trend creates some uncertainty around what the final electorate will look like, and indicates that Republicans will have to rely on a large Election Day turnout to stay competitive, Fowler says.

Americans will receive a final reading on the country's gross domestic product and the state of inflation today before next week's midterm election. The report will show whether the economy grew faster in the summer compared to spring. Economists expect GDP to be higher, but some say the growth feels delicate.



🎧 The tech industry's continued investment in artificial intelligence and consumer spending are driving the GDP, NPR's Stephan Bisaha says. But economist Mark Zandi tells him it's a "very, very fragile growth." Zandi blames inflation for this sense of fragility. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, and prices are outpacing wage growth. After keeping interest rates steady yesterday, the Fed will be paying close attention to today's inflation reading from the Commerce Department.

Israel's election is in a deadlock. More than 90% of the votes have been counted, and no candidate has a clear path to forming a coalition. Parties need 61 seats in parliament for a majority. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have secured 53 seats, while his top rival Gadi Eisenkot and his allies have garnered 48.



🎧 NPR's Daniel Estrin says there are several options for breaking the impasse. Eisenkot's camp could win by partnering with Arab-led parties, which recently secured a record 19 seats in parliament, NPR's Daniel Estrin says. But this partnership seems unlikely due to the political risks. Estrin says Arab political leaders in Israel have been demonized. Israel could hold repeat elections, but Eisenkot doesn't want that because the opposition would have a hard time getting votes a second time. Estrin says Eisenkot will be under pressure to enter a unity government with Netanyahu, especially if Israel launches a new war with Iran.

Sponsor Message

A lawsuit filed yesterday against the Department of Education alleges that the Trump administration is illegally refusing to follow the rules of a program known as "closed school discharge." For more than three decades, federal law has required the U.S. Secretary of Education to cancel debts for qualified borrowers when their schools close unexpectedly. Student Defense, a nonprofit borrower advocacy group, filed the suit on behalf of potentially thousands of borrowers. The Education Department told NPR it stands by its implementation of the program.

Today's listen

toggle caption i Erika Goldring/Getty Images for Americana Music

Bernie Taupin is Elton John's lyricist on nearly every album. Now, for the first time in 40 years, he's stepping into the spotlight. His new album, The Sea Has No Mercy, features a collection of songs entirely written and sung by him. Taupin admits that until recently, he hadn't considered writing for himself, but now he's ready to share his own musical voice. He tells Morning Edition's A Martínez that more so than a songwriter and a lyricist, Taupin thinks of himself as a storyteller. Listen to snippets of the album and hear about how Taupin has been able to keep his and John's relationship so strong.

Life advice

toggle caption i Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

Medicare's open enrollment window runs through Dec. 7. More than half of Americans in Medicare choose a Medicare Advantage plan, which is run by private insurers instead of the federal government. Medicare Advantage is popular because it covers dental and vision, often with lower premiums than traditional Medicare. But private carriers can pick and choose where it's offered, and withdraw from unprofitable communities. Over the last three years, insurers have left regions on an increasingly large scale, according to recent JAMA research. Here are some tips to help navigate Medicare open enrollment this year:

➡️ Check if your Medicare Advantage plan is still offered. Plans closing should have sent letters in early October. You can also log in to Medicare.gov to verify your plan's status.

➡️ Try calling your state's State Health Insurance Assistance Program. It's free, federally mandated and offers unbiased information on all options. Visit shiphelp.org to find your state's program.

➡️ Look for local Medicare counseling services. Brokers can be helpful, but make sure to choose one who discusses all your options, including traditional Medicare and supplemental plans.

➡️ Double-check anything you see on Medicare's Plan Finder with your doctor's office or other Medicare assister.

➡️ Be cautious about sharing your personal information, such as your phone number. Some online agencies may sell it, leading to spam calls and potential scams.

3 things to know before you go

American automakers reported increased revenues for the third quarter but face serious challenges. They are paying more for key components like computer chips, steel and copper, as well as higher transport fuel costs. A hacking group breached the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's personnel files yesterday, exposing the names, phone numbers and addresses of over 40,000 DHS agents and associates, including those in undercover operations. The Department of Health and Human Services announced a new policy that will let small compounding pharmacies make six peptides that haven't been approved by the Food and Drug Administration.
