World.title: Canadian Dental Care Plan working but costing more than expected, AG says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

While the Canadian Dental Care Plan has improved access to affordable dental care, the cost of the program exceeded projections by more than $1 billion in its first two years and will do so by another $1.2 billion by 2032, according to a new report by Auditor General Karen Hogan.

The report also found that confusion over how the program works persists, with call centres and government resources failing to provide useful information.

"We found that across the 2024-25 and 2025-26 fiscal years, payments for dental benefits to oral health providers exceeded the initial budget commitments by a total of $1.1 billion, resulting in funds moved between years to compensate," the report found.

The cost overruns were explained by what the reports said were "higher than anticipated claim payments" for each member of the program.

While moving the money from later years forward helped plug the immediate financial hole, to get a better sense of the cost for services under the plan, Health Canada asked the Office of the Chief Actuary to provide a more accurate forecast of what claim payments would look like going forward on a quarterly basis.

The audit said the forecasting "improved the credibility of the forecasts for claim payments … under the plan as the use of actuarial expertise to forecast payments for dental benefits is an accepted practice in the insurance industry."

Hogan's report found that when comparing the actuary forecasts for the annual cost of providing oral care from 2026-27 to 2031-32, there will be a further shortfall of about $2.4 billion in total.

Hogan later explained in a news conference that just after her audit was published, a new quarterly update from the Office of the Chief Actuary forecasted that gap would be reduced from $2.4 billion to $1.2 billion.

The report said that while Health Canada could address this gap by moving funding from later years, as it did for the earlier $1.1-billion gap, doing so "would reduce funds available for future years when demand is forecasted to be higher than the amounts currently allocated each year."

To remedy this, the audit said Health Canada could make changes to the program to lower the costs by modifying the services it funds, changing eligibility criteria, requesting more funds from the treasury or some combination of all three.

Reducing costs for plan members

Under the plan, Canadians with an adjusted net family income under $70,000 pay no fees for eligible services, members with an income from $70,000 to $79,999 pay about 40 per cent of the cost of services, while families with an income between $80,000 and $89,999 pay 60 per cent.

The report, which looked at how efficiently the program is managed from its launch on Dec. 1, 2023, to May 31, 2026, found that Canadians using the plan paid an average of $264 in out-of-pocket expenses, compared to the $536 households paid in 2023.

About 560,000 plan members, or 16 per cent of the plan members that accessed services in 2025, had their procedures fully covered.

Poor communication

The report received survey results from almost 5,000 dental care providers and found that a third of them said information about the plan was hard to find and access.

"For example, enrolment confirmation letters prominently displayed the percentage of eligible fees covered by the plan — most often 100 per cent — but did not clearly explain that members may still have to pay some costs themselves," the Auditor General's Office said in a statement.

A key complaint was that the information was spread across too many sources, requiring dental providers to spend an average of about an hour a day explaining the plan to members.

The audit said that Health Canada received almost 800,000 calls between March 2025 and February 2026 asking how the program works. A Health Canada survey analyzed 180 of those calls and said only two-thirds managed to meet required quality benchmarks.

LISTEN | Canadian Dental Care Plan has room for improvement: All Points West 9:39 Canadian Dental Care Plan has room for improvement Dentist Rachel Staples and dental office manager Heather Sawyer from Urban Smiles in Colwood provide reaction to a new report from the Candian Dental Association assessing the Canadian Dental Care Plan and how it could be improved for patients and providers.

The audit said that when it looked at the 180 calls examined by Health Canada, it challenged that finding, saying it found it "difficult to come to a conclusion on the quality of the answers provided."

The auditor general's report found that scripts and frequently asked questions approved by the department did not cover key questions.

The report concluded by saying that while "Health Canada efficiently managed the Canadian Dental Care Plan to provide affordable dental care for eligible Canadian residents" it needs to do a better job of assessing claims, providing clear information and monitoring the impact on Canadians' oral health.

Use and barriers to access

The report said that, across most of the country, take up of the program was strong with 6.9 million of the 10.5 million Canadians eligible having registered, and 4.2 million having submitted claims for procedures as of March 31, 2026.

The report also found that uptake was much better in the provinces than it was in the territories. It said that 65 per cent of the people enrolled in the plan in Ontario had submitted claims, the highest utilization rate, while the lowest provincial rate was found in Saskatchewan at 52 per cent.

In Nunavut the rate was just nine per cent, in Northwest Territories 25 per cent and in Yukon it was 45 per cent, "reflecting regional gaps in the availability" of care.

The audit says that, to improve access in the territories, Health Canada should work to "remove barriers to access, including for children in provincial and territorial care."

In her news conference, Hogan said 61,000 children in care across the country currently cannot access the program.

World.title: EU chief continues to push making Canada an associate member despite objections
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen continues to champion making Canada an associate member of the European Union, despite objections from members of the 27-member bloc.

In a keynote speech in Montreal on Thursday morning, the head of the European Union's executive body renewed her pitch to carve out a partnership with Canada "that comes closer to membership than anything we've done before."

Von der Leyen and other European Union officials are in the Quebec city for a two-day summit aimed at forging a new phase in the Canada-EU relationship, as they both seek to lessen dependence on the United States under an unpredictable and protectionist President Donald Trump.

What to call that alliance has loomed over the gathering.

The day before von der Leyen's speech, it was revealed the words "associate membership" were removed from a joint statement and replaced with a commitment to an "ever closer association," as objections within the bloc percolate.

However, von der Leyen — who surprised many last month when she announced that the EU would begin the process of making Canada its first associate member — marched on with her vision in her Thursday speech.

"It is an association without accession," she said.

The leader said becoming an associate member would see a close alignment on policies, including AI, climate, energy, security and governance.

"It means more work shared by the European Commission and the Canadian government," von der Leyen said, suggesting that could mean "parliament to parliament" and "court to court" co-operation.

As European Commission leader, von der Leyen can advocate for policies but it's up to the bloc to decide what happens next.

Sources speaking to CBC said Germany in particular opposes the "associate member" term, calling it a red line.

WATCH | EU agreement 'names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney: EU agreement 'names or nomenclature' don't matter, says Carney | Duration closed caption 0:42 Prime Minister Mark Carney says what 'matters' at the EU summit set to take place later this week in Montreal is 'Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation so we can live our lives as we choose.'

Carney has said the title of Canada's relationship to the EU shouldn't matter.

"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians … and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose," he said before a cabinet meeting in Ottawa on Tuesday.

Trump has threatened retaliation

Talk of making Canada an associate member has irked Trump, who previously said if he interpreted the move as a "hostile act," he might stop trading with Europe "on many things."

It raises the question of whether the president will look unkindly at this week's gathering in Montreal.

Asked Wednesday about the possibility of retaliation from Trump, a senior Canadian government official, speaking on background, told reporters the summit isn't directed against anyone but reflected deep interests between Canada and the EU.

The version of the EU-Canada statement seen by CBC News commits to reinforcing "a predictable trade environment, deepening collaboration in the Arctic, countering foreign information manipulation and interference and continued support for Ukraine."

It also promises to launch negotiations toward deeper participation in Erasmus, the European Union's student and youth exchange program.

A source speaking to CBC News on the condition they not be named says this statement is now finalized by EU member countries, but Canada could still ask for changes before the summit wraps on Friday.

On Thursday, Carney will host a roundtable with business leaders on the margins of the summit. He will then host a dinner in honour of von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.

World.title: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski found guilty of fraud at his jury trial in Toronto
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Aiden Pleterski, the self-described "Crypto King," was found guilty of fraud over $5,000 by the jury at his Toronto trial Thursday morning.

Pleterski, who represented himself at trial, appeared emotional after the verdict was read in Ontario Superior Court.

The jury began deliberations around 10:30 a.m. and came back with their verdict 10 minutes before noon.

Pleterski will be under house arrest as he awaits sentencing. His parents, who were in court for the verdict, will act as his sureties.

Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson denied a request for comment after the verdict.

His co-counsel described Pleterski as "a thief" in the prosecution’s closing statement Wednesday.

"Mr. Pleterski was no 'Crypto King.' Far from it. As it turns out he was no king at all. He was a thief. A thief who stole investor money and used it as he pleased. A thief who stole investor money using calculated lies," Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora told the jury.

"As you've seen, he burned through that money.… He lived his best life, all while his investors pleaded for updates on their money, only to be ignored."

Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora delivered a roughly 90-minute closing statement at Pleterski's fraud trial on Wednesday. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Pleterski took more than $36 million from investors for trading, but never put a cent of it into the trading platform FXChoice on their contracts. Instead, the Crown provided financial records at trial showing Pleterski spent $16.3 million of it on himself and gave another $16.1 million back to investors as returns.

At the end of the Crown's case, they dropped a second charge of money laundering against him.

Pleterski was denied a mistrial earlier this week. He argued that he didn’t have a fair trail without a lawyer. Pleterski only cross-examined the first of 14 witnesses the Crown called at his trial and decided not to call any evidence in his defence or testify himself.

He did make a brief closing statement to the jury Wednesday.

Pleterski addressed the jury for the first time at his fraud trial yesterday in Toronto, giving a brief closing statement on Oct. 28, 2026. (Pam Davies/CBC)

"I am the least qualified person here to give a closing statement," said Pleterski, addressing the jury for the first time.

"However, that being said, I am innocent of these charges. That is why I pled not guilty. Had I not been forced to represent myself, that would have been proven. That's all I have to say."

Justice Shaun Nakatsuru gave his full decision denying Pleterski’s request for a mistrial Thursday morning after the jury began deliberations.

"I'm still confident if Mr. Pleterski had chosen to do so he would have been able to make full defence," Nakatsuru said in his ruling.

"Nothing I have seen at this trial has changed my view on that.... He has not brought a computer or a tablet, he has not brought any Crown disclosure…. He has not made a single note that I have seen.... I'm not even sure he was paying attention to the witnesses."

Pleterski will be back in court on Nov. 13 to schedule dates for his sentencing.

World.title: Canada to invest up to $1.6B in Toronto-based AI company Cohere
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian government is taking an equity stake in Cohere, joining a funding round led by Germany's Schwarz Group targeting ‌$7 billion for the Toronto-based AI lab, Cohere said on Thursday.

The round would value Cohere at about $36 billion. Schwarz, which owns the Lidl and Kaufland retail ​chains, pledged $780 million to lead the round in ​April as part of Cohere's merger with the German AI developer Aleph Alpha.

Cohere said the money will fund ​model development, products for regulated industries and computing infrastructure.

Prime Minister Mark Carney made the announcement Thursday as he welcomed European Union leaders to Montreal for a summit aimed at forging closer ties.

He said ‌Ottawa would invest up to $1.6 billion in Cohere. Other investors included Nvidia and BCE's Bell Canada subsidiary, he said.

"Cohere will stay Canadian, creating more opportunities for our workers and businesses. ⁠Its incorporation and headquarters will remain here," he said in a speech.

Company to invest $1.7B in new infrastructure by 2030

Carney said Canada won't wait for the future of artificial intelligence to be decided elsewhere by those Canadians don't know or trust.

Cohere will invest at least $1.7 billion in new computing infrastructure in Canada ‌by 2030, he added.

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez called the government's investment "a huge honour."

WATCH | What it would take to pace the AI race: Why slowing the AI race won't be easy | Duration closed caption 4:13 Silicon Valley tech CEOs are calling for a slow down of artificial intelligence development — but is that even possible? For The National, CBC's Ashley Fraser looks at what it would take to pace the AI race and why experts say it won't be easy.

Schwarz, which owned more than 20 per cent of Aleph Alpha, spent almost $25 billion on new data centres in Germany. Schwarz ​Digits CEO Christian Müller said the group plans to run Cohere's models on its STACKIT ⁠cloud, calling the investment the next step after the Aleph Alpha ⁠deal.

Cohere has completed only an initial close of the round ⁠and did ⁠not say how much ​has been committed so far or when it expects the round to ​close.

The company said ⁠annual recurring revenue grew 165 per cent year over year as of the third quarter and that its customer count has grown to 300.

World.title: Canada's new national security strategy will shield economy, modernize military
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Defending the economy and preparing for the possibility of war in a more unstable world top the list of priorities in Canada's new national security strategy.

The long-awaited framework plan, released on Thursday, sets the stage for an overhaul of the defence, security and intelligence sectors, details of which will come in future policies.

One of the key aims of the new strategy, the first in more than two decades, is to modernize the country's intelligence capabilities, including the ability to gather and analyze intelligence on emerging threats to sovereignty.

The strategy pledges to ramp up Canada’s intelligence-gathering capabilities and "prepare for all contingencies up to and including war."

The rebuilding of Canada's military and defence industrial base also forms part of the plan released on Thursday, but those measures are already underway.

Increased defence spending

The government of Prime Minister Mark Carney has already begun a substantial increase in defence spending, which will eventually see the country allocate more than $163 billion toward the military by midway through the next decade.

It has also introduced legislation to create a Crown corporation dedicated to defence procurement.

Entirely redrawn defence and foreign policies will be released in the coming months.

At the heart of the new foreign policy will be "diversifying" Canada's trading relationships. The new strategy does not name specific countries as threats, even though U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly mused about making Canada the 51st state in the American union.

The strategy does, however, commit to a "co-operative, clear-eyed relationship with the United States."

WATCH | Trump threatens new tariffs over Canada-EU alliance: Trump threatens new tariffs over Canada-EU alliance if it's 'a hostile act' | Duration closed caption 2:32 U.S. President Donald Trump lashed out at a possible Canada-EU trade alliance, threatening new tariffs if he finds it to be 'a hostile act.' Meanwhile, Democrats in Washington expressed sympathy for Canada and said trade talks should resume.

The Trump administration's own National Security Strategy, released almost a year ago, seeks to make the U.S. the pre-eminent power in the Western Hemisphere.

The Canadian plan will see Ottawa "work to maintain a relationship with the United States based on mutual respect, national sovereignty and shared responsibility for the security of North America."

Strengthening public safety

Over the last several years, the federal government was seized with allegations and reports of foreign interference by China. While the new strategy makes no mention of that, it does commit to strengthening public safety against criminal and national security threats.

One of the more highly anticipated portions of the report had been whether it would set Canada on course to create its own foreign intelligence service.

At the moment, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service has a mandate to collect intelligence on domestic threats. While it occasionally operates overseas, it has no clear authority to operate in the same manner as the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency or Britain's MI6.

Senior federal officials, who walked journalists through the report on Thursday, said the matter is still under consideration, with no decision at this time.

"I don't think we're on the verge of announcing a separate agency that would be akin to the CIA or MI6. But at the same time we're looking at the capabilities that our intelligence agencies have and making sure that they are fit for purpose and for the challenges that we face today," said one senior official who spoke on background.

Creating a foreign intelligence service would require changes to legislation and investment by the federal government.

Wesley Wark, one of the country's leading security and intelligence experts, described the overall plan and commitment to review national security legislation within a year as hugely ambitious.

"It will take money, in some cases bucket loads. It will require some profound institutional changes in how national security is organized and led. Allies and partners will need convincing, and it will take public buy-in," Wark said.

"It’s a steep climb over years of effort."

World.title: At 71, this B.C. man has donated blood 500 times. He hopes others will consider rolling up their sleeves
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s in his blood, so to speak.

George Cavey’s mother suggested he donate blood when he was just 17, shortly after he’d left his home in Manitoba for post-secondary education in British Columbia.

His mother donated blood herself, and Cavey later learned his grandfather was a regular blood donor in Ottawa.

"I did it and it was pretty painless, and I thought, oh, this is OK," he told CBC’s On The Coast.

Now, at 71, he’s just rolled up his sleeve for the 500th time, and he hopes his story will encourage others to consider making a donation.

According to the Canadian Blood Services, one in two Canadians will need blood or blood products at some point in their life, or know somebody who will need it. And while about half of all Canadians are eligible to donate blood, only about one in 76 actually do.

A single donation could save three lives, Canadian Blood Services says.

Cavey said he kept going back, not just for the cookies, but because it’s an easy thing to do, and he enjoys catching up with the staff on site each time he goes in.

"That's a really encouraging part … they greet you, they know your name, they chat with you, [ask] how are your kids. It's a warm feeling going and I'm really happy to keep doing it."

George Cavey, now 71, has been donating blood for more than 50 years. (Submitted by George Cavey)

Originally, Cavey solely donated blood, he said. But the program changed following the tainted blood scandal of the 80s and 90s, and he learned about the importance of donating plasma and platelets. While those donations take longer than donating whole blood, he was able to do it more often.

"I did a lot of plasma over the years after the blood scandal, and then lately they've asked me if I could just switch over. In the last 100-plus donations or so I've been doing platelets."

Plasma is collected for plasma transfusions and for making medications out of plasma, according to the Canadian Blood Services, while platelets are used for platelet transfusions, which, as Cavey learned, can be used in cancer care.

One day, he was speaking with a friend who was being treated for cancer, when she mentioned her program was using donated platelets.

"I suddenly realized, hey, this is a real person that is getting platelets. That's probably not mine. But in our system, she's getting platelets from someone to help her," he said.

"It's real people that are benefiting from this."

The friend is now cancer-free, many years later, he said.

Three of Cavey’s four children joined him for his milestone donation on Monday, all of whom donate whenever they can, Cavey said.

"It is in the family," he said.

Having donated hundreds of times, Cavey has no intention of calling it quits.

"I plan to keep going as long as I'm healthy."

World.title: Edmonton and Calgary rejected her referendum. Does Danielle Smith have a city problem?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This week the Alberta government pivots back to governing, with MLAs returning to the legislature for the first time since a contentious referendum on separation exposed the divide between, among other things, urban and rural Albertans.

Much of the pushback on the 10 referendum questions came from the province’s two largest centres. Calgary collectively voted "no" on all questions except proof of citizenship to vote, while Edmonton was a "no" across the board. Nowhere was the prospect of a second separation vote less popular.

“We all know there’s an urban-rural divide in Alberta politics,” says Lisa Young, a political scientist at the University of Calgary. “But the referendum results make it really stark.”

This presents a quandary for Premier Danielle Smith, who has historically been supported by — and focused her attention on — rural Alberta. Now, she must contend with a sizable group of urban Albertans who appear to have rejected her latest political project, while she publicly spars with councillors over local issues such as zoning.

Meanwhile, it remains to be seen whether her list of priorities for the upcoming sitting, which include public sector hiring based on "merit ," protections for data centre development and the future of bike lanes, will speak to the cities.

“I think a lot of the recent focus on the more performative politics has served the UCP minority base really well,” said Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas on Tuesday.

“But the more we debate … which books should be in a library,” he said, referring to a recent bill to limit sexually explicit material in public libraries, “the more you lose the mainstream Calgarians who actually just want to get things done, want to know that life is safe and affordable.”

Smith herself has talked about the need to refocus on voters in Edmonton and Calgary, telling CBC News last week that her government needed to “identify the issues” that were important to residents of the two urban centres, which together make up just over half of the provincial population.

Urban voters are focused on issues like education, health care and affordability, which is why her government has (temporarily) paused the gas tax at the pumps and rolled out “ complexity teams ” in classrooms, Smith said.

“The issues that were of the referendum, I think it’s pretty clear those are ... of greater interest to those who are in political parties and punditry circles and in rural Alberta than they were in Calgary or Edmonton."

WATCH | Mapping out where Albertans voted to remain (or not) in Canada: Mapping out where Albertans voted to remain (or not) in Canada | Duration closed caption 4:38 Alberta voters overwhelmingly chose "remain in Canada" in the Oct. 19 referendum. CBC's Helen Pike maps the ridings that favoured Option 2 to explore separation, and the results may surprise you.

It’s a change of script from 2022 when Smith, then a newly-minted party leader, made waves by suggesting she didn’t need much urban support. Instead, she had mapped out a “rural-based” path to electoral victory, telling a columnist that she’d done the math and would only need a relative handful of city seats if she won everywhere else.

Smith delivered, winning a majority the following year. She took a dozen seats in Calgary and a few on the outskirts of Edmonton, but painted most of the map blue everywhere else.

But Calgary has since rejected most of Smith’s referendum questions and, Young points out, flipped the reliably right-leaning riding of Calgary-Shaw to the NDP in a recent byelection .

“It looks like Calgary is in a different place than it was a couple of years ago,” Young said.

It may not help that Smith, a frequent critic of federal overreach, has waded into municipal issues in recent months, essentially overturning the decisions of city councils on issues like infill housing and zoning, and now appears to have her sights set on bike lanes, Young added.

It “doesn’t really signal wanting to have a relationship of respect with these urban governments,” she said.

“It’s going to be really interesting to watch and see whether there’s a softening of the hostility with Edmonton and Calgary city governments.”

Mayor Jeromy Farkas says he's not surprised most Calgarians rejected the referendum questions, and he will be looking to see how the provincial government prioritizes investment in his city over the next year. (Brendan Coulter/CBC)

But as Farkas points out, a year away from a provincial election, there’s still time for Smith to turn it around. He’s waiting to see what’s in the provincial budget: “I don’t watch what the politicians are saying; I watch what the politicians are doing.”

“We want to see much more substantive investment here locally in Calgary around affordability, public safety and essential infrastructure.”

The idea of Alberta as the land of cowboys and open prairie can clash with its urban reality as, contrary to stereotypes, Alberta is actually one of the country’s most urbanized provinces.

According to Statistics Canada , it had the third smallest proportion of rural residents as of 2021 at roughly 15 per cent. That makes it more urbanized than the national average, and close on the heels of uber-urban provinces like Ontario and British Columbia.

But rural issues play a big role in provincial politics here, Young notes. That’s in part a result of the electoral map, which allows for a smaller number of residents in some rural ridings, in order to ensure remote areas have adequate representation.

Drawing the map to ensure each riding has roughly the same number of people while making sure some don’t become unmanageably large is a longstanding struggle in Alberta. The report from the 2017 electoral boundary commission noted that at the time, the constituency of Lesser Slave Lake had a population of 28,858 people while Calgary-South East had 92,148.

In other words, a vote in Lesser Slave Lake had about three times the punch of a vote in Calgary.

But there’s also the consideration of the economic importance of rural areas, given the extent to which the actual action of key industries like oil and gas take place outside of urban centres, Young said.

History plays a role, too: “There’s a sense, historically, of people in rural communities seeing themselves as the authentic Albertans, the people who are generating value and prosperity for the province,” said Young.

The issues faced by urban and rural communities are actually not that different, but they show up in different ways, said Colin Aitchison, a former United Conservative press secretary who is now a managing director at communications and public affairs firm Enterprise Canada.

Whether it’s pressure from immigration or the need for jobs, the real challenge for governments is tailoring the message to respect the different ways each community is affected, he said.

“The policy solutions are going to be different, but the overarching issues are the same.”

Most of the priorities Smith’s government laid out for the new session were likely put in place before the referendum and do represent issues that are important to conservative voters regardless of where they live, Aitchison said.

But he expects to see Smith start speaking to a more general audience as the election approaches.

Under Jason Kenney, the United Conservative Party made inroads in Calgary, and could do so again, argues Colin Aitchison, a former press secretary who is now a managing director at Enterprise Canada. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Aitchison points to the 2019 election as an example of when the United Conservative message was heard loud and clear in the cities. That year, the party under Jason Kenney formed government with the help of most of the seats in Calgary and even a few on the outskirts of Edmonton.

“When [the UCP] made significant gains in Calgary, they focused on jobs, economy, pipelines,” he said. “A very simple message, and issues that resonate for both urban and rural communities.”

In interviews, Smith has pointed out that hers is not the only conservative government to struggle in urban areas. But Aitchison, who was involved with the campaign, said the recent victory of the B.C. Conservatives, in which they picked up seats even in parts of tony downtown Vancouver, shows that the UCP shouldn’t be counted out.

“[B.C. Conservatives] focused on affordability, they focused on pocketbook issues, jobs,” he said. “Those are issues that affect both rural and urban communities.”

For her part, Smith said she’s focused on cracking the urban code, to figuring out which issues are important to voters in Calgary and Edmonton and “prioritizing them in a serious way.”

“That’s what the job of politics is,” she said. “You’ve got to find out what’s bugging people and then you’ve got to focus on solving the problems,” she said. “I’m committed to doing that.”

World.title: Joly says she'll meet with Stelco owner if company gives 'concrete' plan to bring workers back
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she's willing to meet with the president of Stelco and the head of its parent company, Cleveland-Cliffs, but only if the company brings back laid off workers first.

In a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon dated Thursday, Joly said she wanted to see a "concrete and credible" plan to return workers to their jobs before she would meet with the Stelco head and Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves.

"My message to [Goncalves] is, first, bring back the jobs and then we'll meet. I want a plan, I want a timeline. And I'm serious about it. You have commitments toward Canada. You have to make sure that you respect them," Joly reiterated to reporters at a news conference on Thursday.

Joly wrote in the letter that the plan to re-engage workers would form the basis of a conversation with Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs about the company's compliance with its requirements under the Investment Canada Act.

Goncalves has previously asked to meet with Joly to discuss a path to bring laid off workers back to the Hamilton plant, where Stelco said last month it was idling some operations.

Joly also demanded the company bring all laid-off employees back to work "immediately."

On Wednesday, Goncalves said in a statement that he hoped to return all 175 laid-off workers to their jobs by Christmas if the company's plan to boost its Canadian sales is successful.

WATCH | Joly warns Stelco boss to honour job commitments: Joly warns Stelco to restore jobs or 'face the consequences' | Duration closed caption 1:28 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, who released a letter sent to Stelco leaders, said she's willing to use the 'full force of the law' if needed in an ongoing fight over a Hamilton, Ont., steel plant, saying Stelco's U.S.-based owner 'failed' its obligation to keep jobs and champion tariff-free access of Canadian steel to the United States.

The letter is the latest in the public back-and-forth between the federal government and the American owners of the steel plant since the layoffs were announced.

Following the decision, Joly demanded that it reverse layoffs announced last month or face potential legal action for violating Investment Canada Act undertakings. The government says the company agreed in those undertakings to keep the number of unionized Stelco employees at 2024 levels through to 2029 when the purchase was made.

Goncalves and Simon have maintained that the company is in compliance, and say the layoffs are necessary to ensure the survival of the company as its been pressured by high U.S. tariffs on steel products.

Last week, Joly gave Cleveland-Cliffs 15 days to reverse its layoffs before taking the company to court. That would mean asking the courts to issue monetary penalties against Cleveland-Cliffs and potentially direct the company to divest from Stelco, the minister said previously.

On Wednesday, Joly said she had contacted government lawyers about comments made by Goncalves a day before on CBC's Power & Politics, which Joly said were "confessions" about his true reason for buying Stelco.

WATCH | Stelco owner's live TV admission prompts industry minister to call lawyers: Stelco owner's live TV admission prompts industry minister to call lawyers | Duration closed caption 2:49 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said she called the government's lawyers after the head of Stelco's American parent company told CBC News that he only bought the Hamilton steelmaker to stop it undercutting his production facilities in the U.S.

Goncalves said in the interview that he bought Stelco because its products were "undercutting our prices in the United States." A legal expert told CBC News that those comments raise questions about Cleveland-Cliffs's original intentions in acquiring Stelco but aren't a slam dunk for the government.

Joly not satisfied with company's proof of compliance

Earlier this week, the company said it had performed an "exhaustive review" of its obligations under the Investment Canada Act and determined it was in full compliance.

But Joly said in her latest letter she was not at all satisfied with the evidence given in that report, saying it "repeatedly asserts compliance" without giving enough proof.

"I find the report far from satisfactory," Joly wrote. "Assertions of compliance are not a substitute for the information and evidence necessary to establish compliance."

An industrial worker walks near the Stelco Hamilton Works on Oct. 9, 2026. The American steel-maker announced 300 to 350 layoffs at the plant amidst an ongoing trade war between the U.S. and Canada. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

The minister said she would need to see data, documents and other necessary evidence from Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs that fully addresses the issues she had laid out in a previous letter in order to be convinced that they are in compliance.

With Cleveland-Cliffs's leadership now indicating they're hopeful they could bring workers back to the Hamilton plant, McMaster University economics professor Colin Mang says it's possible the situation could "resolve itself," since the government has said their ultimate concern is protecting those jobs.

But he says it's difficult to say how successful Stelco might be in boosting that Canadian business. Stelco sells product in the construction and auto industries, both of which Mang points out have been battered by U.S. tariffs.

"Given the state of Canada's relations with the United States, the current state of the trade war, there's still a lot of uncertainty over where the steel market is going," Mang said.
