“It is difficult to reconcile the position taken in our Parliament yesterday with the decision made at the United Nations today. What has changed in the space of 24 hours? If the Government has determined that Jamaica’s position on this matter should change, then it has a responsibility to explain the basis for that decision. Foreign policy cannot be conducted in a manner that leaves the Jamaican people uncertain about where their country stands,” Scott-Mottley stated.

The Opposition spokesperson, in emphasising that Jamaica’s relationship with Cuba has been characterised by decades of friendship, mutual respect, and meaningful cooperation, particularly in health and education, said the principles of sovereignty, non-interference, and respect for international law remain especially important to small states such as Jamaica.

“Jamaica is a small State, but we have never regarded that as a reason to surrender our independent voice in international affairs. Indeed, it is precisely because we are a small State that the principles of sovereignty, non-interference, and respect for international law must remain central to our foreign policy,” Scott-Mottley declared.

She said Johnson Smith must provide an immediate explanation of Jamaica’s abstention and clarify whether it signals a change in the Government’s policy towards Cuba.

“The Jamaican people are entitled to know whether this decision reflects a considered change in national policy and, if so, what circumstances have brought it about. Our international positions must be guided by principle, consistency, and the national interest,” Scott-Mottley added.

Johnson Smith on Wednesday in referencing the motion entitled, ‘Motion on the Economic and Humanitarian Situation in Cuba’, which was passed by Parliament, said it was “consistent with the perspective that a broader view of the complex situation in Cuba is needed”.

“Rather than simply calling for an end to the embargo as has been done in previous years, the motion called on the Parliament to express its deep concerns regarding the economic and humanitarian challenges confronting the Cuban people and affirms that their welfare and aspirations must remain central to efforts to address these challenges; recognise the importance of intensified economic and institutional reforms as well as respect for fundamental human rights and freedoms as well as other essential elements of sustainable development; and support constructive engagement between Cuba and the United States grounded in mutual respect and peaceful dialogue aimed at reducing economic restrictions and other barriers to international trade, finance and investment while facilitating Cuba’s progressive integration into the international economic system, rather than its isolation under the blockade,” she stated.

“These broader contexts are not included in the resolution before the United Nations and there is no scope to adjust the language of the resolution, so we therefore abstained,” the foreign affairs minister told the briefing.

She further pointed to remarks by Prime Minister Andrew Holness at the opening ceremony for Caricom heads meeting in St Kitts Nevis in July of this year, at which he expressed concern at the worsening humanitarian suffering, the impact on Cuba’s circumstances on the region, and affirmed solidarity with Cuba, but also called for US-Cuba dialogue aimed at stability and improving the circumstances of the people. Speaking then, Holness called for reform and suggested that, if, possible Caricom member states could play a constructive role in engagement and cooperation.

World.title: ‘A who mi murder?’
World.content:
Ruddock is on trial in the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston in relation to the October 17, 2021 human sacrifice-type killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James. He is accused of cutting the woman’s throat on instructions from his now deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith, seen here

A former detective testified on Wednesday that when he informed Andre Ruddock that he would be charged for murder, he inquired of the cop who the victim of that murder was, and when told he would be charged for conspiracy to murder, he demanded a lawyer.

This happened three days after he had already confessed during a caution statement at the Freeport Police Station in Montego Bay, St James, on October 18, 2021. The confession was recorded on a video in which Ruddock appeared calm while telling detectives that he was guilty of killing a woman at a church. After he gave that caution statement, detectives then proceeded to conduct a question-and-answer session to get more information out of him about the incident. The question-and-answer session was also video-recorded and Ruddock was in fact heard confessing. He then signed to written versions of the said statement as well as the answers he gave to the detectives.

Ruddock is on trial in the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston in relation to the October 17, 2021 human sacrifice-type killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James. He is accused of cutting the woman’s throat on instructions from his now deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith.

On Wednesday, the witness, who was the lead detective in the matter, told the court that Ruddock was transported from Montego Bay to Kingston on October 21, 2021 and was housed at the headquarters of the Major Investigations Division.

“I approached him whilst in custody and informed him of the charge of murder and conspiracy to murder. I cautioned him for the offence of murder and when cautioned he then said, ‘A who mi murder?’ I then charged him with murder. I cautioned him for conspiracy to murder and he said, ‘Call mi lawyer, please.’”

During the caution statement and question-and-answer session in Montego Bay, no attorney was present. However, in that interview room were two justices of the peace along with two detectives and Ruddock. The accused was not heard requesting an attorney at any point during those sessions.

Prosecutor Latoya Bernard asked the witness on Wednesday if prior to Ruddock being taken to Kingston to be charged, if the accused had complained to him about being beaten, threatened, or harmed in any way by a detective constable. The witness said no.

“He did not have any injuries on him. He did not make any complaints about being assaulted by him or any other officers,” the witness said.

The trial resumes on Friday, when the last witness for the prosecution, a pathologist, will begin testifying.

World.title: Andrew Tosh, Anthony B lead musical salute to Peter Tosh
World.content:
Son of Peter Tosh, Andrew Tosh, performs one of his father’s most famous hits during the recent staging of Tosh Fest 2026.

“I am moved by the turnout of patrons who came out to pay tribute to the legacy of my father despite the rains,” said Niambe McIntosh, head of the Peter Tosh Foundation, reflecting on a celebration that underscored the enduring power of Peter Tosh’s music and message.

That spirit of devotion was on full display at Woodstock Beach in Negril, Westmoreland, on Saturday, October 17, as artistes, cultural enthusiasts, and music lovers turned out in droves for Tosh Fest 2026, despite the inclement weather. They gathered with one purpose in mind: To honour the reggae icon while celebrating 50 years since the release of his landmark album Legalize It.

From the spiritual grounding of Nyabinghi drumming to the impassioned performances of established and emerging acts, the celebration brought Peter Tosh’s revolutionary catalogue and uncompromising principles into focus, reminding those gathered that his legacy extends far beyond the music.

Among the evening’s most moving moments was the appearance of Peter Tosh’s son, Andrew, whose striking vocal resemblance to his father lent added poignancy to renditions of some of the reggae legend’s hits.

As he delivered the familiar songs, patrons joined in, transforming the performances into a collective expression of remembrance for a man whose voice continues to resonate across generations.

Anthony B brought his own intensity to the tribute, combining high-energy delivery with the conscious messaging that has long defined his artistry. For the artiste, following in Peter Tosh’s ideological footsteps was a deliberate choice rather than a passing musical influence.

“While others were doing other things, I chose not to follow the crowd; I chose to follow Peter Tosh,” he remarked, underscoring the enduring influence of the late singer’s fearlessness and willingness to challenge convention.

The evening also featured performances and selections from poet Mutabaruka, Grammy Award-winning songwriter Medisun, conscious music act Karbon, young artistes Dahvid Slur and Aza Lineage, and selector Rory Stone Love, whose selections contributed to a programme rooted in reggae’s cultural and revolutionary traditions.

The celebration opened with a Nyabinghi drumming ceremony, paying homage to the spiritual traditions that helped shape reggae music, followed by a screening highlighting Peter Tosh’s musical legacy before the stage came alive with performances.

Yet, at the heart of the celebration was the message behind the music.

Released in 1976, Legalize It became one of the artiste’s career-defining works, boldly confronting the stigma surrounding cannabis while speaking to broader themes of personal freedom, human rights, and political advocacy. Fifty years later, its message remains inseparable from the legacy of an artiste who used his platform to challenge injustice and demand equality.

McIntosh said the anniversary provided an opportunity to revisit the album not simply as a landmark in reggae history, but as a powerful statement of freedom and human rights.

Despite the rain delaying the start of the festivities, the turnout in Peter Tosh’s home parish held particular significance for the foundation, reinforcing the importance of keeping his legacy alive in the community most closely associated with his roots.

“We made the intentional commitment to hosting the celebrations in the parish he loved,” McIntosh said, adding that the foundation anticipates Tosh Fest growing in local and international patronage, bringing economic benefits to Westmoreland residents while establishing the event as a fixture on Jamaica’s cultural and entertainment calendar.

Tosh Fest formed part of a wider week of activities celebrating the singer’s life and work. Taste of Tosh, held at the Peter Tosh Museum on October 14, brought members of the music fraternity together in tribute to the legend.

Tosh Talks, staged on October 15 and 16 at Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts and The University of the West Indies, respectively, featured academic presentations on Tosh’s life, legacy, and Legalize It, alongside panel discussions.

The commemorations continued on October 19, National Heroes’ Day and Peter Tosh’s earthstrong, with dawn Nyabinghi drumming and a blessing by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church at his resting place in Belmont, Westmoreland.

World.title: JCF calls for review of ganja law amid tensions with Rastas
World.content:
Senior Superintendent of Police Arielle Brown Blake (left), head of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Legal Affairs branch, speaks as JCF Legal Officer Jamie Brown-Bailey looks on during Wednesday’s meeting of the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Green Paper on the National Policy for Culture, Entertainment and the Creative Economy 2025–2035..

THE Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) is calling for a comprehensive review of the Dangerous Drugs Act, saying gaps and ambiguities in the law governing sacramental ganja use by Rastafarians must be addressed to clarify the community’s religious protections and guide police enforcement.

The force says uncertainty over how officers should verify religious authorisation, identify approved cultivation sites and recognise places of worship has contributed to tensions with Rastafari adherents, whose use of ganja is recognised under Jamaican law for sacramental purposes.

Head of Legal Affairs at the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), Senior Superintendent of Police Arielle Brown Blake, told the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Green Paper on the National Policy for Culture, Entertainment and the Creative Economy 2025–2035 on Wednesday that the law governing sacramental ganja use by Rastafarians should be reviewed to address ambiguities that have contributed to tensions between the community and the police.

Responding to questions from Opposition Senator Allan Bernard following the JCF’s presentation to the committee, who asked whether Jamaica should move away from criminalising ganja towards a broader legislative framework that better recognises Rastafari’s religious and cultural rights, Brown Blake said the JCF supports a comprehensive review of the legislation and a shift towards an approach that better protects the community’s constitutional rights.

“In supporting our citizens’ rights and freedoms under the constitution, I do think that it is something that we can consider moving away from, and not just can consider, should consider, instead of moving away from a criminalisation framework into a framework that allows them to take hold of the rights that the constitution enshrines them with,” Brown Blake said.

She said the force recognised that the current system had created difficulties for both police officers and members of the Rastafari community, adding that the law’s gaps and the lack of updated information on authorised spaces had contributed to disputes.

Brown Blake said the JCF had already been discussing a review of the legislation with its parent ministry, the Ministry of National Security and Peace, and the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

She added that the force supported reform that would improve Rastafari adherents’ ability to practise their religion, while allowing police to enforce the law with greater certainty.

The JCF’s submission also focused on the practical challenges officers face when determining whether ganja-related activities fall within the law’s sacramental exemptions. It called for clear guidance covering possession, cultivation, storage, transportation, smoking and events where ganja is used as a sacrament.

The force recommended that the policy explain when authorisation is required, what conditions apply and how officers should verify relevant information. It also called for clarity on identification letters or other documents issued by recognised Rastafari priests, elders and leaders, including how their authenticity should be checked.

JCF Legal Officer Jamie Brown-Bailey said the proposed policy should establish clear procedures for transferring responsibility for sacramental ganja matters from the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs to the ministry responsible for culture.

She said the transfer should identify the functions being moved, explain how decisions and authorisations would be communicated to police, and ensure that existing authorisations remain valid while outstanding applications are addressed.

The force also recommended that the responsible ministry maintain current records of designated cultivation lands, authorised individuals and organisations, and events exempted under the law.

Brown Bailey noted that the Dangerous Drugs (Designation of Land for Cultivation of Ganja for Sacramental Purposes) Order, 2023, came into operation on July 20, 2023, and was amended on August 3 that year.

She said the policy should also clarify how places of Rastafari worship are identified and registered for relevant legal purposes, with accessible procedures and clear criteria.

The debate comes amid ongoing Government consultations on Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis framework, which were announced in July following recommendations from the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce. The consultations are aimed at clarifying the rules governing sacramental organisations, approved cultivation sites, possession and transportation, as well as enforcement procedures.

The earlier discussions also followed reports of Rastafarians facing prosecution despite legal provisions for sacramental ganja use. In the case of Westmoreland resident Troy Harrison, the Crown offered no evidence on possession and dealing charges, which were subsequently dropped in the parish court. Harrison’s attorney, Marcus Goffe, told the Jamaica Observer that some police officers continued to interpret the law as they saw fit, arguing that members of the community were being unfairly targeted despite the 2015 amendments to the Dangerous Drugs Act.

On Wednesday, Committee chair and Culture Minister Olivia Grange acknowledged that practical difficulties remained and said the policy must allow Rastafari adherents to exercise their rights with certainty while enabling the police to enforce the law fairly.

“The regime, which is put in place, is defined so that Rastafari, the community, who it’s meant to be, they are meant to be the beneficiaries of this regime, can exercise their rights with certainty. And equally, the JCF can enforce with certainty,” Grange said.

Senator Bernard also questioned, during the sitting, whether the difficulties identified by the JCF pointed to a deeper problem with the continued criminalisation of ganja, rather than administrative shortcomings alone.

He asked whether the policy should address the historical relationship between the Jamaican state, the police and Rastafari, including decades of discrimination and criminalisation alleged by members of the community.

Bernard also asked whether Jamaica should consider replacing the existing prohibition-based approach with modern legislation that distinguishes ganja from more harmful controlled substances.

Brown Blake said she believed the policy should focus on protecting Rastafari’s identity and rights and look towards the future, rather than detailing past tensions.

“I am not of the view that the tensions need to be articulated in that paper, just their identity and their rights, and that those rights should be preserved. And the policy looks towards the future rather than taking a backward view. That is my personal and professional opinion,” she said.

Government Senator Kavan Gayle said the JCF’s participation would be valuable when Rastafari representatives appear before the committee, arguing that engagement could help address perceptions of conflict between the community and the police.

The committee is reviewing the Green Paper on the National Policy for Culture, Entertainment and the Creative Economy 2025–2035, which proposes transferring specific responsibilities relating to sacramental ganja use from the justice ministry to the ministry responsible for culture.

World.title: HIGHER HEIGHTS
World.content:
Australia forward Samantha Kerr (fourth left) vies for the ball with Jamaica forward Khadija Shaw (fourth right) during their France Women’s World Cup Group C match at the Alpes Stadium Grenoble, central-eastern France, on June 18, 2019. (Photo: AFP)

WITH Khadijah “Bunny” Shaw now recognised as a top three player in women’s football, former Reggae Girlz Head Coach Charlie Edwards believes the national senior women’s team should reach another level and move closer to being a serious contender at the FIFA World Cup.

Manchester City striker Shaw is still celebrating her third-place finish in the Ballon d’Or Féminin rankings on Monday at the awards ceremony in London. The achievement adds to her Women’s Super League Player of the Season, Professional Footballers Association Player of the Year and Football Writers’ Association Footballer of the Year recognition, which she claimed over the past few months for her impressive 2025/2026 season.

Shaw won her third-consecutive WSL golden boot after scoring 21 goals in 22 games, leading City to their second-ever league title. Her 35 goal contributions across all competitions were also pivotal in City’s FA Cup title win.

Along with her club objectives, Shaw is looking to lead Jamaica to a third-consecutive FIFA Women’s World Cup in November, as the Reggae Girlz takeonCostaRicaintheConcacaf W Championship quarterfinals in Texas, USA.

Edwards, who led the national team from 2007 to 2008, told the Jamaica Observer that Shaw’s Ballon d’Or ranking must be used as a stepping stone for the Reggae Girlz to better their finishes at previousWorldCupappearances.

After failing to advance from the group stage on their debut in France in 2019, Jamaica made history by reaching the round of 16 in 2023 in Australia and New Zealand, where they were narrowly beaten by Colombia.

“Now that [teams] are realising that we have a top-class player, it is going to force coaches now to start sitting down, putting game plans together to play against Jamaica,” Edwards said. “But what I’d love to see it do, though, is motivate the rest of the players in the squad to step their game up and propel Jamaica to another level.”

“The last time [at the World Cup] we made the final cut for the round of 16. I’d love to see us get back to the round of 16 and win a game or two and I really don’t think it’s far-fetched. I think we have the quality in the squad that can perform and do well, so let’s hope that this becomes the momentum or the drive behind us performing even better in the World Cup, once we get to the World Cup.”

Shawhasanincredible67goals in 49 caps for the national team and Reggae Girlz Head Coach Hubert Busby says their success in future tournaments depends heavily on their captain.

“If you look at the stats of what shemeanstoManCitywhenshe’s intheline-upandwhatshemeans for us when she’s in the line-up, they’re almost the same — they’re about a 75 win percentage, she averages a goal a game per programme. So, there’s no getting away from the impact that she has, both at Man City and with the national team,” he told the Observer.

“We’re a different team when she’s in there, there’s no doubt about it. Teams have to play us differently, we can play differently. When you have one of the best players in the world, it’s only natural that she lifts the ability, or not so much the ability, but she lifts the confidence of the group. Also, she inspires a group both on and off the pitch so she’s our leader and when she’s with us, you can see what an impact she has on the team.”

Edwards, who also won 12 women’s league titles with Barbican FC, says Shaw’s Ballon d’Or ranking shouldn’t only have animpactonthepitch.Hesaysthe Jamaica Football Federation and other stakeholders must use the accolade as a springboard to help boost women’s football locally.

“This is a momentum that Jamaica could use in a very significant way in the sense of motivating the young, talented female players in Jamaica. You’re looking at the Women’s Premier League, you’re looking at the high school [level] — this is mileage that we need to capitalise on and utilise it in a very significant way to help develop and grow what we are working so hard to accomplish,” he said.

“I personally think her accomplishment should create a lot more inspiration for the young players in Jamaica and maybe evenaroundtheCaribbean.What she has done is shine a light where nobody else in the Caribbean has ever shone light. I really hope that they capitalise on it and realise that if we can produce a Ballon d’Or third-place finisher, young girls will say if I work hard enough,IcouldbethenextBunny Shaw and that is a mentality that I want the young players to start adopting.”

World.title: ‘They are not criminals’
World.content:
An image shared by US White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt depicting people boarding a deportation flight in January 2025. (Photo: @PressSec / via X)

FOREIGN Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith has reiterated that individuals sent to Jamaica under the third-country national (TCN) agreement with the United States (US) have zero criminal antecedents other than breaching that country’s immigration laws.

Speaking during Wednesday’s Post Cabinet Press briefing at Jamaica House in St Andrew, Johnson Smith said that detail was worth repeating given apparent confusion in some quarters about the individuals transiting the country under the arrangement.

“There are countries which have agreed to receive criminals. They exist; when the United States speaks about sending criminals under TCN agreements they send them to those countries. Jamaica is not one of them. Our country has negotiated arrangements whereby persons with criminal antecedents will not be sent to Jamaica,” the foreign affairs minister stressed.

“Other than having broken the United States immigration laws, that is having illegally entered the US, they are not criminals, those are the persons who are sent to transit Jamaica. So, when the US says that under TCN agreements criminals are being sent, they are not including Jamaica,” she emphasised.

On Tuesday, United States Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin shared on social media that “through engaging in fully legal third-country removals, [and] thanks to TCN agreements with various countries, we have been able to deport some of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the US, including those who are so barbaric that even their home countries won’t take them back“.

According to Johnson Smith, the individuals are “vetted on the US side and they are vetted on the Jamaica side before they enter Jamaica”.

“Our arrangement does not agree to receive any criminals… so I just wanted to make that clear,” she added.

In the meantime, in providing an update on the 22 third country nationals sent here, Johnson Smith said compared to Tuesday when she reported that one person returned home and 21 continue to be in country with one requesting to stay, nine have since departed while departure arrangements are at various stages of processing for the remaining 11.

The first 22 TCNs – 15 males and seven females – arrived at the Norman Manley International Airport in Kingston on October 13. They are under the care of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) while arrangements are made to facilitate their return to their respective home countries.

The governments of Jamaica and the US, earlier this year, signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to facilitate the temporary reception of individuals in Jamaica before return to their countries of origin. The MOU was inked amidst US efforts to manage regional structured migration. The MOU provides for its suspension if 10 third country nationals apply to remain in Jamaica through asylum applications or other humanitarian processes. The full details of that MOU are yet to be made public.

The Jamaican Government has previously stated that under the agreement the country will not accept more than 25 individuals per fortnight.

World.title: The Art of Dining: Posh Table Brings a Fresh Taste of Asia to Montego Bay
World.content:
Sweet chilli tuna tartar (Photo: Aceion Cunningham)

Posh Table restaurant is celebrating its first anniversary. Located at Whitter Village, Ironshore, Montego Bay, the stylish eatery is redefining what guests can expect from Indian cuisine. Guided by the tagline “The Art of Dining,” the restaurant combines authentic Indian flavours, Pan-Asian influences, impressive cocktails, and an inviting atmosphere to create a dining experience unlike any other in the city.

At the centre of the concept is co-owner Vinod Balandram, whose lifelong passion for food and cocktails inspired the venture. A talented cook himself, Balandram’s appreciation of flavours and hospitality helped shape a restaurant that balances authenticity with innovation.

Opened on October 1, 2025, Posh Table faced an early setback when Hurricane Melissa which devastated western Jamaica on October 28 and forced its temporary closure. Undeterred, the team reopened on December 1, reaffirming its commitment to bringing something unique to Montego Bay’s culinary landscape.

“We wanted to create something authentic but also exciting and contemporary. The goal wasn’t simply to open another typical Indian restaurant but to have a fusion and a mix to introduce guests to the diversity of Asian cuisine through an Indian lens,” explained co-owner Amrita Balandram.

While Indian cuisine forms the heart of the menu, Posh Table is far from your typical Indian restaurant. The offerings are rooted in authentic North Indian cooking, complemented by touches of South Indian cuisine, while also embracing a wider Pan-Asian concept that introduces diners to flavours from across the continent.

“We offer two distinct types of cuisine, authentic Indian and Pan-Asian. To break down the Pan-Asian, first comes the Indo-Chinese. It has a fusion of Indian and Chinese spices used in Indian street food and then cuisines from across Asia,” co-owner Vinod Balandram.

The Indo-Chinese cuisine features popular street food dishes such as Hakka noodles, chilli chicken, and Manchurian chicken which deliver bold flavours rarely found elsewhere in Montego Bay, offering guests a fresh take on both Indian and Chinese cuisine. Other offerings include southern Indian cuisine such as Black Pepper Chicken made with curry leaves and freshly ground black pepper and northern Indian cuisine featuring the heavy use of the Tandoor. The spice profile for the eatery relies heavily on coriander, cumin and mustard seeds as well as curry leaves, old red chilli and Chinese seasonings.

The Pan-Asian menu extends beyond India, featuring dishes inspired by Korea, Japan, Thailand, and China. Popular options include a Korean Bowl with three types of protein, a hearty steamed bowl with pork, chicken, and shrimp, fresh sushi selections, and flavourful Thai dishes using red and green curry. The result is a menu that encourages diners to explore a variety of Asian culinary traditions in one setting.

“We’re celebrating our first year of opening and our customers are demanding more of the sushi and dumpling dishes. This will see us doing a new menu with items to include more options including a Caribbean Roll and Crystal Dumplings. We tested some of the new items a few weeks ago and the response was extremely positive,” Vinod added.

Complementing the cuisine is a carefully curated cocktail menu that reflects the restaurant’s attention to detail and creativity. Whether paired with spicy Indo-Chinese specialties or classic Indian dishes, the cocktails elevate the overall dining experience.

Beyond the food, Posh Table prides itself on creating a welcoming environment. The owners encourage guests to ask questions about unfamiliar dishes and are eager to share the stories and traditions inspiring the menu. The restaurant also offers space for private events, making it an appealing venue for celebrations, corporate gatherings, and special occasions.

In a city with a developing vibrant food culture, Posh Table stands out by offering something refreshingly different: Authentic Indian cuisine, adventurous Pan-Asian flavours, handcrafted cocktails, and genuine hospitality, all delivered through its commitment to The Art of Dining.

World.title: WATCH: Holness hits back at Beenie Man after Hurricane Melissa relief comments
World.content:
This file photo shows Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness addressing a special press briefing at Jamaica House on Tuesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

ST ELIZABETH, Jamaica — Against the backdrop of criticism from dancehall veteran Beenie Man over the Government’s hurricane relief efforts, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness on Wednesday took a swipe at the artiste.

He said over $300 million of the Government’s $3.8 billion allocation to the health sector post Hurricane Melissa was spent to rebuild the Black River Hospital.

“[With] all the dignitaries… who are here, I thought to myself the Minister [of Health Dr Christopher Tufton] neglected to invite Beenie Man, because then he would see first-hand how the Government has been spending on the recovery,” Holness said on Wednesday during the reopening of the Black River Hospital.

Beenie Man criticised the Holness administration’s handling of millions of dollars in donations it received to assist Jamaicans devastated by the storm.

World.title: Meet the front-runners to replace Lagarde
World.content:
The choices will also be influenced by horse trading over what will likely be a package deal with the opportunity to fill the two executive board seats that will be vacant in January and May.

Softly spoken de Cos

An economist with a Ph.D. from the University of Madrid, de Cos joined the Bank of Spain in 1997, moved to Frankfurt in 2004 to be an adviser to the ECB’s executive board, before returning to the Spanish central bank. He rose through the ranks to become governor, serving from 2018 to 2024. In this role he restored the Bank of Spain’s reputation after a series of missteps before and during the financial crisis.

His achievement was implicitly acknowledged by his appointment to two terms as chair of the Basel Committee for Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for bank regulation. He now runs the Bank for International Settlements, the institution often described as the central bankers’ central bank.

His style is low-key: a modest dove, meaning that he is more attentive than hawks to growth and employment alongside inflation. Still, when inflation surged in 2022, de Cos backed the ECB’s shift toward higher rates. Equally, he has little time for governments that put off essential pension system reforms, having published a sharp critique of the Pedro Sanchez government while at the Bank of Spain.

His case

De Cos has long been groomed by Lagarde’s predecessor Mario Draghi, whose voice continues to carry a heavy weight in European economic debates and may influence the preference of some countries as they mull who to place at the top of the Frankfurt institution.

As France faces mounting debt pressures, de Cos’ experience as a senior Bank of Spain economist during the eurozone crisis could convince EU governments that he is the best fit. Galo Nuño, vice dean and professor of economics at IE University and a former alternate member of the ECB governing council, called it “a huge advantage.”

World.title: Britain’s spy agency doesn’t know where thousands of its memory sticks are
World.content:
He noted that the devices “may contain IPA-related data” — which has a high level of sensitivity.

IPA-related data refers to information collected or held under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. That could include intercepted communications such as emails, texts and telephone calls, as well as information extracted from people’s computers or phones.

The report added that GCHQ currently estimates the number of devices “to be in the thousands” and is currently undergoing work so it can report how many of the devices have been confirmed as lost.

“We remain very concerned about this issue and are disappointed with the time it has taken GCHQ to investigate,” the report notes.

Last year IPCO disclosed that GCHQ and fellow intelligence agency MI5 had been unable to locate considerable numbers of storage devices, some of which potentially containing information classified as "TOP SECRET."

A GCHQ spokesperson said: “As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations.

"We recognise the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken."

World.title: Von der Leyen touts ‘associate member’ status for Canada over objections of EU capitals
World.content:
No sooner had von der Leyen finished speaking than German Chancellor Friedrich Merz issued a statement saying that the EU and Canada were establishing an “Alliance for the Future” — without mentioning the associate member status. Germany has led the opposition to using the term, according to EU diplomats.

The Commission president said in her speech that talks about associate membership would focus on deeper cooperation across AI, climate and energy policy, as well as bolstering shared work between the European Commission and the Canadian government as well as “Parliament to Parliament” and “Court to Court,” a reference to the European Court of Justice and Canada’s Supreme Court.

Such a status, she said, would be open “only to our closest partners outside of Europe, who are ready to open a new frontier together — and to chart the course together, to think beyond the terms of our partnership today, toward the most ambitious vision we can build.”

Von der Leyen’s use of the term associate membership — which she first mentioned in September — is likely to rub some EU capitals the wrong way after a group of countries led by Germany objected to including a reference to the term in a joint EU-Canada statement that was seen by POLITICO and is due to be published on Friday.

After days of talks, EU countries opted for softer language to describe the two sides’ future relations, including the “Alliance for the Future” — the term used by the Canadian side — as well as an “even closer association ... short of full membership.”

EU diplomats have told POLITICO that while capitals support the broader aim of closer ties with Canada, they are wary of offering a status that has never been proposed before and whose legal contours remain undefined. Berlin had previously floated associate member status for Ukraine, including specific privileges such as observer status in the European Commission, but that effort was rejected.

World.title: Canada to join EU network of supercomputers
World.content:
The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an €8.2 billion budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers.

The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of €30 billion.

Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start.

“Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term ‘middle power’ cooperation plays in AI,” said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

But he added that for now “it doesn’t put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S.

“As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn’t result in massive buildouts will help,” he said.

World.title: Former Spanish employment minister died in train crash
World.content:
Báñez served in center-right Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy’s government from 2011 to 2018 and played a central role in Spain’s response to the eurozone crisis. During that period, she developed a warm personal relationship with Ursula von der Leyen, now European Commission president, who was then her counterpart in Germany’s labor ministry.

As employment minister, Báñez oversaw the conservative government’s controversial 2012 labor-market reform, which made it easier for companies to dismiss workers and drew fierce opposition from trade unions. The administration argued the changes would make hiring more flexible and accelerate the country’s economic recovery.

Speaking from the crash site Wednesday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared three days of national mourning. “All of Spain is mourning,” he said.

“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” Sánchez added. “We are going to get to the bottom of this, and if there has been negligence, it will be revealed, and if there have been failures in the system, we will act decisively.”

Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the initial investigation suggested the collision was caused by an official at the national railway control center in Madrid who “inexplicably” instructed one high-speed train to proceed along a track where another had stalled.

Puente insisted Spain has “a safe transport system,” but acknowledged that “human action plays a role” and that, despite extensive safety regulations and protocols, “failures can occur.”

World.title: Lagarde’s bandages due to a ‘little skin cancer,’ not ‘kick-boxing in Thailand’
World.content:
In a video to staff, seen by POLITICO, the outgoing ECB president says her coverings are due to “a little skin cancer that had to go.”

FRANKFURT — Christine Lagarde’s announcement that she will leave the European Central Bank in February quickly drew attention to more than her departure date: the two bandages on her face visible in a video statement she posted.

They prompted speculation on social media, which Lagarde addressed in a follow-up post. She said they were from a “small surgery” earlier in the week and urged people to follow medical advice and get their skin checked regularly.

In a separate internal video message to all ECB staff, seen by POLITICO, Lagarde offered a little more humor and detail: “I know I look funny. This is not kick-boxing in Thailand,” she said after attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings in Bangkok earlier this month. “It is just a little skin cancer that had to go.”

World.title: Russian strike on busy train platform kills at least 14 in Dnipro
World.content:
KYIV – Russia struck a railway platform in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday, killing at least 14 people in what Mayor Borys Filatov described as an act “of genocidal war.”

“In Dnipro, the Russian forces directed a drone straight at the railway station platform, where many people were waiting for a train. As of this moment, 14 people have been killed, and at least 14 others have been wounded,” State Emergency Service of Ukraine said in a statement.

Russia also killed civilians in residential districts of Kremenchuk in сentral Ukraine and in the center of Chernihiv in the north of the country, emergency services said. Three people were killed in Kremenchuk and another 15 were injured, while two children died in the strikes on Chernihiv, where 23 people were injured, including a 10-month-old baby girl. Houses, shops, and cars were also damaged, the statement says.

World.title: EU will nationale Social-Media-Verbote stoppen
World.content:
„Die Kommission hat beschlossen, alle Entwürfe nationaler Gesetze, die sich mit den künftigen harmonisierten Regeln überschneiden, für zwölf Monate aufzuschieben“, sagte Kommissionssprecher Thomas Regnier am Donnerstag vor Journalisten.

Österreich hatte die Kommission bereits im Juli gebeten zu prüfen, ob sein geplantes Gesetz, das den Zugang für unter 14-Jährige verbieten würde, mit EU-Recht vereinbar ist. Die Frist für eine Antwort der Kommission lief am Donnerstag aus. Die EU-Kommission forderte Österreich daraufhin auf, die Verabschiedung des Gesetzes für ein Jahr auszusetzen, sagte Regnier.

„Ein europäisches Problem erfordert eine gemeinsame europäische Antwort“, sagte Regnier. „Wir müssen uns nun auf die Verhandlungen zum EU Kids Act konzentrieren.“

Die Mitgliedstaaten müssen sich nun mit dem Europäischen Parlament und der Kommission auf die Einzelheiten des Kids Act einigen, bevor die Regeln umgesetzt werden können.

Nach dem Vorschlag der Kommission wäre der Zugang zu sozialen Medien für Kinder unter 13 Jahren in den meisten Fällen verboten. Für Jugendliche unter 15 Jahren würde er stark eingeschränkt. Zudem sollen Plattformen zu mehr Sicherheit bereits bei der Gestaltung ihrer Dienste verpflichtet werden. Die Vorgaben sollen auch für Videospiele und KI-Begleiter gelten.

Wie die Mitgliedstaaten auf die Aufforderung reagieren werden, ist zunächst unklar.

World.title: Death toll from Spain train crash rises to 74 as royals visit victims
World.content:
The death toll from Wednesday's train crash in Spain has risen to at least 74, according to the country's transport ministry.

 

The update came as Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited a hospital in Toledo on Thursday afternoon to meet survivors and relatives of the victims.

The royal couple were welcomed by emergency workers, whom they thanked for their efforts, before speaking with injured passengers and victims' families. The hospital is currently treating 15 patients in intensive care and another eight on general wards.

Visibly moved, Felipe VI and Letizia cancelled their official engagements to travel to Toledo and hear firsthand about the condition of those receiving treatment.

Following the crash, the king expressed his sorrow over the "terrible accident", offered his condolences to the victims' families and friends during "such a difficult time", and praised the work of emergency services.

As a mark of respect, the Royal Household has suspended its official engagements for the coming days. The decision coincides with the start of three days of national mourning on Thursday and affects events scheduled in both Madrid and the Canary Islands.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 29th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Major strikes planned across Italy on Friday against cost of living and military spending
World.content:
Strikes are planned across Italy on Friday, with widespread disruption expected as trade union Unione Sindacale di Base called on both public and private sector workers to strike, mobilise and protest, including at a major demonstration in Rome.

 

Renewed student protests are also expected to return to the street in major cities across Italy.

Meanwhile, the Cobas unions, together with Adl, Clap and Sial, have also called for a general strike across the public and private sectors, excluding transport.

The strike will also be a new test for public order, as students are set to return to the streets in all the main cities across Italy.

Friday's protests are directed against the rising cost of living, which unions say makes it increasingly difficult for people to cover essential expenses, as well as military spending.

Rail services are expected to be disrupted from 21:00 on Thursday until 20:59 on Friday, while the strike in air transport is expected to last for the entirety of Friday.

In local public transport, the impact will vary from city to city. The strike is also expected to affect taxi services throughout Friday, while motorway staff will begin their strike in the evening on Thursday.

Also on Friday, dock workers will mobilise globally against arms trafficking, rearmament policies and the militarisation of ports.

The action has been organised by several unions, including USB in Italy, the CGT in France and other trade union organisations in Greece, Turkey, Morocco and the Basque Country.

According to the organisers, workers from more than 100 ports in 17 countries and four continents have joined the mobilisation.

In Italy the protests will affect, among others, the ports of Genoa, Livorno, Trieste, Civitavecchia, Ancona, Ravenna and Gioia Tauro.

What are unions demanding?

Among USB's key demands is for wages to rise in line with the cost of living, including through the reintroduction of the "scala mobile", a mechanism previously used to automatically adjust wages in line with inflation.

The union is also calling for measures to bring down the costs of essential goods, household bills and rents, and for a reduction in VAT on basic necessities.

According to USB, the government is allocating too many resources to military spending, while funding for health care, education and other public services remains inadequate.

World.title: Deadly train crash puts Sánchez on the ropes a month before elections
World.content:
Wednesday's train crash near Toledo has added pressure on Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of the early general election he called for next month.

 

His government has already faced a succession of crises this year, including another deadly rail accident in Adamuz in January and the migration crisis in Ceuta in July. The latest accident represents another political shock in the middle of the pre-election period and comes as the government's handling of public services faces renewed scrutiny.

Although the main parties suspended their pre-campaign events after the tragedy, with the exception of Vox, political confrontation has continued.

The Partido Popular has questioned the government's management of the rail network. Far-right Vox has filed a criminal complaint for homicide against Transport Minister Óscar Puente while Frente Amplio has demanded that he appear before parliament to explain what happened.

FILE: The acting prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, shakes hands with party member Óscar Puente, in Madrid, Spain, on 29 September 2023. AP Photo

The investigation still has to establish what caused the collision and whether human, technical or coordination failures were involved. But the political debate is already moving faster than the investigation.

While investigators try to reconstruct the minutes leading up to the crash, the parties are already disputing the narrative of what happened and, above all, who should bear its consequences.

One crisis after another

The crash is the latest in a series of crises that have shaped public debate in Spain in recent years and are now feeding into the election campaign. These include protests over housing, migration tensions in Ceuta, the nationwide blackout, devastating floods in Valencia, the handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, and corruption cases involving figures close to Sánchez and the PSOE.

For the public, the more immediate questions are what happened, why it happened and what will be done to prevent it from happening again.

Related Sánchez pledges tough line on possible safety failures after Toledo train crash

The tragedy in Urda has once again put rail safety at the centre of the national debate, barely nine months after the Adamuz accident, which killed 46 people. The two incidents have renewed questions about infrastructure oversight, safety protocols and accountability.

What were the polls saying before the Urda tragedy?

Even before this week's train crash, polls were already pointing to a difficult electoral landscape for Pedro Sánchez, although some showed signs of recovery for the PSOE.

According to a poll published by El Mundo on 26 October, the Partido Popular was on 30.6% of the vote and between 125 and 131 seats, compared with 26.1% and between 103 and 109 seats for the Socialists. Vox was on 19.9% and between 66 and 69 seats.

Another poll published by El Español around the same time put the Partido Popular at around 32% of the vote and 135 seats, the PSOE at 27% and 108 seats, and Vox at 18.6% and 63 seats.

Both polls suggested that the PP and Vox together could secure an absolute majority.

The Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), however, has presented a very different picture, placing the PSOE well ahead of the PP in its latest barometer.

The sharp differences between polls add further uncertainty to a pre-election period already dominated by political and management crises, with the Urda rail tragedy now added to the debate barely a month before the general election.

World.title: EU countries push back against Brussels plan to tax gas more than electricity
World.content:
More than a dozen EU countries have pushed back against European Commission plans to make electricity cheaper than gas through preferential taxation, warning that Brussels is overstepping its powers.

 

At a meeting of EU energy ministers in Luxembourg on Thursday, Germany, Italy, Malta, the Czech Republic, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Finland, Romania, Croatia, Poland, Latvia, Estonia and Hungary were among the countries calling for the controversial provision to be scrapped.

The proposal is part of the Commission's efforts to encourage households and businesses to switch from fossil fuels to electricity, as demand from industry, data centres, heat pumps and electric vehicles continues to grow.

But the rising cost of expanding and operating Europe's electricity grids is increasingly being passed on to consumers through higher bills.

The Commission proposal comes amid an energy crisis, exacerbated since the US-Israeli war against Iran which has sent prices soaring and intensified pressure on Brussels to ease the burden on households and industry.

Related Germany warns EU electricity tax plan threatens national sovereignty

Even before the Middle East conflict, European electricity prices were twice those in the US and China, prompting European manufacturers to demand "urgent and bold" action.

During an informal summit last February, EU leaders vowed to drop energy prices by making electricity taxation more favourable than natural gas in a bid to lower bills.

But several EU countries argue that tax policy should be dealt with in the ongoing revision of the Energy Taxation Directive, which requires unanimity, rather than being decided by a qualified majority vote, as the European Commission proposes.

Sweden's energy minister Ebba Busch called for better regulation instead of more bureaucracy.

“Given the very significant differences in grids and the grid characteristics across the Union, there is no one-size-fits-all solution for tariff design,” Busch said.

Spain, Denmark and Luxembourg have backed the Commission, though they called for some flexibility.

"The proposals should include flexibility for member states to set clear political priorities for ambitious electrification policies to ensure pace and scale of grid expansion," said the Danish permanent representative diplomat, Søren Jacobsen.

France sought a middle path, calling for the legal basis to be secured and suggesting the measure be tied to specific circumstances such as a gas crisis.

Luxembourg floated replacing the provision with a general obligation to promote electrification.

Brussels versus national control

The strongest opposition centred on the Commission’s plan to let it set common rules for how electricity grid charges are calculated across the EU, without having to seek fresh approval from member states and the European Parliament each time.

Italy, France, Germany, Slovakia, Poland, Spain, Finland and other countries argued that the plan would undermine the independence of national regulators and give Brussels too much power over decisions that they believe should be made at national level.

Finland noted that its parliament had formally concluded the proposal violates that principle.

"Member states must retain sufficient flexibility to reflect their national circumstances, investment needs and electricity systems. We are also concerned by the lack of comprehensive impact assessment," Finland's state representative Mika Nykänen said.

Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen held his ground in his closing remarks, saying the EU executive's proposal "makes a lot of sense".

The EU's top energy chief said that the legal services of both the Commission and the Council judged the proposal legally sound.

"It (the legal clause) could have both an immediate and a structural impact on reducing our electricity bills. We should not deprive our consumers and industries of the benefits of this proposal," Jørgensen told energy ministers.

The Irish Presidency, currently mediating EU negotiations, says it wants a compromise on network charges in December.

World.title: German serial rapist sentenced to 12 years as police investigate 44 more cases
World.content:
The court sentenced Frank S. to 12 years in prison, followed by preventive detention. The 69-year-old is unlikely ever to be released.

 

One of the worst serial rapists in German criminal history is believed by investigators to have drugged and raped 58 women, filmed his crimes and shared the footage online with other men. It was this that ultimately led to his capture.

After his chat partner was arrested, police tracked down Frank S., searched his flat and found the video recordings.

Frank S. had filmed a total of 58 women after drugging their drinks and sexually assaulting them. Some of the women were still conscious and begged him to stop. Afterwards, many were unable to remember what had happened because of the heavy sedation. As a result, Frank S. was not reported to police, while other women suppressed memories of what they had experienced.

It was only when police visited some of the women at home during the investigation that they first learned what Frank S. had done to them.

On Wednesday, Berlin Regional Court sentenced Frank S. to 12 years in prison, followed by preventive detention, for 22 rapes involving 14 women. In nine cases, he also violated their intimate privacy by recording them.

During the three-month trial, all 14 women testified as witnesses, with six also participating as joint plaintiffs. The perpetrator's videos were also used as evidence.

According to the court, the women were completely helpless and defenceless because they had been sedated with various medications. The judges found that Frank S. took advantage of this. The now 69-year-old filmed his acts and is said to have stored the video recordings digitally "like trophies in a cabinet". The court described his actions as particularly "contemptuous towards women".

Despite the confession delivered by S.'s defence lawyer at the start of the trial, the court ordered preventive detention after he serves his sentence. This measure is considered one of the harshest tools available to the judiciary. By the time he could be released from prison, he will already be over 80 years old.

After viewing Frank S.'s video recordings, the police assume that he drugged and raped a total of 58 women. Euronews

The court did not consider his advanced age sufficient reason to conclude that S. would not reoffend. The presiding judge stated that the defendant had not fully understood what he had done to the women or the serious consequences his actions had had for them. The verdict is not yet legally binding, and S. can still appeal.

Frank S.'s devious methods

Over a seven-year period from 2016 to 2022, the now 69-year-old met the 14 women through dating platforms and deceived them. He gained their trust in a way that was, according to a court spokesperson, "particularly devious". He told one woman he was a police inspector and another that he was a helicopter pilot. Ultimately, the trained electrician invited the women to his flat and offered them drinks.

However, the alcoholic drinks were laced with substances that, combined with alcohol, left the women helpless and unable to resist. Some still tried to protest verbally, but S. ignored them. "What really mattered to him was to exercise power over these defenceless women," a court spokesperson explained. S. raped the sedated women, in some cases several times, in his bedroom, where a video camera was permanently installed.

The judge described S.'s methods as systematic and highly organised. His crimes followed a pattern. The court also stated that he acted like an archivist and, as became particularly clear from the videos examined, carried out his crimes in a calm and routine manner. He is said to have rewatched some of the footage while smoking a cigarette.

Four expert witnesses, including specialists in IT, toxicology and psychiatry, provided evidence during the trial. Six of the victims participated as joint plaintiffs during the three-month proceedings. Two of them attended the sentencing but declined to speak publicly.

Women avoid public attention as organisations show solidarity

"What is very important for me and also for my client is the preventive detention that has now been ordered, because the propensity to offend and the danger he poses, at least as things stand today, are very clear," said Silke Studzinski, lawyer for one of the joint plaintiffs.

Laura Leogrande, a lawyer for another joint plaintiff, also said "that there was indeed a reluctance to speak in public". She stressed that this was not a criticism, however. At the plaintiffs’ request, the closing statements were delivered behind closed doors. They decided to speak about the rapes they had suffered without members of the public present.

"I do find it remarkable that there was so much shame," Leogrande said, "about having been in this situation, about having become a victim of this crime, and having trusted this man enough to go home with him, and then something like this happens." The victims were not to blame.

Outside the courthouse, organisations such as Terre des Femmes and initiatives like "Die Scham muss die Seite wechseln" ("Shame must change sides") showed their solidarity. They called for protests and rallies.

"Terre des Femmes is here because we stand in solidarity with those affected and because we want to send a signal against sexualised violence," explained Sina Tonk, a department head at the organisation, in an interview with Euronews. "We know that only around three percent of rapes are ever reported to the police, and that happens out of fear or shame, or because many obstacles are placed in the way of those affected."

Another trial could follow. Police now believe there are 58 victims, and investigations into a further 44 cases are ongoing. Ten women believed to appear in the videos have not yet been identified.

Leogrande stressed that this is not a new phenomenon. Rather, rape after a victim has been drugged is "something that has only now come to the surface, that is only now being talked about and that is only now being investigated in real detail". The Pelicot case in France has drawn particular attention to the issue.

Berlin police became aware of Frank S. after officers in Lower Saxony passed on a tip based on a chat log. S. had exchanged information about his crimes with a suspected rapist in Verden, Lower Saxony. He was arrested in March 2026 and has remained in pre-trial detention since then.

The series of rapes is considered the largest case to date involving drug-facilitated sexual assault before the Berlin Regional Court. Germany has also recently tightened its laws on sexual violence, including provisions concerning the use of incapacitating drugs and the recording of crimes.

World.title: Netenyahu's Likud party alleges interference and fraud in Israel's election
World.content:
Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party are alleging election interference and fraud after Israel’s election results left his bloc short of a parliamentary majority.

 

The final count, expected on Thursday evening, is set to confirm that Netanyahu's bloc has fallen short of the 61 seats needed for a majority. With around 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 seats, the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot 48, and Arab-led parties 19.

The result represents major gains for the Arab-led parties, potentially giving them a decisive role in determining whether a government without Netanyahu can be formed.

The election saw record participation by Arab citizens of Israel, many of whom are descendants of Palestinians who remained after the country's creation in 1948. The campaign had seen Netanyahu and his far-right allies repeatedly portray Arab-led parties as a threat.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to his supporters at Likud party headquarters in Jerusalem. 28 October 2026 AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg

Netanyahu alleges interference

Netanyahu, who has served as Israel's prime minister on and off since 1996, has accused Arab parties of benefiting from foreign interference and funding. Neither he nor his allies have publicly provided evidence to substantiate those claims.

In a post on the social media platform X, Netanyahu quoted his Likud party, saying: "The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state through serious criminal offences of bribery, threats, violence, forgeries, and the use of prohibited software to mobilise voters."

A post on X from Benjamin Netanyahu alleging interference by Arab-led parties

In another post on Thursday morning, he wrote: "Why did Ahmad Tibi visit Qatar 4 days before the elections?" Ahmad Tibi is a Palestinian-Israeli politician and a senior figure in the Ta'al party.

Israel's Central Election Commission has asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate alleged foreign interference. However, the request itself reportedly did not specifically accuse Arab-led parties of wrongdoing. AP also reported that the commission said there was no basis, to its knowledge, for claims of systematic violations of election integrity.

The Arab-led Joint List rejected the accusations, saying Netanyahu’s camp was trying to delegitimise the Arab vote because of its increased political influence. It accused Netanyahu of "working to steal the election".

Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas said he welcomed an investigation into allegations of wrongdoing but said his party had "no connection" with them.

Netanyahu himself has previously faced scrutiny over alleged links between aides and Qatar, after two of his aides were arrested last year on suspicion of receiving payments from the Gulf state.

Qatar has categorically denied interfering in the election. Its Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed Al Ansari, said: "They accuse Qatar of buying off Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli political left and now, in this latest campaign, the Arab vote. These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure."

Israel's President Isaac Herzog has also called for a full investigation, while warning against stigmatising the country’s entire Arab community.

Israeli lawmaker Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra'am party, raises his fists as he greets supporters after the release of the first exit poll. 27 October 2026 AP Photo/Mahmoud Illean

What happens next?

The full count is expected on Thursday evening, although the official election results are due to be certified by 4 November.

President Herzog will then decide whom to ask to try to form a government.

The next Knesset is due to be sworn in on 10 November.

If no coalition can be formed after several attempts, Israel could face another election early next year.

The political uncertainty is unfolding alongside the possibility of renewed Israeli or US strikes on Iran, which could further complicate coalition negotiations.

World.title: Palestinian President Abbas signals readiness for talks with Israel, seeks Cyprus mediation
World.content:
Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas said on Thursday that he hoped the election of a new Israeli government would allow for the resumption of peace talks.

 

During a meeting with Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides in Nicosia, Abbas asked Cyprus to mediate the efforts.

"For many years now, we have been extending a hand to the Israeli side in order to achieve peace with them, so that Israel and Palestine may live in security, stability and peace," Abbas said.

"We hope that, immediately after a new Israeli government is formed, we will be able to engage in dialogue together," he added.

Christodoulides said Abbas' visit comes at an "important moment" for the region.

"How can we work together, always through a positive approach? To create conditions of security and stability in the region. Of course, we are also at Palestine’s disposal, so that we may play whatever role they deem necessary for the Republic of Cyprus, in order to achieve our common goals," Christodoulides said.

Later during a working lunch attended by delegations from both sides, Abbas' highlighted the importance of Cyprus' role.

"I will not dwell on the excellent relationship that exists between the Palestinian people and the Cypriot people and the Republic of Cyprus, but you also have excellent relations—and rightly so—with Israel," Abbas said.

"So you can play a role in mediating between the two sides, based on a political solution that is grounded in international law and the resolutions of the Security Council and the United Nations," he concluded.

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Egypt's mahrganat music: from the streets to five-star hotels
World.content:
Born in Egypt’s working-class neighbourhoods, mahraganat music is loud and raw, and these days it is practically impossible to escape. But for the artists behind it, mahraganat is more than just party music: they see it as the latest chapter in Egypt’s rich musical history.

Advertising

In this third episode of the season, we travel to the Egyptian capital, Cairo, to discover the origins of a genre that has become the soundtrack to urban life, despite receiving no official airtime.

Mahraganat evolved from shaabi: music by the people, for the people. Although it rose to prominence during the revolution of 2011–12, it has since become less overtly political.

It remains the music of happiness, partying, joy, and celebration.

Its fast rhythms and loud beats may be a far cry from the golden age of Egyptian music, but mahraganat has been on the scene since the early 2000s and it isn’t going anywhere, any time soon.

We trace its origins and evolution as we speak to one of the godfathers of the movement, his musical partner and a specialist in the genre.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora. Special thanks to Elisa Schouten for her contribution.
