World.title: From Takumi to Gonta, a New Chapter for Japanese Food in Prague
World.content:
For those craving a taste of Japan without leaving Prague, Takumi offers a chance to explore Japanese cuisine in the heart of the city.

Located behind Quadrio, near the moving head sculpture of Franz Kafka, the restaurant recently celebrated its first anniversary this September.

We spoke with co-owner Euntaek Kim about the restaurant’s history, his journey to Prague, and his latest project, Gonta, a Japanese tonkatsu restaurant.



From Korea to Prague

The Takumi franchise was founded in Düsseldorf, Germany, in 2007 by Haruhiko Saeki and Kenjiro Komatsubara. Kim and his business partner, Viet Hung Phung, later partnered with the founders to bring Takumi Ramen to Prague, opening their first branch on Senovážné náměstí in 2019.

Kim’s connection to the restaurant business began long before that. Before he moved to Prague, his uncle owned several Hanil restaurants in Vienna and planned to expand into the Czech market. This led Kim’s family to move to Prague in 2000, when he was just 12 years old.

Later, Kim and his sister took over the Hanil restaurant their parents had run. He eventually sold it to a Korean chef he had worked with for several years.

Over time, Prague became much more than a place to do business.

“Prague has become like my second home. After having lived here for almost 26 years, I feel connected to its culture as well as my own Korean culture. In business settings and everyday life, I always try to find a balance between both,” Kim says.

His decision to open a Japanese restaurant was driven by what he saw as a gap in Prague’s dining scene.

“I felt like something was missing in Prague. Previously, Asian cuisine was close to nonexistent here. I wanted to make a change,” he explains.

Since moving to Prague, Kim has noticed growing interest in Asian food and culture among local residents, reflecting the city’s changing culinary landscape.

Introducing Gonta, a Japanese Tonkatsu Restaurant

Kim’s latest project, Gonta, brings another Japanese specialty to Prague. Located at Jungmannova 750/34, near Můstek metro station, the restaurant focuses on tonkatsu, a Japanese dish made with breaded, deep-fried pork cutlets, typically served with rice and a tangy sauce.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Gonta Prague (@tonkatsugonta.prague)

“When people think about Japanese cuisine, most people tend to think of sushi or ramen. Tonkatsu is a delicious dish that has not yet reached Prague. I craved it a lot,” Kim says, explaining what inspired him to launch Gonta.

The restaurant is scheduled to open in October 2026, adding another option to Prague’s growing selection of Japanese dining spots.

World.title: Why October 28 Is a National Holiday in the Czech Republic
World.content:
October 28th is Czechoslovak Independence Day, marking the establishment of Czechoslovakia in 1918.

Although Czechoslovakia peacefully split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993, October 28 remains one of the most important dates in Czech history.

It commemorates the struggle for independence and the emergence of modern Czech statehood. It should not be confused with Czech Statehood Day, celebrated on September 28.



Why Czechoslovakia Declared Independence in 1918

Before 1918, the Czech lands and present-day Slovakia were part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Bohemia, Moravia and part of Silesia belonged to the Austrian half of the monarchy, while Slovakia was part of Hungary. For decades, Czech and Slovak political leaders had sought greater autonomy and the right to determine their own future.

World War I, which began in 1914, weakened the empire and intensified nationalist movements. Food shortages, economic difficulties and growing public discontent increased support for an independent state.

Politicians working abroad played a crucial role in the independence movement. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, Edvard Beneš and Milan Rastislav Štefánik coordinated diplomatic efforts to win support from the Allied powers. France, Great Britain and the United States recognised the Czechoslovak National Council as a provisional government in 1918.

Czechoslovak legions also fought on several fronts during the war, including in France, Italy and Russia, helping draw international attention to the independence movement.

How Independence Was Declared

On October 18, 1918, Masaryk issued the Declaration of Independence of Czechoslovakia in the United States, known as the Washington Declaration. It outlined the ambition to establish a democratic state based on the right of the Czechs and Slovaks to self-determination.

The decisive events took place in Prague on October 28, as news spread that Austria-Hungary had agreed to armistice terms. Many people interpreted the reports as a sign that the empire was collapsing and gathered in public squares to celebrate.

The Czech National Committee took control and issued the first law establishing an independent Czechoslovak state. October 28 subsequently became the official date of its founding.

Who Founded the New State?

Masaryk became Czechoslovakia’s first president after independence. A philosopher, educator and politician, he had spent years persuading foreign governments to support the creation of a new state.

Beneš was instrumental in diplomatic negotiations and later served as foreign minister and president. Štefánik, a Slovak politician, astronomer and military officer, helped organise the Czechoslovak legions and strengthen cooperation between the Czech and Slovak independence movements.

Politicians working in Prague, including Alois Rašín, Karel Kramář and Antonín Švehla, also helped organise the transfer of power.

What Happened After 1918?

During the interwar period, Czechoslovakia became a parliamentary republic with one of Central Europe’s most developed industrial economies. However, tensions between its different national communities presented ongoing challenges.

In 1938, the Munich Agreement led to the loss of the Sudetenland. Nazi Germany occupied the Czech lands in March 1939, while Slovakia became a separate state aligned with Berlin. Czechoslovakia was restored after World War II but later came under communist rule.

The Velvet Revolution ended communist rule in 1989. On January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia peacefully split into two independent countries.

World.title: Where to Celebrate Halloween in Prague: 6 Events for Children and Adults
World.content:
Prague will mark Halloween 2026 with events for children and adults, ranging from pumpkin carving and lantern parades to costume competitions and late-night club parties.

Here are some of the events planned across Prague, including admission prices where available.

Blackout Halloween Rave at SaSaZu

Blackout Events will hold its first Halloween rave on Tuesday, October 27, at SaSaZu, bringing hard techno, Halloween costumes and stage productions to the Prague club.

The lineup includes WYNTER at 9 p.m., HOOOR at 10:30 p.m., A.N.I. at midnight, NOTMYTYPE at 1:30 a.m. and KLAR at 3 a.m. The event is scheduled to finish at 4 a.m.

An afterparty will follow at Club Mecca in Holešovice from 3 a.m. The event is restricted to visitors aged 18 and over. Organizers say further program details will be published on Blackout Events’ Instagram account.

Halloween at Hybernia Theatre

Hybernia Theatre, near Náměstí Republiky, is also listed as a venue for a Halloween electronic music event. The program is set to combine electronic music, Halloween decorations and the historic theatre’s interior.

Italian DJ SPADA is announced as a special guest. Admission is listed at CZK 499, although the event date should be confirmed with the organizer before publication.

Spooks at Žluté lázně

Žluté lázně in Podolí will host a Halloween afternoon on Saturday, October 31, from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Children can follow a spooky trail featuring a spiderweb tunnel, a mysterious castle and a series of challenges. The program will also include pumpkin carving, face painting and dancing.

The organizers will announce the winner of the best-costume competition at 6:10 p.m. Admission costs CZK 150, while children wearing costumes can enter for free. Pumpkins for carving will be available for CZK 100.

Halloween Among Dinosaurs at DinoPark Harfa

DinoPark on the rooftop of Galerie Harfa will offer Halloween activities on Saturday, October 31, including a trail where children can complete tasks among the dinosaurs.

The afternoon program will feature Stegoušek Kvído, a walking dinosaur character who will lead two lantern parades, at 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. Visitors should bring their own lanterns.

DinoPark will be open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Children in Halloween costumes can enter for CZK 50.

Pumpkin Carving at the Public Transport Museum

The Public Transport Museum in Střešovice will combine Halloween activities with a look at Prague’s historic trams and buses on Saturday, October 31.

Visitors can carve pumpkins and explore the museum’s collection of historic vehicles. Those arriving in costume will receive a gift.

At 4:45 p.m., the carved pumpkins will be lit in the museum courtyard. The museum will be open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Bloody Sexy Halloween Returns to SaSaZu

Bloody Sexy Halloween will return to SaSaZu on Friday, October 30, and Saturday, October 31, for two nights of music, performances and themed productions.

Founded in 2009, the event has become one of the region’s established Halloween parties, attracting more than 4,000 visitors in previous editions, according to the organizers.

One of the weekend’s main attractions is the Bloody Sexy Costume Contest. Participants can register at SaSaZu between 9 p.m. and midnight. Costumes are judged on creativity, originality and presentation, with the winner selected by audience applause at midnight and awarded CZK 40,000.

World.title: Thirty Seconds to Mars to Play Prague in 2027 With Special Album Tour
World.content:
Thirty Seconds to Mars will return to Prague on May 18, 2027, for a concert at the O2 arena.

The Jared and Shannon Leto-led band will revisit two of its best-known albums, A Beautiful Lie and This Is War, as part of a special world tour.

The American rock band will perform without an opening act, with the show expected to last approximately two hours. Tickets start at CZK 1,500, excluding ticketing fees, and VIP packages will also be available.



The concert is part of the band’s A Beautiful Lie vs This Is War tour, which focuses on two records that helped establish Thirty Seconds to Mars as a major name in alternative rock.

Tickets will be available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal from October 30, 2026, at 10 a.m. Fan club members will have access to a presale beginning October 27 at 10 a.m. Live Nation, Spotify and O2 presales will follow on October 29 at 10 a.m.

Two albums that defined the band’s sound

Released in 2005, A Beautiful Lie marked a turning point in the band’s career, bringing its music to a much wider international audience. The album features some of Thirty Seconds to Mars’ best-known songs, including The Kill, From Yesterday and the title track.

The follow-up, This Is War, arrived in 2009 and expanded that sound. Tracks such as Kings and Queens, This Is War and Closer to the Edge became signature songs, helping the band reach a broader audience.

From alternative rock to global tours

Led by brothers Jared Leto, the band’s vocalist, and Shannon Leto, its drummer, the group continued to develop its sound on Love, Lust, Faith and Dreams in 2013 and America in 2018. The latter included the singles Walk on Water and Rescue Me.

In 2023, the band released its sixth studio album, It’s the End of the World but It’s a Beautiful Day, exploring a different musical direction while maintaining its focus on melody and emotional themes.

The band has also received several MTV awards and a Billboard Music Award. Its touring history includes a Guinness World Records recognition for the longest concert tour.

The 2027 tour will take Thirty Seconds to Mars across Europe, the United Kingdom, South Africa and other destinations. Its Prague stop will bring the band’s anniversary celebrations and catalogue of established hits to the Czech capital for a show centred on two of its most influential albums.

World.title: Viktor Orbán reported to police over controversial speech about ‘handing out appropriate tools’
World.content:
Hungary’s National Bureau of Investigation has confirmed receiving a criminal complaint against former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán over remarks about distributing ‘appropriate tools’ for resistance. Authorities are now examining the complaint, but it’s unclear whether a criminal investigation will follow.

Hungary’s National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) has confirmed that a criminal complaint has been filed against former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán over controversial remarks he made at a gathering of the Digital Civic Circles (Digitális Polgári Körök, DPK) in Lakitelek earlier this month.

According to Hungarian broadcaster ATV, the authorities are currently examining the contents of the complaint as part of a preliminary procedure to supplement it. It is not yet known whether a formal criminal investigation will be launched or what suspected offence, if any, it would concern.

Orbán’s comments triggered a strong reaction from Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who accused his predecessor of referring to an armed uprising and the violent overthrow of Hungary’s constitutional order.

If you missed it: Vučić allegedly considered a coup after election defeat – Did Orbán help stop him?

What did Orbán say at the Lakitelek event?

At the DPK gathering in Lakitelek on 18 October, Orbán was asked about the ‘national resistance’ he had previously called for against the Tisza-led government.

The former prime minister responded that the country was not yet in a suitable state for such resistance, but his own camp was ready.

“Our country is not yet in a state suitable for this. We already are. We could hand out the appropriate tools here, whoever gets what, blunter or sharper – that is not the question,” Orbán said.

The remarks drew attention because of the reference to distributing tools of varying sharpness. Magyar subsequently argued that the comments amounted to a reference to armed rebellion and the violent alteration of the constitutional order.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Magyar accuses Orbán of referring to armed rebellion

Magyar reacted to the remarks on social media on the same day, citing provisions of Hungary’s Criminal Code concerning crimes against the constitutional order.

He pointed to legislation under which acts directly aimed at violently changing Hungary’s constitutional order, or threatening to do so, can carry prison sentences of five to 20 years or even life imprisonment. Preparatory acts intended to facilitate such a crime can also be punishable by one to five years in prison.

Orbán had previously called for ‘national resistance’ and a fight against the Tisza government at political events in Tusnádfürdő over the summer and at the Kötcse gathering in September. He claimed that Hungary was facing a new form of colonialisation under the new administration.

Police confirm complaint after fresh media inquiry

ATV first contacted the National Police Headquarters (ORFK) on 21 October to ask whether a complaint had been filed over Orbán’s comments. At that point, the authorities said no proceedings had been initiated in the matter by the time they responded.

The broadcaster sent a further inquiry earlier this week to establish whether the situation had changed.

In its latest response, the National Bureau of Investigation confirmed that the complaint had arrived at the office and that its contents were being examined as part of a procedure to supplement the complaint.

World.title: Budapest to Prague in just 3 hours? Magyar announces push for V4 high-speed railway after talks with Babiš
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and his Czech counterpart Andrej Babiš have pledged closer cooperation on energy, migration and transport, while Magyar delivered a sharp response to speculation about Viktor Orbán becoming the next UN secretary-general.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar described himself as an “easygoing guy” after holding the first-ever joint Czech-Hungarian government meeting in Prague on Thursday. Speaking alongside Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, Magyar stressed that the two countries wanted to focus on practical cooperation rather than their political differences.

The talks covered energy security, migration, European Union affairs and plans for a high-speed railway connecting the Visegrád Four (V4) countries. Magyar also took the opportunity to criticise his predecessor, Viktor Orbán, over reports that the former Hungarian prime minister could be considered for the post of UN secretary-general.

Photo: MTI

‘I’m an easygoing guy’, Magyar says

Asked about his approach to cooperation with Babiš, Magyar said he was interested in Hungarian interests rather than ideological debates.

“I’m an easygoing guy. I’m interested in the interests of Hungarians,” he said, adding that he wanted to discuss concrete issues with international partners instead of focusing on subjects that divide them.

Babiš, who previously enjoyed a close relationship with Orbán, said he represented the interests of his own country and respected the choices made by other nations. He praised Magyar’s strong electoral mandate, saying he envied the Hungarian prime minister for winning such a decisive victory without needing coalition partners.

Magyar welcomed the renewed momentum behind the V4, which brings together Hungary, Czechia, Poland and Slovakia. He said cooperation between the four countries could strengthen their position in the European Council, particularly on energy and migration.

Magyar mocks prospect of Orbán leading the UN

One of the most striking exchanges came when CNN asked Magyar how he would react if US President Donald Trump backed Orbán for the UN secretary-general position.

“If someone wants to destroy the UN, take an Orbán – that would be a good start,” Magyar said.

He acknowledged that the international organisation had shortcomings but rejected the idea that it was a criminal organisation. He also referred to alleged criminal cases involving former members of Orbán’s government as part of his criticism.

The comments followed reports that Orbán’s candidacy had been discussed in US political circles. However, no confirmed appointment or selection has been announced, and the process for choosing the next secretary-general remains ongoing.

High-speed railway could connect Budapest and Prague in three hours

Transport and energy cooperation also featured prominently in the talks. Magyar said the two governments wanted to turn broad commitments into concrete projects, including encouraging energy companies to invest in each other’s countries.

The leaders also discussed a proposed high-speed railway linking the V4 capitals. Magyar said the route could eventually cut travel time between Budapest and Prague to around three hours, while a Budapest–Warsaw journey could take approximately five hours.

The project could cost more than €10 billion, and the four countries want to secure substantial funding from the EU’s next seven-year budget. Hungary and Czechia also signed a memorandum on transport cooperation, including railway investment.

Prague. Source: Pixabay

Hungary hopes to end daily €1 million EU fine

Magyar also confirmed that the Hungarian budget contains no allocation for the daily €1 million EU penalty imposed over the country’s migration policy.

He said he hoped Hungary could secure an exemption before the end of the year. Babiš also criticised the fine, calling it absurd that Hungary should pay for protecting its borders against illegal migration.

The Czech government is expected to visit Budapest in the spring for the next bilateral government meeting, with both leaders expressing confidence that closer cooperation could deliver tangible benefits for their countries.

World.title: Spar turns to Brussels again: ‘Euphoria about Hungary’s new government proved unfounded’
World.content:
The Austrian parent company of supermarket chain Spar has urged the European Commission to intervene, accusing Hungary of systematically discriminating against foreign retailers despite hopes of a fresh start under the new government.

Spar’s Austrian parent company has renewed its call for the European Commission to take action against Hungary over the retail sector’s special tax, which the government has no plans to abolish. The company’s leadership has expressed disappointment with the new administration, arguing that recent changes have failed to address what it sees as unfair treatment of foreign supermarket chains.

According to Austrian newspaper Die Presse, Hans Reisch, head of Spar’s Austrian parent company, has written to the European Commission again, urging it to intervene in the dispute. He reportedly described the government’s retail policy changes so far as a smokescreen and said he had little confidence that the sector-specific tax would be scrapped any time soon.

Spar calls for EU infringement proceedings

Reisch claims that foreign retail chains continue to face systematic discrimination in Hungary and argues that the government is unwilling to establish a level playing field for domestic and international businesses.

The company believes the European Commission should therefore launch infringement proceedings against Hungary over its retail taxation policy.

The dispute centres on the special retail tax, which will remain in place under the government’s plans for the 2027 budget. The highest tax band, applying to the portion of the tax base exceeding HUF 50 billion (approximately €125 million), will continue to carry a rate of 4.5%.

‘Euphoria about the Magyar government proved unfounded’

Peter Manhartsberger, a director at Spar’s Austrian parent company, voiced his frustration in an interview with Die Presse.

“Unfortunately, the euphoria surrounding the Magyar government proved unfounded,” he said.

Manhartsberger also pointed to the government’s plans to abolish the mandatory retail margin cap while retaining the special tax. In his view, the tax represents a considerably greater financial burden for the company.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Dispute costs Spar €130 million a year

According to Manhartsberger, the two measures together cost Spar around €130 million annually. Of this amount, approximately €90 million is attributable to the special retail tax, while the margin cap accounts for a further €40 million.

The figures illustrate the scale of the financial dispute between the supermarket group and the Hungarian government. With the special tax set to remain in place in 2027, Spar’s Austrian parent company is once again turning to Brussels in an effort to secure a change in policy.

World.title: Portuguese man brutally assaults Hungarian partner’s stepfather in their home
World.content:
A Portuguese man who travelled to Hungary to visit his partner following the birth of their child is facing prison after allegedly beating her stepfather so severely that the victim required life-saving surgery.

Came to witness the dawn of life, almost took one

According to the indictment, the defendant, a Portuguese national living in the Netherlands, came to Hungary to see his partner, who had temporarily returned to her home country for the birth of their child. She was living in a village in Borsod County with her mother and stepfather.

During the visit, the defendant and the older man began drinking together in the kitchen. They communicated through gestures as they didn’t speak each other’s language, but the situation eventually deteriorated into a loud argument. The Portuguese man allegedly slapped his partner’s stepfather, and the two began fighting before the victim was pulled to the ground.

The Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Chief Prosecutor’s Office has brought charges of attempted murder over the incident, which took place in October 2024. Prosecutors say the victim’s survival was down to chance, as the assault carried a genuine risk of life-threatening injuries.

The attacker even smashed a car window with a shovel

The confrontation briefly subsided when the victim and the woman’s mother went outside and got into a car. However, the defendant followed them. He allegedly threw a sack of corn at the vehicle’s windscreen before threatening, through gestures, to cut the older man’s throat.

The victim got out of the car and attempted to keep the Portuguese man at a distance using a shovel with a handle approximately 1.5 metres long. The defendant wrested the tool from his hands and used it to smash the car’s rear window.

The woman’s stepfather then tried to flee, but the defendant caught up with him in the yard. Prosecutors allege that he punched the victim repeatedly in the head with considerable force. After the man fell to the ground, the attacker continued kicking and stamping on him, including striking him in the ribs.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Only the police could stop him, prosecutors seek prison sentence

The assault only stopped when police arrived after being alerted by family members. The victim was taken to hospital by ambulance, where he underwent emergency surgery followed by further surgical treatment. Prosecutors say there was a realistic possibility that he could have suffered life-threatening injuries, and that his death was prevented only by chance.

The Portuguese man has no previous criminal record. Nevertheless, prosecutors have requested a prison sentence and a ban on holding public office. They have also asked the court to rule that he should not be eligible for parole. The case will now proceed through the Hungarian judicial system.

Read also: Hungarian authorities ambush criminal network behind overpriced Covid ventilator deals linked to former government – Video

World.title: Hungary to triple fee-free bank transaction limit, announces PM Magyar
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has announced plans to triple the threshold for fee-free bank transfers for private individuals, raising it from HUF 50,000 to HUF 150,000. The change is expected to take effect in 2027 and could reduce banking costs for millions of customers.

Prime Minister Magyar announced the decision on social media

“Bank transfers will be exempt from the transaction levy up to HUF 150,000,” Magyar wrote on Facebook on Wednesday, confirming the government’s intention to increase the limit. The proposal had been reported earlier by Hungarian financial website biztosdöntés.hu, which said the higher threshold was being planned as part of the government’s 2027 measures.

Hungary’s transaction levy applies to a range of financial operations, including bank transfers, cash withdrawals, currency exchanges and card payments. Although financial institutions are legally responsible for paying the levy, they commonly pass the cost on to retail and business customers through their fees.

What will change for customers?

The existing exemption allows private individuals to transfer up to HUF 50,000 (EUR 136.62) per transaction without incurring the levy. Under the proposed change, that threshold would rise to HUF 150,000 (EUR 409.87), meaning transfers up to three times the current limit would qualify for the exemption.

The government is not planning to reduce the levy’s percentage rate, according to the earlier report. Instead, it reportedly intends to increase the maximum charge per transaction from HUF 20,000 to HUF 30,000 (from EUR 54.65 to EUR 81.97).

The broader levy was introduced in 2012 and its rate was increased in August 2024. The current charge on transfers is 0.45 per cent, subject to the applicable cap, while cash withdrawals and certain currency transactions face separate charges.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Could banks hit back at customers?

Raising the fee-free threshold could encourage more people to use bank transfers for everyday payments rather than relying on cash. It may also help households avoid some banking costs as they pay bills or send money to others.

However, the full effect will depend on how banks adjust their account fees and when the measure is formally implemented. The announcement concerns the planned exemption for private individuals; customers should check their bank’s terms for details of any additional charges. The government has yet to provide further implementation details beyond the announced increase.

Read also: Hungary shuts down bank, but what happens to customers’ money?

World.title: Record-breaking month for Hungarian exports: Billions flow in, but there’s a catch
World.content:
Hungary’s exports reached an all-time high of €16.2 billion in September, helping the country record a €907 million trade surplus as export and import volumes both increased year on year. However, the latest figures also reveal contrasting trends in trade with the European Union and countries outside the bloc.

According to data published by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH) on Thursday, the value of exports rose by 21% in euro terms compared with September 2025, while imports increased by 20%. The trade surplus improved by €266 million year on year.

Record-breaking exports, stronger imports

Hungary exported goods worth HUF 5,932 billion (€16.2 billion) in September, while imports totalled HUF 5,601 billion (€15.3 billion).

Compared with the same month last year, export volumes increased by 4.6%, while import volumes grew by 5.4%. After seasonal and working-day adjustments, export volumes were 1.1% higher than in August, while imports fell by 1%.

The figures suggest that Hungary’s external trade gained momentum following a weaker August, although imports continued to grow faster than exports in volume terms.

The terms of trade also improved by 1.7% year on year, meaning Hungary’s export prices moved more favourably relative to its import prices. Meanwhile, the forint strengthened by 6.8% against the euro and 5% against the US dollar compared with September 2025.

Machinery drives trade growth, while energy exports fall

Machinery and transport equipment played a major role in the September figures. Export volumes in this category increased by 9.9%, while imports surged by 18%.

Processed products showed a more mixed picture: export volumes rose by 0.8%, but imports fell by 7.2%. This decline helped limit the overall increase in Hungary’s imports.

Energy trade also moved in the opposite direction. Export volumes of energy products plunged by 28% compared with a year earlier, while imports declined by 7.9%.

Food, drinks and tobacco performed relatively steadily, with export volumes edging up by 0.3% and imports falling by 1.8%.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

EU trade delivers a surplus, but non-EU trade remains in deficit

Trade with EU member states provided a significant boost to Hungary’s overall balance. Export volumes to the bloc increased by 5.1%, while import volumes from EU countries decreased by 1.1%.

As a result, Hungary’s trade surplus with EU partners reached €2.2 billion in September, an improvement of €1.2 billion compared with the same month in 2025. EU member states accounted for 73% of Hungary’s exports and 63% of its imports.

Trade with countries outside the EU told a different story. Both export and import volumes increased by 23%, but the balance deteriorated by €946 million, leaving Hungary with a €1.3 billion deficit in trade with non-EU partners.

What do the figures show for 2026 so far?

Between January and September, Hungary’s exports were worth €124.8 billion, while imports reached €118.6 billion. The country therefore recorded a trade surplus of €6.2 billion over the first nine months of the year.

Export volumes increased by 1.3% compared with the same period in 2025, while import volumes grew by a much stronger 8%. The trade surplus consequently narrowed by €1.4 billion year on year.

September’s record export value is an encouraging sign for Hungary’s external trade. However, the faster growth in imports over the first nine months and the persistent deficit with non-EU trading partners show that the broader picture remains mixed.

World.title: Budapest airport bus gets a long-awaited upgrade: You can now pay by card!
World.content:
Passengers travelling between Budapest Airport and the city’s metro network can now buy a bus ticket with a bank card directly on board the 200E service, making one of the Hungarian capital’s key airport connections more convenient for visitors.

The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) introduced the new payment option on 28 October, extending a system already available on three other popular bus routes. The change means passengers no longer need cash to purchase a paper single ticket from the driver.

How to pay for your 200E airport bus ticket

Passengers can buy a paper single ticket when boarding the 200E bus, which runs between Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport and Kőbánya-Kispest, the southern terminus of metro line M3.

Payment can now be made through an onboard POS terminal using a conventional bank card. Digital wallets and virtual bank cards stored on smartphones and other devices are also accepted.

However, there is one important detail: buying a ticket does not automatically validate it. Passengers must still validate their paper tickets in the usual way after purchase.

The development is intended to make boarding quicker and easier for passengers while reducing the amount of cash drivers need to handle.

More Budapest bus routes now accept card payments

The 200E is not the first bus service to introduce this payment option. BKK launched onboard bank card payments on the 105, 210 and 210B routes in early September, focusing initially on services particularly popular with tourists.

The extension to the 200E brings the option to another important route for international visitors, connecting the airport with Budapest’s public transport network.

According to BKK, further expansion is possible based on passenger feedback and experience with the system. More routes are expected to offer onboard card payments in the first quarter of 2027.

If you missed it: BudapestGO receives useful new update to make metro journeys easier

Budapest is expanding its digital ticketing options

BKK is also working to extend its Budapest Pay&GO service, which allows passengers to pay for public transport using a bank card and is already available across all metro lines and on the 100E Airport Express.

Until then, travellers can continue to buy tickets and passes through the BudapestGO app, which also offers journey planning and real-time public transport information to help users find the most suitable route.

World.title: Hungary plans exit tax on wealthy people moving abroad – Who would pay?
World.content:
Hungary’s new government has unveiled plans for a 15% exit tax on unrealised investment gains for wealthy individuals who move their tax residence abroad. The proposed measure, which could take effect on 1 January 2027, would mean some people face a tax bill even if they have not sold their investments.

The detailed rules were published on Tuesday evening alongside the government’s wealth tax bill, according to Hungarian financial news outlet Portfolio. The government says the measure is intended to prevent capital from leaving Hungary in ways that reduce the country’s right to tax it.

Who would be affected by Hungary’s new exit tax?

Under the proposal, the tax would apply to individuals who meet all three of the following conditions:

They were Hungarian tax residents for at least five of the previous ten tax years.

Their relevant assets have a combined market value exceeding HUF 500 million (approximately EUR 1.36 million), or they own at least a 20% stake in a company worth at least HUF 250 million (approximately EUR 681,000).

Moving their tax residence abroad would end or restrict Hungary’s right to tax gains from the subsequent sale or disposal of those assets.

The proposed tax rate is 15%, matching Hungary’s standard personal income tax rate.

Crucially, the measure would target unrealised capital gains – increases in the value of investments that have not yet been converted into actual profits through a sale.

Under the proposed rules, the tax authorities would calculate the gain using the asset’s market value on the day before the individual’s Hungarian tax residence ends. This means that moving abroad could trigger a tax liability even if the investor continues to hold their investments.

Which assets would be covered?

The proposed legislation covers a broad range of financial assets, including:

Shares and other securities

Company ownership stakes

Certain options and derivative positions

Cryptocurrency assets

Certain rights associated with long-term investment and retirement savings accounts

Residual rights under life insurance policies, including pension insurance.

Ordinary cash, money held in standard bank accounts and bank deposits would not be covered in their own right. However, cash held within certain long-term investment or retirement savings arrangements could fall within the scope of the rules.

Another important detail is that gains on individual assets would be added together, but losses could not be offset against gains when calculating the taxable amount. This could increase the tax burden for investors whose portfolios contain both profitable and loss-making assets.

Moving to the EU could mean a payment delay

The proposed rules distinguish between people moving to EU or European Economic Area (EEA) countries and those relocating elsewhere.

Individuals moving to an EU or EEA country would generally receive an automatic, interest-free deferral of payment, provided they meet the relevant tax return and reporting requirements. The tax would still be assessed, but payment would typically be postponed until the assets were sold or otherwise realised.

The deferral could end earlier in certain circumstances, including when assets are transferred without payment, substantial value is withdrawn, the individual moves to a country outside the EU or EEA, or serious reporting obligations are breached.

Those moving to countries outside this framework would generally have to pay the tax by the filing deadline for the relevant tax year.

This distinction could be particularly important for wealthy Hungarians considering a move to the United States or another destination outside the EU and EEA.

Why is the government introducing the tax?

The exit tax is part of a larger package of proposed tax changes, including a new wealth tax planned for 2027.

The government argues that the measures are intended to discourage people from moving assets abroad to avoid Hungarian taxation. Prime Minister Péter Magyar has previously indicated that the government wants to prevent wealthy individuals from escaping the proposed wealth tax by transferring their assets overseas.

The wealth tax proposal would impose an annual levy on substantial personal fortunes, with different rates applying to different levels of wealth. The exit tax is intended to address a related issue: the potential loss of Hungary’s right to tax investment gains when a person changes their tax residence.

The government’s position is that people who accumulated wealth in Hungary should continue to contribute to public services through an appropriate share of taxation.

Concerns over the practical implications

The proposal is likely to raise questions about how the market value of certain assets, particularly privately held companies, would be established. Tax experts consulted by Telex have previously highlighted the potential difficulties of valuing businesses and the additional administrative burden such rules could create.

Exit taxes also raise legal questions within the EU, where rules must be consistent with the principles governing the free movement of capital and people. The proposed payment deferral for qualifying moves to EU and EEA countries is intended to address some of these concerns.

The legislation is currently a proposal, meaning its final wording could change during the parliamentary process.

World.title: Prosecutors and Police Officers Suspended in Kosovo After Latest Femicide
World.content:
Protest in Ferizaj/Urosevac, Kosovo, on October 29, 2026 against the femicide case. Photo: BIRN

On Thursday, the Kosovo Prosecutorial Council suspended Lumturije Vucetaj and Arlinda Nallbani Gacaferri, the chief prosecutor and deputy chief prosecutor of Peja/Pec. Nallbani Gacaferri served as the coordinator for domestic violence cases in addition to serving as deputy.

The suspensions come after a local woman was murdered on Sunday evening just minutes after being escorted home from the police station, where she had been to report her husband for domestic violence.

Dardan Vuniqi, a member of the Kosovo Prosecutorial Council, told BIRN after the conclusion of the council meeting that “both have been suspended”.

Kosovo Police suspended 11 members of the police from the Peja/Pec region upon request of the Police Inspectorate. The suspended include the regional director, a police station commander and the head of investigations.

Albert Sylaj, Zekaj’s brother-in-law, is suspected of murdering Zekaj with an axe in the presence of Zekaj’s son and Sylaj’s children and mother. The suspect fled the scene of the crime and was arrested two days later. On Wednesday, he was remanded in custody for 30 days by the Basic Court of Peja/Pec.

Zekaj’s ex-husband, Jeton Sylaj, who was detained after she reported him for domestic violence on Sunday, was remanded in custody for 30 days on Tuesday for violating a court order.

BIRN found that although Zekaj had warned the police three days before her murder that Albert Sylaj had threatened to kill her, he was interviewed only as a witness.

On October 22, 2026, Arlinda Zekaj stated to police that Albert Sylaj had said to her: “Go away or I’ll kill you.” Three days later, he allegedly carried out his threat. The now suspended prosecutor Nallbani Gacaferri was informed of the case.

On the same day, Zekaj sent a letter to the now suspended chief prosecutor Vucetaj, asking for an investigation against officials who were neglecting her case, warning that she feared for her life.

Hundreds of protesters rallied on Wednesday in Kosovo’s capital Pristina to demand institutional accountability, resignations and urgent measures against femicide and gender-based violence.

“The state’s hands are bloody, women’s murders are forewarned, how many more Arlindas,” protesters chanted as they marched from Pristina’s main square to the Ministry of Justice and then on a circuit of a number of other government buildings.

At Wednesday’s protest, activists, civil society groups and members of the public demanded the resignation of Justice Minister Donika Gervalla, Internal Affairs Minister Xhelal Svecla and Peja/Pec Mayor Gazmend Muhaxheri.

They also demanded the dismissal and prosecution of various justice system employees in Peja/Pec – chief prosecutor Lumturije Vucetaj; prosecutor Suada Rama Hamza; president of the basic court Shemsedin Haxhiaj; acting director of the welfare centre Shpresa Lukaj; and judge Migjen Kastrati, who had ruled that Zekaj and her ex-husband Jeton Sylaj could continue living in the same household if they maintained a distance of two metres from each other.

The protesters further demanded the provision of social housing for survivors of gender-based violence, the vetting of the justice system, the legalisation of self-defence for women, and for femicide be treated as a national emergency.

Activists have announced that the protest will continue on Thursday.

World.title: Change in Power in Serbia Brings Headaches for Central Europe’s Governments
World.content:
While crowds across Serbia celebrated the landslide victory of the protest Student List movement over Aleksandar Vucic’s regime, populist and pragmatic leaders across Central Europe have been left facing a major geopolitical headache.

The electoral victory of a grassroots protest movement over Belgrade’s deeply entrenched political-economic network came as a shock in Central European capitals, where at least a tight race – or another Vucic victory – was widely anticipated. It remains to be seen how effectively this experimental movement will assume power and fulfil its promises to root out state corruption. But one thing is already clear: the regime change in Belgrade will have far-reaching and potentially disruptive implications for Serbia’s relations with Central Europe.

Over the last decade, governments in Czechia, Hungary and Slovakia, despite their divergent political profiles, all systematically cultivated and deepened ties with Vucic’s regime. They did so primarily out of economic pragmatism and strategic interest, backed by personal and ideological affinities. Today, those carefully built networks are threatened by tectonic shifts in Serbian politics.

The contrast in immediate reactions – with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar congratulating the Student List while his Czech and Slovak counterparts, Andrej Babis and Robert Fico, remained silent – signals emerging friction across Central European capitals. However, Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia alike have developed deep ties with Vucic’s Serbia over the past decade. Ties that the new Serbian leadership will find hard to simply move past.

World.title: Serbia’s Public Broadcaster RTS Faces Uncertainty as Director-General Resigns
World.content:
Questions over the future of Serbia’s public broadcaster RTS and who will lead it emerged after director-general Manja Grcic bowed to pressure and resigned on Wednesday evening, after having ruled out stepping down just a day earlier.

Grcic’s resignation came amid mounting public pressure following the parliamentary elections on Sunday in which the Student List won an absolute majority against the outgoing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has been in power for 14 years.

The Student List issued an open letter to RTS on Tuesday identifying the removal of political influence from the broadcaster as one of its key priorities. The letter demanded the immediate resignation of the broadcaster’s management and news editors, accusing them of political bias and a failure to uphold professional standards.

In her resignation statement on Wednesday, Grcic acknowledged the growing demands for change. “I am aware that some members of the public see my remaining in office, even temporarily, as an obstacle to change,” Grcic said.

Branislav Klanscek, the president of RTS’s governing board, told the news service FoNet on Wednesday that the board would meet on Friday to consider appointing an acting director-general, denying reports that deputy director-general Dejan Jovanovic had already been appointed to this position. Before resigning, Grcic dismissed editor-in-chief of news Bojana Mladjenovic and proposed Borivoje Uskokovic as her replacement.

According to N1, a group of 70 RTS employees proposed popular television journalist and presenter Jovan Memedovic as acting director-general and Milica Janjic as marketing director.

Grcic, who was appointed in February 2026 for a five-year term, became the first woman to lead Serbia’s national public broadcaster.

Explaining her decision to step down, she said: “I made this decision after carefully considering the circumstances in which the public broadcaster is currently operating, believing that it is in the institution’s best interests to ensure the continuation of its work.”

In the same news bulletin announcing Grcic’s resignation, Student List parliamentary candidate Nemanja Karovic criticised RTS’s coverage of the student movement, accusing it of spreading “blatant falsehoods” and maintaining “a servile attitude towards the SNS regime, which was not one of cooperation, but complicity”.

“The student movement does not want to impose its own management, control or dominance over RTS, but wants the broadcaster to return to operating within the law, follow established procedures and serve citizens, regardless of who is in power,” Karovic said, adding that he counted on professional and honest RTS employees to help achieve this.

The student movement, which has protested against SNS’s government for nearly two years, has regularly criticised RTS’s reporting on the protests and the students’ demands. In April 2025, students blockaded RTS buildings in Belgrade for two weeks in a protest against the broadcaster’s coverage of the student demonstrations.

Grcic’s resignation followed changes at Radio Television of Vojvodina (RTV), Serbia’s provincial public broadcaster, which is separate from the RTS. On Monday, the day after the elections, RTV publicly apologised to viewers for years of one-sided and uncritical reporting.

During its 5 pm news bulletin, presenter Goran Eror acknowledged that RTV had failed to fulfil its public service role by withholding information and failing to ask critical questions. The apology coincided with the resignation of Nenad Cacic, acting editor-in-chief of RTV’s Channel 1.

World.title: The Invisible Mountain: A Toxic Wasteland at the End of Athens
World.content:
“We’re ashamed to say we live here,” says Gogontina Atzabou, the owner of an arts studio in Ano Liossia, who grew up in the neighbourhood. “I saw how, with the growth of the landfill, there was a growing sense of inferiority among the locals.” She trained and worked as a naval architect before giving it up for choreography, her true passion. Like many from Ano Liossia, she said, she faced racist prejudice when she left the neighbourhood – in her case, for university. “The other students immediately assumed I was Roma. This type of prejudice has left a lasting impression on everyone who grew up here.”

Fyli can often be a charming neighbourhood, with its low-rise housing and wide, open spaces at the foot of the mountain. But the landfill is never far from residents’ minds, or nostrils. “How can I describe the stench to you, so you can capture it on the microphone,” said Vangelis Lekatou, a pensioner I met in the central square of Ano Liossia. “In the summer, when the south wind blows, you can’t stand on your balcony. You have to go inside and close the windows.” The smell was particularly bad at night, when the landfill was covered with a layer of soil and compost. “Then the square empties out in five minutes – the young people have to leave the cafes, go elsewhere.”

Fires tend to break out on the landfill in hot, dry weather, spreading toxic fumes across the neighbourhood. The rotting waste generates huge quantities of flammable methane gas – a common problem with uncontrolled landfills. A UCLA study of methane-emitting landfills, drawing upon satellite imagery, ranked Fyli the 19th worst offender worldwide. A blaze in September 2020 was severe enough to trigger automated civil defence alerts to phones in the area, urging residents to stay inside and keep doors and windows sealed. Local residents worry about the health impact of all the smoke. Lekatou observed how cancer seemed to be everywhere: many around him had the disease or were living with someone that did. “The cancer patient at home – isn’t that our everyday reality here?”

While cancer mortality rates have risen across Attica, the rate in Western Attica has increased at double the rate elsewhere in the region, according to official data analysed by social scientist Dimitris Bourikos. Using numbers collected by the Hellenic Statistical Authority, ELSTAT, for the 20-year period between 1999 and 2019, Bourikos showed that there had been a 25 per cent increase in the mortality rate from cancers in Western Attica, a 1,000 square kilometre zone that is home to more than 150,000 people. Across the rest of Attica, the mortality rate from cancers had gone up by 14 percent over the same period.

World.title: Bonuses for Albanian Police on Protest Frontlines Spur Calls for Accountability
World.content:
Earlier this month, Prime Minister Edi Rama addressed the rank-and-file of the Albanian State Police, and promised a bonus for every one of them facing down protesters calling for his resignation.

The 2,500 euros per officer was “for all the resistance, all the sacrifice, all the courage and, above all, the dignity” Rama said they had shown in confronting the protests, which turned violent this month.

Later the same day, Rama’s government allocated 759 million lek, roughly 7.7 million euros, to reward 2,821 officers.

Security experts, however, have questioned the message such bonuses send, not least because for the past two weeks the State Police has deployed tear gas, water cannon, batons and rubber bullets against the young protesters, many of them students.

World.title: Security Services Must Be Reformed to Dismantle Serbia’s Mafia State
World.content:
The student-led electoral list won a landslide victory in Serbia’s parliamentary elections on October 25, 2026, despite a highly uneven playing field. According to preliminary results, the Student List is set to secure around 140 seats out of 250 in the National Assembly, giving it an absolute majority and a strong mandate for change.

This provides a strong political foundation for far-reaching reforms – a foundation that the Democratic Opposition of Serbia, the broad coalition of diverse political parties that ousted Slobodan Milosevic’s authoritarian regime in 2000, did not enjoy.

This is where triumphalism must end. During its 14 years in power, Aleksandar Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) profoundly undermined the country’s security apparatus. Rather than serve the public, the security apparatus was turned into a protector and enforcer of the SNS’s power and illicit activities. Urgent reforms are needed.

World.title: Kosovo Protesters Demand Ministerial, Judicial Resignations After Latest Femicide
World.content:
Hundreds of protesters rallied on Wednesday in Kosovo’s capital Pristina to demand institutional accountability, resignations and urgent measures against femicide and gender-based violence.

The eruption of anger came after a woman, Arlinda Zekaj, was murdered on Sunday evening in Peja/Pec after the police accompanied her home from the police station where she had reported domestic abuse by her husband.

“The state’s hands are bloody, women’s murders are forewarned, how many more Arlindas,” protesters chanted as they marched from Pristina’s main square to the Ministry of Justice and then on a circuit of a number of other government buildings.

Arlinda Zekaj was murdered on Sunday evening in the village of Vitomirica, near Peja/Pec, shortly after returning home from the police station. Three days earlier, she had asked the local prosecution to intervene to protect her against violent attack.

World.title: Serbia Raises Terror Alert After Attack on Israeli Embassy
World.content:
Serbia’s caretaker Interior Minister Ivica Dacic announced on Wednesday that the terrorism threat level had been raised to high alert after an attack in front of the Israeli embassy in Belgrade the night before, in which a gendarme was injured and the assailant killed.

Dacic said that the measures include tighter security checks and increased police deployments at critical infrastructure sites and places where large numbers of people gather.

These measures are being imposed three days after the snap parliamentary elections that led to defeat of the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, and its strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic.

The announcement, published on the Serbian Interior Ministry’s website, followed what Dacic described as a terrorist attack on a gendarme guarding the Israeli embassy in Belgrade shortly after midnight.

“An unidentified minor, believed to be from Sabac, attacked a member of the gendarmerie with two knives while shouting ‘Allahu Akbar’,” Dacic said.

Dacic added that the gendarme shot and killed the attacker in self-defence, but sustained minor injuries, including a knife wound to his face.

“The investigation is ongoing and all the details will be known during the night. Given that a terrorist attack took place on our territory, as the interior minister responsible for security, I have raised the terrorism threat level to the highest possible level, namely red alert,” he said.

The final results of Sunday’s elections still haven’t been published, but according to the latest preliminary results from the Republic Electoral Commission, the opposition Student List won 52.85 per cent and the SNS-led list won 39.1 per cent. The results mean that the Student List will have an absolute majority in the assembly.

The election results sparked two days of celebrations across Serbia, with large crowds gathering in public spaces to celebrate the victory.

Serbia’s caretaker government issued a statement on Tuesday evening in which it stressed that, while the right to peaceful assembly, freedom of expression and publicly voicing demands are guaranteed by the constitution, exercising these rights cannot justify violence, threats, intimidation or the imposition of decisions that must be made through legally prescribed procedures.

The Israeli Foreign Ministry said in a post on X that an attempted terrorist attack had taken place near the Embassy in Belgrade, stating that the attacker had been “neutralised” by Serbian police.

It added that no embassy personnel were injured and that the embassy was closed at the time of the incident, which occurred late at night.

World.title: Croatia Plans Demanding Navy Modernisation
World.content:
October the 29th, 2026 – Croatia is currently planning navy modernisation, with Rijeka’s 3 Maj shipyard wanting to take full control over this demanding project.

The President of the Management Board of the 3 Maj shipyard, Roko Vuletić, said that the situation on the EU market is once again favourable for shipbuilding after very many years. Poslovni reports that Andrija Ljulj, from the University of Defence and Security “Dr. Franjo Tuđman” spoke to representatives of the shipbuilding industry recently. In doing so, he presented the long-term development plan and projects of the Croatian Navy (HRM) and invited them to get involved and participate in the process of modernisation.

a boost for croatian shipbuilding

The first and key project of the Croatian Navy is the procurement of two multipurpose corvettes, whose construction and outfitting is planned from 2025 to 2028, which is a short deadline for such a demanding project, Ljulj said at a conference entitled “Perspective of the Development of Croatian Shipbuilding in Kvarner” at the Faculty of Engineering in Rijeka. He hopes that the deadline will be met, with possible minor delays. Regarding the current status of the project, after obtaining information from 23 companies from around the world, and after collecting initial information, the Ministry of Defence (MORH) conducted an analysis of which of those projects could meet the requirements.

After the selection of potential partners, in the second round of the tender final offers will be sought from those selected, which is expected very soon, and the decision is made by the Minister of Defence, he said.

An unfinished project of coastal patrol vessels was also presented, in which two ships were built, and three remained unfinished after Brodosplit ran into financial problems. Captain of the battleship Andrija Ljulj mentioned that there were problems with financing and the increase in the cost of equipment, but also that the owner of the shipyard may not have been so open to cooperation in which that project would still be completed. MORH has taken legal steps to protect itself, and until the court proceedings are completed those three ships, finished to about 45 percent, will not be completed, he said, adding that it is possible that they will be finished at Brodosplit but also elsewhere.

croatian navy modernisation implies modern unmanned systems

The project of a mine countermeasures ship was abandoned and a switch was made to the procurement of unmanned systems for mine countermeasures, detection, identification and destruction of sea mines, which will be installed on the HRM ship Faust Vrančić. Given that this ship is quite old, the acquisition of a new ship of up to 60 metres is also being considered.

One of the projects in the initial phase is the equipping of the HRM with new landing assault ships, and four such ships are planned from 2029 to 2034, Ljulj said.

The fifth project is the development and production of maritime surface unmanned systems. He said that work is also being done on appropriate new training programmes and that the next step would be the realisation of concrete projects through cooperation with industry and scientific institutions. He added that individual companies have already presented their solutions. Regarding the overhaul and maintenance of ships, he noted that they were mainly carried out in the shipyards in Šibenik and Trogir and that after the modernisation of the HRM this part should also be expanded. In the discussion, it could be heard that the profession is ready, that there are technologies in design and in execution and that the processes that precede them need to be accelerated.

the rijeka shipyard seeks to take control

The President of the Management Board of the 3 Maj shipyard, Roko Vuletić, said that the situation on the EU market is once again favourable for shipbuilding after many years. This Rijeka shipyard has two slipways, and although it does not build the ship in its entirety, more than 85 percent of the workers are from the local pool, and for about 10 percent of the jobs the customer has to engage help from abroad, he said.

He pointed out that they have applied for the announced construction of two multipurpose corvettes for the Croatian Navy, assessing at the same time that it will be difficult to meet the deadline until 2028. He also mentioned the renewal of the domestic passenger fleet and Jadrolinija’s announcement related to the renewal of the fleet and green technologies and the construction of four ships with alternative propulsion, in which the Rijeka shipyard also wants to participate. He added that it is necessary to think in a timely manner about charging stations for these ships as well. Vuletić emphasised that in Rijeka he recognised positive energy, a kind of last oasis that wants a shipyard, from local authorities to the public, and highlighted the strong presence of engineering offices and cooperating companies that work for the whole world, as well as the merits of the faculty.

In just a few months, the Rijeka shipyard plans to launch a brand new polar cruiser for the company Scenic, and besides that they are preparing several projects of floating piers and small yachts, while serious preparations are underway for the upcoming tenders, Vuletić said. Other shipbuilding and design companies from across the wider Kvarner area also presented themselves at the aforementioned conference, including the Viktor Lenac Shipyard, Rheinmetall Naval Systems, AITAC, Navis Consult and others.

World.title: Omiš Residents Left Without Answers: “I Don’t Know Who to Turn to”
World.content:
October the 29th, 2026 – Over two months after the catastrophic fire, Omiš residents are still trying to recover from the tragedy that claimed six lives and left behind around €100 million in damage.

Behind the scorched earth, destroyed homes and business premises remain the still bewildered people who, in just a few hours, lost everything they had been building for years. Lucija Zderic reports for Index that while some of the injured are still fighting for their lives, and the cause of one of the worst fire tragedies in Croatia remains unknown, those who lost their homes and property in the fire are fighting their own battle to return to normal life.

“i just don’t know who to turn to”

Marina Ozretić is one of those who lost everything they had been building for years in the fire. She found temporary accommodation with relatives, and is still waiting for concrete answers about the reconstruction of her house. “The situation is the same today as it was after the fire. No one can tell me what I should do or who to turn to. I don’t know whether it’s the City, the state, the County or somebody else. I can contact the City, but when I do, they tell me they know nothing. I don’t know what the situation is with my case or what I should specifically do, and financially I am not in a position to rebuild the house myself,” says Marina Ozretić.

Recalling the evening the fire broke out, she says she made the decision to flee herself, aware of the danger that threatened her. She believes that if she had not left the house in time, she herself would have become one of the victims of the firestorm. “If I hadn’t thought with my own head and if I hadn’t started running myself, I would probably have burned together with the house. If I had stayed ten minutes longer, I wouldn’t have survived,” Marina recalls.

Besides the lost home, what weighs on her most is that even after two months she still doesn’t know how she will rebuild the house or whether she will receive help. “Maybe for them this is a short time, given that such a situation has never happened before, but for me it’s a lot. I need to see somewhere that something is moving so that I can have hope for a better tomorrow,” says Marina.

“there’s been no progress”

After the fire a large clean-up action was organised, volunteers stepped in to help, and neighbours joined forces to ease one another’s first days after the tragedy. But the initial wave of solidarity gradually subsided, the city’s capabilities proved limited, and state financial aid got stuck in bureaucracy. People were thus left relying on each other, but that help, as Goran Lović tells us, is no longer enough.

“More than two months have passed since the fire, and we are currently in a very difficult situation. It’s not easy for people. They have been left without houses, their houses have been charred or burned down, and there is no financial aid. People are in shock and no longer know who to turn to. They have simply been driven to the wall. The state has not paid people any funds for reconstruction.

At the beginning we started arranging fire-fighting paths and cleaning, but the works have decreased. We have come to a wall because we cannot saw on private land, and we cannot independently intervene on state land either. Property-legal relations are tangled, and we don’t have an appropriate legal framework that would enable cleaning and remediation,” says Goran Lović, owner of a beach bar that was hit by the fire in the Lokva Rogoznica area.

He adds that in the remediation of the burned area more concrete help is missing from institutions that should play an important role in this, such as Croatian Waters, Croatian Roads and Croatian Forests. “The most important thing is how we will rebuild the area and how we will prevent this from happening again. When will Croatian Waters come and install hydrants? When will Croatian Roads clear the terrain so that trees don’t fall along the road? We have a problem how to bring life back to our area. These large state services have so many employees, and they are not able to send people who would come here and do the job. We have already been in grief for months. Not everything has even been cleaned yet, let alone that anything has been replanted. Everything that has been done so far is the result of the voluntary work of citizens. Time is passing, we are late, and in five months the new season begins,” says Lović.

residents are demanding answers regarding the investigation and the failed early warning system

Even 75 days after the fire in Omiš its cause is still not known. The police launched a criminal investigation and seized surveillance camera footage, among other things those handed over by Goran Lović, whose restaurant is located near the place where the fire broke out.

Lović suspects that the fire was set, but the investigation has not yet been completed. The prolonged uncertainty among residents, he says, is causing growing unrest and anger because, according to the information reaching them, there is no visible progress in establishing responsibility. “Omiš has been a very sad city since then. People’s grief has not yet passed, and now they are already a little angry because nothing is happening in the process of finding the culprit for this event, at least nothing is being communicated about it to the people and the public,” believes Julija Hrstić. The non-activation of the SRUUK, a system worth around eight million euros, has raised numerous questions about why the population was not timely warned of the danger and whether some of the tragic consequences could have been prevented thereby.

“We want answers as to why the SRUUK was not activated. That interests many people. The system was activated during the fire on Brač, and why not in Omiš? The largest number of people died and were injured in Mala Luka, which is actually distant from the place of Lokva Rogoznica where the fire started. If action had been taken as it should have been, the question is what would have happened. Everyone can grieve and ask themselves, but those people are no longer here.”

the tragedy has claimed six lives so far

The fire that initially broke out in the area of Lokva Rogoznica claimed six lives, and dozens of people were injured. Among the victims were retired Omiš firefighter Drago Lelas (79) and seasonal workers Dragana Antešević (34) and Katica Nikolić (58). The last victim died in the Split hospital, more than two months after the fire. As Hrstić says, the restoration of nature and homes will be a long and difficult process, but it will be hardest for those who will return to their houses in which their loved ones will no longer be. That is precisely why, she says, Omiš and the people who went through this tragedy must not be forgotten.

“From one family three people died. A man lost his wife, father and mother. He is still recovering. How strong you have to be in the head to continue living for the sake of the children, I don’t even know myself. This is a tragedy that hit Omiš. Besides what burned, human lives were lost. For many families nothing will ever be the same again and that must not be forgotten and neglected.” For Omiš residents, the fire did not end on the day the flames themselves were finally extinguished. For some, it left totally destroyed homes, and for others losses that cannot be compensated. While reconstruction and answers about the causes of the tragedy are awaited, the question remains how much more time will pass before life begins to be rebuilt again in the burned area.

World.title: Top Gear Tests Out New Tourbillon, Praises Rimac and Croatia
World.content:
October the 29th, 2026 – Mate Rimac hosted the Top Gear team in the magnificent new Bugatti Tourbillon, which resulted in praise for Rimac and Croatia.

British Top Gear journalist Ollie Marriage was among the first to experience the new Bugatti Tourbillon on the road, sitting in the passenger seat while Mate Rimac was at the wheel. Poslovni reports that after a drive along scenic French roads and bends in the foothills of the Vosges, he made no secret of his enthusiasm. He was particularly impressed by the naturally aspirated V16 engine, whose sound and character, he claims, represent a complete departure from previous Bugattis. After just a few powerful accelerations, Marriage concluded that he had never experienced anything like it. The pivotal moment comes at around 3,000 rpm, when the engine completely changes character, and the sound becomes increasingly intense as it approaches the 9,000 rpm limit. Rimac, meanwhile, was thoroughly enjoying himself behind the wheel. At one point, after a particularly strong acceleration, he even admitted that the Tourbillon might even be too fast.

The V16 that completely changed Bugatti

Unlike the Chiron, which used a massive W16 with four turbochargers, the Tourbillon has a naturally aspirated 8.3-litre V16 developed in collaboration with Cosworth. The petrol engine alone develops around 1,000 hp, while three electric motors add another 800 hp. Marriage points out that it is precisely the character of the engine that is the biggest change. While the Chiron felt like a giant machine that brutally overpowered everything in front of it, the Tourbillon leaves the impression of a much livelier and more explosive car.

He was particularly delighted by the sound. At lower revs the V16 has a deep and powerful tone, then begins to resemble two V8 engines, and at the top of the rev range it produces an almost racing scream. Rimac insisted during the drive that the journalist lower the windows so he could hear the engine without muffling. The experience then became even more intense, and Marriage concluded that among the engines he has experienced so far, only the V12 from the Gordon Murray T.50 can offer a comparable sonic performance. Interestingly, Bugatti did not artificially amplify the sound. Rimac explained that the engine sounds exactly as it was developed, without additional sound channels or electronic aids.

zagreb will hold a key role in production

“The car will be produced in Molsheim, but everything starts at Rimac’s campus in Zagreb. Most of the engineering is done in Croatia; the main part of the work is carried out in Zagreb, and even the painting. Final assembly is done in Molsheim, where a completely new production facility has been built,” writes TopGear, as reported by Tportal. Rimac explained to the journalist that Bugatti wants to reduce dependence on external suppliers and take over as many production processes as possible within its own organisation. Such an approach should speed up production and shorten customer waiting times, which currently exceed three years. Interest in the first 250 planned examples is already so great that Bugatti’s problem is not finding buyers, but producing enough cars.

a faster feeling than the nevera…

One of the most interesting moments of the drive came when Rimac compared the Tourbillon with his own Nevera. Although the Nevera is faster in acceleration to 200 km/h according to factory data, Rimac believes that the Tourbillon subjectively feels even more brutal. Marriage agrees with him and explains that the big difference is created precisely by the sound of the V16 engine, which further amplifies the feeling of acceleration. The Tourbillon reaches 200 km/h in approximately five seconds, while the Nevera needs around 4.4 seconds for the same task. But the numbers, the journalist concludes, cannot convey the intensity of the experience.

It is particularly interesting that the driver can completely switch off the electric part of the powertrain and use only the naturally aspirated V16. The Tourbillon then becomes a rear-wheel-drive car with approximately 1,000 hp. Rimac also insisted that the car must be able to slide the rear wheels in a controlled manner. When the engineers explained to him that drifting is not a traditional Bugatti characteristic, he replied that from now on it would be.

Marriage also found a few criticisms. He was not entirely satisfied with the shape of the seat backrest, and the passenger does not have a sufficiently practical armrest. The cabin is very narrow, and the seats cannot be moved forward or backward, only adjusted for height and backrest angle. Nevertheless, most of these details remained in the background because of the impression the car leaves. He was particularly fascinated by the instrument panel made up of approximately 2,000 mechanical parts, which despite its complexity weighs only 600 grams. It is made like a luxury mechanical watch and represents a complete departure from huge digital screens.

After the drive, the journalist concluded that the Tourbillon is more agile, changes direction more lively and provides a more direct feeling of connection with the road than its predecessors. At the same time it remains exceptionally stable, although it has probably lost some of the refinement for which the Chiron was known. The biggest change, Marriage believes, is not in power or top speed, but in philosophy. Bugatti is no longer trying only to make the fastest car in the world. Under Rimac’s leadership it wants to create a car that will give the driver the most intense experience possible.
