World.title: Azerbaijan's female judoka wins historic Judo Grand Slam gold in Abu Dhabi
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 29. Konul Aliyeva, a member of the Azerbaijani national team, has achieved a historic result at the Judo Grand Slam tournament held in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

This was reported by the Azerbaijan Judo Federation.

"Competing in the 48 kg weight category, our judoka defeated all her opponents to win the tournament. With this, Konul Aliyeva has made history as the first Azerbaijani female judoka to become a champion at a Grand Slam event," the report noted.

According to the report, Aliyeva, who began her campaign in the Round of 16, first defeated Ulbusin Khakimova from Uzbekistan, followed by a victory over Amber Gersjes of the Netherlands in the quarterfinals, and French judoka Mélanie Vieu-Clément in the semifinals.

"In the decisive bout, Konul Aliyeva faced Merve Azak from Türkiye; she outperformed her opponent to secure the gold medal.

This also marks the first gold medal Konul Aliyeva has won on the senior-level World Judo Tour," the report added.

World.title: Why President Ilham Aliyev skips the OTS Summit in Türkiye
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 29. For a month now, a vicious campaign has been underway in Türkiye against Azerbaijan, its leader, the Azerbaijani people and the state.

In fact, this process began earlier. Over the past three years, Azerbaijan has been repeatedly targeted, albeit with occasional lulls. The main issue has been Azerbaijan's cooperation with Israel. Those behind the campaign believe Azerbaijan should shape and conduct its foreign policy and economic relations according to their wishes.

This is a demeaning approach to Azerbaijan that denies its independence. It is a completely distorted interpretation of the principle of “one nation, two states.”

At the same time, numerous facts about Türkiye's own cooperation with Israel have come to light, and none of them has been officially refuted. Under these circumstances, why should the accusations against Azerbaijan be taken seriously?

The campaign flared up again with particular intensity in early October, using as a pretext the fact that an Azerbaijani representative did not leave the hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's address at a UN session. Shortly afterward, following a decision by Azerbaijan's Cabinet of Ministers concerning a standard school uniform, the campaign became more vicious and repugnant than ever before, almost turning into a trending national issue in Türkiye's information space.

During this period, Azerbaijan and its leadership were subjected to an unprecedented torrent of criticism and insults. Even during the 30 years of confrontation with Armenia, such degrading rhetoric had never been directed at Azerbaijan on this scale.

Azerbaijan had expected such an attack from Iran, but instead suffered the harshest blow from Türkiye, a country it considered brotherly. Those delivering this blow were the ruling AKP and its supporters among Islamist and Nurcu groups.

Six rallies were held outside Azerbaijan's embassies in Ankara and Istanbul, with participants voicing serious accusations and insults.

Turkish media and social media distorted the issue of the hijab and carried it into the Arab world's information space, becoming a major driving force behind the anti-Azerbaijan campaign there.

Official Ankara intervened very late in the process and only then tried to take some action. Had these steps been taken in time, and had Ankara avoided not only incitement but also a passive, bystander stance, matters would never have reached this point.

As a result of the deliberate and sustained campaigns to demonize Azerbaijan, an unhealthy attitude toward the country and an unfavorable atmosphere have taken shape in Türkiye.

Reminder

In July 2024, the President of Türkiye did not attend the informal summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Shusha. The reason was that he attended the football match between the Turkish and Dutch national teams at the time.

Furthermore, Erdoğan did not attend the World Urban Forum held in Azerbaijan in May 2026 or the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in October.

Naturally, both objective and subjective factors determine whether a head of state attends an event in another country. However, one should not overlook the fact that reciprocity also matters in diplomacy.

On October 24, Azerbaijan hosted the opening of the FIFA U-15 World Championship and Festival for the first time in its history. The event will conclude on October 30.

None of this means that Azerbaijan is withdrawing from the OTS or scaling back its activities within the organization. Azerbaijan is one of its founding members and has made considerable efforts to develop the organization and expand its activities. It will continue working to advance the OTS.

Taking all these factors into account, it can be argued that the Azerbaijani president, Ilham Aliyev, made the right decision by not attending the OTS summit in Türkiye.

World.title: Spain begins three days of mourning as train crash death toll reaches 74
World.content:
Spain has begun three days of mourning after its second high-speed rail collision this year killed 74 people.

One of Europe's deadliest train disasters this century has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain's rail network after the transport minister said an "error" and "inexplicable circumstances" caused the crash.

During a visit to the crash site, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faces a general election on November 29, pledged to establish the cause of the crash.

"We are working day and night not only to support the victims' families, but also to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again," he said.

Cranes help remove the wreckage of the trains involved in the collision. (Reuters: Ana Beltran)

The collision happened in the central region of Castilla La Mancha on Wednesday morning when a train from state operator Renfe rear-ended a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.

Emergency services combed through the wreckage overnight in search of victims on the key line that links Madrid with the southern city of Seville.

Sniffer dogs and thermal drones were deployed at the crash site a few kilometres from the village of Urda on Thursday to search for bodies, the regional government said.

Rescue personnel worked overnight, using sniffer dogs and drones in the search of victims and survivors. (Reuters: Ana Beltran)

The death toll was raised from 68 to 74, and dozens of people remain in hospital.

Minute of silence observed

A minute of silence was observed at midday on Thursday across the country, including by lawmakers outside Parliament, rail workers and union leaders in Madrid's main train station.

Flags flew at half-mast on public buildings in Spain, with official ceremonies and public events cancelled or scaled back.

Spain's Minister of Transport, Oscar Puente said an automatic control system had interfered with rail operations just before the crash. (Reuters: Juan Barbosa)

On Wednesday transport Minister Oscar Puente, who faces calls to resign, said an automatic control system shut down on 69 kilometres of track, causing all trains on the stretch to be stopped, including the Renfe train.

But the control centre decided to "resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable," Mr Puente said.

The Renfe train travelled 25 kilometres on the stretch before striking the the back of the Iryo train.

The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it" he added.

Witnesses recount collision

Josimar Medina from Peru is holidaying in Spain with his girlfriend, and said he was sleeping on the Renfe train when "I woke up and I was in the air."

Pablo Mejia escaped with injuries to his head, telling AFP that a last-minute change of seat saved his life.

Rail crash survivors tell of horror Residents of a rural village in central Spain race to provide help after the deadliest rail disaster in Europe in more than a decade.

Wearing a bloodstained grey jumper and holding his tattered suitcase, he recounted "a very strong hit."

"A lot of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos,

"I think I've been born again," Mr Meija said.

Families in shock

A school near the crash site in Urda is being used as a temporary support centre, for relatives to enquire about their loved ones.

Two people waiting for updates outside a support centre for relatives of missing train passengers. (AFP: Oscar Del Pozo)

Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said "long and hard hours" were in store because "every person will manage it in their own way."

"We have people who are in shock, who haven't taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated," Ms Garcia said.

A man waits to hear news about a relative following the incident near Urda, in Spain. (Reuters: Susana Vera)

Jose Miguel Fernandez works as a parish priest in the area and joined emergency services in offering support to victims' families.

"Many of them were calm, others were nervous and desperate. They wanted to know straight away and get news" he said.

Train staff strike

In January, two high-speed trains collided in the southern region of Andalusia, after one derailed and crossed onto the adjacent track, killing 46 people.

In its wake Spain's government faced heavy criticism over its management of the country's railways.

The investigation into the January incident is ongoing.

Groups of protesters and police face off outside Spain's Ministry of Transportation during a demonstration to demand the government's resignation. (Reuters: Juan Barbosa)

Train workers held a strike on Thursday that was planned before the crash, to demand the government carry out safety improvements to the rail services.

Unions say changes were promised after the first deadly collision in January.

Union leaders questioned the why the minister had placed blame on one controller, and criticised the leaking of the control room's conversations to the media.

"The focus should not be on if there was a human error, but rather what is wrong with the system," said Pepa Páez, the general secretary of the railway sector of CCOO, the largest trade union in Spain .

"What situations must be improved so that if there is a human error we don't find ourselves in this situation," he said.

World.title: Russian drone strike on Ukrainian train platform kills 14
World.content:
A Russian drone has slammed into a busy platform at a railway station in Ukraine's Dnipro killing at least 14 people in what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called a "horrific" attack that demands a response from Kyiv's allies.

The strike came as Ukraine and Russia strive to uphold a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky -- under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages.

The truce was holding into its third day, both countries said, with the Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets announcing that he had "set out with the Ukrainian delegation towards Oleshky" through Belarus and Russia.

But elsewhere, Moscow continued to pummel Ukraine.

Images released by Ukrainian emergency services showed bodies scattered across the platform. (Reuters)

The strike at the Dnipro train station hit a platform "where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing", Mr Zelenskyy said.

By early afternoon, Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha said the death toll from the strike had risen to 14.

Another 14 had been wounded, he said, adding that six of them were in severe condition after suffering "multiple shrapnel wounds", including an 11-year-old boy and a man who had "both legs amputated".

Mr Zelenskyy slammed the attack as "horrific" and insisted that "sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues".

Images released by Ukrainian emergency services showed bodies on the platform, rescuers helping victims to safety and two burnt-out passenger trains with their windows shattered.

French President Emmanuel Macron reacted with outrage to the attack, stressing the need for "far more than a localised ceasefire" like the one in Oleshky.

"It is intolerable that Russia continues to reject all proposals to this end, choosing instead to pursue escalation and target civilians," he said.

Zelenskyy slams sanctions relief

Russia has fired drones on trains across Ukraine since the first days of its 2022 invasion -- destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing several railway workers.

Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three jet-powered drones in a daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.

Trump's threats to Ukraine It is hard to see Donald Trump's shifting position on Ukraine as a clear strategic change, and not one driven principally by soaring fuel prices ahead of the US mid-term elections.

In the aftermath of the attack, Mr Zelenskyy refreshed his criticism of a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to ease some sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel onto global markets.

"How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and the energy sector, instead of de-escalating," he asked.

At least six others were killed across Ukraine in separate Russian attacks, according to local officials.

Two teenagers killed

Another Russian strike on the city of Chernihiv killed two teenaged girls. (Reuters)

A strike on the city centre of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded nearly two dozen others, including four children, the head of the city's military administration, Dmytro Bryzhynsky, said.

A drone also slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing three and wounding several -- including a six-year-old -- the local governor said.

Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.

The Kremlin earlier this week vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under US mediation.

As Russia-Ukraine war changes, Zelenskyy could be 'losing a strong partner' Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has taken on a different complexion lately, and it has shone a light on Kyiv's strained relations with the White House.

Russia and Ukraine are to meet next month with US envoys to discuss ways to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II, with no firm dates set for the talks yet.

Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.

Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.

Ukraine and its allies say ceding ground to Moscow would be tantamount to a capitulation and leave Kyiv vulnerable to future Russian attacks.

AFP

World.title: Triple-murderer Erin Patterson to learn her appeal fate today
World.content:
Triple-murderer Erin Patterson will learn within hours whether she has won her appeal against her convictions.

Patterson is serving three life sentences with a non-parole period of 33 years after a jury found her guilty of murdering her parents-in-laws Don and Gail Patterson, along with Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson, in 2023.

The victims had been invited to lunch at Patterson's Leongatha home, in Victoria's south-east, where she served them death cap mushrooms inside beef Wellington.

Patterson, 52, was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Mrs Wilkinson's husband, Korumburra church pastor Ian Wilkinson, who survived after falling gravely ill from the poisoning.

Don Patterson (left), Heather Wilkinson (centre) and Gail Patterson (right) died after consuming a beef Wellington meal laced with death cap mushrooms. (ABC News)

Patterson lodged an appeal against the jury's verdicts, claiming there was a substantial miscarriage of justice during her trial, which was held in the regional town of Morwell in 2025.

Patterson's lawyers told a two-day appeal hearing in August there had been a "catastrophic" accommodation bungle during the deliberations over the verdicts, which saw the jury staying at the same hotel as the main police witness for the prosecution, as well as two members of the prosecution team.

The defence made lengthy submissions about the risk of the jury being influenced by any direct and indirect contact with the parties, even as simple as a jury member seeing one of the others through a hotel window.

It also argued that prosecutor Nanette Roger SC's cross-examination of Patterson was "unfair and oppressive".

Patterson's lawyers told the court the five-day questioning included, at times, terse exchanges which posed a risk of creating improper inferences in the jury members' minds.

They also accused Dr Rogers of changing the prosecution case during her closing addressing by implying there was a motive for the murders after telling the jury there was no evidence of a motive when she was opening the case.

Prosecution's fight to lock up Patterson for life

When handing down Patterson's life sentence, Justice Christopher Beale set a 33-year non-parole period.

That means Patterson could be released back into the community when she's in her early 80s.

Erin Patterson is not expected to attend today's appeal decision in person. (AAP Image: James Ross)

The prosecution's appeal against that minimum term focused on the severity of Patterson's crimes and the conditions she would face in jail.

The team argued that a life sentence without parole was the only option given the number of Patterson's victims, the amount of planning that went into the deadly lunch, the continuation of the offending by not revealing the poisoning to medical staff when there was a chance to treat the victims, and a lack of remorse displayed by Patterson.

The prosecution also argued Justice Beale should not have made an allowance for Patterson facing years in protective custody because of her notoriety.

The appeal court heard Patterson had access to a library, recreation centre, exercise yard and treadmill, had regular video calls with her children and engaged in hobbies such as crocheting.

What could happen today

Despite already hearing the appeal arguments, Court of Appeal judges Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd must first rule whether Patterson's case has met the requirements to be granted leave to appeal.

The Court of Appeal heard two days of arguments in August by Erin Patterson's lawyers and the prosecution. (ABC News: Karen Percy)

That means there are four possible outcomes for Patterson's appeal:

The court may rule leave has not been granted to appeal, which means Patterson's appeal was judged to be without merit before her detailed arguments were more deeply considered.

Leave to appeal may be granted but the case may be dismissed, meaning the judges were not convinced by Patterson's lawyers that there had been a miscarriage of justice.

Leave to appeal may be granted and the judges may announce that "the appeal has been upheld". That would mean that Patterson has won her appeal against her convictions. The judges may then order the entire trial be held again.

Leave may be granted, the appeal upheld but the judges may decide, based on the evidence presented to support Patterson's submissions, that the jury's verdicts should be quashed and Patterson be acquitted of all charges and released from prison.

If a retrial is ordered or the court acquits Patterson, the prosecution's appeal against the sentence is no longer relevant.

Listen to The Case of podcast | Mushroom Lunch Mushroom Lunch continues to follow all proceedings related to Erin Patterson's triple murder conviction in July 2025.

If Patterson loses her appeal, the judges will then turn to the prosecution's appeal.

If that appeal is dismissed, the original sentence of life imprisonment with a minimum term of 33 years set by Justice Beale remains in place.

If the appeal is upheld, the Court of Appeal will announce Patterson's new sentence.

Due to the large media and public interest in the case, the decision will be handed down in Court 1 of the Victorian Supreme Court, not in the usual Court of Appeal building.

Patterson is not expected to attend today's hearing in person.

World.title: Russell Brand's wife tells court actor's promiscuity left her 'heartbroken'
World.content:
Russell Brand's wife has told a London court the British entertainer's promiscuity left her "heartbroken" and caused their relationship to end years before they married.

The actor and comedian is on trial in London's Southwark Crown Court charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The 51-year-old is accused of committing the crimes against six women in the United Kingdom between 1999 and 2009.

Brand tells jury friends won't defend him over sex crime allegations Russell Brand told the court he did not commit the crimes and believed sexual consent was "fundamental, essential, necessary" and "more important than sex itself".

On Wednesday, Mr Brand told the jury himself no friends, acquaintances or colleagues were prepared to give evidence in his defence and had not touched him "with a bargepole" since the allegations became public.

But on Thursday, Laura Brand took the stand, telling the jury her husband of nearly 10 years was a "very caring" sexual partner.

Ms Brand was 19 when she met the then-31-year-old Mr Brand after his show "Shame" at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe in August 2006.

Ms Brand is the sister of well-known British model and television presenter Kirsty Gallacher, which the court heard Mr Brand knew "within moments" of the pair meeting.

The jury heard the two exchanged phone numbers, met up the next day and started dating shortly after.

"I felt entirely cared for and looked after by Russell," she told the jury, referring to their sex life together.

Brand nodded along with his wife's evidence in court. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

Laura Brand tells court she wanted monogamy

Ms Brand told the jury she was left "heartbroken" when the relationship ended a few months later, in February 2007.

"I was aware that he liked women and I was aware towards the latter part of the year that he was engaging with other women," she told the court.

"I was not interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people.

" It was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous. "

The pair started dating again in 2015, Mrs Brand told the court, before marrying in 2017.

Russell Brand's wife Laura has accompanied the actor to court on almost every day of the trial. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

"Russell, my husband, is caring, he's kind, he's a wonderful father," she told the jury.

"I feel very seen by him; I love him very much.

"Our relationship has always been about honesty."

The jury heard after the birth of the pair's first child, Mr Brand went on an American talk show and described his relationship with his wife while they were going out.

The court heard that on the program Mr Brand said they "loved each other very much" but "I was in a phase where I thought the world was an amusement park full of orgasms".

Ms Brand told the court she probably did not watch the program but did not dispute the comments.

The court also heard that Ms Brand told a podcast in 2020 that when the pair rekindled their relationship years later, Mr Brand was "so different to how I knew him before".

Under cross examination, Ms Brand said she did not know her now-husband during some of the period of his alleged offending.

Mr Brand nodded along to much of his wife's evidence in court and at times closed his eyes, playing with the red scarf he was wearing.

The jury also heard from two of Mr Brand’s former partners.

A dance teacher who had a three-year relationship with Mr Brand from 1996, described the comedian as “gentle, warm, kind and adventurous” despite having acquired a “bad boy reputation”.

In a statement read to the court, the woman said when she was with Mr Brand, he was very different to the person he was in front of an audience.

"At home he was more introspective, gentle and loving," she said, but went on to say their relationship ended after she felt she could no longer trust him to be faithful.

Another previous partner, who met Mr Brand in 1999 at an English school in London, said the actor was “undoubtedly promiscuous” but described him as "very loving, thoughtful, patient and charming".

She said they never engaged in sexual activity without consent.

The trial continues.

World.title: WA Labor MP vows to 'vigorously defend' US lawsuit over $1m loan
World.content:
A Western Australian MP embroiled in a legal dispute over a million-dollar loan in the United States insists everything he did was above board.

Jags Krishnan has been the Labor member for the southern suburbs seat of Riverton since 2021.

The Nine network yesterday revealed he had been named in a lawsuit in the New Jersey District Court.

In a court document, seen by the ABC, Kenyan Consulting LLC is suing Dr Krishnan, his wife and three companies for breach of contract and unjust enrichment over an alleged failure to pay back a $US655,000 ($930,500) loan plus interest.

Dr Krishnan has engaged Perth legal heavyweight Martin Bennett to defend his case.

Dr Krishnan has engaged the services of Perth legal heavyweight Martin Bennett. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Dr Krishnan said he would also be suing a representative of Kenyan Consulting and another person for defamation.

Mr Bennett said he represented both Dr Krishnan and his wife, and that both would fully defend the case.

"I'll vigorously defend my position in court," Dr Krishnan told reporters on Thursday afternoon, reading from a prepared statement.

"I understand there's interest in this matter, but given it's now before the courts, it wouldn't be appropriate for me to go into details or comment on the claims.

"I am confident I have acted appropriately, and it's important we allow the legal action to run its course."

Dispute over repayment term

According to the court document, the American company said Dr Krishnan reached out to a representative through a mutual friend in May 2024 and "urgently requested short-term financial support" in the form of a $US250,000 loan.

The money was paid to Codd Technologies, according to the document.

Dr Krishnan's wife, Yaamini Jagadish, is currently the sole director of that company.

"[Dr Krishnan] expressly promised that the funds would be repaid upon the successful completion of his fundraising efforts in the United States," the writ reads.

Dr Krishnan says he will defend the allegations. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Once Dr Krishnan was in the US, the case alleges, the Kenyan Consulting representative arranged a limousine for the MP to "pitch" a separate business, Spectrum Health, for investment.

Later, at a meeting at the representative’s home — according to the writ — Dr Krishnan said he was in "dire need of immediate funding", which led to an extra $US405,000 being loaned.

In Kenyan Consulting’s view, it was agreed the total loaned amount would be paid back within a year.

Dr Krishnan’s lawyer disputes this allegation, claiming the agreement was that the loan was to be repaid over nine years.

Krishnan 'assisting my wife'

Kenyan Consulting's case alleges it eventually recalled the entire loan in January 2026, saying it had "lost confidence in [Dr] Krishnan's willingness and ability" to resolve the dispute and demanded payment within 30 days.

The writ states Dr Krishnan replied the same month to say the loan would be repaid "at the earliest possible time", but the American company claims no money has been received.

Dr Krishnan was named in the suit in the New Jersey District Court. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The company claimed it was not until October 2026 that it was aware of Dr Krishnan's claim that the money would be repaid over nine years.

Asked whether it was appropriate to be engaged in business dealings while a sitting MP, Dr Krishnan said: "I was not actively engaged in any business dealings; I was assisting my wife."

A staffer physically pulled Dr Krishnan back into his office as a journalist continued to ask questions.

Do you know more? Contact Keane Bourke on encrypted email. Please note you will need your own encrypted email account, such as Protonmail, to ensure end-to-end encryption.

Premier Roger Cook said he was first made aware of the "specifics" of the dispute in the past week.

"I understand that this is a legal situation that [Dr Krishnan] is engaged in and I won't comment in relation to that court action," he said.

World.title: Israeli election chief demands foreign interference probe as neither bloc wins majority
World.content:
The fallout from Israel's inconclusive election has taken another turn as the head of the country's elections panel demands an investigation into allegations of foreign interference in Tuesday's vote.

Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, the head of the Central Elections Committee, has written to the chief of intelligence agency Shin Bet to call for an immediate inquiry and asking for its findings within a week.

"Serious suspicions have been brought before me of improper influence on the elections through foreign funding from foreign entities operating against Israeli interests," Justice Sohlberg said in the letter to Shin Bet director David Zini.

"I cannot attest to the nature of the above suspicions, but it seems to me that, given the fact that these are suspicions concerning foreign entities, there is a duty to investigate them properly."

Protesters in Tel Aviv have called for Arab parties to be included in a future government. (Reuters: Jamal Awad)

Justice Sohlberg described the "purity of elections" as being at "the heart of democracy".

Israeli media outlets are reporting that the allegations include a claim that Qatar provided funding to encourage higher voter turnout in predominantly Arab-Israeli communities.

The letter followed allegations from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party that Arab-Israeli politicians had "stolen" the election.

Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of hyposcrisy after making the allegations. (Pool via Reuters)

The vote count has since been completed and shows the two Arab-Israeli parties, the Joint List and the United Arab List, have secured 19 seats between them in the next Knesset.

It is a record level of representation in the parliament for the groups, primarily representing the marginalised Arab and Palestinian citizens who make up 20 per cent of the nation's population.

The result gives the two parties significant influence on who might be able to form a coalition government, particularly as there is no clear path for the other anti-Netanyahu parties, including lead challenger Gadi Eisenkot, to form government without them.

Mr Netanyahu's likely coalition has only secured 53 seats, short of the 61 needed to govern in majority, while Mr Eisenkot's likely bloc has locked in 48 seats.

The Likud allegations went to far as to say envelopes had been stuffed with cash alongside ballot papers for the United Arab List in some communities. There were also claims of identity fraud.

Arab-Israeli parties complained of intimidation at polling stations, accusing right wing activists of trying to stop people from voting.

Before the letter from Justice Sohlberg on Thursday, numerous Israeli media outlets had cited police sources in claiming the allegations from Likud were baseless.

"The Israel Police has declared that it will safeguard the integrity of the elections with the utmost vigilance — and that is exactly what it will do," Police Commissioner Daniel Levy said in an official statement.

"Every complaint received, and any suspicion of an offense related to the integrity of the elections, will be examined and investigated thoroughly and impartially.

"Regarding any suspicion of an offense, the Police will act with determination to uncover the truth and ensure that those involved are held fully accountable, without exception."

'Attack on democracy'

Likud described the allegations in the letter as an "unprecedented shock".

"This is an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of right-wing rule in order to lead to retreat and defeat of the IDF in all arenas — and primarily Iran," it said in a statement.

It challenged the "change"-camp parties not to cooperate with the Arab-Israeli politicians in any attempt to try to replace the Likud speaker of the Knesset and take control of the parliament before a new government was formed.

Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot said the matter should be investigated, but questioned the motive behind Likud's comments.

"Netanyahu, who has grown accustomed to confronting reality through lies, manipulation of public perception and the spread of chaos, is leading, together with his partners, an illegitimate influence operation targeting the Israeli public," Mr Eisenkot said.

Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, was Benjamin Netanyahu's main opponent in the election. (Reuters: Shir Torem)

The Joint List labelled it a "smear campaign"

"We are done apologising and defending ourselves against vile lies and baseless accusations from elements on the Right who refuse to accept the election results," the party said in a statement.

" These racist accusations only highlight how much they fear the power of our community. "

Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said the country categorically denied the allegations.

"These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure," Majed Al Ansari said on X

"The repeated invocation of Qatar in Israeli electoral rhetoric reveals an excessive obsession with our country among certain Israeli political and media figures.

"Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians."

Democrats leader Yair Golan said it was rich for Mr Netanyahu and Likud to make allegations about Qatari money when a senior aide accused of taking funds from Doha had not been sacked.

"Until then, Netanyahu can keep barking. We will keep working. The public fired him. We will make sure he vacates his seat," Mr Golan posted on X.

"Netanyahu has suffered a crushing democratic defeat. The public has fired him, and he refuses to accept the voters' verdict."

Mr Golan has been publicly advocating for the 'change' camp to consider working with the Arab-Israeli parties.

Anti-Arab slogans the centrepiece of Netanyahu's campaign

For much of the election campaign, Mr Netanyahu leant on anti-Arab slogans as he implored voters to back his party or risk Palestinian influence on the next government.

On polling day he posted photos he claimed showed large crowds in Arab-majority communities lining up to vote as he encouraged his supporter base to show up to cast their ballots. Voting in Israel is not compulsory.

US President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. (Reuters: Ronen Zvulun)

At least one of those images has been labelled as AI-generated, after analysis from the BBC.

Mr Netanyahu's political partners, including far-right finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, seized upon the letter from the Central Elections Committee.

Where to next in the Israeli election? The inconclusive result of the Israeli election with neither Netanyahu nor the opposition gaining majority, means weeks of messy and complicated negotiations.

"The suspicion of election interference with foreign Islamist money is a litmus test for the State of Israel," he said.

"The heads of the Arab parties must be interrogated by the Shin Bet today.

"The State of Israel will not be sold to radical Islam with terrorist money."

Mr Smotrich's Religious Zionism party lost support at the election and is on track to hold only six seats in the next Knesset.

He has been sanctioned by many countries, including Australia, for his policies and rhetoric against Palestinians.

He had been promising to "Judaise" parts of Israel that have Arab-majority populations, effectively suggesting that more Jewish Israelis should move to those areas to diminish the influence of locals.

World.title: Zacharia blames media for troubled stint as White House press secretary
World.content:
Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has broken her silence 10 days after her abrupt departure from the administration.

Ms Zacharia's legal credentials came under scrutiny after a truncated first press briefing raised questions over her suitability for the position.

It all seemed to come crashing down for Ms Zacharia after two appearances on Fox News, where she admitted she had failed the bar exam.

Katie Zacharia only answered three questions from conservative-leaning news outlets at her first White House press briefing. (AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

In a media appearance at the time, US President Donald Trump told reporters he had advised her to reconsider the position, bringing her tenure after just five days in the office.

The pair appeared to part ways cordially, with Mr Trump accusing the media of treating her "pretty nastily".

Ms Zacharia later penned an op-ed for the New York Post saying the "call" to serve the president was an "honor" she was proud of.

"I've always wanted to work for President Donald Trump," she wrote.

"Being back in California feels like an interlude, a temporary pause between the work that matters most," she wrote.

Katie Zacharia was asked about her legal credentials before heading to Alaska. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Appearing on Piers Morgan Uncensored this week, Ms Zacharia doubled down on her loyalty to Mr Trump and did not rule out working for his administration if the opportunity arose again.

"I would love to work for the president again," Ms Zacharia told Morgan on Wednesday, local time.

She said she had since returned to her home state of California, where she plans to continue to "fight" for Mr Trump, whom she described as a "force of nature" and an "incredible president to serve".

Loading Instagram content

When Morgan asked about the firestorm after her first press briefing and the backlash over the misrepresentation of her legal credentials, Ms Zacharia blamed the media for leading the public down a "red herring trail" that distracted attention from Mr Trump ahead of crucial midterm elections.

As she continued to pledge her loyalty to Mr Trump, Morgan accused her of being a "robot".

"Has Donald Trump got some program plugged into you to make you say all of this?" he asked.

The United States goes to the polls next week, where voters will decide which major party will control the House of Representatives and the Senate for the remainder of Mr Trump's administration.

Trump is very unpopular in the US Donald Trump wants American voters to "pretend" he's on the ballot these midterm elections. Voters don't need to be reminded how much they dislike him.

Ms Zacharia, a staunch supporter of Mr Trump since his first term in office, told Morgan that initial polling showed the Senate race would be "tight" and the House would prove to be an "uphill battle".

In the lead-up to the midterms, Mr Trump has drawn criticism for attempting to block alleged non-citizens from voting in California.

Meanwhile, he has continued to host rallies around the country, recently addressing Ms Zacharia's departure from the White House at one such event.

"She was a perfect, beautiful woman when she walked into that press room," he told the crowd.

He blamed the media for "scaring" the former press secretary, telling the crowd that he told her there were easier ways to make a living.

Mr Trump has yet to appoint the next press secretary, having earlier said he had no plans to do so until after the midterms.

ABC

World.title: Darwin man who ran over partner during argument to spend five months in jail
World.content:
A 63-year-old man will spend five months in jail after running over his partner during an argument, leaving her with multiple skull and facial fractures, at a caravan park just outside of Darwin at the beginning of the year.

The sentencing judge said the incident left the woman with "horrendous" life-threatening injuries, including brain bleeds, that left her in hospital for months and faced with a long process of recovering her ability to walk.

Christopher Morley pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and breaching a domestic violence restraining order earlier this month after spending a little over four months in jail on remand.

On Thursday morning, before sentencing in the Northern Territory Supreme Court, he also pleaded guilty to the summary charge of driving under the influence of drugs.

Christopher Morley pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and breaching a domestic violence order earlier this month. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

According to the agreed facts, Morley and his then-partner were drinking at the Oasis Caravan Park in Virginia when the pair got into a verbal argument.

Earlier that day, Morley had texted his daughter saying the victim had threatened to burn the caravan down unless he paid her $1,500 — a threat the victim denied when speaking to the daughter at the time.

In another message to his daughter, Morley said the victim was drinking, refusing to leave and talking to another male at the bar.

The court heard the incident occurred earlier this year at the Oasis Caravan Park in Virginia. (ABC News)

In handing down his sentence, Justice Stephen Southwood said the victim had walked in front of Morley's Range Rover Discovery as he was trying to leave and "faced the vehicle head-on".

"As the offender accelerated the vehicle, the victim reached out in front of her and placed both hands on the centre of the vehicle," he said.

He said Morley then accelerated forwards, pushing the victim backwards, causing her to lose her balance and fall under the front passenger side of the car.

"The offender then continued to drive for approximately 10 metres before coming to a stop," Justice Southwood said.

Justice Stephen Southwood says Christopher Morley misrepresented the incident to police when they arrived. (Supplied: NT Supreme Court)

The court heard Morley called Triple Zero (000) immediately, but made false statements to police when they arrived.

"The offender suggested that the victim had jumped out in front of the car in an act of self harm. That is not correct," Justice Southwood said.

He said Morley had also told police he was only driving 5km/h, when in fact it was closer to 10km/h, and that his vehicle's dash camera was not working, although it was.

The court heard Morley's blood alcohol level was at 0.045, and that he tested positive for benzodiazepine, amphetamines and another substance at the time of the incident.

The judge took Christopher Morley's criminal history into account during sentencing. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

In handing down his sentence, Justice Southwood said Morley's criminal history could not be ignored.

The court heard the victim had taken out a domestic violence order against Morley two years prior, after he assaulted her.

In 1990, he spent a month in prison for a separate assault, and was later fined after damaging property and resisting police.

In 1991, he was sentenced to three months jail for breaching an intervention order.

The Supreme Court heard the victim had previously taken out a domestic violence order against Christopher Morley, following an assault. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

While Morley's defence counsel had previously submitted their client was attempting to leave the situation in question voluntarily, an argument Justice Southwood accepted, the judge said the "very serious injuries" sustained by the victim were "significant".

"The volatile domestic situation preceding the offending explains but does not excuse it," he said.

"They should have adhered to the domestic violence orders in place and none of this would have happened."

Morley was sentenced to two years and three months in jail, suspended after nine months and backdated, leaving him with five months' remaining jail time.

He was also ordered to pay a $194 fine and disqualified from driving for six months.

World.title: Sydney Southwest Metro opening LIVE updates: Relief for commuters as mega rail project’s final stage opens after two years of disruptions
World.content:
Commuters who have had to catch pink-coloured replacement buses while the southwest metro project was underway will know exactly how long the passenger rail corridor between Bankstown and Sydenham has been closed.

But for those who are not regular southwest commuters, a bit of history is in order.

Under the original plans of the previous Coalition government, the south-west section of the M1 metro line was meant to open in 2024, at the same time as the rest of the second stage between Chatswood and Sydenham.

A decision was made about four years ago to open the southwest section later amid rising construction costs and challenges turning a century-old rail line into one for driverless trains.

In mid-2018, the then Coalition government told commuters the T3 heavy rail line would need to be closed for three to six months before the metro conversion was completed. Before the T3 was shut in September 2024, the Minns government said the shutdown might last longer than its earlier estimates of 12 months.

World.title: ‘This really is Albo’s cabinet’: How the PM’s razor gang hindered the treasurer’s saving plans
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘This really is Albo’s cabinet’: How the PM’s razor gang hindered the treasurer’s saving plans Paul Sakkal October 30, 2026 — 4:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ push for tighter fiscal discipline was obstructed by the prime minister’s razor gang ahead of the last budget, intensifying scrutiny on Anthony Albanese’s economic credentials as Labor scrambles to find savings to offset new spending. High-level government sources said that in the run-up to the May budget and years past, Chalmers had often advocated for the lowest-cost option when proposals came to the cabinet’s expenditure review subcommittee. Budget proposals usually come with a range of options on the cost, giving ministers the option to spend more or less. Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers during a vote in the House of Representatives this week. Alex Ellinghausen Chalmers told this masthead’s Inside Politics podcast this week that he had become a “lightning rod” for criticism at a time when inflation is running hotter in Australia than the UK and the US and the G7 average. But the role of Albanese and his close allies on the secretive budget spending committee has not attracted the same level of scrutiny.



Related Article Inflation Chalmers weighs infrastructure cuts as inflation locks in Cup Day rate hike The prime minister’s allies Finance Minister Katy Gallagher, Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Health Minister Mark Butler dominate the nine-person group. Chalmers is not factionally aligned with Albanese. While it is not the first time a treasurer has been unable to convince colleagues to tighten belts, several party sources said that they’d heard Chalmers comment on the fact that he had pushed for lower spending than the razor gang approved. “[Chalmers] has told people he wanted to do more both on the revenue side and spending side,” one source familiar with the matter said. “It shows that this really is Albo’s cabinet, at the end of the day. But it also begs the question of how much authority the treasurer commands in the cabinet.” Even if the treasurer had found extra savings, it would have probably trimmed spending at the margins rather than overhauled Labor’s broader economic strategy.



Renewed scrutiny has been placed on the relationship between Albanese and the treasurer this week. Inflation was revealed to be well above target on Wednesday – fuelled by domestic pressures, soaring oil prices and the war in Iran – and the RBA is expected to raise rates for a fifth time this year on Melbourne Cup day. Party colleagues took note when Chalmers told Inside Politics that he was attuned to criticism that he was isolated from colleagues and said he took responsibility for his part in Labor’s polling decline, which he pointed out had begun before the budget was unveiled in May. Albanese’s approval ratings started to drop following the Bondi massacre in December. “It’s up to other ministers and the prime minister how they describe their part in that,” Chalmers said. Treasurer Jim Chalmers arrives for question time this week. He will deliver a crucial mid-year budget update in December. Alex Ellinghausen Chalmers was previously reported to be pushing for a tax on gas exports, a popular idea that would have created a fight with multinationals but was ultimately not taken up by the cabinet. Chalmers wanted the revenue to fund a broader incentive package to stimulate business investment.



Albanese was also critical in conversations with colleagues about Chalmers’ proposal for a road user charge, which Albanese thought would have been too controversial. Plans to introduce this charge, widely viewed as a necessary move as more people buy EVs, have not advanced in months. A push for each department to find cuts worth 5 per cent – to spend on other priorities – did not materialise in a major budget saving, as the size of the public service continues to balloon. Federal spending increased by 4.3 per cent last financial year, more than double the projection of GDP growth from the last budget. Albanese and Chalmers have said they are aiming to find savings in the December budget update to take heat out of the economy and put downward pressure on interest rates. However, they have not committed to finding enough savings to offset new spending. Sources in the government said it would be difficult to create net savings given a series of backflips and blocked measures, such as a $3 billion private health insurance change blocked by the Coalition, had blown a hole in the budget. The Australian Financial Review reported Labor would need to make up $11 billion to offset the gap, which is increasing through higher interest payments and bond yields.



Related Article Exclusive

Australian economy What would you cut? Chalmers challenges critics of government spending Labor ministers argue they receive little credit for finding $64 billion in savings and reprioritisations in the last budget, and $180 billion over the life of the government. But economists including Chris Richardson have noted that an unexpected $400 billion-plus revenue boost since coming to government in 2022 meant Labor had been wasteful. “We know that economic reform in this country can be difficult,” Chalmers told parliament on Thursday after passing a bill on tax reform tweaks. “If it wasn’t, those opposite would have done some in their nine years of office, but they didn’t do any economic reform or any tax reform.” Chalmers accused the Coalition of dealing in “post-truths” in their assessment of inflation, but shadow treasurer Tim Wilson demanded Chalmers “finally take responsibility”. Wilson also sledged Albanese for his upcoming travel to international summits, saying the prime minister was “jetting off to the Caribbean” as the RBA was expected to hike rates.



Albanese also laughed off criticism from former treasurer Peter Costello, who used an Institute of Public Affairs to condemn Labor’s economic settings. “Peter Costello is a partisan participant,” Albanese said. “I’ll make this prediction, when the election’s on in 2028, there’ll be a splash in a broadsheet which is, ‘Howard condemns Albanese government’. Wait for it.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Lyon does a Warne impression as Test twists towards classic finish
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Lyon does a Warne impression as Test twists towards classic finish Daniel Brettig October 30, 2026 — 4:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cape Town: Nathan Lyon has seldom celebrated a wicket more vibrantly. In his 14th and last over of the day, Lyon succeeded in teasing South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma into coming down the wicket and aiming a flick over the leg side. The ball turned viciously out of the footmarks that had made Lyon (1-31) fiendishly difficult to face all afternoon, and the clatter of stumps was accompanied by a collective roar from Lyon and his teammates. South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma is bowled out by Nathan Lyon. AP Photo/Halden Krog As a moment, it was the kind that Shane Warne used to conjure for Australia, and in keeping with the quality of a tantalising, undulating Test match where the tourists overcame an awful first session of the match to keep themselves in front more or less ever since.



“Yeah it was satisfying,” centurion Josh Inglis said. “I think we controlled the tempo really well in that last session. Although they put on a pretty good partnership, they weren’t really getting away from us. Gaz bowled brilliantly and looked threatening the whole time. “And when you work for a couple of hours there, and then get the rewards right at the end, it’s really satisfying.” At 4-140 and leading by just 40 with six wickets left, the Proteas are up against it in terms of setting a big target, but the Australians will not want to chase any more than about 200 on a surface that is now tinder dry. They were grateful, too, for further heroics from Mitchell Starc (2-29), who gave another demonstration of his incredible durability. Australian players celebrate the wicket of South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma. AP Photo/Halden Krog



Shortly after coaxing Aiden Markram to punch a drive to mid-off for his seventh consecutive South African wicket to start the innings, Starc had looked briefly uncomfortable on the boundary. Consorting with a sub-fielder at fine leg, he looked to be flexing something, and when the strike turned over from left-hander to right his jog into position had the look of exploration about it. Related Article Australian cricket Australia vs South Africa LIVE: Mitchell Starc’s searing Cape Town Test puts series win in sight Not too long later and Starc jogged up the steps to the dressing room for some time in the physio room and a patch-up to whatever fast bowler's niggle he had picked up this time. Having returned to the field and swung around to the Kelvin Grove End, Starc promptly produced one of the balls of the series, a searing bouncer that did for Marques Ackerman via edge and helmet to slip. The exchanges that followed, as Ackerman tried to review a fraction after his 30 seconds were up, prompting the umpires and then Travis Head to send him on his way, underlined the high pitch of competitiveness at which this series has been fought.



Starc's physical and cricketing exploits at the age of 36, meanwhile, have been just one of many high points in a tremendous Test match, now winding towards the likelihood of a classic finish over the final two days. Australia played some marvellous and sensible cricket on day three, once again watched by a healthy crowd. But so too did South Africa, cutting back the dimensions of the tourists' first innings then fighting heartily with the bat as Nathan Lyon spun the ball treacherously at times and Pat Cummins used his bowlers in short bursts. The day had begun with Inglis’ advance to a second Test hundred, getting there wonderfully by lacing a reverse sweep to the backward point boundary. Inglis celebrated heartily, making the most of an opportunity that arrived through the last-moment withdrawal of Steve Smith. Inglis (102) has undoubtedly made the strongest case to stay in the team for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth in December, and should Smith be fit the most logical man to make way will be Marnus Labuschagne. Two hundreds in six Tests for Inglis should certainly trump Labuschagne’s three years without one. “It’s tough playing all three forms, or at least being away for all three forms,” Inglis said. “I guess those conversations, they’re always had between those three format players and [selection chair Bailey] and the selection committee. So those conversations will probably be had over the next couple of weeks in terms of what I need to prepare for the white ball series coming up, but then obviously the Test summer as well.”



It was a surprise to all at the ground when the very next ball, Inglis leaned forward and got a thin edge behind off Simon Harmer, who remained threatening throughout. Inglis marched off frustrated, and the next few overs only added to his sense of irritation. Alex Carey (80) snicked Harmer to slip, Cummins was lbw for a duck, and only Cooper Connolly's composed 29 ensured a three figure lead. Australia’s Travis Head celebrates with teammates after the dismissal of South Africa’s Aiden Markram on day three. AP Still, the benefits of two nights' rest was evident in how the Australian attack set about the Proteas, even if Cummins' run of bowling without a wicket has now stretched beyond 200 runs. Markram and David Bedingham were each drawn into intemperate shots by fresh bowlers, before Ackerman was bounced out and Bavuma cornered so effectively that he felt the claustrophobic urge to get away from the crouched fielders. “There’s many ways to skin a cat,” Harmer said. “As an off-spinner, you want to bowl a right-hander through the gate. That’s the dream delivery. But there are a lot of nuances in how you can set batters up, get them to play on the back foot or front foot by using fielders.



“That’s the art of spin bowling. Understanding what’s easy and what’s difficult, how a batter is trying to play you, and you’re going to have moments where you can take a risk. But yeah, it’s about trying to play with the batter’s mind by using your field.” In 2001 at Trent Bridge, Warne had brought about a similar rash-looking shot by Mark Ramprakash in a tight contest, paving the way for Australia to secure the Ashes. Having been in and out of the team recently, Lyon would cherish nothing more than to do likewise. Starc, too, has a South African Test series victory firmly in his sights. World.title: Australia vs South Africa LIVE: Mitchell Starc’s searing Cape Town Test puts series win in sight
World.content:
Mitchell Starc’s golden Cape Town Test has helped Australia edge closer to a famous series victory as the pace great struck twice on day three to leave South Africa 4-140 and with a lead of just 40.

After taking six wickets on the opening day to help set up the Test for Australia, Starc removed openers Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman.

His double blow came after a second Test century for Josh Inglis had helped lift Australia to 429 in their first innings early on day three, in reply to the Proteas’ 329.

The third and deciding Test still remains somewhat in the balance, with a fourth-innings chase looming as tricky on a wicket that’s offering plenty of turn.

But thanks to Starc (2-29) and Nathan Lyon’s crucial late dismissal of stubborn homer skipper Temba Bavuma, Australia can for now claim the upper hand.

South Africa were guilty of throwing away some of their wickets on Thursday, with Markram driving Starc straight to Travis Head at mid-off for two.

David Bedingham then top-edged a Josh Hazlewood short ball to deep backward square on 11, after being one of three Proteas caught hooking in the first innings.

And while Marques Ackerman and Bavuma appeared to have steadied the ship for the Proteas, it was a brute of a ball from Starc that broke a 64-run partnership.

Brought back on midway through the last session, the left-armer had a bouncer follow Ackerman as he tried to uppercut on 62.

It hit the left-hander’s bat and helmet on the way through to the slips, leaving the Proteas 3-95 and still five runs short of drawing level.

Ackerman did try to review the call and was told to start walking by Head with time having just elapsed, but replays showed the call would not have been overturned anyway.

Lyon then bowled Bavuma for 35 just five minutes before stumps, when the Proteas captain inexplicably tried to hit hard across the line with the offspinner getting prodigious turn.

Pat Cummins has again gone wicketless, with his drought now extending to 358 balls and back to the first Test in Durban.

But he still bowled particularly well, with Bavuma edging Australia’s captain to just in front of slip and surviving an lbw review on height.

South Africa have not lost a home Test series for almost six years, and now need a serious recovery effort in a three-match contest full of twists and turns to keep that record.

Earlier, Inglis’s century headlined one of Australia’s most complete batting performances in years, with Alex Carey (80), Matt Renshaw (74) and Cameron Green (65) also posting half-centuries.

Cooper Connolly also made a crucial 29 alongside the lower-order, helping add another 49 for the final few wickets after Australia lost 3-10 on Thursday.

Those extra runs could prove crucial, with the pitch showing signs of turn and spinner Simon Harmer taking 4-107 for the Proteas before Lyon’s late work.

After being called in late to replace the injured Steve Smith, Inglis brought up his hundred when he reverse-swept Harmer to the boundary.

At that point the Proteas had started the day reasonably flat, with a number of misfields at Newlands under the warm Cape Town sun.

But when he was caught behind later in the same Harmer over and a 185-run stand with Carey was ended, the Proteas were suddenly back in the contest.

Carey edged Harmer to slip four overs later, before Pat Cummins was trapped lbw by Kagiso Rabada in the mini collapse.

World.title: New wave of Australian antisemitism comes from progressive social justice critics, says antisemitism envoy
World.content:
Exclusive NationalAntisemitism New wave of Australian antisemitism comes from progressive social justice critics, says antisemitism envoy Clair Weaver October 30, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The most pervasive form of discrimination against Jewish Australians comes from progressives motivated by social justice who give antisemitism a “respectable veneer”, argues a new report from Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism (ASECA). The report describes this mainstream group as combining the hostility of Islamist extremism with far-left ideology delivered through a progressive lens, singling them out for making antisemitism acceptable and even fashionable. ASECA Priorities, a new road map report to be released on Friday, identifies evolving threats and progress in tackling antisemitism, with envoy Jillian Segal also levelling heavy criticism at universities and the ABC. It includes recommendations for reforms across society, from health and the arts to migration and the digital world. Jillian Segal believes a new progressive antisemitism is conflating the actions of the Israeli government with Jewish Australians. Janie Barrett



In an interview with this masthead before the report’s release, Segal acknowledged antisemitism has always come from the far-right, far-left and Islamist extremism, but pointed to a newer, more palatable form that gives it “intellectual and cultural credibility”. “What we have is antisemitism that I describe as much more in the middle: well-intentioned people who are concerned about the policies of the state of Israel and feel critical of them,” she said. “And they transfer that criticism to Jewish members of society in Australia … through a lens of thinking that they are upholding progressive values and human rights. “It’s really conflating criticism of policies of the government of Israel onto Jewish Australians. And actually, Jewish Australians have got no influence on the state of Israel. They may not support any of those policies, and yet, they are suffering.” Impacts on Jewish people have ranged from hostility, online abuse and exclusion to doxxing, graffiti and violence, Segal said. Zionism, or the belief in Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state, has also become a proxy for antisemitism, according to the report, even though it doesn’t equate to excluding Palestinian self-determination or sovereignty.



“Increasingly, and often to avoid appearing transparently and obviously antisemitic, it has become common to vilify, target and ostracise ‘Zionists’ rather than ‘Jews’,” the report said. “Jews, generally in Australia, are supportive of the existence of the state of Israel,” Segal said. “But not necessarily, of course, for all the policies.” With caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political future uncertain in the fallout of Israel’s deadlocked election this week, Segal said Israel and its government should be subject to scrutiny and criticism like any other democratic state. Online environment A febrile online environment, in which conspiracy theories and hate flourish, is also singled out in the report as “one of the most significant accelerators of contemporary antisemitism”.



The report comes amid renewed government focus on online hate and abuse, as Indi MP Helen Haines recovers after losing both legs in an alleged attack by a 43-year-old man outside her electorate office. Segal said there’s been “an explosion of hate” online, which ramped up against Jews after Hamas’ October 7 terror attack. “We saw a further increase after the Bondi terror attack,” she said. “And we saw all those absolutely terrible allegations online that Bondi was staged: it was not real, the people staged their own blood on their head. “Not only was it incredibly traumatic for the people who were there, but even more traumatic then for that real experience to be trivialised and made fun of online.” Following the Bondi terror attack, the report said “social media was flooded with a cascade of denials of the killings, conspiracy theories.” Flavio Brancaleone



Media One of the more controversial recommendations of the ASECA report is the call for an external, independent watchdog for the ABC and SBS to be installed by the federal government. Segal reported significant concern in the Jewish community about the public broadcasters’ reporting on issues related to Israel and the Middle East, with allegations of “disproportionate, misleading or inaccurate” coverage. “Jewish Australians have reported being abused, harassed and accused of being ‘baby killers’ or supporters of ‘genocide’ simply for their belief in the right of Israel to exist,” the report stated. “That perception of a link between coverage and hostility is itself a matter of public importance.” While the ABC and SBS have internal ombudsmen, Segal argues more serious complaints should be handled externally to ensure accountability and public confidence.



“Many other industries – such as telecommunications, superannuation and financial services – have external complaints dealt with transparently and independently by ombudsman services,” she said. “And I think that should apply to the public broadcasters as well.” The ABC and SBS defended their Middle East reporting and internal complaints processes at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion earlier this year. Public funding cut Taxpayer funding would be withheld or stripped from people or organisations that engage in or tolerate antisemitism, under several recommendations in the report. This applied to arts, culture, sport and university research and included government grants. Previous proposals have been met with resistance on the grounds of freedom of artistic expression.



“My principle is that government money should not be used to foment hate in any sphere,” said Segal. The report also calls for doxxed or excluded Jewish artists to be re-engaged by the arts sector. Universities ‘slow to act’ Universities come under fire for “serious shortcomings”, including failing to act on antisemitism and adopt an agreed definition. “University leaders have periodically expressed regret, but actions have been slow and inadequate on campus encampments, office invasions, activism in learning environments, and disruptive actions hostile to Jewish staff, students and visitors,” the report states.



While an agreed Universities Australia definition of antisemitism was endorsed by vice chancellors in 2025, this year it emerged that no university had adopted a uniform definition. Western Sydney University chancellor Jennifer Westacott acknowledged a failure by the sector to tackle antisemitism. Louie Douvis Western Sydney University chancellor Professor Jennifer Westacott said there was “a collective failure to address the escalating severity of antisemitism” by the sector and that more work was needed. “Universities have to be places where ideas can be respectfully contested,” she said. “They have to be places of debate, and they can be places of peaceful protest, but they should never be places of hate or fear.” Other recommendations include training for visa decision makers to recognise antisemitism, education and training in schools, the public sector and business, and the establishment of a national healthcare antisemitism taskforce.



Multicultural Affairs Minister Dr Anne Aly, who was the first Muslim woman elected to Australia’s parliament, said antisemitism was “a serious and deeply troubling challenge in Australia” and Jewish Australians have a right to feel safe. “We must never allow international conflicts to become a licence for hatred here at home,” she said. “Australians can hold different views, including on events overseas, without turning against one another. Multiculturalism is one of Australia’s greatest strengths, but it cannot be taken for granted.” The royal commission will deliver its final report on December 18.
