World.title: ‘A game-changer’: How a brick box without windows won an architecture award
World.content:
NationalQueenslandArchitecture ‘A game-changer’: How a brick box without windows won an architecture award Nick Dent October 29, 2026 — 11:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It looks like a layered slice of rock dug out of the earth and placed on the University of Queensland grounds. A pair of greenhouses sitting on top enhance this illusion, while inside, hidden from view, researchers are working like so many ants on how to feed a changing world. This is the Plant Futures Facility at the University of Queensland, and when the head of the School of Agriculture and Food Sustainability first walked in, he knew it was “a game changer”. The Plant Futures Facility at the University of Queensland supports research into biotechnology. Christopher Frederick Jones “It had a wow factor,” Professor Sagadevan Mundree said. “It’s state of the art, and the only one of its kind in the Southern Hemisphere.”



The building houses research into sustainable food, fibre and fuel production in response to climate change, environmental degradation, and population growth. It contains about 40 “growing rooms”, cabinets and glasshouses where climatic conditions of any environment can be recreated. One room might be like the sub-Saharan desert. Another might be like Finland; another, a tropical region. Laboratories can manipulate light, heat, humidity, CO2 and other environmental factors. Christopher Frederick Jones Academics can book rooms for two or three-month trials, then check out when they have their results. “It feels like a very luxurious hotel for plants,” Mundree said. “For the university, I would say [it’s had] a huge impact because it gives us a chance now to mimic microclimates.



“That gives us the edge of being able to do speed breeding, and one of the areas that is fast evolving is genome editing of crops.” Designed by Brisbane firm M3Architecture, the Plant Futures Facility has won a National Award for Educational Architecture 2026, bestowed by the Australian Institute of Architects. Corridors utilise adaptable coloured lighting and mirrors. Christopher Frederick Jones Jury member Alice Hampson said the building was “astounding” both for its technology and its aesthetic. “Conceptually, it’s like a walled garden [with] a pixelated brick facade, it reminds me of sedimentary rock samples,” Hampson said.



“The patterning in the brickwork is from basically a cross-section through the Great Artesian Basin, the geological profile of Queensland,” architect Michael Christensen said. Brick was chosen as a response to the neighbouring Hartley Teakle Building, a well-loved 1969 brick edifice originally built for the Agriculture and Entomology departments. Christensen said the new building’s main challenge was the fact it could not have any windows, “because that will change the amount of light, or the temperature. “It’s a big brick box, right? So we were thinking about how can we make working in there a more pleasant experience.



“In these grow rooms, the researchers are playing with the environmental conditions for the plants. So we thought, well, why don’t we do the same to the academics?” Related Article Architecture Peter designed a Brisbane house that breaks all the rules. Now it’s an award winner The building’s central corridor features variable light and colour settings. There are also distorted mirrors adding visual interest, “like at the Ekka”. “It could have been boring and sterile,” Hampson said. “If I was a kid and visited, I’d be going, ‘How can I make a career to work in this building?’ Seven of the 34 National Architecture Awards were won by Queensland projects.



Two houses in the Mount Coot-tha foothills won residential awards. A renovated 1920s home in Burleigh, Woodside Cottage, won the Eleanor Cullis-Hill Award for Houses (Alterations and Additions). A spectacular city apartment block, 443 Queen St, won the award for Multiple Housing, while commercial office tower 205 North Quay won the Harry Seidler Award for Commercial Architecture. City restaurant Golden Avenue won an award for its interiors. Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: ‘I have created my own legacy’: McReight wins first John Eales Medal
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘I have created my own legacy’: McReight wins first John Eales Medal Jonathan Drennan Updated October 29, 2026 — 10:33pm ,first published 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Fraser McReight has won the John Eales Medal as Australian rugby’s best player of the year after his international teammates recognised his consistently excellent performances for his country this season. McReight received the game’s highest honour at the Rugby Australia awards in Sydney on Thursday night, while 21-year-old inside centre Faitala Moleka was crowned Wallaroos Player of the Year and Reds star Treyvon Pritchard named rookie of the year. Fraser McReight has been recognised by his peers for Rugby Australia’s highest honour Getty Images The John Eales medal is based on votes submitted by Wallabies players after every Test match. McReight joins a long list of outstanding back-rowers to have won the award since it was established in 2002, including David Lyons, Phil Waugh, George Smith (twice), Rob Valetini (twice), David Pocock (twice) and former captain Michael Hooper, who won the award a record four times. Like Hooper, McReight has played some of his best rugby when the Wallabies are under the greatest pressure. A ferocious competitor at the breakdown, McReight has also developed an accomplished all-around game, establishing himself as one of the best openside breakaways in world rugby.



Related Article Analysis

Wallabies Why Wallabies are a better chance of winning World Cup than Bledisloe McReight acknowledged the significant legacy of the previous John Eales medal winners, including Hooper, after winning the award. “I think it means I have created my own legacy, those players that have come before me are fantastic players and we’re all so different,” McReight said. “They’re all unbelievable players and I was lucky enough to play with Hoops and I idolised a lot of them. “I think for me now to carve my own path and knowing that I’ve got the World Cup next year and other things that I’m really targeting is really special to me...



“You don’t play the game for these [individual] honours. You play to win as a team and that’s all I care about... winning and having a beer in the sheds with my mates.” McReight was also recognised for his outstanding defensive performances – particularly in the 16-point defeat to France in Brisbane in July, in which he scored two tries as well as making 19 tackles, with the award for Defender of the Year. McReight has also become the first Queensland Reds player to claim a John Eales medal since former Wallabies fullback Chris Latham 20 years ago. The late Peter Meagher who has been recognised by Rugby Australia for his outstanding service to the game. Meagher family Brisbane Junior Rugby Union Western Region chair Paula Watkins was honoured with the inaugural Peter Meagher Spirit of Rugby Award, in recognition of her dedication and tireless support for the community game.



Meagher, a much-loved figure in the Randwick rugby community, was one of 15 people tragically killed in the terrorist attack at Bondi Beach last year while taking photographs of the Hanukkah festival as a volunteer. “Rugby Australia decided to honour Marzo”, who held a longtime association with Randwick rugby club, by rebranding the award previously named after Nick Farr-Jones in his honour. National team captains Isabella Nasser and Henry Hutchison took home the Shawn Mackay Awards for the Women’s and Men’s Sevens Player of the Year, respectively. 2026 Rugby Australia Awards - winners list John Eales Medal - Fraser McReight

Wallaroos Player of the Year - Faitala Moleka

Shawn Mackay Award for Men’s Sevens Player of the Year - Henry Hutchison

Shawn Mackay Award for Women’s Sevens Player of the Year - Isabella Nasser

Swyftx Super Rugby Pacific Player of the Year - Jock Campbell

Swyftx Super Rugby Women’s Player of the Year - Siokapesi Palu Sekona

Santos Men’s Rookie of the Year Award - Treyvon Pritchard, Queensland Reds

Santos Women’s Rookie of the Year Award - Amelia Whitaker, Wallaroos

Junior Men’s Player of the Year - Edwin Langi, Australia U20 and NSW Waratahs

Junior Women’s Player of the Year - Waiaria Ellis, Wallaroos and NSW Waratahs

Cadbury Try of the Year - Siokapesi Palu Sekona, Wallaroos vs. Scotland, Canberra

Defender of the Year - Fraser McReight, Wallabies vs. France, Brisbane

Fedex Referee of the Year - Nic Berry

Peter Meagher Spirit of Rugby Award - Paula Watkins, Queensland Rugby Union

Joe French Award for Outstanding Contribution to Rugby - Craig Robberds, ACT Rugby

Geoff ‘Bunter’ Shaw Community Coach of the Year Award - Kieran Smith, NSW Rugby

Andrew Cole Community Match Official of the Year - Julius Ambat, NSW Rugby First-time winner Nasser led the Australian Women’s team to the World Championship title while Hutchison, who last achieved this accolade in 2021, guided the Men’s side to their first tournament win since 2023 when they claimed gold in Valladolid.



Japan-bound fullback Jock Campbell won the Super Rugby Pacific Player of the Year title after an outstanding year for the Reds, while ACT Brumbies and Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona was named Super Rugby Women’s Player of the Year. Amelia Whitaker was also named women’s rookie of the year after her first season for the Wallaroos. Australian U20 and NSW Waratahs prop Edwin Langi won Junior Men’s Player of the Year for his performances across the year in both programs, while 19-year-old Waiaria Ellis picked up Junior Women’s Player of the Year after shining on the international stage. Referee of the Year Award was awarded to the experienced Nic Berry, who has taken charge of 41 Tests over the last ten years since retiring from playing professional rugby. World.title: Sydney Southwest Metro opening LIVE updates: Relief for commuters as mega rail project’s final stage opens after two years of disruptions
World.content:
Commuters who have had to catch pink-coloured replacement buses while the southwest metro project was underway will know exactly how long the passenger rail corridor between Bankstown and Sydenham has been closed.

But for those who are not regular southwest commuters, a bit of history is in order.

Under the original plans of the previous Coalition government, the south-west section of the M1 metro line was meant to open in 2024, at the same time as the rest of the second stage between Chatswood and Sydenham.

A decision was made about four years ago to open the southwest section later amid rising construction costs and challenges turning a century-old rail line into one for driverless trains.

In mid-2018, the then Coalition government told commuters the T3 heavy rail line would need to be closed for three to six months before the metro conversion was completed. Before the T3 was shut in September 2024, the Minns government said the shutdown might last longer than its earlier estimates of 12 months.

World.title: ‘This really is Albo’s cabinet’: How the PM’s razor gang hindered the treasurer’s saving plans
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘This really is Albo’s cabinet’: How the PM’s razor gang hindered the treasurer’s saving plans Paul Sakkal October 30, 2026 — 4:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ push for tighter fiscal discipline was obstructed by the prime minister’s razor gang ahead of the last budget, intensifying scrutiny on Anthony Albanese’s economic credentials as Labor scrambles to find savings to offset new spending. High-level government sources said that in the run-up to the May budget and years past, Chalmers had often advocated for the lowest-cost option when proposals came to the cabinet’s expenditure review subcommittee. Budget proposals usually come with a range of options on the cost, giving ministers the option to spend more or less. Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers during a vote in the House of Representatives this week. Alex Ellinghausen Chalmers told this masthead’s Inside Politics podcast this week that he had become a “lightning rod” for criticism at a time when inflation is running hotter in Australia than the UK and the US and the G7 average. But the role of Albanese and his close allies on the secretive budget spending committee has not attracted the same level of scrutiny.



Related Article Inflation Chalmers weighs infrastructure cuts as inflation locks in Cup Day rate hike The prime minister’s allies Finance Minister Katy Gallagher, Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Health Minister Mark Butler dominate the nine-person group. Chalmers is not factionally aligned with Albanese. While it is not the first time a treasurer has been unable to convince colleagues to tighten belts, several party sources said that they’d heard Chalmers comment on the fact that he had pushed for lower spending than the razor gang approved. “[Chalmers] has told people he wanted to do more both on the revenue side and spending side,” one source familiar with the matter said. “It shows that this really is Albo’s cabinet, at the end of the day. But it also begs the question of how much authority the treasurer commands in the cabinet.” Even if the treasurer had found extra savings, it would have probably trimmed spending at the margins rather than overhauled Labor’s broader economic strategy.



Renewed scrutiny has been placed on the relationship between Albanese and the treasurer this week. Inflation was revealed to be well above target on Wednesday – fuelled by domestic pressures, soaring oil prices and the war in Iran – and the RBA is expected to raise rates for a fifth time this year on Melbourne Cup day. Party colleagues took note when Chalmers told Inside Politics that he was attuned to criticism that he was isolated from colleagues and said he took responsibility for his part in Labor’s polling decline, which he pointed out had begun before the budget was unveiled in May. Albanese’s approval ratings started to drop following the Bondi massacre in December. “It’s up to other ministers and the prime minister how they describe their part in that,” Chalmers said. Treasurer Jim Chalmers arrives for question time this week. He will deliver a crucial mid-year budget update in December. Alex Ellinghausen Chalmers was previously reported to be pushing for a tax on gas exports, a popular idea that would have created a fight with multinationals but was ultimately not taken up by the cabinet. Chalmers wanted the revenue to fund a broader incentive package to stimulate business investment.



Albanese was also critical in conversations with colleagues about Chalmers’ proposal for a road user charge, which Albanese thought would have been too controversial. Plans to introduce this charge, widely viewed as a necessary move as more people buy EVs, have not advanced in months. A push for each department to find cuts worth 5 per cent – to spend on other priorities – did not materialise in a major budget saving, as the size of the public service continues to balloon. Federal spending increased by 4.3 per cent last financial year, more than double the projection of GDP growth from the last budget. Albanese and Chalmers have said they are aiming to find savings in the December budget update to take heat out of the economy and put downward pressure on interest rates. However, they have not committed to finding enough savings to offset new spending. Sources in the government said it would be difficult to create net savings given a series of backflips and blocked measures, such as a $3 billion private health insurance change blocked by the Coalition, had blown a hole in the budget. The Australian Financial Review reported Labor would need to make up $11 billion to offset the gap, which is increasing through higher interest payments and bond yields.



Related Article Exclusive

Australian economy What would you cut? Chalmers challenges critics of government spending Labor ministers argue they receive little credit for finding $64 billion in savings and reprioritisations in the last budget, and $180 billion over the life of the government. But economists including Chris Richardson have noted that an unexpected $400 billion-plus revenue boost since coming to government in 2022 meant Labor had been wasteful. “We know that economic reform in this country can be difficult,” Chalmers told parliament on Thursday after passing a bill on tax reform tweaks. “If it wasn’t, those opposite would have done some in their nine years of office, but they didn’t do any economic reform or any tax reform.” Chalmers accused the Coalition of dealing in “post-truths” in their assessment of inflation, but shadow treasurer Tim Wilson demanded Chalmers “finally take responsibility”. Wilson also sledged Albanese for his upcoming travel to international summits, saying the prime minister was “jetting off to the Caribbean” as the RBA was expected to hike rates.



Albanese also laughed off criticism from former treasurer Peter Costello, who used an Institute of Public Affairs to condemn Labor’s economic settings. “Peter Costello is a partisan participant,” Albanese said. “I’ll make this prediction, when the election’s on in 2028, there’ll be a splash in a broadsheet which is, ‘Howard condemns Albanese government’. Wait for it.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Lyon does a Warne impression as Test twists towards classic finish
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Lyon does a Warne impression as Test twists towards classic finish Daniel Brettig October 30, 2026 — 4:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cape Town: Nathan Lyon has seldom celebrated a wicket more vibrantly. In his 14th and last over of the day, Lyon succeeded in teasing South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma into coming down the wicket and aiming a flick over the leg side. The ball turned viciously out of the footmarks that had made Lyon (1-31) fiendishly difficult to face all afternoon, and the clatter of stumps was accompanied by a collective roar from Lyon and his teammates. South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma is bowled out by Nathan Lyon. AP Photo/Halden Krog As a moment, it was the kind that Shane Warne used to conjure for Australia, and in keeping with the quality of a tantalising, undulating Test match where the tourists overcame an awful first session of the match to keep themselves in front more or less ever since.



“Yeah it was satisfying,” centurion Josh Inglis said. “I think we controlled the tempo really well in that last session. Although they put on a pretty good partnership, they weren’t really getting away from us. Gaz bowled brilliantly and looked threatening the whole time. “And when you work for a couple of hours there, and then get the rewards right at the end, it’s really satisfying.” At 4-140 and leading by just 40 with six wickets left, the Proteas are up against it in terms of setting a big target, but the Australians will not want to chase any more than about 200 on a surface that is now tinder dry. They were grateful, too, for further heroics from Mitchell Starc (2-29), who gave another demonstration of his incredible durability. Australian players celebrate the wicket of South Africa’s captain Temba Bavuma. AP Photo/Halden Krog



Shortly after coaxing Aiden Markram to punch a drive to mid-off for his seventh consecutive South African wicket to start the innings, Starc had looked briefly uncomfortable on the boundary. Consorting with a sub-fielder at fine leg, he looked to be flexing something, and when the strike turned over from left-hander to right his jog into position had the look of exploration about it. Related Article Australian cricket Australia vs South Africa LIVE: Mitchell Starc’s searing Cape Town Test puts series win in sight Not too long later and Starc jogged up the steps to the dressing room for some time in the physio room and a patch-up to whatever fast bowler's niggle he had picked up this time. Having returned to the field and swung around to the Kelvin Grove End, Starc promptly produced one of the balls of the series, a searing bouncer that did for Marques Ackerman via edge and helmet to slip. The exchanges that followed, as Ackerman tried to review a fraction after his 30 seconds were up, prompting the umpires and then Travis Head to send him on his way, underlined the high pitch of competitiveness at which this series has been fought.



Starc's physical and cricketing exploits at the age of 36, meanwhile, have been just one of many high points in a tremendous Test match, now winding towards the likelihood of a classic finish over the final two days. Australia played some marvellous and sensible cricket on day three, once again watched by a healthy crowd. But so too did South Africa, cutting back the dimensions of the tourists' first innings then fighting heartily with the bat as Nathan Lyon spun the ball treacherously at times and Pat Cummins used his bowlers in short bursts. The day had begun with Inglis’ advance to a second Test hundred, getting there wonderfully by lacing a reverse sweep to the backward point boundary. Inglis celebrated heartily, making the most of an opportunity that arrived through the last-moment withdrawal of Steve Smith. Inglis (102) has undoubtedly made the strongest case to stay in the team for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth in December, and should Smith be fit the most logical man to make way will be Marnus Labuschagne. Two hundreds in six Tests for Inglis should certainly trump Labuschagne’s three years without one. “It’s tough playing all three forms, or at least being away for all three forms,” Inglis said. “I guess those conversations, they’re always had between those three format players and [selection chair Bailey] and the selection committee. So those conversations will probably be had over the next couple of weeks in terms of what I need to prepare for the white ball series coming up, but then obviously the Test summer as well.”



It was a surprise to all at the ground when the very next ball, Inglis leaned forward and got a thin edge behind off Simon Harmer, who remained threatening throughout. Inglis marched off frustrated, and the next few overs only added to his sense of irritation. Alex Carey (80) snicked Harmer to slip, Cummins was lbw for a duck, and only Cooper Connolly's composed 29 ensured a three figure lead. Australia’s Travis Head celebrates with teammates after the dismissal of South Africa’s Aiden Markram on day three. AP Still, the benefits of two nights' rest was evident in how the Australian attack set about the Proteas, even if Cummins' run of bowling without a wicket has now stretched beyond 200 runs. Markram and David Bedingham were each drawn into intemperate shots by fresh bowlers, before Ackerman was bounced out and Bavuma cornered so effectively that he felt the claustrophobic urge to get away from the crouched fielders. “There’s many ways to skin a cat,” Harmer said. “As an off-spinner, you want to bowl a right-hander through the gate. That’s the dream delivery. But there are a lot of nuances in how you can set batters up, get them to play on the back foot or front foot by using fielders.



“That’s the art of spin bowling. Understanding what’s easy and what’s difficult, how a batter is trying to play you, and you’re going to have moments where you can take a risk. But yeah, it’s about trying to play with the batter’s mind by using your field.” In 2001 at Trent Bridge, Warne had brought about a similar rash-looking shot by Mark Ramprakash in a tight contest, paving the way for Australia to secure the Ashes. Having been in and out of the team recently, Lyon would cherish nothing more than to do likewise. Starc, too, has a South African Test series victory firmly in his sights. World.title: Australia vs South Africa LIVE: Mitchell Starc’s searing Cape Town Test puts series win in sight
World.content:
Mitchell Starc’s golden Cape Town Test has helped Australia edge closer to a famous series victory as the pace great struck twice on day three to leave South Africa 4-140 and with a lead of just 40.

After taking six wickets on the opening day to help set up the Test for Australia, Starc removed openers Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman.

His double blow came after a second Test century for Josh Inglis had helped lift Australia to 429 in their first innings early on day three, in reply to the Proteas’ 329.

The third and deciding Test still remains somewhat in the balance, with a fourth-innings chase looming as tricky on a wicket that’s offering plenty of turn.

But thanks to Starc (2-29) and Nathan Lyon’s crucial late dismissal of stubborn homer skipper Temba Bavuma, Australia can for now claim the upper hand.

South Africa were guilty of throwing away some of their wickets on Thursday, with Markram driving Starc straight to Travis Head at mid-off for two.

David Bedingham then top-edged a Josh Hazlewood short ball to deep backward square on 11, after being one of three Proteas caught hooking in the first innings.

And while Marques Ackerman and Bavuma appeared to have steadied the ship for the Proteas, it was a brute of a ball from Starc that broke a 64-run partnership.

Brought back on midway through the last session, the left-armer had a bouncer follow Ackerman as he tried to uppercut on 62.

It hit the left-hander’s bat and helmet on the way through to the slips, leaving the Proteas 3-95 and still five runs short of drawing level.

Ackerman did try to review the call and was told to start walking by Head with time having just elapsed, but replays showed the call would not have been overturned anyway.

Lyon then bowled Bavuma for 35 just five minutes before stumps, when the Proteas captain inexplicably tried to hit hard across the line with the offspinner getting prodigious turn.

Pat Cummins has again gone wicketless, with his drought now extending to 358 balls and back to the first Test in Durban.

But he still bowled particularly well, with Bavuma edging Australia’s captain to just in front of slip and surviving an lbw review on height.

South Africa have not lost a home Test series for almost six years, and now need a serious recovery effort in a three-match contest full of twists and turns to keep that record.

Earlier, Inglis’s century headlined one of Australia’s most complete batting performances in years, with Alex Carey (80), Matt Renshaw (74) and Cameron Green (65) also posting half-centuries.

Cooper Connolly also made a crucial 29 alongside the lower-order, helping add another 49 for the final few wickets after Australia lost 3-10 on Thursday.

Those extra runs could prove crucial, with the pitch showing signs of turn and spinner Simon Harmer taking 4-107 for the Proteas before Lyon’s late work.

After being called in late to replace the injured Steve Smith, Inglis brought up his hundred when he reverse-swept Harmer to the boundary.

At that point the Proteas had started the day reasonably flat, with a number of misfields at Newlands under the warm Cape Town sun.

But when he was caught behind later in the same Harmer over and a 185-run stand with Carey was ended, the Proteas were suddenly back in the contest.

Carey edged Harmer to slip four overs later, before Pat Cummins was trapped lbw by Kagiso Rabada in the mini collapse.

World.title: New wave of Australian antisemitism comes from progressive social justice critics, says antisemitism envoy
World.content:
Exclusive NationalAntisemitism New wave of Australian antisemitism comes from progressive social justice critics, says antisemitism envoy Clair Weaver October 30, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The most pervasive form of discrimination against Jewish Australians comes from progressives motivated by social justice who give antisemitism a “respectable veneer”, argues a new report from Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism (ASECA). The report describes this mainstream group as combining the hostility of Islamist extremism with far-left ideology delivered through a progressive lens, singling them out for making antisemitism acceptable and even fashionable. ASECA Priorities, a new road map report to be released on Friday, identifies evolving threats and progress in tackling antisemitism, with envoy Jillian Segal also levelling heavy criticism at universities and the ABC. It includes recommendations for reforms across society, from health and the arts to migration and the digital world. Jillian Segal believes a new progressive antisemitism is conflating the actions of the Israeli government with Jewish Australians. Janie Barrett



In an interview with this masthead before the report’s release, Segal acknowledged antisemitism has always come from the far-right, far-left and Islamist extremism, but pointed to a newer, more palatable form that gives it “intellectual and cultural credibility”. “What we have is antisemitism that I describe as much more in the middle: well-intentioned people who are concerned about the policies of the state of Israel and feel critical of them,” she said. “And they transfer that criticism to Jewish members of society in Australia … through a lens of thinking that they are upholding progressive values and human rights. “It’s really conflating criticism of policies of the government of Israel onto Jewish Australians. And actually, Jewish Australians have got no influence on the state of Israel. They may not support any of those policies, and yet, they are suffering.” Impacts on Jewish people have ranged from hostility, online abuse and exclusion to doxxing, graffiti and violence, Segal said. Zionism, or the belief in Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state, has also become a proxy for antisemitism, according to the report, even though it doesn’t equate to excluding Palestinian self-determination or sovereignty.



“Increasingly, and often to avoid appearing transparently and obviously antisemitic, it has become common to vilify, target and ostracise ‘Zionists’ rather than ‘Jews’,” the report said. “Jews, generally in Australia, are supportive of the existence of the state of Israel,” Segal said. “But not necessarily, of course, for all the policies.” With caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political future uncertain in the fallout of Israel’s deadlocked election this week, Segal said Israel and its government should be subject to scrutiny and criticism like any other democratic state. Online environment A febrile online environment, in which conspiracy theories and hate flourish, is also singled out in the report as “one of the most significant accelerators of contemporary antisemitism”.



The report comes amid renewed government focus on online hate and abuse, as Indi MP Helen Haines recovers after losing both legs in an alleged attack by a 43-year-old man outside her electorate office. Segal said there’s been “an explosion of hate” online, which ramped up against Jews after Hamas’ October 7 terror attack. “We saw a further increase after the Bondi terror attack,” she said. “And we saw all those absolutely terrible allegations online that Bondi was staged: it was not real, the people staged their own blood on their head. “Not only was it incredibly traumatic for the people who were there, but even more traumatic then for that real experience to be trivialised and made fun of online.” Following the Bondi terror attack, the report said “social media was flooded with a cascade of denials of the killings, conspiracy theories.” Flavio Brancaleone



Media One of the more controversial recommendations of the ASECA report is the call for an external, independent watchdog for the ABC and SBS to be installed by the federal government. Segal reported significant concern in the Jewish community about the public broadcasters’ reporting on issues related to Israel and the Middle East, with allegations of “disproportionate, misleading or inaccurate” coverage. “Jewish Australians have reported being abused, harassed and accused of being ‘baby killers’ or supporters of ‘genocide’ simply for their belief in the right of Israel to exist,” the report stated. “That perception of a link between coverage and hostility is itself a matter of public importance.” While the ABC and SBS have internal ombudsmen, Segal argues more serious complaints should be handled externally to ensure accountability and public confidence.



“Many other industries – such as telecommunications, superannuation and financial services – have external complaints dealt with transparently and independently by ombudsman services,” she said. “And I think that should apply to the public broadcasters as well.” The ABC and SBS defended their Middle East reporting and internal complaints processes at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion earlier this year. Public funding cut Taxpayer funding would be withheld or stripped from people or organisations that engage in or tolerate antisemitism, under several recommendations in the report. This applied to arts, culture, sport and university research and included government grants. Previous proposals have been met with resistance on the grounds of freedom of artistic expression.



“My principle is that government money should not be used to foment hate in any sphere,” said Segal. The report also calls for doxxed or excluded Jewish artists to be re-engaged by the arts sector. Universities ‘slow to act’ Universities come under fire for “serious shortcomings”, including failing to act on antisemitism and adopt an agreed definition. “University leaders have periodically expressed regret, but actions have been slow and inadequate on campus encampments, office invasions, activism in learning environments, and disruptive actions hostile to Jewish staff, students and visitors,” the report states.



While an agreed Universities Australia definition of antisemitism was endorsed by vice chancellors in 2025, this year it emerged that no university had adopted a uniform definition. Western Sydney University chancellor Jennifer Westacott acknowledged a failure by the sector to tackle antisemitism. Louie Douvis Western Sydney University chancellor Professor Jennifer Westacott said there was “a collective failure to address the escalating severity of antisemitism” by the sector and that more work was needed. “Universities have to be places where ideas can be respectfully contested,” she said. “They have to be places of debate, and they can be places of peaceful protest, but they should never be places of hate or fear.” Other recommendations include training for visa decision makers to recognise antisemitism, education and training in schools, the public sector and business, and the establishment of a national healthcare antisemitism taskforce.



Multicultural Affairs Minister Dr Anne Aly, who was the first Muslim woman elected to Australia’s parliament, said antisemitism was “a serious and deeply troubling challenge in Australia” and Jewish Australians have a right to feel safe. “We must never allow international conflicts to become a licence for hatred here at home,” she said. “Australians can hold different views, including on events overseas, without turning against one another. Multiculturalism is one of Australia’s greatest strengths, but it cannot be taken for granted.” The royal commission will deliver its final report on December 18. World.title: ‘A game-changer’: How a brick box without windows won an architecture award
World.content:
NationalQueenslandArchitecture ‘A game-changer’: How a brick box without windows won an architecture award Nick Dent October 29, 2026 — 11:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It looks like a layered slice of rock dug out of the earth and placed on the University of Queensland grounds. A pair of greenhouses sitting on top enhance this illusion, while inside, hidden from view, researchers are working like so many ants on how to feed a changing world. This is the Plant Futures Facility at the University of Queensland, and when the head of the School of Agriculture and Food Sustainability first walked in, he knew it was “a game changer”. The Plant Futures Facility at the University of Queensland supports research into biotechnology. Christopher Frederick Jones “It had a wow factor,” Professor Sagadevan Mundree said. “It’s state of the art, and the only one of its kind in the Southern Hemisphere.”



The building houses research into sustainable food, fibre and fuel production in response to climate change, environmental degradation, and population growth. It contains about 40 “growing rooms”, cabinets and glasshouses where climatic conditions of any environment can be recreated. One room might be like the sub-Saharan desert. Another might be like Finland; another, a tropical region. Laboratories can manipulate light, heat, humidity, CO2 and other environmental factors. Christopher Frederick Jones Academics can book rooms for two or three-month trials, then check out when they have their results. “It feels like a very luxurious hotel for plants,” Mundree said. “For the university, I would say [it’s had] a huge impact because it gives us a chance now to mimic microclimates.



“That gives us the edge of being able to do speed breeding, and one of the areas that is fast evolving is genome editing of crops.” Designed by Brisbane firm M3Architecture, the Plant Futures Facility has won a National Award for Educational Architecture 2026, bestowed by the Australian Institute of Architects. Corridors utilise adaptable coloured lighting and mirrors. Christopher Frederick Jones Jury member Alice Hampson said the building was “astounding” both for its technology and its aesthetic. “Conceptually, it’s like a walled garden [with] a pixelated brick facade, it reminds me of sedimentary rock samples,” Hampson said.



“The patterning in the brickwork is from basically a cross-section through the Great Artesian Basin, the geological profile of Queensland,” architect Michael Christensen said. Brick was chosen as a response to the neighbouring Hartley Teakle Building, a well-loved 1969 brick edifice originally built for the Agriculture and Entomology departments. Christensen said the new building’s main challenge was the fact it could not have any windows, “because that will change the amount of light, or the temperature. “It’s a big brick box, right? So we were thinking about how can we make working in there a more pleasant experience.



“In these grow rooms, the researchers are playing with the environmental conditions for the plants. So we thought, well, why don’t we do the same to the academics?” Related Article Architecture Peter designed a Brisbane house that breaks all the rules. Now it’s an award winner The building’s central corridor features variable light and colour settings. There are also distorted mirrors adding visual interest, “like at the Ekka”. “It could have been boring and sterile,” Hampson said. “If I was a kid and visited, I’d be going, ‘How can I make a career to work in this building?’ Seven of the 34 National Architecture Awards were won by Queensland projects.



Two houses in the Mount Coot-tha foothills won residential awards. A renovated 1920s home in Burleigh, Woodside Cottage, won the Eleanor Cullis-Hill Award for Houses (Alterations and Additions). A spectacular city apartment block, 443 Queen St, won the award for Multiple Housing, while commercial office tower 205 North Quay won the Harry Seidler Award for Commercial Architecture. City restaurant Golden Avenue won an award for its interiors. Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: ‘I have created my own legacy’: McReight wins first John Eales Medal
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘I have created my own legacy’: McReight wins first John Eales Medal Jonathan Drennan Updated October 29, 2026 — 10:33pm ,first published 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Fraser McReight has won the John Eales Medal as Australian rugby’s best player of the year after his international teammates recognised his consistently excellent performances for his country this season. McReight received the game’s highest honour at the Rugby Australia awards in Sydney on Thursday night, while 21-year-old inside centre Faitala Moleka was crowned Wallaroos Player of the Year and Reds star Treyvon Pritchard named rookie of the year. Fraser McReight has been recognised by his peers for Rugby Australia’s highest honour Getty Images The John Eales medal is based on votes submitted by Wallabies players after every Test match. McReight joins a long list of outstanding back-rowers to have won the award since it was established in 2002, including David Lyons, Phil Waugh, George Smith (twice), Rob Valetini (twice), David Pocock (twice) and former captain Michael Hooper, who won the award a record four times. Like Hooper, McReight has played some of his best rugby when the Wallabies are under the greatest pressure. A ferocious competitor at the breakdown, McReight has also developed an accomplished all-around game, establishing himself as one of the best openside breakaways in world rugby.



Related Article Analysis

Wallabies Why Wallabies are a better chance of winning World Cup than Bledisloe McReight acknowledged the significant legacy of the previous John Eales medal winners, including Hooper, after winning the award. “I think it means I have created my own legacy, those players that have come before me are fantastic players and we’re all so different,” McReight said. “They’re all unbelievable players and I was lucky enough to play with Hoops and I idolised a lot of them. “I think for me now to carve my own path and knowing that I’ve got the World Cup next year and other things that I’m really targeting is really special to me...



“You don’t play the game for these [individual] honours. You play to win as a team and that’s all I care about... winning and having a beer in the sheds with my mates.” McReight was also recognised for his outstanding defensive performances – particularly in the 16-point defeat to France in Brisbane in July, in which he scored two tries as well as making 19 tackles, with the award for Defender of the Year. McReight has also become the first Queensland Reds player to claim a John Eales medal since former Wallabies fullback Chris Latham 20 years ago. The late Peter Meagher who has been recognised by Rugby Australia for his outstanding service to the game. Meagher family Brisbane Junior Rugby Union Western Region chair Paula Watkins was honoured with the inaugural Peter Meagher Spirit of Rugby Award, in recognition of her dedication and tireless support for the community game.



Meagher, a much-loved figure in the Randwick rugby community, was one of 15 people tragically killed in the terrorist attack at Bondi Beach last year while taking photographs of the Hanukkah festival as a volunteer. “Rugby Australia decided to honour Marzo”, who held a longtime association with Randwick rugby club, by rebranding the award previously named after Nick Farr-Jones in his honour. Shawn Mackay Award for Men’s Sevens Player of the Year - Henry Hutchison

Shawn Mackay Award for Women’s Sevens Player of the Year - Isabella Nasser

Swyftx Super Rugby Pacific Player of the Year - Jock Campbell

Swyftx Super Rugby Women’s Player of the Year - Siokapesi Palu Sekona

Junior Women’s Player of the Year - Waiaria Ellis, Wallaroos and NSW Waratahs

Cadbury Try of the Year - Siokapesi Palu Sekona, Wallaroos vs. Scotland, Canberra

Joe French Award for Outstanding Contribution to Rugby - Craig Robberds, ACT Rugby

Geoff ‘Bunter’ Shaw Community Coach of the Year Award - Kieran Smith, NSW Rugby

Andrew Cole Community Match Official of the Year - Julius Ambat, NSW Rugby First-time winner Nasser led the Australian Women’s team to the World Championship title while Hutchison, who last achieved this accolade in 2021, guided the Men’s side to their first tournament win since 2023 when they claimed gold in Valladolid.



Japan-bound fullback Jock Campbell won the Super Rugby Pacific Player of the Year title after an outstanding year for the Reds, while ACT Brumbies and Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona was named Super Rugby Women’s Player of the Year. Amelia Whitaker was also named women’s rookie of the year after her first season for the Wallaroos.
