World.title: Cost of living, youth drain, and marine protection dominate final Nelson debate
World.content:
Last election, less than 30 votes separated the top two candidates in Nelson.

On election night, it looked like National's Blair Cameron was going to be Nelson's MP. He was out in front with a 54 vote lead, but Labour's Rachel Boyack claimed the victory with a 26 vote lead after an official recount. It could be a different story this election, if the new talent running for Opportunity and the Green Party split the left vote.

At the last debate before election night hosted by the Nelson Tasman Chamber of Commerce and the Blue House, candidates had a final chance to make their case to an audience of around 80 people gathered at the Tides Hotel in Nelson.

Cameron said despite losing the seat, he'd worked hard over the last three years to advocate for the electorate while continuing his work remotely for the World Bank.

"Every single one of our national cabinet ministers has visited Nelson over the last three years and I've put a lot of time and effort to make that happen, that's what I've done in my spare time, he told the audience of around 80 people gathered at the Tides Hotel in Nelson.

"If I'm your MP, that'll be my job."

He said he wanted to see Nelson become a more attractive place for young people.

National's Blair Cameron. LDR/Sara Hollyman

"My goal, if I get to be your MP, is to shift the perception of our region from somewhere that's just a nice place to retire to somewhere where it's an exciting place for young people to start their careers. I want 18 to 35 year olds to look at our region and think, Nelson Tasman, that's somewhere where I want to build my future."

Boyack said in the last three years, life had become more expensive and access to healthcare more difficult.

"Every person I speak to talks to about the challenges they're facing with the increase in the cost of fuel, the increase in the cost of groceries, increase in the cost of doing business. All of these things that are affecting business and also everyday working, ordinary people in New Zealand, many of whom are now having to rely on food banks to be able to feed themselves and their families. "

The conversation turned to the fishing sector and Boyack said while Labour was open to phasing out bottom trawling, an outright ban would be devastating for the region.

"We do have to address the impacts of bottom trawling, there's no doubt about that and it can cause absolute devastation on some of the most precious parts of our ocean. Our policy is to put limits on bottom trawling and over time, we are very open to having that conversation around what a phase-out would look like. "

Labour's Rachel Boyack. VNP/Louis Collins

Opportunity's Nelson candidate Jodie Kuntzsch has spent the last 20 years working in the seafood and aquaculture sectors and said it was possible to find a balance between sustainability and innovation, and there were business in the region that had proved that.

"You can have a resilient sustainable marine environment and have thriving innovative high-value businesses and support our community to have natural resilience along the coast and support our cultural and recreational practices."

At number six on the list, Kuntzsch will make it into Parliament if the party gets over the 5 percent threshold.

MC and Chamber of Commerce chief executive Ali Boswijk asked the candidates how they would deal with coalition partners making public statements that conflicted with their party's values.

She cited NZ First candidate Ron Mark's recent comments blaming 'woke b******t' for the HMNZ Manawanui sinking.

Green candidate Rohan O-Neill-Stevens, the city's former deputy mayor said that behaviour had not just begun during the election campaign.

Nelson candidates at the Last Chance Nelson Candidate Debate at the Tides Hotel. RNZ / Samantha Gee

"We have had senior ministers, we have had our deputy prime minister say horrific things, racist and sexist things, and not be called out on it at all.

"To me your values, if you don't stand up for them, aren't your values."

O-Neill-Stevens said his time on council meant he was used to working with people of all stripes, including mayor Nick Smith, with whom he disagreed on things, but the two had worked well together as they had mutual respect for one another's values.

"I think fundamentally if you believe in something, you have to stand up for it, you have to fight for it and that doesn't compromise your ability to work collaboratively."

At 16 on the Green Party list, O-Neill-Stevens has also got a good shot of making it into Parliament.

ACT candidate Chris Baillie encouraged people to party vote ACT, but made it clear he wasn't seeking a return to Parliament.

"I've spent three years up in Wellington and I think you're all mad if you want to go back there. But we need to continue the way we're going.

"ACT is committed to reducing the size of government, making it much more manageable. New Zealand has a spending problem, not necessarily a tax problem."

World.title: Affordable and easy to access: Why peptide users say they’re injecting unregulated drugs
World.content:
An increasing number of New Zealanders are using unapproved peptides purchased through social media to help with weight loss and chronic health conditions.

It comes as Health New Zealand started providing pharmacies with peptide-injecting kits as part of its needle exchange programme.

Are you or someone you know using peptides? We want to hear your story and are open to discussing anonymity. Get in touch at: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Medsafe has warned many of the unapproved peptides are illegal, untested and potentially dangerous.

Oceane Ceballos, had lost about 4kg over a 10-week period while using retatrutide, known as "Reta", a weight-loss peptide which is not approved for use in Aotearoa.

She had seen "incredible transformations" for people using the drug on social media but found for her, it was not so successful.

In May 2026, Medsafe warned against anyone using them if they were not prescribed or sourced from a pharmacy.

"There is a very real risk that these products may be of poor quality, not contain the substance claimed on the label (if they are labelled), contain other harmful substance not on the label or not be sterile (and so may contain substantial quantities of germs or mould).

"These products... are illegal and potentially harmful. Using them can cause serious and potentially life-threatening reactions."

Ceballos had been doubtful about injecting peptides until she saw the weight loss results a friend was having.

"I've got Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), so it's hard for me to lose weight. I've been a big girl all my life.. and would like to get back to my pre-baby body.

"My friend was in the same boat and I saw her lose 24kgs in three months and she just looked amazing... so I was like, I'm gonna give it a go, if my friend had really good results, I'm gonna jump on."

In the past, Ceballos said she'd considered getting weight loss surgery and had discussed taking a GLP-1, like Wegovy, with her GP but was put off by the price which was between $365-$470 per month.

Ordering Reta was "super easy" Ceballos said and was cheaper at a price of $200, through a "friend of a friend", who had a supplier in China.

"It was as easy as a bank transfer through my friend and then the supplier ships it to you. I ordered on a Friday and it came by Monday.

"The seller sent me the wrong needles to use which was really dangerous, it would be so easy to give yourself way more than what you should be having."

A vial of Retatrutide Oceane Ceballos had in her fridge. OCEANE CEBALLOS / SUPPLIED

Three weeks into the weekly injections, Ceballos said she didn't notice any difference.

"I thought did I get a dud Reta? I messaged the seller and she was like 'no, no, here's all the paperwork I have.... I'll add you to my group, hundreds of women can vouch for it'."

At week seven, Ceballos said she was told to increase her dose, which is when the negative side effects began. These included waking up in the night with headaches, becoming extremely uncomfortable after eating, diarrhoea and experiencing sulphur burps.

"I hadn't heard anyone experiencing what I was so I ended up speaking with a GP about my side effects and they recommend I stop before it gets any worse."

Ceballos said she didn't listen and continued for another three doses. Until the side effects became too much.

"In these groups I was open about what I experienced and I started thinking is this all just a marketing scheme? Are these AI bots replying to me?

"There was no one I could speak with who was going through what I was going through... it just didn't work for me at all... I'm not going to go and promote Reta, people need to be more informed."

She urged anyone considering injecting peptides to "do it the right way" and speak with their GP.

Molly* who spoke to RNZ on condition of anonymity, is also no longer injecting peptides, but planned to go back on them to help with inflammation caused by endometriosis. She said it also helped her quit drinking and smoking.

She had used Reta before moving to KLOW, a four-peptide blend and GLOW peptide stack.

Molly said she'd had no bad side effects and her doctor was aware she was on them.

"I've been off for four weeks now and my inflammation is coming back."

Molly said she knew lots of other women who were injecting peptides and she was able to source it online.

"My sister had someone she bought it off and I sampled that one, but I wanted to do my own research and supply. I've known plenty of people who have snorted so much up their nose... do you know where it comes from? Some people are so quick to put down someone who has found a good source."

She said she found her supplier though community pages on social media.

Molly was able to source peptides through social media. (File photo) Samuel Boivin / NurPhoto via AFP

Molly used a needle exchange as she used to buy her own boxes from an Auckland supplier but they recently changed its rules so only registered companies could buy them.

She wanted to see peptide testing come into New Zealand.

"You can get drugs tested at a concert, but no where to safely take your peptides.

"There's so many people that are on it... my mum's on it, my sister's on it, my neighbours are on it… everyone I know is on it. You'd be surprised."

What is in imported peptides?

Dr Paul Harris runs the Harris Peptide Laboratory and had found concerning results in his analysis of imported peptides.

"In one case, [I tested] a 'Wolverine Stack' which is a mixture of two peptides, there's the Body Protective Compound and TB-500, and I couldn't see any evidence of TB-500 in that sample... In fact, it was an unknown peptide and I'm still not quite sure what it is," he said.

"I also analysed a couple of samples of retatrutide, which claimed there were 10 milligrams in each vial, and my analysis found they were different amounts in each vial."

He said people didn't know what they were injecting into their bodies.

"A lot of these things are arriving with so-called 'data sheets' which I think have mostly been falsified, because you don't actually know how they've analysed them."

'Touted as a wonder drug'

Social media touted peptides as a "wonder drug", Professor of policy and health at Massey University Chris Wilkins said.

Massey University Professor Chris Wilkins. (File photo) RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

"People are probably most familiar with the weight loss ones, which are actually clinically trialled pharmaceutical products you can get through your doctor, so there is real evidence for some of those peptides in specific areas.

"The problem is there's a whole range of peptides and a whole range of claims about them, and we're talking about ones that are not manufactured under medical-grade conditions, and are not purchased or obtained through the health system."

The products may not be the substances users think they're getting, Wilkins said and since they were manufactured in unregulated conditions, they could come with their own contaminants.

Injections were also risky, Wilkins said, as people weren't always aware of health risks involved in terms of clean needles and good injection practice.

Wilkins said good information needed to get out to people using peptides about some of the risks involved, especially in purchasing online from unknown sources.

University of Auckland molecular medicine and pathology Professor Peter Shepherd said there was no real way of knowing the quality of the products.

"There's huge risks, risks of infection, of overdosing, because we just don't know what's in them."

He said it showed people were really desperate to lose weight and was a real "cry for help".

"We should really be doing something about this bu supplying legitimate products through proper channels.

"There's a very worrying degree of people believing anything they see on social media, and taking risks as a result. It's very disturbing."

World.title: New Zealand First commits to introducing bill forcing Ngāpuhi to sign Treaty settlement if in government
World.content:
New Zealand First deputy leader Shane Jones has committed to introducing a bill forcing Ngāpuhi to sign a Treaty settlement in the first 100 days of the next government, if re-elected.

Jones made the commitment during TVNZ's Kaupapa Māori Debate on Thursday night, where he said he would "deal to it in the first hundred days after the election".

He told RNZ last year the bill would force Ngāpuhi, the largest iwi in Aotearoa, into a single commercial and ensure there was no mention of hapū sovereignty.

At the time, he said a Ngāpuhi claim should be focused on good governance, a strong economic base and not get distracted by "insoluble debates pertaining to indigenous sovereignty".

Speaking to media following the debate, Jones said the bill had been worked on and would "crystalise" the cost and "way forward" of the claim.

"We're not going to tolerate any more taxpayer money being wasted on pursuits such as parallel sovereignties within the broader Ngāpuhi community."

Jones said if introduced, the bill would go to select committee then all the "factions of Ngāpuhi" would be able to apply to appear before the committee.

"This was done for the original Ngāi Tahu bill, and it'll be done for Ngāpuhi if we have our way," he said.

TVNZ's Kaupapa Māori Debate. Screenshot / TVNZ

Labour's Māori campaign chairperson Willie Jackson said the bill was "absolute nonsense" and would get rejected by Ngāpuhi.

"You cannot just force our people into settlement, you have to work with our people, [and] Shane knows that better than anyone," he said.

Jackson said he "understood his frustration" but Ngāpuhi would not settle just because "Shane Jones makes a declaration".

Asked if forcing a settlement through Parliament was a good way to get Ngāpuhi to settle, National's Tama Potaka said it was something he "never contemplated" himself.

"Let's see what happens after the election, but that's something that the matua and the rangatira have opined on and have been very bold in their position on," he said.

ACT's Nicole McKee said ACT supported the treaty settlement process but government forcing the issue was the right approach.

"What we can do is encourage them to actually come together so that we can get a settlement because the longer that it is delayed the harder that it is on the people of Ngāpuhi," she said.

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rāwiri Waititi said Jones was a mokopuna of the North, and ultimately, it was an issue North would "have to reconcile".

"I've got my own issues and my own iwi, so Te Whānau a Apanui also hasn't settled, nor has my neighbouring iwi and iwi I whakapapa to, Ngāi Tai."

"I'll let Shane focus on the North, and I've got my own iwi that I need to get settlements over the line in the first 100 days," he said.

The John Key-National government sought to get a settlement over the line in 2009 by recognising the mandate known as Tuhoronuku, initiated by previous rūnanga leader Sonny Tau.

World.title: Firefighter training deficiencies report includes disputed claim of 'beasting' recruits
World.content:
A Fire and Emergency report has revealed major flaws in the way firefighters are trained - including a claim that an old-school military style approach called "beasting" is used to belittle trainees.

In response, FENZ has launched a training reset but didn't share the report with firefighters or the Minister of Internal Affairs.

The report found training was often outdated, disjointed, or did not teach new recruits or firefighters getting a refresh what they needed for the job, and was unsafe for learners.

"Trainers use old military-style approaches (beasting) to belittle learners if they fail to meet the required standard," it said.

"These mindsets and behaviours do not promote our courses as safe learning environments."

Fire and Emergency said the reset would be "short" and aim to improve safety.

However, it was confined to new recruits and volunteers, and not extend to the 1000-plus professional firefighters.

National training leader Joe Stanley said he blocked the extension, saying: "We're going down the wrong path."

Joe Stanley. RNZ

He faulted the training report for taking aim at individual instructors when they were doing their best in an underfunded system that needed to change.

Minister finds out

FENZ is under intense pressure.

Its chief executive quit last week over a month after Minister Brooke van Velden said she did not have confidence in him.

She told RNZ on Tuesday: "I was not made aware of the 2025 report you refer to, which I understand was an internal Fire and Emergency working document.

"I am advised the report helped shape this year's redesign of recruit and volunteer training. I expect the board to ensure Fire and Emergency provides recruits and volunteers with safe, effective training that meets operational requirements and prioritises firefighter safety."

Minister Brooke van Velden. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Bill Butzbach, head of the United Fire Brigades' Association that represents 12,000 volunteers, said he would be asking to see a copy.

"We're quite disappointed that we didn't see it."

He put that down to an oversight.

Beasting or not

The training deficiencies are long-running and systemic, according to the report.

Butzbach said this came as no surprise.

"It's been on our radar."

Firefighters RNZ has spoken with have for several years said training did not get high enough priority.

The problems with it come on top of the fire truck fleet management woes investigated by MPs.

A few lines in the report refer to "beasting", and the extent or nature of it are not detailed.

Historically, it is a military practice of verbally dressing down or ordering a trainee to do arduous physical exercise - 100 push-ups - as a reprimand.

FENZ told RNZ it "does not condone or tolerate the behaviour described, and it is not part of our training".

The United Fire Brigades' Association said it knew of one case in the last two years, of a volunteer recruit. The details were confidential but verbal rather than physical belittling was the issue.

Bill Butzbach, head of the United Fire Brigades' Association. ufba.org.nz

They worked on it with FENZ, and Butzbach recalled one instructor was censured.

"We were satisfied with the outcome."

He would tell recruits and their families that there were sufficient safeguards in place and FENZ had changed that culture.

But Stanley rejected the "beasting" assertion entirely.

"That's wrong. I've never seen any beasting," he said.

He works at the Rotorua national training centre, running officer development, and is also national president of the Professional Firefighters' Union (NZPFU).

They ran fitness "boot camps" but these were voluntary, he said.

Other sources said non-uniformed staff may have got the wrong idea. The training report was authored by an educationalist rather than a firefighter, though it drew on some firefighter input.

'Safety training is not woven through'

The report goes into much more detail about other training shortcomings.

It cast deep doubts on whether "we do enough to embed safety in the training we provide".

Citing the deaths of two volunteer firefighters in a landslide in Muriwai in Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023 and a volunteer firefighter injured by a car last year, it said: "While these examples relate to volunteers, feedback from interviewees suggests there is not a strong safety culture in career firefighting either."

"Personal and crew safety training is not woven through all training activities."

Stanley once again said that was wrong.

"That's a backhanded insult against the programmes that I run.

"I wear the deaths of those two firefighters in Muriwai as a motivation to ensure that everyone that comes through the national training officer development function knows how to make good decisions."

Butzbach said FENZ and his association had the safety of personnel as a top priority.

'Systemic inconsistency'

Recruits do a 12-week course at the Rotorua centre. Firefighters undergo refreshers and specialised training there, as well as at fire stations.

The report featured a long list of deficiencies in training generally:

"Significant concerns" about learner experience and safety. Trainees did not feel supported; for instance, there was no proper gym and recruits "must eat the meals at the hotel (that's 84 buffet dinners in a row)."

"Systemic inconsistency" leading to highly variable outcomes and assessment.

Old facilities; for instance, there has been no training on real fires for over a year because the steel containers set up for this had twisted and begun leaking smoke.

"Old information" presented in old ways that were not updated to catch up with new firefighting approaches in rail tunnels, or involving electric vehicles or lithium batteries.

Overall, "there is no clear and documented alignment of course content to an overarching purpose".

"This exposes the organisation to operational and reputational risk," said the report.

Short reset

FENZ's board got the training report in February. A team was set up to improve training but it has recently been shedding staff and a request for more funding was turned down, RNZ understands.

The report was used to begin redeveloping recruit and volunteer training.

Stanley said he blocked that being extended to career officers.

FENZ said it recently reviewed its improvement programme to "further improve delivery, effectiveness, and value for money".

Changes would be put in place during a short reset period.

A key initiative would be improving the main safety concepts, it added.

RNZ understands managers have talked about slowing the pace of the reset to find a more sustainable model.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

'It's miles away'

Stanley said FENZ was wasting resources on a training reset that had far too little front-line input.

"Perversely, it's become an opportunity to save money rather than reinvest the organisation's resources into better training outcomes," he said.

"I'm very, very protective over the programmes that I'm running. There is constant pressure on reducing the cost of those programmes and I push against that."

Butzbach said the reset was at a very early stage with his association in talks with FENZ about it.

"It's just started. It's miles away from being completed and it will require significant investment."

Cost cutting on training had not come up with FENZ, and any move towards that would be counterproductive, he added.

One problem was what training should cover, Butzbach said: It had to match firefighters' core jobs but these were still being debated in the face of a greater range of emergency demands.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Fire and Emergency said late on Thursday that there had been isolated instances of poor behaviour by its instructors but called them "issues of the past".

"Like any large organisation, we are not immune to pockets of poor behaviour and are aware that in the past there have been isolated instances of poor behaviour by some of our people. Where known, these instances were addressed," said deputy chief executive of prevention Stephen Hunt in a statement.

Instructors had a critical role and influence so FENZ had strengthened the standards they were held to, including how they were selected and supported.

"We have revised guidelines that set clear expectations of professional conduct in the training environment."

Behaviour on courses was monitored.

"We are confident these changes have addressed the issues of the past," Hunt said.

He added FENZ had put a lot of work into training in general to embed safety concepts in the last two years, with help from with operational personnel to close any gap in knowledge that existed.

Revised safe-person and risk assessment were "now built into every practical lesson".

The career recruit course had clear outcomes and assessment to ensure people got the skills they needed, and similar for volunteer recruits.

"We have not yet completed the reviews in full. We deliberately prioritised the recruit courses because they set the foundation for every firefighter. We will advance to the officer programmes through the review cycles."

World.title: Is there an easy fix to card surcharge problem?
World.content:
Audio player for " When does my property become relationship property? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2230547%2Fis-there-an-easy-fix-to-card-surcharge-problem

Could redirecting point-of-sale systems so that contactless payments go to eftpos transactions, rather than Visa or MasterCards, be the answer to New Zealand's surcharge worries?

While Australia has moved to ban credit card surcharges, plans have stalled on this side of the Tasman.

The Commerce Commission has introduced limits on the interchange fees that can be charged on credit card transactions but so far the impact on consumers has been muted.

Organisations such as Consumer NZ are still calling for a surcharge ban, because they do not think the reduction in fees will be passed on. Retail NZ has called for a full investigation to determine what sort of surcharge cap might be appropriate for businesses to charge to cover their costs.

David Cunningham. Supplied / Squirrel

But David Cunningham, chief executive of Squirrel, said he had prepared a submission to the Reserve Bank's modernising retail payment systems consultation, arguing that there was an easy fix.

"When you tap your card, it goes through Visa or MasterCard. That is criminal in my mind. It should go through our eftpos network, which is a fraction of the cost, a fraction of the cost. It gets rid of this whole surcharging thing."

He said it would save New Zealand businesses $100 million in fees if people could be directed to eftpos instead.

"Tap payments that aren't credit should be routed through the eftpos system rather than the Visa or MasterCard system. And that will create efficiency for New Zealand … and it can be implemented in months."

Peter Hansen, general manager of Eftpos New Zealand, said it was possible but not simple.

"It's very complicated and would require a lot of change across multiple industry participants. At the very least it would require a combination of regulatory and/or industry agreement on changes to current routing rules for card transactions, and technical changes at terminal, switch and card issuer level to support the different card acceptance profile."

He said because eftpos transactions require a PIN, while contactless payments below $200 do not, even if transactions were rerouted through the eftpos system they would decline.

"To solve that, we would need to either prompt for PIN on all contactless transactions, requiring terminal development and impacting the consumer benefit of contactless, or get issuers to agree to new transaction types that can be authorised without PIN, which requires switch and issuer development and increased risk for the issuer, as well as change routing rules at a processing level.

"And even then it wouldn't necessarily solve for mobile wallets that use a card token instead of a card number and include other costs - Apple charge fees per transaction - that the current eftpos commercial model doesn't currently support."

Julia Nicol, head of public affairs for Paymark said the main hurdles were rules set by international card schemes.

"Banks and merchants are bound by these rules so they can't just decide to change it. In some other jurisdictions like Australia, US, Europe and Singapore merchants can choose to use either a local processor or the international card schemes.

"In NZ, how the transaction is processed depends on the way the bank set the card up, the way customer chooses to pay and the payment options available on the terminal."

Nicol said a single debit card could be processed two ways in New Zealand. "Which way it goes is decided by scheme and industry rules, not by the merchant, not by the consumer, and not by any technical constraint."

When a card was tapped, it had to go via the international schemes, she said. When it was inserted or swiped, it was settled by the merchant servicing bank at materially lower cost.

"There is no security, fraud or cryptographic reason for the difference. Least cost routing (LCR) or merchant choice routing means giving the consumer and/or the merchant the choice which network it wants to use. Here in New Zealand, this can be enabled at the terminal or, similarly to Australia, 'dual-network' cards could be issued, allowing consumers to choose how they want their contactless transactions to be routed."

She agreed businesses could save well over $100m a year if they could route contactless debit cards locally.

"This estimate does not account for the change in consumer behaviour that would likely result from the ability to access LCR through contactless, rather than being obliged to access it through the cumbersome insert and swipe method.

"The Commerce Commission could require it by issuing an access standard under the Retail Payment Systems Act. For example, Visa's rulebook already contains a payment system selection rule for Australia, Europe and the United States; New Zealand is simply outside its scope."

Drew Franklin. Supplied / University of Auckland

Drew Franklin, associate dean at the University of Auckland business school, said he expected Commerce Commission limits on interchange fees to eventually bring the costs down for shoppers.

"The extent to which consumers benefit depends on how those savings are carried through the system - through two main stages. Banks and payment providers need to reflect lower interchange fees in what they charge businesses, and businesses then need to reflect those savings in surcharges or prices. Because interchange is only one component of the overall payment fee, we'd need to look at the total cost businesses face before knowing how much pressure this might have on downstream pricing. Lower fees are a useful start, though. The test is whether the savings reach the checkout, so to speak.

"This is a familiar or similar argument around structural separation in supermarkets, so I think these interventions are rather complementary, as well as the calls for more competition in the payments market. Fee limits and structural reform should work together - caps reduce one component of payment costs, while opening the payments system to independent competitors gives retailers alternatives and puts pressure on providers to lower their overall fees. Together, these changes should lower retailers' payment costs and give them more scope to reduce surcharges."

World.title: Does a free-trade agreement affect prices you pay?
World.content:
Audio player for " When does my property become relationship property? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2230546%2Fdoes-a-free-trade-agreement-affect-prices-you-pay

New Zealand's free-trade agreement with India has been in force for a little over a week - but will consumers notice any change in the prices they pay?

Economists say the answer isn't clear cut.

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said the effect would depend a lot on whether India was a large importing country or not, for any particular product.

When it was, its trade policies would have an effect on the world price.

"Reducing the amount of international product that its consumers are willing to buy, as domestic products are effectively relatively cheaper. This lower demand for international product effectively reduces the world price … and given New Zealand's situation where consumers effectively pay the world price for products that we export, prices end up being lower here as well, as do production levels because there's not as much profit or incentive to squeeze out the last marginal unit of production at a higher cost. So reversing that situation out, by removing a tariff, will lead to greater demand globally and a higher global price.

"However, if India is not a large importing country, then any change to its trade policies will have little or no effect on the world price. For example, if India removed an import tariff on beef, but there were still no beef imports because everyone in the country was Hindu and didn't eat beef, then the world price would remain unchanged - even though the price of available beef for Indian consumers had fallen. Thus there would be no effect on prices for NZ consumers (and no effect on exporters' revenue or volumes either)."

He said the question then became whether Indian demand for New Zealand products was expected to increase materially due to a reduction in tariffs, and whether the demand was significant enough that it would affect global activity.

"In reality, there will be a continuum between India having a large effect on the world price and having none at all.

"Having had a quick skim through NZ's key export categories to India, wool and apples look like the shift in Indian demand could be significant enough on a global scale to have some effect on the price, although wool prices are so poor that it might not make much difference, whereas Indian demand for lamb and wine is so low from a global perspective that it seems unlikely to affect prices."

Murat Ungor. Supplied

Murat Ungor, an economist at Otago University, said free-trade agreements could create lower prices for local consumers by letting cheaper goods in to be stocked on shop shelves.

But that was not always what happened.

"Trade creation occurs when cheaper imports from a partner replace higher-cost domestic production, so prices fall, consumers gain, and resources shift towards what the country does best," he said.

"Trade diversion occurs when imports switch from a cheaper outside supplier to a partner who is now cheaper only because of the tariff preference. Prices may still fall, but by less than under a non-discriminatory tariff cut, and the country loses tariff revenue and ends up buying from a higher-cost source. The gain shrinks and can turn negative."

He said which outcome dominated in any particular scenario would depend on a range of factors.

"Creation is more likely when the partner is a low-cost producer and the two economies make overlapping products at different costs, because there is domestic production to displace. Strict rules of origin can push firms to source inputs from partners even when outsiders are cheaper, adding to diversion. And the more of world supply the bloc covers, the less room there is for diversion."

Ungor said another important consideration was how much was actually passed on to shoppers.

"Even when a tariff cut lowers import costs, market structure determines how much of that reaches consumers. Where retail or distribution is concentrated, pass-through can be well below 100 percent. The overall effect on prices can therefore be modest, gradual and a one-off shift in the price level, not a change in ongoing inflation."

Gareth Kiernan. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

Kiernan said a big part of the rationale for the free-trade agreement with India was to allow some diversification away from the Chinese market.

He said that had served New Zealand well over the past 17 years but came with geopolitical risks, as well as the issue of being overly reliant on a single market.

"Risks that we saw demonstrated a few years ago when the Chinese government effectively turned off the tap on several Australian export categories, such as wine. Additionally, there's a widespread expectation that Chinese economic growth will be slower going forward than it has been over the 1990-2020 period, meaning that there are fewer gains to be made for exporters in that market.

"In contrast, Indian's outlook for economic growth and population growth remains relatively strong - and that's before one considers the rapid growth in the size of the country's middle class that has yet to occur, much like we've seen in China over the last 30-odd years. So the growth potential for exporters is considerable given the confluence of those factors, and the FTA's removal of impediments to realising that growth is key."

World.title: NZ facing fourth-largest increase in fuel costs
World.content:
Audio player for " When does my property become relationship property? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2230545%2Fnz-facing-fourth-largest-increase-in-fuel-costs

New Zealanders are facing the fourth-highest increase in fuel costs in the world, on a per capita basis, new data shows.

Statistics from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air show that the global oil price shock this year has added US$468 billion (NZ$833b) to the world's fuel bill.

The United States has felt the largest impact, with an additional US$160b (NZ$285b) added to its fuel costs. Canada was just behind, followed by Australia and then New Zealand.

New Zealand had the 10th highest increase in diesel prices in the world compared to pre-conflict, up US55c (NZ99c) a litre.

Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the impact was because New Zealand had high levels of car ownership.

"A lot of people don't live in very large, developed metropolitan areas where you have a lot of public transport available."

He said New Zealand's price movement was not as large on a per litre basis as some of the other countries in the report - Laos had experienced diesel jumping by US$1 (NZ$1.78) - because some developing countries had regulated fuel prices.

"What tends to happen in those cases is they sometimes have very large percentage moves when the government has to move what's typically a subsidised price up by a relatively long way when a big shock occurs. We don't really have that in New Zealand because fuel pricing basically reflects market pricing."

He said fuel spending was up 27 percent per person compared to the same time a year ago but the implied volume of fuel purchases was lower by about 12 percent.

"We're spending more, we're driving less, and you can see one of the effects of that in that public transport spending on our cards is also up 18 percent since February … so that does reflect a change in behaviour because the cost of driving has gone up."

He said New Zealand households were being disproportionately affected.

Many were having to spend money on fuel that might otherwise have gone on other things, including "nice-to-haves", he said.

"I think it's self-evident that, you know, if we hadn't seen this Iran war and the big increase in oil and fuel prices, then the economy would probably be stronger for it."

Shamubeel Eaqub. Supplied

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said New Zealand was "very exposed" to the fuel price movements, not just because of the use of cars but because the cost of getting items to New Zealand was high. "We are quite dependent on imported products so everything is transported here."

Gaspy data shows that the average price of 91 on Thursday was $3.51, up 3 percent over 28 days. Diesel was at $3.17, up 1.46 percent.

Thursday is often a discount day for retailers.

The cheapest 91 petrol in the country was at Tasman Epsom, at $3.19.

World.title: What a typical first-home buyer looks like now
World.content:
Audio player for " When does my property become relationship property? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2230544%2Fwhat-a-typical-first-home-buyer-looks-like-now

A typical New Zealand first-home buyer is now 35.5 years old and buying a standalone house for about $715,000. They are helped by a KiwiSaver withdrawal and maybe borrowing more than 80 percent of the house's purchase price.

Cotality and Westpac have released their latest first-home buyer report, which shows first-time buyers were responsible for 29.5 percent of all property purchases in the third quarter of the year. That is another new record market share.

They paid a median $715,000 for their purchases. In Auckland the median was $868,000, in Wellington $720,000 and in Christchurch, $650,000.

Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said the median price had lifted from $700,000 last year but they were getting more house for their money. "The share of first-home buyer purchases that are standalone dwellings has just continued to rise."

He said there were about 25,000 first-home purchases on a rolling 12-month basis, a level last seen briefly during the post-Covid boom.

First-home buyers were particularly strong in Wellington, where they made 37 percent of the purchases so far in 2026. But they were also at least 30 percent of the Hamilton and Auckland market, as well as Gisborne, Rotorua, Hastings, Palmerston North and Invercargill's.

More than three-quarters of their purchases were standalone houses, and more than half of first-home buyers' loans were taken out with a deposit of less than 20 percent.

The average age of first-home buyers increased a little from 35 late last year to 35.5 but Davidson said that could just reflect that buyers felt they had more time to make a decision about a purchase.

"The average age ticked up a bit in the third quarter, which at face value might not be so encouraging but I think as opposed to the past where it's been linked to lack of housing affordability, I think this little edge up is more about we don't need to rush, we've got time, the market's not running away. We might as well wait a bit and get what we actually want."

Satish Ranchhod. Supplied

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod said buyers were helped by the large number of properties available for sale.

"Those looking to get their foot on the property ladder have had plenty of options, As a result first-home buyers have often been able to get into newer and larger standalone homes without having to pay significantly more."

He said mortgage rates being relatively low had also helped.

"For the average first-home buyer, lower mortgage interest rates in recent years shaved around $560 off their monthly mortgage payments compared to 2023 when interest rates were at their peak. And in Auckland, where first homes tend to be more expensive, the saving is around $685 a month."

Davidson said first-home buyers were active across the price spectrum. They accounted for 30 percent of purchases in the middle 40 percent price bracket of transactions so far this year, up from 28 percent in 2025 and 25 percent in 2020, and from only 21 percent in 2015.

He said there were some signs that the number of first-home deals was starting to tail off a bit.

"Up until now their market share has been going up because they've simply been doing more deals. There's just a sense now that the market share is starting to take a bit of a boost because other groups are actually falling even faster. So first-home buyers are maybe just buying a few less properties, but the fall for other groups is even faster, so their market share is still going up. But that's very, very early days, the wider point is they're still very strong, they're still buying high numbers of properties and market share is strong."

Kelvin Davidson. SUPPLIED

Davidson said housing affordability had been a problem for so long that it was important not to get complacent about it. "I have to acknowledge it's not easy. It hasn't just become a free-for-all in terms of buying a first house. But the fact is that more people are being successful at the moment than has been the case for quite some time."

He said that was likely to remain the case for the time being.

"If you look at first-home buyers themselves, some of those supports they've had look likely to be in place. We're not really seeing house prices going anywhere. They don't seem likely to turn around any time soon so there's a chance to save that deposit. There's plenty of low deposit finance available, KiwiSaver funds are building up. There's still a lot of listings, but also just a bit of caution from other buyers.

"Owner occupiers are sort of fairly cautious about the economic cycle and tending to stay where they are. There's still a lot of new builds coming online too, so that's presenting more choice for first home buyers. And investors are fairly cautious as well."

He said it was not always the case that first-home buyers and investors were interested in the same houses.

"I don't think it's direct competition. But the fact is investors are a little bit more cautious right now, there's obviously political considerations, what might happen over the next year or two in terms of taxes. It is simply harder to get investment sums to stack up at the moment with higher costs and flat rents, so there's just a little bit less competition out there. First-home buyers have a fairly open platform at the moment to get the house they want. They don't have to rush. There are good times ahead for first-home buyers, still."

World.title: WBBL season gets underway with Thunder thumping of Renegades
World.content:
Anika Learoyd has carved out a career-best innings as the Sydney Thunder began its WBBL campaign with a convincing six-wicket win over the Melbourne Renegades in the season opener.

Learoyd made 48 off 37 balls after off-spinner Georgia Voll (4-26) did most of the damage in the first match of a double-header at Junction Oval today.

The Melbourne Stars host the Hobart Hurricanes in the night game.

In at first drop, after Voll made 25 off 18, including the Thunder's only six of the match, Learoyd hit nine boundaries and put on 62 with Heather Knight in a match-winning third-wicket partnership.

The pair took 28 runs from the power surge, putting the Thunder within sight of victory.

Knight (29 not out off 22 balls) and Nadine de Klerk (12no off six) finished the job, guiding their team to 4-140 with 18 balls to spare.

Learoyd admitted feeling "really nervous" batting near the top of the order, but will take confidence from starting the season with a strong performance.

Earlier, Voll's four wickets and hand in a run-out were crucial in restricting the Renegades to 9-138 from their 20 overs.

Renegades opener Hayley Matthews gave her side a strong start, blasting 45 from 30 balls before holing out in the deep.

Matthews put on 56 for the first wicket with Courtney Webb (22 from 24), and Georgia Wareham made a handy 23 from 19, but a late-innings collapse ended their chances.

The Renegades lost 5-2 in seven balls through the 17th and 18th overs as Voll wreaked havoc.

AAP

World.title: Late Lyon wicket puts Australia in control of deciding Test
World.content:
The late wicket of Proteas skipper Temba Bavuma has given Australia the upper hand over South Africa on a fascinating third day at Newlands in Cape Town.

Nathan Lyon clean bowled Bavuma with less then five minutes to go before stumps on a wearing pitch, leaving the hosts 4-140, with a lead of just 40 runs.

Josh Inglis scored a century as part of a 185-run fifth wicket partnership with Alex Carey to give Australia a 100-run first innings lead before tea.

South Africa overhauled that deficit before the close, but not before losing three wickets at Mitch Starc (2-29) and Josh Hazlewood (1-37) made early inroads to the Proteas' top order.

Australia resumed on day three with a one run lead and two well-set batters in Carey (51no) and Inglish (85no) in the middle, the pitch wearing but, at that stage offering no genuine assistance to the bowlers.

Carey and Inglis continued their excellent partnership to build Australia's lead, looking entirely untroubled as Inglis bought up his second Test century.

However, moments later Simon Harmer came into the attack and extracted an edge from Inglis's bat to have him out for 102, ending a hugely profitable 185-run partnership.

Carey (80) departed just nine runs later, Harmer again extracting an edge with Aiden Markram taking a good low catch.

Simon Harmer, left, made the breakthrough in the first hour of day three. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Cooper Connolly managed the tail, turning down singles as Pat Cummins (bowled by Kagiso Rabada for 0) and Nathan Lyon (caught Harmer off the bowling of Mulder for 1) departed.

But his innings ended when Marco Jansen caught and bowled him for 29, ending the innings with a lead of exactly 100 runs.

In response, Markram (1) was caught by Travis Head driving Starc, and David Bedingham (11) fell to a top edged pull shot off Josh Hazlewood to leave the Proteas 2-31.

Travis Head, second right, caught Aiden Markram dfor just a single run. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Marques Ackerman and Temba Bavuma combined for a 64-run partnership before Starc brutally bounced Ackerman out for 62.

Starc delivered a head-hunting bouncer right into the grill of the Proteas opener, knocking him backwards.

A clearly shaken Ackerman wanted to review after conversing with his skipper, but was controversially ruled to have taken too long to ask for it and had to depart.

In the end, the replay showed a fine top edge as Ackerman attempted to get his bat up to protect his face so the decision saved South Africa a review, although Marnus Labuschagne chastising Travis Head for checking on the South African opener's welfare left a sour taste in the mouth.

Temba Bavuma played a watchful innings after tea. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke built a steady 36-run partnership as the shadows lengthened across the ground.

But Lyon, who was extracting increasingly vicious spin and bounce in the dusty pitch, had one last say before stumps were called to put them in an ideal position heading into day four.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Brewers complete underdog story with maiden World Series title
World.content:
The small-ball Milwaukee Brewers, playing in the smallest market in the majors, are World Series champions for the first time.

Young ace Jacob Misiorowski threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings, rookie Cooper Pratt had two more hits and two runs batted in (RBIs), and the Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 to set off a long-awaited celebration among thousands of Brewers fans in attendance at Tropicana Field.

"It's the best feeling ever. All of our fans are here. I know the city's waited a long, long time for this," Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said.

"We're so happy to bring it home to them. I can't wait to get back there and celebrate."

World Series MVP William Contreras hit an RBI double and Misiorowski allowed just two hits before leaving the game because of a right calf cramp. He got a standing ovation from the Brew-Crew fans, who took over the section behind Milwaukee's dugout for the last three games.

The 22-year-old Pratt set a series rookie record with six straight hits before a sacrifice fly in the sixth. Jackson Chourio set a five-game series record with 11 hits.

"This is one of the greatest moments of my life. Oh my gosh. It doesn't even feel real," said Pratt, who made his major league debut in June.

"This is surreal. It only took four months."

The championship comes in the 58th season for a franchise that began as the Seattle Pilots in 1969 and moved to Milwaukee the following year. The Brewers' only previous trip to the World Series in 1982 ended in heartbreak when they blew a 3-1 lead in the sixth inning of Game 7 and lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals.

But this team displayed the toughness and resilience of 67-year-old manager Pat Murphy, who survived a heart attack in 2020 and was the NL Manager of the Year in his first two full seasons at the helm in 2024 and 2025.

"This group of guys right here, the 2026 team, will be remembered forever — and they deserve that because they were a team," Murphy said.

"When you talk about this team, you've got to talk about people who care about each other. They're not worried about their own stats. No-one cares about that. They care about coming together and winning tonight."

AP

World.title: Aussie captain most expensive player at WPL auction
World.content:
Australia captain Sophie Molineux has proved the most expensive buy in India's Women's Premier League auction, and she'll suit up for a UP Warriorz side captained by former national team skipper Meg Lanning.

With many of the world's top players having already been retained for the 2027 edition of the lucrative Indian league, Molineux's signature was the most coveted one still left and the Lucknow-based franchise captured the T20 World Cup-winning skipper for the biggest price, INR 1.1 crore ($A164,000).

The spinning all-rounder won't be leading the team in the January 14-February 7 tournament, though.

Instead, Molineux will be playing under the captaincy of 34-year-old Lanning, the inspirational figure who skippered Australia when she first came into the side, in a T20I in India eight years ago.

Big life changes for WBBL winning duo A lot has changed since Nicola Carey and Elyse Villani lifted the WBBL trophy last year, as the Hobart Hurricanes prepare to defend their title.

Molineux's base price in the auction in Kochi was 50 Lakh ($A75,000) but she eventually went for over twice that price as a bidding battle began between Royal Challengers Bengaluru and the Warriorz.

With their superior budget, UP also snapped up big-hitting all-rounder Grace Harris going for $45,000, meaning that the side will have four Australians in their ranks with Phoebe Litchfield already on board.

Intriguingly, national skipper Molineux has been bought for less than both Lanning and Litchfield and four others among the 14-strong Australian contingent in the league.

The most expensive Australian in the league — each of the five teams has at least one Aussie World Cup winner in its ranks — will be Ash Gardner, captain of the Gujarat Giants, who was retained for $523,000 in a side that also includes four Aussies.

Gardner is the joint most-lucrative retention, alongside Royal Challengers Bengaluru captain Smriti Mandhana and Mumbai Indians' England skipper Nat Sciver-Brunt.

Of the 11 Australians up for grabs in Wednesday's auction, only three were sold.

Heather Graham, Tayla Vlaeminck, Tess Flintoff, Charli Knott, Samantha Bates, Maitlan Brown, Maddie Penna and Milly Illingworth were the ones to miss out.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Gold Coast Suns AFLW finals feat faces home-ground headache
World.content:
The Gold Coast Suns have earned their place in the AFLW finals — but their reward could be a home final away from home.

After back-to-back seasons near the bottom of the ladder, the Suns have surged into fourth spot with eight wins, booking their first finals appearance since 2023.

A victory over GWS on Sunday would strengthen their grip on a double chance, guaranteeing a home final during the series.

But there's a catch.

Carrara Stadium is unavailable for weeks two, three and four of the finals series, due to Australia's T20 clash with England, leaving the Suns and the AFL searching for an alternative venue.

Springfield, home of Queensland rivals the Brisbane Lions and an hour's drive up the highway, and Southport's Fankhauser Reserve are among the alternatives being considered.

Southport however comes with a significant caveat — any final would need to be played during the day, when November temperatures average around 28 degrees and humidity can hover around 70 per cent.

A spokesperson for the club said it is "working with all stakeholders on home venues for each week of the finals" where Carrara is not available.

"Our playing group and staff have been resolute all season in their efforts to play anywhere, anytime, across eight different venues and we know they'll take that attitude into any scenario that presents throughout the post-season campaign," the spokesperson said.

Despite this, coach Rhyce Shaw said on Tuesday the club is embracing the excitement of a long-awaited finals campaign.

Michael Voss Oval in Springfield is being considered as one option for an alternative venue. (Supplied: Brisbane Lions)

"I took [my son] Henry to swimming the other day and all the staff were getting behind us," Shaw said.

"It is exciting for our footy club … It's been a bit of a tough year all round, but for our girls to pick up the slack a little bit and get going and make finals is really, really cool."

"We've got a big job against the Giants and then we'll think of finals after that."

If the Suns were to fall to GWS on Sunday, there is the potential for them finish as low as seventh on the ladder.

However, a fifth or sixth place finish would mean they would earn a home final next weekend and the ABC can confirm Carrara Stadium would be available in this instance.

Rhyce Shaw, Senior Coach of the Suns, says it's been a "tough year" for the club. (Getty Images: Maya Thompson)

ABC Sport AFLW expert Chyloe Kurdas said regardless of the ladder outcome, the lack of venue certainty is an unwanted distraction.

"I think it is such a valuable home ground advantage [finishing in the top four] but it's also not just that, it's the distraction of this conversation right now that happens in the lead up to," she said.

"It occupies bandwidth and it occupies energy from the playing group and the coaching group and the staff."

Kurdas said not being able to play at Carrara, a venue the side has won their last three games at, would be a missed opportunity.

"I think there's a real sweet spot right now with the number of talented kids that are Gold Coast born and raised … that are now playing at the Suns," Kurdas said.

"Fan engagement is going to be such an important part of this Gold Coast Suns women's team journey … they're so talented."

The Suns have had a 75 per cent increase in AFLW memberships for this season.

A familiar problem

The Suns aren't the only club caught in a scheduling squeeze.

Second-placed Geelong, one win away from securing a top-two finish, also faces a venue clash, with Kardinia Park unavailable next weekend due to the AUSX Supercross Championship.

While, the AFLW Grand Final, should it be played in Melbourne, has already been locked in for Princes Park — with a capacity of 13 thousand that has sold out for the showpiece game within hours in recent seasons.

Docklands Stadium, with a 53,343-capacity is unavailable, with Harry Styles booked across the weekend, despite players calling for a bigger venue.

The Geelong Cats are facing a similar venue problem. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Grand Final has also been scheduled for Friday night, November 27, to avoid a clash with the Victorian State Election.

It's a familiar problem that's haunted the competition since it started in 2017.

In the inaugural season, the Brisbane Lions earned the right to host the Grand Final but were forced to play at Carrara, with the Gabba unavailable due to cricket.

Now in its 11th season, the debate continues about where the AFLW competition belongs in the sporting calendar.

The AFL is reportedly considering an earlier start to align the women's season with the end of the men's competition.

"You do your due diligence and you look at where is there likely to be these kind of clashes," Chyloe Kurdas said.

"But ultimately, whenever you choose to play it, you then have to live and die by those decisions."

She says clubs and the AFL must also be prepared to make commercial decisions that put their women's programs first.

" You can't just buy in when it suits you. "

The AFL and Stadiums Queensland were contacted for comment.

World.title: WBBL winning duo on eve of big life changes
World.content:
A lot has changed since Nicola Carey hit the winning runs for the Hobart Hurricanes in last year's WBBL final.

Cricket-wise, her partner Elyse Villani retired and handed over the captaincy.

Life-wise, they're building a house together and are expecting their first child.

"Now that you've pointed it out, I am a bit overwhelmed," Carey joked.

"We've got a bit going on, don't we?

"Poor thing, Elyse has to carry the baby and do all the admin for the house. We're both very much looking forward to having a little one.

"People keep asking me if I'm excited, but I don't think I know fully what's coming."

The desire to start a family influenced Villani's decision to call time on her WBBL career.

The 37-year-old played in every season since the competition started in 2015 and skippered three different clubs during that time.

Elyse Villani retired last year, and Nicola Carey has since taken over the Hurricanes' captaincy. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"Elyse would've played cricket forever, but I don't think her body would've allowed it," Carey said.

"It definitely did play a part, but it's not a guaranteed thing that you'll fall pregnant either."

Following successful IVF treatment, Villani is due to give birth to a boy in November.

Loading Instagram content

It was a fairly straightforward process, and Carey said she was grateful knowing how tricky fertility could be for some people.

They are adjusting to the new chapter in their lives, as the Hobart Hurricanes open their season against the Melbourne Stars tonight.

Name game

In February, all-rounder Carey played her first match for Australia in four years.

There has been a lot of interstate travel since and overseas tours to the Caribbean and the UK.

Nicola Carey played in Australia's recent T20I series against New Zealand in Sydney. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

"Elyse came over to England for about seven weeks because I was there for the T20 World Cup and The Hundred, and she was calling it a baby moon," Carey laughed.

"She knows a lot of the players obviously, so it was a huge social get-together and cruisy for her.

"While I was stressed playing terrible cricket she was living her best life."

"No-one misses pre-season do they. Maybe when we start playing again here for Tassie, she'll miss it a bit more."

The couple is aligned when it comes to baby names.

"We've got a few names picked out but we haven't nailed one down yet," Carey said.

"Every male that we walk past seems to have an opinion though.

"Our CEO [at Cricket Tasmania] Dominic Baker is like, 'Dom's a good name,' and I'm thinking, that's not even top 100 for us, but thank you for your input."

Reflecting on the final

The Hurricanes' victory last December at Bellerive Oval was a dream come true: playing in front of their home fans, claiming a maiden title and sending off Villani in style.

The Hurricanes celebrate last year's WBBL title. (Getty Images: Steve Ball)

Although Carey was the batter that sealed the result with a boundary, she concedes she had "the easy part" thanks to a record-breaking innings from teammate Lizelle Lee.

The South African opener was the star of the night, as the team chased down 138 runs.

Blasting 77 off 34 balls, Lee equalled the highest individual score in a WBBL finals match.

The women were inspired after watching their male counterparts lift the BBL trophy in January that same year.

It also followed the achievements of a core group of players in the 50-over Women's National Cricket League (WNCL), clinching three consecutive titles from 2022 to 2024.

The result capped off a wonderful career for Villani, who had previously played in three losing WBBL finals.

The Hurricanes' WBBL title win last season was a special occasion for the players. (ABC News)

She caught the team by surprise, deciding to retire on the spot and go out on a high.

"I sort of knew it was Elyse's last season," Carey said.

"What I didn't know was that she was going to announce it right then and there.

"She was panicking because she told the TV broadcast in an interview first and was then like, 'Oh no, now I need to tell the girls.'

Loading Instagram content

"That caught me off guard.

"To finally win one in your last season adds to that fairytale narrative.

"We had a great group and really good people, which made it enjoyable, so to cap it off with that win was really special."

Despite originally hailing from NSW and Victoria, the couple has now been living in the Apple Isle for a long time and is passionate about ensuring the next generation of the state's talent is set up for sustainable success.

"It's been a nice period of cricket in Tasmania," Carey said.

"A lot of us aren't from there originally, but they've taken us in and welcomed us.

"Because it's so small, everyone lives five minutes away, so you spend a lot more time together than you would in the bigger cities, where you're more spread out.

"It's got a real family feel, so it's nice to be able to give back."

World.title: Scans reveal extent of Steve Smith's neck injury ahead of Test summer
World.content:
Australia expects to have Steve Smith back for the home summer after scans confirmed joint damage to the vice-captain's neck in South Africa.

Australian team officials said Smith had scans on Friday before failing in his bid to play in the third and deciding Test.

Those scans detected an injury to a "cervical facet joint", which connects to the spine and acts to guide and stabilise neck movement.

"Due to this and his limited range of motion, he was unfit to participate in the current Test," Cricket Australia said in a statement.

On a day that could have ended Test careers, a few young ones flourish With a reshuffled line-up in questionable form, Australia's batting stocks show the sort of fight and flair the team has been lacking of late.

"Steve will continue to receive treatment and rehabilitation, with a full return to availability anticipated for the upcoming home Test series against New Zealand."

Smith has six weeks to recover for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, which will begin a long run of virtually uninterrupted cricket through to mid-March, with a five-Test tour of India (January 21 to March 3) and the 150th anniversary Test against England at the MCG (March 11-15).

Australia will want Smith available for that stretch of 10 Tests in 14 weeks, just as they had hoped to have him for the return to Cape Town this week.

Even well after Friday's scans on arrival in Cape Town, Australia's coaching staff had been extremely confident Smith would be fit to face South Africa.

The 37-year-old batted in the nets for around 35 minutes on Sunday, two days out from the third Test, before sitting down and stretching his neck.

He then briefly returned to batting, before growing increasingly frustrated and walking out of the nets.

Smith also attempted to bat on Tuesday morning just 90 minutes before the match, then determining he was not able to get his neck right.

"He is huge, one of the greatest batters we have ever had," Cummins said the day before the start of play.

"You don't play 100-odd Test matches without playing Test matches where you're not 100 per cent fit.

"Even though he is probably not going to be 100 per cent, hopefully he can compartmentalise that, like he has done 100 times before with other things, and come out and contribute like he does every week."

The injury means Smith is likely to never play another Test at Newlands, the venue of the ball-tampering scandal in 2018 that cost him the captaincy and a 12-month ban.

World.title: A three-ball statement gives Australia hope of a flourishing future
World.content:
The vague suspicion before play on day two of the Cape Town Test was that Australia — out of form, stalked by rumours of disharmony in the ranks, its batting line-up restocked and reshuffled for the umpteenth time — was one more calamitous batting collapse away from the end of an era.

The day of perfectly calm and controlled Test batting that took place instead was no less arresting, and in the context of this topsy-turvy series, far more surprising. For 90 overs, Australia batted diligently, adaptively, intelligently and at changing tempos, building a series of reassuring partnerships that put it in control of the game.

Elevated to the opening slot, Matt Renshaw looked safe as houses. Slotted into Steve Smith's number four position, Cameron Green hit a commanding half-century. Drafted in at the 11th hour, Josh Inglis was closing in on a century by stumps and had dragged Alex Carey along in his slipstream.

Josh Inglis took the baton from Cameron Green and Matt Renshaw. (AP: Halden Krog)

It all meant that Proteas attack leader Kagiso Rabada, who probably woke up feeling comfortable with the expectation it would be his day to wreak some havoc — perhaps even end some careers — went wicketless, as did too many of his mates.

Thanks to stands of 126 between Renshaw and Green and an undefeated 145 between Inglis and Carey, Australia reached 4-330 by stumps and walked away probably feeling in the box seat on a pitch offering very little assistance to the bowlers.

The weight of numbers was one thing, the problem-solving another. In two testing periods, South Africa made double-strikes and threatened to blow the game back open, only for the tourists to consolidate and rebuild.

Monster Carey-Inglis stand keeps Australia in driver's seat in Cape Town Alex Carey and Josh Inglis put together a handy partnership late on day two in Cape Town to put Australia in firm control of the third Test against South Africa.

The crunch moments came in the 18th over, when off-spinner Simon Harmer ripped out Travis Head and Marnus Labuschagne, and just before tea, when Renshaw and Green were removed by Marco Jansen in the space of a few overs.

Both times Australia took a deep breath, regrouped and pushed on in the same direction as before.

The only major negative of the day for Australia — although the many unkind souls who wish him bad luck will not view it so — was Labuschagne's duck. Out-of-form players often have a knack for attracting unplayable balls. At the moment, poor old Marnus can make almost anything look unplayable.

For a team that has not produced a single 100-run opening partnership in the past three years, Renshaw's 74 from 139 deliveries was a welcome return to normalcy at the top of the order. In a 58-run stand with Travis Head (41) to start off, the Queenslander was deferential and circumspect, showing they could be a fire and ice combination.

But it was Renshaw's union with Green, which stretched across 32 overs, that provided the most welcome glimpse of the future of this Australian team.

At 27 and 30, Cameron Green and Matt Renshaw are the babies of this team. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

They were a study on contrasts: surely no batsman as big as Renshaw has ever made himself such a small target for bowlers; heavy-footed Green, on the other hand, has the awkward tendency to turn himself into a fast bowler's piñata, swaying and ducking into bouncers, and in this case wearing a few painful body blows from the shorter stuff South Africa threw at him in large doses.

In the latter sense, Green again showed he had guts. And as he got going, his fluent stroke play more than made up for the cobwebs he was destined to display after three and a half weeks without a competitive hit.

As Aiden Markram had treated Pat Cummins's bowling with disdain on day one, Green took it upon himself to take down Rabada, who has lorded it over Australia in the past.

The killer blow on that front was when Green moved into the 40s with a trio of swivel-pulls that brought six, six and four off consecutive deliveries.

Green punished a trio of Kagiso Rabada short balls. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

Renshaw, as in his Durban epic, was more watchful and unassuming, content to press, deflect, dab, flick and generally accumulate — precisely the sort of calm, unhurried Test batting Australia has been crying out for in the past two years, and which is the bedrock of the big, defendable totals Australia will need to post when it can no longer rely on its brilliant but aging bowling unit.

As well as re-emphasising Labuschagne's redundancy, the Renshaw-Green partnership might also, in the wash-up, accelerate the conversation about how Australia tactfully moves on from the Smith and Labuschagne era.

What more is there to say about Marnus at this point? Harmer, who weeded him out this time, is a canny bowler and has proved himself a big-moment performer in this series. But geez, his wicket ball this time was not exactly a jaffa.

Labuschagne shuffled back to what might otherwise have been a half-volley, pushed at it with hard hands, his slicing bat plane again a horror story, and Markram gobbled the edge at slip.

And what Labuschagne had made look impossible in that brief and tortured innings was, by the end of the day, looking entirely straightforward thanks to Inglis and Carey, undefeated on 85 and 51 respectively.

Loose and a little too eager to play his shots earlier in the series, Carey took a leaf out of Renshaw's book with nudges, nurdles and strike rotation. Inglis, whose finger injury prevented even net sessions for most of the past two weeks, clobbered nine fours and two sixes to poleaxe a tiring Proteas attack.

Tomorrow, both or either batsmen could feasibly take the game and the series away from South Africa in the space of an hour or two. But then, we've said that before, haven't we?

Tech.title: Data centers could send US climate pollution skyrocketing
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The US power sector could release 42 percent more planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution by 2030 than it did in 2025 as it builds out more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club. That would essentially wipe out 15 years of greenhouse gas reductions.

CO2 emissions from electricity generation would increase by 618 million tons by the end of the decade if planned AI projects are constructed. That’s roughly equivalent to carbon pollution from the electricity use of 128,788,523 homes in a year.

The Sierra Club’s estimate is higher than some previous projections

The Sierra Club’s estimate is higher than some previous projections from other groups. Another study published by academic researchers in June forecast that electricity demand from data centers and crypto mines could push up power sector emissions by 28 percent by 2030 when compared to a scenario with no data center growth. The outcome depends on how many planned data center projects actually come to fruition, as well as on what type of technology is used to power those facilities.

The US is now planning to build more fossil fuel capacity than it has in a decade, according to a separate report published this month by the Environmental Defense Fund.

Tech.title: This open-source project lets you sync Withings data to other apps without a subscription
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

When it was revealed earlier this month that Withings would require new users to subscribe to a Withings Plus subscription to sync heath data from the company’s devices to third-party apps, Tom Anthony, who was already fed up with the Withings mobile app which they describe as a “bloated mess,” became motivated to “free” their scales. Anthony’s solution was to create an open-source project called YourOwnWeigh that reroutes your data away from Withings’ servers so it can be wirelessly synced to other apps and platforms for free.

You can read more about the project on GitHub, where you’ll also find quick-start guides on how to get YourOwnWeigh set up, but it mostly consists of a web app running on a server of your choice. If you don’t already operate your own, Anthony says YourOwnWeigh can run entirely on a free CloudFlare account given how little data it’s moving around.

The YourOwnWeigh web app handles several tasks, including using Bluetooth to update Withings scales with alternate firmware so they upload data to a non-Withings server you’ve configured. Instead of hosting a copy of Withings’ firmware, it’s downloaded and patched as needed. The web app also imports the scale’s current settings and existing user profiles, and downloads the health data generated by regular weigh-ins.

To get that data into Apple Health, Anthony used Apple Shortcuts to create a scheduled automation that pulls the Withings data off the alternate server and imports it into the app, but they’re hoping the community can come up with ways to expand the compatibility to other apps, including Google Health. YourOwnWeigh is also currently limited to just two older models of Withings’ scales. But assuming the firmware on newer models can be patched in a similar manner, expanding the project’s compatibility should be possible.

Tech.title: Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Holdings is acquiring ADT for $7.6 billion
Tech.content:
