Tech.title: 100,000 Folds and Counting for the iPhone Duo in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. How High Will It Go?
Tech.content:
Since Apple’s first-ever foldable phone — the iPhone Duo — launched last Friday, everyone has been examining the hinge and looking for ways to push it to its limits. We braved three hours at the Apple store on Friday morning to snag our own testing model for our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, where I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations.

So, the real question: How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? At 1:30 p.m. ET on Wednesday, we passed 100,000 folds.

Our goal is simple. On Friday, my team and I loaded the Duo into a proprietary machine we built to test foldable phones like Apple’s and Samsung’s rival Galaxy Z Fold 8, which we’ve also already started testing. I’ve overseen the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone. (Read on for how CNET tests foldable phones.)

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube today from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

Tech.title: I Spent Weeks With Keurig’s Posh, Plastic-Free Pod Coffee System: What Works and What Doesn’t
Tech.content:
As a seasoned reviewer of all things coffee, I’ve sampled my fair share of Keurig products. After all, the brand’s presence is far-reaching; Keurig’s single-serve coffee makers are found in tens of millions of American households. So when I heard the brand had completely revamped its hard plastic-encased K-Cup, I knew this was big news. First teased way back in 2024, Keurig’s plastic-free pod coffee system has finally arrived.

Nikita Ephanov/CNET Keurig Alta 8.0 $500 at Keurig Pros & Cons The plastic-free pods are an achievement in themselves

The steam wand is high-quality

On balance, the coffee brewed was impressive

The digital interface was easy to use The espresso lacked body

Keurig's largest coffee brewer, it takes up a good deal of counter space

The price is steep

Individual AltaRounds are packaged in foil (for now)

Called an AltaRound, this puck consists of coffee grounds encased in seaweed-derived gel. The changes go beyond packaging. The transformed pods come with a new machine, the Alta, a revamped brewer that marks Keurig’s first foray into high-pressure espresso extraction. The machine extracts at up to 10 bars, on par with a standard espresso machine.

Put the puck and coffee machine together, and the technology is striking. The coffee maker even scans QR codes printed on the pucks and suggests drinks on a touchscreen. It’s a futuristic reinvention, but what matters most to me is the environmental initiative coupled with coffee quality. It’s an ambitious redesign on Keurig’s consumer scale; I couldn’t wait to see how the new Alta system performs.

More from CNET

The Keurig Alta Brewer is sizable yet stylish

It’s a commitment in both cost and counter space. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Keurig’s range of coffee makers spans from no-frills single-button models to spiffed-up machines. Right out of the box, the Alta is clearly the brand’s most substantial offering yet. The appliance is fairly large, taking up 19 inches by 10 inches of counter space and standing 1 foot tall. The back has a removable 70-ounce water tank, while the front has a steam wand and pitcher.

The 4 Best Pod Coffee Makers We Tested See at CNET

You deposit pods into the top of the machine, directly under an electronic display, so you’ll need 8 more inches of vertical clearance to operate. Spent pucks and liquids collect in a compartment on the machine’s left side. With so many moving parts, the coffeemaker needs ample counter space. I also found the cord on the short side, so plan its placement accordingly.

As of this writing, you can buy Light, Medium, and Dark Roast pucks. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The aesthetics make up for the size. The Keurig Alta looks more like a retro espresso maker than a pod machine. I’m a fan of the smooth, lightly ’70s-inspired shape and the bright white color. The absence of a single button or immediately noticeable display adds to the sleekness. Brewing functions are controlled via a compact digital screen on top of the brewer, roughly the size of a smartphone.

To set it up, the machine syncs to Wi-Fi, and the touchscreen guides the initial configuration. The display enhances the Keurig’s already intuitive process. Each Alta puck comes stamped with a QR code the coffee maker scans, which prompts several suggested beverages. The coffee maker feels like an expanded and modernized Keurig experience. At $500, though, I’d expect all the bells and whistles.

The touchscreen gave me no grief. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Hands-on with the new Keurig Alta pods

Keurig’s new machine is certainly eye-catching, but the accompanying AltaRounds are the real headline. I’ve never handled a coffee product quite like them. Each 14-gram pod resembles a damp espresso puck, yet comes bound with a thin, NSF-certified seaweed film. The material isn’t brittle, so I can pick up an AltaRound and drop it into the brewer with my fingers without worrying about loose grounds. Remarkably, the pucks remain intact even after extraction, altered only by a handful of needle-like piercings.

Compared to the hard plastic-encased K-Cup, it’s a system built with sustainability in mind. Still, I don’t love that every AltaRound is sold in a non-recyclable foil wrapper. A Keurig rep told me paper-based packaging is coming, but for now, the system still generates more waste than traditional espresso, drip or filtered coffee.

Plastic-free pods wrapped in seaweed byproduct are the star of the show. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Sampling the Keurig Alta’s coffee lineup

The newly debuted AltaRound lineup is narrow, but all entirely new to the Keurig ecosystem. As of October 2026, you can buy Light, Medium, and Dark Roast pucks, plus a sole flavored Caramel option. Additional options are in the works. Conveniently, the coffee maker also has a slot for older-generation plastic pods, so you can still brew your favorite K-Cups without committing to the new system.

The pods come in foil packaging, though the brand plans to switch to paper wrappers soon.

The Alta brews a broad range of beverages, from thick, short espresso to foamy lattes or a standard mug of drip. No barista skills are required: The machine scans each pod, recommends a drink, then automates extraction. Even the milk frother is machine-driven, using a magnetic spinner at the bottom of the pitcher to help time and foam dairy.

There is some room for customization, though. You can also froth manually, and adjust coffee to three strengths, temperatures, and sizes. You can also use the steam wand to make cold foam or hot froth. Keurig even offers suggested recipes for more complex drinks, like an espresso martini or salted caramel latte. There’s a lot to sample, and it can take several AltaRounds to find your preferred beverage.

The steam wand worked well in my testing. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

I was most impressed by the double-shot dark roast, which brewed opaque and capped with an aesthetic crema, unlike any K-Cup I’ve brewed. Mixed with steamed milk, it yielded a tasty cappuccino, latte and cortado, approaching espresso machine caliber.

Compared to conventional espresso, the coffee lacked some body, a sensory experience my testing confirmed. Both the single shot and double-shot AltaRounds weighed just shy of 14 grams. The latter produced some 98 grams of coffee, making it a 1:7 ratio far from the ideal 1:2 espresso shot. The dark roast AltaRound tastes pleasantly bold and bitter, but has neither the acidity nor concentrated flavor I’d expect from a barista-quality shot. It’s not true espresso, but considering the ease of brewing and shelf stability (nine months sealed, 30 days opened), I’d be happy to drink it.

The coffee was one-note but perfectly pleasant. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The light and medium roast Alta pods appealed less to me. Brewed into a hot 8-ounce cup (the recommended preparation), both pods delivered more acidity, and the light roast added a touch of fruitiness. While brighter, the two coffees tasted bland, with a flat flavor.

The cups also had a faintly woody, off-putting note, extra pronounced in the medium roast. Served iced, this tasting note intensified. The Keurig Alta lowers the extraction temperature for cold beverages, and this adjustment doesn’t bring out the best of AltaRounds. Mixing either roast profile with milk softens the issue; still, I generally preferred this machine for hot beverages.

I liked the caramel AltaRound more, even though I don’t often sweeten my coffee. Blending sweet and toasted flavors, this puck successfully recreates a housemade syrup experience, especially in a hot drink with milk. Like the other pucks, the underlying coffee flavor is one-note but pleasant, making it a cup I’d sip every now and then.

Overall, I didn’t find the brewed AltaRound coffees a significant improvement over K-Cups in flavor, though the coffee maker’s options are certainly far more comprehensive than previous models.

My verdict on the Keurig Alta

If you’re a longtime Keurig user, the Alta is a significant revamp. The system delivers espresso-like brewing, a sleek machine, and the redesigned AltaRound. I’m all for more environmentally conscious coffee brewing, and this packaging is a step forward for single-serve coffee (plastic wrapper aside). The Alta arrives not long after Lavazza’s plastic-free pod system, and I welcome Keurig’s contribution to brewing waste reduction.

The price may be hard to swallow for casual coffee drinkers. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The brand’s innovation does come at a steep price, though. The new brewer set costs $500 (including 32 AltaRounds to start), a step up from K-Cup brewers available for as low as $50. Puck refills are sold at $11 per eight-count box, discounted $1.50 a box when opting for the AutoRefresh subscription. Even at the lower price, that still works out to over $1 a cup. That’s pricier than making coffee at home using a drip machine, for example.

In my opinion, the coffee flavors don’t warrant the increased cost. At this price, I’d opt for an automatic drip brewer or a semi-automated espresso machine, both of which let you use fresh coffee beans. However, if you want the convenience of shelf-stable pods for espresso drinks while staying loyal to Keurig coffee, the Alta is a worthwhile redesign.

Tech.title: What’s Faster Than an F1 Car? The Data Behind the Race
Tech.content:
Technology has always been central to Formula One, but it’s playing an increasingly important role in how races are brought to fans around the world.

Ahead of the United States Grand Prix, which ran Friday through Sunday in Austin, Texas, I got a behind-the-scenes look at the on-site production facilities and how data is analyzed and turned into broadcast insights that help viewers – newcomers like me included – better understand the action unfolding on the track.

F1 has surged in popularity in the US in recent years, driven by factors like increased social media exposure, new race destinations and a more personal connection with drivers, thanks in part to Netflix’s hit docuseries Drive to Survive. And with cars reaching speeds of up to 230 miles per hour, it’s easy to see what makes the sport so thrilling.

More from CNET

But those cars aren’t just lightning-fast; they’re also data-gathering machines. Each F1 car generates around 1.1 million data points per second from 300 sensors. Technology partners like Amazon Web Services help process and analyze that information, turning complex data into insights that anyone, from casual viewers to die-hard data nerds, can understand and enjoy – including race metrics previously available only to production crews.

F1 is all about high speeds and even faster data. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Then there are people like me, somewhere in between — intrigued by the F1 frenzy but still learning the rules, technical details and strategies that keep millions of fans invested in every race. That’s where a handful of digital tools can help make sense of the fast-moving action, revealing the stories behind the numbers.

“To know a sport is to love a sport,” said Ruth Buscombe, technical adviser and race strategist at Formula One and AWS motorsports ambassador. “When you look at any kind of relationship you have with something that is a passion, it’s about starting as a novice and then learning about it and falling in love with the details of it. And sports has always been that.”

Inside the Event Technical Centre, the backbone of F1’s global broadcast

Feeds from the on-track cameras and microphones go through F1’s Event Technical Centre before the footage makes its way on air. F1/AWS

Nestled behind the swanky Paddock Club and team hospitality units sits a white, temporary hangar-like facility called the F1 Event Technical Centre, or ETC.

This hub is where data from across the circuit is brought together. Dozens of cameras and hundreds of microphones capture the sights and sounds of the race from almost every angle, while each car’s 300 sensors monitor everything from tire pressure to airspeed. For broadcast production, these feeds and data streams are then sent to F1’s Media & Technology Centre in Biggin Hill, UK.

Construction of the tent-like ETC, which spans 375 square meters (about 4,036 square feet), begins 10 days before the race and takes five days to complete. The process includes laying a network of over 58 kilometers (around 36 miles) of fiber-optic cables, as well as data antennas that enable two-way information transfer to and from the cars speeding around the track.

Up to 28 ultra-high-definition trackside cameras capture the action, alongside cable cams, helicopters, drones, free-roaming cameras and slow-motion cameras. More than 90 cameras are mounted directly on the cars, with up to eight views available from each. The 150 microphones positioned around the circuit capture the quintessential sounds of an F1 race, from the roar of the engines to the screech of the tires (now coming in clear to viewers with Dolby Atmos on Apple TV, along with Dolby Vision).

Inside the ETC, around 140 technical, operations and TV production crew members work side by side, surrounded by glowing switchboards, computer screens and monitors displaying the on-track action, including close-up shots of the cars and sweeping aerial views of the circuit.

The ETC houses around 750 pieces of equipment, according to F1. F1/AWS

In one room, timekeepers track lap times to within one ten-thousandth of a second, with additional timekeepers based at the UK’s Media & Technology Centre. Behind them, teams process and relay data from cameras, audio feeds and car sensors to their headquarters in Europe to support real-time strategy decisions. Sensors positioned around the track every 150 meters also help with vehicle tracking and positioning maps, as well as monitoring potential violations, such as speeding in the pit lane. An operations team at the back ensures the ETC and UK command center are in sync.

In another room, directors decide which shots to use and when to cut to replays or add graphics, which are also handled by team members in this area. A separate crew monitors the team radio, which is delayed by around 20 seconds so they can add subtitles and, importantly, bleep out any swear words.

At the far end of the ETC, a wall of routers and servers transmits the live camera feeds, audio and data to the UK’s Media & Technology Centre. There, production teams turn those feeds into the international broadcast watched by around 1.6 billion viewers.

“We have this really diverse fan base, and we have a complicated story to tell,” said Dean Locke, executive director of broadcast at Formula One. It’s not just the fan base that’s diverse, but also the ways people tune in – whether they’re watching on a big screen, a tablet or a phone.

“The way we develop graphics, the way we develop footage, that is something that we keep in mind,” Locke said. “Is it hitting every single fan?”

Giving fans deeper insights with Track Pulse

Formula One partnered with AWS in 2018, moving much of its computing infrastructure from on-premises data centers to the cloud. AWS also helps F1 refine race strategies, improve digital broadcasts and collect and analyze data, of which there is plenty.

Now, F1 and AWS are making Track Pulse, a tool the broadcast team has used since 2023, available to fans for the first time this season.

Track Pulse sifts through vast amounts of data from each car’s sensors to highlight the moments and decisions that can shape a race. From sudden changes in pace to shifting weather conditions to tire strategies, these callouts can help viewers better understand not just what’s happening on track but also why it matters.

“It’s near impossible to have enough pairs of eyes to monitor all 22 cars at the same time and really pick up on the small details of what’s happening,” said Jerome Descreux, AWS senior engagement manager. That’s why broadcast teams have been using Track Pulse to help determine what to spotlight for viewers. And now, viewers can tap into those insights themselves via F1’s data channel, whether they’re watching in the US through Apple TV or internationally with an F1 TV Pro or Premium subscription.

Track Pulse can offer more in-depth insights into what’s unfolding on track, giving viewers a heads-up on what to look out for and why. AWS

The interface is a data-rich dashboard with developing “stories,” as they’re called, on the left side, such as when a driver is quickly catching up to another. Track Pulse also displays live team radio transcripts, allowing viewers to peek into the conversations impacting the race. The goal is to distill the endless raw data into elements viewers may be interested in exploring and following.

For instance, during the 2026 Australian Grand Prix, Track Pulse flagged a moment when George Russell rapidly closed the gap between him and Lewis Hamilton. The tool highlighted this point because of just how quickly Russell was catching up. Track Pulse also noted that Hamilton was using the same tires for an unusually long time, giving fans further insight into the decisions shaping the action on track.

“We need to make sure that we’re bringing our fans on the journey,” said Formula One IT Director Chris Roberts. “For those people that are really technical, we’re not dulling things down so that it’s a bit boring for them, but also for those fans that are on a learning journey, we’re giving them the information that allows them to understand the sport at different levels.”

Most people might not get the chance to sit trackside, but data feeds for viewers at home can make the action feel closer. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

On the broadcast side, Track Pulse’s AI insights complement the F1 production team’s work, helping them sift through millions of data points to identify key race moments and turn them into digestible insights for people hungry to understand more of the action.

“We originally designed [Track Pulse] to be a producer’s tool,” Locke said. “Then we realized the power of it as a storytelling device. And it could crunch data and create story cards and tell us things that are going on in the races that even an entrenched producer of 20 years wasn’t seeing.”

He added, “Once someone gets into Formula One, they realize how much depth there is, and I think Track Pulse explains it quite well.”

Getting deeper insights with AI

Insights powered by AWS can help distill the fast-moving action on the track. AWS

AWS also powers around two dozen data-driven F1 Insights, as they’re called, which add real-time analysis to live broadcasts. One example is the Battle Forecast, which estimates how many laps it might take for a chasing car to get close enough to attempt an overtake. The prediction is based on information like track history and projected driver pace, giving viewers a better sense of when the action could heat up.

Tire Performance is another insight that helps fans understand how different driving styles affect tire longevity and how tire condition can influence pit stop timing. And Close to the Wall uses specialized cameras and deep neural network algorithms to track a car’s trajectory in real time and calculate just how close it is to a wall, since even a slight brush at high speeds can affect lap times or damage the car’s carbon-fiber components.

Today, fans can essentially tap into the same data that teams and strategists have long used to gain even the slightest edge over their competitors.

On-screen blurbs can help viewers understand why a team made a particular decision. AWS

“[Teams and strategists] have been doing this for 70 years before anybody at home got to see it,” Buscombe said. “And now, AWS is using the exact same data, doing the exact same math, creating the exact same insights. But rather than it just being a black box where the Formula One teams get to have all the fun, now you, as a fan sitting on your sofa – whether it’s your first race or your 1,000th – you get to see the same kind of data. And those are the F1 insights that pop up on screen.”

Tech and data are set to play an even bigger role in the sport, particularly with AWS now serving as the official AI and cloud computing partner of the FIA, Formula One’s governing body. The partnership could influence everything from race operations to the design of future cars. Running aerodynamic simulations using AWS cloud computing, for instance, allows the FIA to virtually test how air flows around a car without building physical components, which can potentially speed up development.

This past weekend was my first foray into the world of F1, but the combination of technology, data and high-speed racing has already piqued my interest. I may still have plenty to learn, but at least I have some tools to help me make sense of it all.

Editors’ note: Abrar Al-Heeti’s travel costs for the F1 United States Grand Prix in Austin were covered by AWS. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro Hands-On: Apple Finally Lets Us Swipe the Screen
Tech.content:
Surpassed only by the iPhone Duo, this year’s most anticipated Apple announcement is its launch of both a 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen display — the company’s last-to-the-party use of both technologies in one of its laptops. And despite the awful “PROLED” name, it’s more than just a fancy new display. It’s a complete design overhaul that, at least on paper, brings its feature set up to the front of the class for professional content creation, albeit with the same processor options and ports as the other MacBook Pros.

Aside from a screen that brings its capabilities more in line with the Studio Display XDR, the new model adds:

Touch support

The iPhone’s Dynamic Island

A 16TB configuration

Improved speakers with Dolby Atmos support and better mic

A thinner and lighter design

Genlock support

It doesn’t come cheap, though; as predicted, you pay a $400 premium over the standard models. The 14-inch M5 Pro model starts at $2,899 compared with $2,499 for the same non-OLED version, and the M5 Max model begins at $4,499 compared with $4,099. If you want to upgrade to 16TB, you have to bump to the M5 Max — that’s a minimum buy-in of $11,499 with only 36GB of memory. Preorders started on Wednesday, and systems are slated to start shipping Nov. 6.

One of the most popular changes won’t be the whizzy features, but the drop in weight to 3 pounds for the 14-inch model (down from 3.4 pounds) and to 4 pounds (down from 4.7 pounds) for the 16-inch. Also, while Apple updated its sound system to deliver better bass and incorporated Dolby Atmos support to its spatial audio, one of the more notable enhancements is the claimed improvements to the sound when the MacBook is closed.

Hands-on impressions from Executive Producer Bridget Carey

From my brief moments with the laptop, I can tell the touchscreen is something you may use as a supplemental feature — a quick zoom here, a drag-and-drop there. But even if you don’t see yourself needing to poke a screen, the vibrant OLED display is a noticeable leap in quality.

I was expecting to see rows of smudged up screens on demo tables. Yes, there are plenty of Apple staff with polishing cloths to give it a quick buff between tests, but my screens were not looking too smudged up after dragging my fingers around. It’s also less reflective — so those true blacks can be enjoyed without light reflections getting in the way.

I got a chance to see Apple’s display side by side with another Windows OLED Touchscreen, the Lenovo Yoga 9i. It was no contest — the new MacBook Pro was far superior with a more vibrant display, and it kept the detail even in extremely bright light, plus it was less reflective.

Apple brought back the illuminated logo on the cover. Bridget Carey/CNET

I was worried it might be a little hard to control certain aspects of MacOS with a clumsy finger, but it was able to accurately pick up on my touch. Controls would enlarge when I wanted to screen or expand a window, to make sure I pressed what I intended, and I quickly got used to dragging and locking windows to the sides. You have to do it with a little swivel in your hips and a flick of the wrist.

An impressive screen

A lot of the traditional advantages of OLED over alternatives like IPS with array backlights — such as a wider color gamut and true blacks — are less pronounced than they used to be.

That’s even more true for the current MacBook Pro’s mini-LED-backlit Liquid Retina XDR screens: They already deliver excellent deep blacks and 100% P3 gamut coverage, along with great color accuracy sufficient for prosumer creative work.

But the PROLED XDR screen sounds top-notch. While I take Apple’s claim of a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with 10,000,000 grains of salt — the arithmetic ratio of peak brightness to minimum black isn’t really meaningful, especially beyond about a million — the display has an expanded gamut that covers the Adobe RGB color space and more of Rec. 2020, a space for mastering video.

The latter is still only 80%, but at the moment, that’s the best you can get in a laptop display.

Tara Brown/CNET

Peak brightness is also similar to the desktop display at 2,000 nits. As with the current screens, though, you can set the SDR brightness only up to 1,000 nits; above that, it’s automated to compensate only for bright sunlight. That can get frustrating for people like me who find auto- brightness distracting.

The display can do 1,000 nits full screen in both SDR and HDR, though. Microsoft’s recently shipped Surface Laptop Ultra also hits 2,000 nits, the first Windows laptop that does, but uses mini-LED.

Oddly, Apple still quotes a 1-nit minimum brightness spec, similar to its mini-LED screens, though OLED’s native minimum is a lot lower: Theoretically, it’s zero, but professional colorimeters have measured it a lot lower. That may be because Apple has adopted it as a standard, and possibly clamped it, to tonally match its mini-LED models.

Apple also refers to its panel technology generically as “tandem OLED,” which is a little annoying, since there is a raft of tandem OLED types. But it is “state of the art!”

The letdowns

There are a couple of potential disappointments, though. For one, the battery life is unchanged. While the MacBook Pro’s battery life has always been good, it’s clear that the OLED display didn’t provide any power savings, or at least savings that weren’t spent elsewhere in the system.

Touch looks like the biggest mixed bag, though. The hardware is only a small aspect of the implementation; operating system interfaces like those of iOS and iPadOS are built around considerations like your finger is bigger and fatter than a cursor. Simply porting the mobile interfaces to a laptop isn’t necessarily a solution, either.

Playing a keyboard on a touchscreen that can’t open wide? Bridget Carey (that’s her hand) says, “You should not play piano like a doofus, finger stabbing the screen.” Tara Brown/CNET

We use laptops in part because a hardware keyboard is sometimes the best input choice, and even navigating the mobile devices via touch can get annoying, so those interfaces don’t necessarily translate optimally.

The point is, a lot is riding on how Apple has adapted MacOS for touch. For instance, the Touch Bar floundered in part because it felt grafted on rather than integral to the OS’ interface, as well as arguably superfluous.

And since Apple didn’t launch the capability with MacOS 27 at its developer conference, WWDC, this year, it sounds like the applications will be behind. That’s not something you beta test on a pro-level production system. Pros rely heavily on muscle memory. It should really have launched with a MacBook Air.

Plus, to adapt to touchscreen use, Apple had to stiffen the hinge — poking the screen makes that necessary — and add image stabilization to the webcam in case you poke the screen during video calls.

Apple seemed like it was really stretching to find meaningful uses for touch. Playing piano on a screen that forces your hand to an awkward angle? No thanks. The one application that sounded like it might be OK was for developers to simulate mobile app interfaces.

I was also kind of hoping for increased refresh rates beyond 120Hz or the ability to manually set it above 60Hz. Apple seems to position ProMotion as a power-saving technology rather than for gaming. Apple also seems to think 60fps is a great frame rate, so it’s not surprising.

Tech.title: Daylight Saving Time Ends on Sunday. Get Ready to Change Your Clocks
Tech.content:
It’s almost time to change your clocks. Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, when clocks across most of the US move back to 1 a.m. The timing lines up neatly with Halloween: Trick-or-treaters on Saturday still get the later sunset, and the extra hour of sleep arrives overnight. Phones and computers update on their own, but oven, microwave and car clocks usually don’t. Here’s what else to know about the switch, including which states skip it — and when the clocks spring forward again.

The time shift is notorious for disrupting sleep patterns and schedules. Some politicians are advocating for the abolition of time changes and the permanent adoption of daylight saving time, or DST. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July, but it still needs Senate approval and the president’s signature to become law — meaning that, for now, we still have dark winter hours coming.

If you, too, dislike how early it gets dark each day through winter, just remember that brighter evenings will return in mid-March.

More from CNET

When does daylight saving time end?

Daylight saving time in the US ends at 2 a.m. local time Sunday. It will return at 2 a.m. local time on March 14, 2027. The end of DST is when we “fall back,” whereas in March, we “spring forward.”

The US isn’t alone in observing daylight saving time. Check out this list of other countries that use DST, along with their start and end dates.

Daylight saving time vs. standard time

The official US time website shows where time zone boundaries are located. Time.gov/Screenshot by CNET

The exact start dates for daylight saving time and standard time float a little. DST kicks off on the second Sunday of March and ends on the first Sunday of November with the return of standard time.

We spend about eight months of the year in DST. We can thank the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for bringing some order to what had been a complicated history of time changes in the US.

“Motivated by transportation improvements, this act mandated standard time within the existing time zones and established a permanent system of uniform DST, including the dates and times for twice-yearly transitions,” the Bureau of Transportation Statistics states in a history of time zones.

The country’s time zones date to the railroad boom of the late 1800s. DST formally entered the chat in 1918, but its application was inconsistent until 1966. The country tried year-round daylight saving time in January 1974 under President Richard Nixon to address the energy crisis. It didn’t go over well. Congress and President Gerald Ford restored standard time in October 1974.

If you truly hate time changes, then consider moving to Arizona (except for the Navajo Nation) or Hawaii. Those states are on standard time all year long, and their residents don’t have to deal with the physical and mental health impacts of the change. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands also skip DST.



Sleep experts seek year-round standard time

Organizations such as the National Sleep Foundation, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms are united in calling for permanent standard time, saying it’s better for human biology.

“There’s a mismatch between the outside world and our internal clocks during daylight saving time that can result in some negative health consequences,” says Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation.

Dzierzewski cites mental health concerns and upticks in cardiovascular events and drowsy driving. He also calls out safety issues with young children walking to school or sitting at bus stops in the dark. Those safety issues were a big reason why permanent DST didn’t last in 1974.

Will we ditch these time changes for good?

Time changes aren’t popular. An October 2024 YouGov poll (PDF) of more than 1,100 US adults found that 63% would like to see the changing of the clocks eliminated. Only 17% wanted to keep time changes, and 20% weren’t sure.

Efforts to end the time changes have so far failed to pass into law. The bipartisan Sunshine Protection Act, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, passed the Senate in 2022 — the new version of the bill passed the House earlier this year and was sent on to the Senate to review in July.

While many people agree on eliminating time changes, the schism between daylight saving time and standard time remains. Standard time may have a bit of an image issue compared to DST.

“Part of the issue is that people associate daylight saving time with summer. People love summer, right?” Dzierzewski said. “But the simple fact of the matter is, it would still be summer if we were on permanent standard time.”

President Donald Trump criticized time changes in a 2024 Truth Social post: “The Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn’t! Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient and very costly to our Nation.”

Bills and resolutions at the state level haven’t had real-world impacts yet. Politicians are still split on whether they want permanent daylight saving or standard time. Dzierzewski is hopeful that permanent standard time will win out.

“This is the first time in several years where I’ve seen more legislation introduced at a state level in support of permanent standard time as the solution,” he said.

If you’d like to see time changes end and want to advocate for either daylight saving or standard time, contact your state and national representatives and express your opinion.

"You're in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally." Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation

Adjust your body clock to daylight saving time

Daylight saving time is happening, so now it’s a matter of figuring out how to deal with it. It’s not just about the day of the time change.

“You’re in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally,” Dzierzewski said. He recommends exposure to bright light in the morning, physical activity during the day, eating meals at regular times and practicing a relaxing wind-down routine at night.

The majority of Americans struggle to get the National Sleep Foundation’s recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep for most adults. A CNET survey found that more than half of US adults use some method to cope with sleep-related challenges. Check out some expert-backed tips for improving your sleep quality.

“If you’re doing these healthy sleep behaviors, you’re probably more resilient to some of these changes,” Dzierzewski said. “If you have poor sleep to begin with, you’re probably going to feel it a little bit more.”

Establishing a better sleep routine can take time. There are two things you can do in direct response to the time change. Dzierzewski suggests adjusting your bedtime and wake-up time gradually ahead of the change. For example, you could shift your schedule by 15 minutes per day and ease yourself into DST. He also recommends getting a good dose of bright morning light on the day of the time change to help set your internal body clock.

Think of DST as another kind of wake-up call, one that can motivate you to evaluate your sleep routine and quality and make positive changes. Start with these six simple habits. And don’t forget to change your clocks. Do it the night before, and you won’t have to worry about it later.

Tech.title: You Can Spend Nearly $15K on Apple’s New Touchscreen MacBook Pro. Why?
Tech.content:
The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, announced on Wednesday and available on Nov. 6, brings touchscreen control to Apple’s most premium laptop. Pricing starts at $2,899 for the entry-level M5 Pro with the smaller 14-inch display, or $3,399 for the 16-inch model, before any applicable education discounts.

If you go ham on Apple’s preorder configurator and max out the processor, memory and storage, the price balloons to an eye-watering $14,549. That’s wild, especially in today’s economy. Will anyone actually spend that?

Fully loading the M5 MacBook Pro

Let’s see what it means to reach that top-tier configuration of the new touchscreen laptop, starting with the larger, more expensive 16-inch PROLED XDR model at $3,399. Color doesn’t affect price, so take your pick of silver or space black.

More from CNET

The first upgrade you’ll pay for is Nano-texture glass, an antireflective glass finish physically etched at the nanometer scale to diffuse ambient light and eliminate glare, for an additional $150.

Then, stepping up from the M5 Pro’s 20-core GPU to the M5 Max’s 35-core GPU brings the total to $4,949. Bumping to the even more potent 40-core GPU adds another $300, while unlocking horsepower for complex tasks like gaming, video editing and AI-driven operations such as machine learning and coding. (In our testing, CNET found that the Max 40-core is the best fit for pro creatives who work with 8K or raw video, data scientists and intensive users of generative AI imaging and video.)

Next comes memory and storage, which is where things get really expensive. Our starting M5 Max configuration comes standard with 48GB of unified memory and 2TB of storage, but we can pump those numbers considerably. Upgrading to 128GB of memory adds $2,000. Going for 16TB of storage adds $7,000, the most expensive upgrade on the list, roughly doubling the price of the machine.

Pricey high-capacity memory and storage were par for the course long before the RAMpocalypse, but the current AI-fueled spike in RAM and solid-state storage prices has made things worse.

“It’s so expensive because 16TB drives cost a fortune, as does 128GB, and professionals have been paying those workstation prices for years,” Lori Grunin, CNET senior editor for computers and gaming hardware, told me.

Maxing the RAM boosts bandwidth and performance, allowing the Mac to more easily work with the massive files used in high-resolution video, complex 3D models, large datasets and complex mathematical equations. The extra terabytes of storage mean more and larger files can be saved to the device, since neither the MacBook’s memory nor storage can be upgraded after purchase.

All in, our fully loaded MacBook Pro M5 Max with 16-inch PROLED XDR Display comes to $14,549.

Grunin said she’d want more for the money. “For that price, I’d expect the M5 Ultra chip,” she said. “But I don’t think they can put the Ultra in a laptop yet.”

The top-spec MacBooks are aimed at companies that can absorb the high costs of high-capacity storage and memory. Apple

These upgrades aren’t for everyday people

So who buys a laptop that costs more than a used car? Is this just a flex for the super-rich?

“It’s for people who don’t have to pay for it,” said CNET Managing Editor Joshua Goldman.

Configured-to-order, powerful mobile workstations like these are most commonly bought through enterprise procurement by companies, startups and institutions — so the employer is paying, not the individual. Think engineering and architecture firms, Hollywood VFX and post-production houses or AI, machine learning and data science teams. They have big budgets, can put the extra digital horsepower to use and can easily absorb the exorbitant price.

For context, Grunin pointed me to a Dell Precision workstation that I was able to trick out to over $18,000. Five-figure enterprise-scale machines from HP or Lenovo are also not out of the question.

Yes, there will be well-heeled individuals buying at this level, but they’re a relatively small slice of the pie. More likely, the majority of the new touch-enabled MacBook Pros sold will be at still-expensive but easier-to-fathom prices.
